Of animals, machines and men: melting and reshaping of inequalities over troubled water and energies 70 years of agrarian change in dryland Southern India [SOURCE: Page_3]

Painting by Monique Poirier, 2022 [SOURCE: Page_3]

Des animaux, des machines et des hommes : fonte et refonte des inégalités au fil de l’eau et de l’énergie 70 ans d’histoire agraire en Inde du Sud semi-aride [SOURCE: Page_3]

3 [SOURCE: Page_3]

4 [SOURCE: Page_4]

Abstract ENGLISH [SOURCE: Page_5]

Agriculture in the region of Rapthadu (Anantapur district, state of Andhra Pradesh) in dryland Southern India has evolved at the expense of important social, economic and technical inequalities. Since the 1950’s, the Indian government has made strong political choices and implemented an agrarian reform, a “yellow” agricultural revolution (aimed at boosting the oil sector, particularly groundnut in the study area), a “green” revolution (development of borewell irrigation) and a “white” revolution (dairy sector). In this PhD, we combine two methodological frameworks to analyse the agrarian dynamics of this small region from the 1950’s to today: comparative agriculture which is commonly used to examine agrarian dynamics and the process of social differentiation of farms; and social metabolism largely used to study interactions between society and nature and analyse them from an environmental perspective, using flows of energy and matter. We chose to focus on flows of energy (human and animal muscular energies, gross calorific energy of products and fossil energy) because they can account for the changes of agriculture in the area, from an agriculture harnessed by human and animal muscular power to an agriculture blending muscular and motor-mechanised energies. Based on water balances, we also consider flows of water to account for the changes in the use of this limiting resource in this semi-arid environment. This study has been carried out at the scale of the plot, the herd, the farm and also at territorial level by reconstructing an archetype village of the study area. We show that despite the agricultural policies mentioned previously, inequalities persist between the 1950’s and today but they have been reshaped: the agrarian system in the 1950’s was chiefly structured by flows of human and animal labour energies while the current agrarian system is structured by flows of fossil energy and flows of calorific energy (in particular groundnut hay and manure). Furthermore, a new (non-conscious) form of exploitation has emerged between production systems recharging the groundwater table and others pumping it. In this dryland area, even if the use of groundwater has not yet led to an over-exploitation of the resource as it has in other areas in India where the level of the groundwater table is declining, we show that this equilibrium is fragile and embedded in strong social inequalities. This work is innovative because it takes into account social diversity in metabolism analysis and also because it reconstitutes the metabolism of a territory at two-time intervals (the 1950’s and the current period) by associating a dense fieldwork (observation, interviews, including retrospective ones) and archival data. The combination of the two approaches enables to better approach environmental issues in the analysis of agrarian dynamics and also to integrate in return, social diversity and inequalities in environmental assessment studies with importance given to the understanding of agricultural practices. Metabolism studies often consider society as « a whole » and do not take into account the social categories and the social relations of production. Our combination thus brings awareness on the power relations behind environmental sustainability issues. [SOURCE: Page_5]

## FRANCAIS

La mise en valeur de la petite région agricole de Rapthadu (district d’Anantapur, état d’Andhra Pradesh) en Inde du sud semi-aride s’est faite au prix d’importantes inégalités sociales, économiques et techniques. Depuis les années 1950, les choix politiques de l’état Indien ont été forts et matérialisés par une réforme agraire, une révolution jaune (secteur des oléagineux, notamment l’arachide), une révolution verte (développement de l’irrigation par forage) et une révolution blanche (secteur laitier). Dans cette thèse, nous combinons deux approches pour étudier les dynamiques agraires de cette région depuis les années 1950 : celle de l’agriculture comparée communément utilisée pour étudier les dynamiques agraires et la différenciation sociale des exploitations agricoles d’un territoire ; celle du métabolisme social largement utilisée pour rendre compte des interactions entre sociétés et nature et les évaluer d’un point de vue environnemental, notamment par l’analyse de flux physiques d’énergie et de matière. Nous avons choisi de nous intéresser aux flux d’énergie (énergie du travail humain, animal, énergie brute calorifique des produits et énergie fossile) car ils permettent de rendre compte des changements d’une agriculture entièrement manuelle et à traction animale vers une agriculture qui s’appuie sur l’hybridation entre forces musculaires humaines et animales et moto-mécanisation. A travers des bilans hydriques, nous nous intéressons également aux flux d’eau afin de rendre compte des changements d’usages de cette ressource limitante dans cette région semi-aride. Cette étude se fait à l’échelle de la parcelle, du troupeau, de l’exploitation agricole mais aussi à l’échelle territoriale, par la reconstitution d’un village archétype de la région d’étude. Nous montrons ainsi que malgré les révolutions citées précédemment, les inégalités perdurent entre 1950 et aujourd’hui mais qu’elles ont pris de nouvelles formes : le système agraire des années 1950 était régi par des flux d’énergie du travail humain et animal tandis que le système agraire actuel est structuré par des flux d’énergie fossile et des flux d’énergie brute calorifiques des produits (notamment des fanes d’arachide et du fumier). Par ailleurs, une nouvelle forme d’exploitation (non consciente) entre systèmes de production qui rechargent l’eau de la nappe et d’autres qui la puisent a émergé. Dans ce milieu semi-aride, si l’utilisation de la ressource en eau souterraine ne s’est pas encore traduit comme dans d’autres endroits de l’Inde par un abaissement problématique du niveau de la nappe, nous montrons que cet équilibre est fondé sur de profondes inégalités sociales et est fragile. Ce travail est novateur car il prend en compte la diversité sociale dans les analyses de métabolisme et aussi parce qu’il reconstitue le métabolisme d’un territoire à deux pas de temps différents (les années 1950 et à la période actuelle) grâce à un long travail de terrain (observation, enquêtes, notamment rétrospectives) couplé à des données d’archives. La combinaison des deux approches permet d’une part de mieux intégrer les enjeux environnementaux dans les analyses des dynamiques agraires, et d’autre part de prendre en compte la diversité sociale dans les évaluations environnementales avec une considération importante des pratiques agricoles. En effet, les analyses de métabolisme considèrent souvent la société comme un « tout » et ne considèrent pas les catégories sociales et les rapports sociaux de production. Cette combinaison permet de révéler les enjeux de pouvoir derrière les enjeux de durabilité environnementale. [SOURCE: Page_6]

Acknowledgements This PhD thesis began on December the 1st 2020. Today is October 25th 2023 and I am reaching the finishing line. Note on using the first person: This PhD manuscript is partly written in the first person. Most of the material of this research stems from personal up-close interactions and observations, making this work in essence “sensorial, intimate and comprehensive” (Filion, 2011). Using the pronouns “we” or “I” is was a way of acknowledging a degree of subjectivity of this work (Olivier de Sardan, 2015a). This research is the product of a collaborative work, fuelled by many discussions, advice and comments. The interpreters played a central role, for retrieving the information and also for building the relationships with the interviewees. Some of them even actively participated in the reflections. The use of the pronoun “we” therefore represents this collective work (fellow researchers, interpreters and myself). When expressing my own thoughts and impressions I use the first-person singular. Introduction [SOURCE: Page_17]

India is a world agricultural giant: first in the production of milk, pulses and in the size of the cattle population; second in the production of wheat, fruits, vegetables, sugarcane, cotton and groundnut; fighting of the first place for rice production with China. Agriculture is one of the main sectors of the country’s economy, making 23% of the GDP (Gross Domestic Product) (FAO, 2023). Behind this colossus, there is a teeming population of 1.4 billion, of which 70% live from agriculture (FAO, 2023). The performances of the Indian agriculture are the results of strong agrarian policies which have taken place since its Independence from British rule in 1947. [SOURCE: Page_17]

Taking the bull by the horns: India’s post-independence agrarian policies Since the 1950’s, the Indian government has made strong political choices to boost agricultural production. It implemented an agrarian reform and three “coloured” agricultural revolutions^1, each of them focusing on boosting the production of a particular type of food: the Green Revolution (1960’s) targeted the production of rice and wheat, the White revolution on the dairy sector (1970’s) and the Yellow Revolution on oil seeds (1980’). [SOURCE: Page_17]

The Green revolution provided a necessary increase in food production through technological changes such as the introduction of high-yielding varieties, the use of synthetic fertilisers and the development of borewell irrigation (Dorin and Landy, 2009; Hazell, 2009). The boom in groundwater use for agriculture is also more specifically known as the “pump revolution” (Shah, 2009). In 2018, 51% of the net sown area in India was irrigated, out of which 63% used groundwater^2 (GOI, 2023). India’s groundwater consumption for agriculture has skyrocketed from the 1960’s onwards and today by far exceeds all the other countries in the world (Fig. 1). The vast majority of the pumped groundwater is used by the agricultural sector (84%) while the industry consumes only 12% and the remaining 4% are attributed to domestic use (Dhawan, 2017, p. 13). [SOURCE: Page_17]

1 The word “revolution” is commonly used to refer to the technologies which have been implemented and which had a revolutionary potential (Pearse, 1974) 2 48% by borewell irrigation and 15% by well irrigation [SOURCE: Page_17]

17 [SOURCE: Page_17]

Figure 1. Agricultural groundwater usage since the 1940’s in the world Source : (UN World Water Development Report, 2015), initially made by (Shah, 2009) Then came the White Revolution, also known as Operation Flood, which structured the dairy sector through a network of dairy cooperatives. Those cooperatives strengthened the transport, processing supply and marketing of milk, thus increasing its production (Cunningham, 2009). Finally, the Yellow Revolution, also known as Operation Golden Flow, aimed at increasing the production of edible oilseeds to meet demand and be less dependent on imports. The production of oilseeds – majorly groundnut, mustard, rapeseed, soyabean - was multiplied by approximately 4 since the 1950’s (Dorin and Landy, 2009). [SOURCE: Page_18]

The successes in agricultural production are undeniable: Dorin and Landy (2009) estimate that the production of food grains, milk and sugar cane was multiplied by 4 to 5 between 1950 and 2000. But those successes are bittersweet from both environmental and socio-economic perspectives. The environmental performances are poor. Dependency on fossil fuel energy rose (Gulati et al., 2018; Kumar and Singh, 2001; Rathore et al., 2018). In some areas nitrate concentrations in groundwater was proved to be linked to the groundwater development of agriculture (Buvaneshwari et al., 2017), posing new health and environmental issues : in some areas nitrate concentration being 7 times higher than European standards! (Buvaneshwari et al., 2017). Greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture were multiplied by 1.75 between 1970 and 2010 (Pathak et al., 2014). Moreover, poverty and inequality in India is still striking. It is one of the most unequal nations with 1% of the population capturing 29.4% of the pre-tax national income, while the bottom 50% of the population captures only 11% (Chancel and [SOURCE: Page_18]

18 [SOURCE: Page_18]

Piketty, 2018). A quarter of the world’s undernourished population lives in India (World Food Programme, 2023). Even though the proportion of poor people among the total population has decreased (Dorin and Landy, 2009), 14% of the total population is still poor and the vast majority of them live in rural areas (NITI Ayog, 2023), making the study of agriculture inseparable from the question of poverty. Farmer’s income are utterly disparate among states - an average farmer in Punjab earns 3.5 times more than the average farmer in Bihar- (Gov. India, 2019) and the gap between farm-income and non-farm income tripled between 1983 and 2011 (Chand et al., 2015). [SOURCE: Page_19]

The role of livestock in social and environmental sustainability Historical studies show the importance of livestock in building an agriculture which is both sustainable and has a decent labour productivity (Aubron, 2021). In pre-industrial societies for instance, crop and livestock were highly integrated (Bonaudo et al., 2017). The production systems were based on low input and output flows, and high internal flows between crop and livestock farming systems. It was precisely these low, multiple and combined biomass flows that enabled soil fertility to be maintained (Krausmann, 2004). In some areas today, fertility is still managed by livestock by recycling biomass between the cropping and livestock farming systems (Diarisso et al., 2015) and by ensuring fertility transfers from the saltus to the ager (Audouin et al., 2015; Cochet, 1996). With livestock, non-arable land could be used and by-products inedible to human could be consumed (Kemp and Michalk, 2007). Livestock also played a major role in providing draft power to prepare land, harvest and irrigate crops (Costa, 1991; Huguenin and Lhoste, 1988; Krausmann, 2004). The access to draft animals was therefore shown to be a major factor of social differentiation in some agrarian societies (Cochet, 2011). [SOURCE: Page_19]

The shift from pre-industrial to industrial societies has substantially changed the role of livestock. With moto-mechanisation and the use of fossil fuels, the role of livestock in providing draft power was considerably reduced, and in some areas even disappeared (Harchaoui, 2019). Nonetheless, in some areas, livestock farming systems have not disappeared: they have specialised in the production of milk or meat (Domingues et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020). With specialisation, the role of livestock in nutrient recycling, in the use of non-arable land and consumer of by-products inedible to human, has strongly decreased, with many environmental consequences (Garnett et al., 2017) and stronger feed-food competitions (Wilkinson, 2011). Livestock was held responsible for 18% of world greenhouse gas emissions, mostly due to methane emissions from enteric fermentation (Steinfeld et al., 2006, p. 113). [SOURCE: Page_19]

19 [SOURCE: Page_19]

Livestock has become one of the black sheep of environmental sustainability and reducing methane enteric emissions is often put forward as one of the greenhouse gas emissions mitigation option (Herrero et al., 2016), to the detriment of a more systemic vision of agriculture and an analysis of the long-term trajectories of evolution of agriculture which are sometimes overlooked. There can indeed be a trade-off between reducing enteric methane and increase carbon dioxide emissions from the production of feed concentrates to feed livestock (Hemingway et al., 2023). Looking at a higher scale than the mere scale of the herd, synthetic fertilisers, and in particular nitrogen-based ones manufactured through the Haber-Bosch process, have also replaced the role of animal manure in providing nitrogen. In India, the use of synthetic fertilisers have disrupted the recycling of nutrients between crop and livestock farming systems, with nitrogen flows from synthetic fertilisers largely outweighing the ones from manure (Aubron et al., 2021). With specialisation, the crop-livestock integration and the relations of livestock farming systems with the ecosystem have simplified (Swift and Anderson, 1994) and the dependence on external inputs has increased (Moraine et al., 2017; Schut et al., 2021; Vigne et al., 2013b). In some areas, livestock is however still a valuable source of employment for farmers (Basu and Scholten, 2012), wealth (Alary et al., 2011; Faye and Duteurtre, 2009), and seems to play an important role in lifting farmers out of poverty (Aubron et al., 2023). The changing role of livestock has therefore played a major role in agrarian transformations (Gingrich et al., 2018), with consequences on both environmental and social sustainability. The examples above call for a consideration of the plurality of forms of livestock. [SOURCE: Page_20]

Bonding the inequality question and the environmental one The previously mentioned environmental downsides -of the changes of Indian agriculture and the changes of the role of livestock- are subject to many debates on the mitigation of the adverse effects of this agricultural development. Those debates encompass all sectors -not only the agricultural one- and are held worldwide. A number of policies are conducted with the same guideline that each and every country and citizen must adapt and participate in reducing their environmental footprint. This is seen for instance in the reduction of waste, which has been produced as a consequence of the decoupling of production and consumption (Bonaudo et al., 2017). The political dialogue has gradually drifted towards thinking global and a focus on development without transgressing planetary boundaries and the preservation of finite resources. However, thinking “global” is partly misleading, because it often overlooks the importance of social drivers in the ecological crisis and it ignores regional [SOURCE: Page_20]

20 [SOURCE: Page_20]

and local particularities (Brand et al., 2021). The flows of waste are in fact “intimately connected to global flows of capital, processes of uneven development and marginalization” (Peet et al., 2010, p. 133) and are not purely technical matters solved by technocratic operational approaches (Brand et al., 2021). Flows of waste are “political issues, deeply infused with power relationships, questions of justice and governance, and shaped by representational practices.” (Peet et al., 2010, p. 133). Inequalities and the study of agricultural transformations and environmental assessments have to be bridged together. “We have to think of ecology and power relations together if we are to understand the formation of social and environmental inequalities. We then have to envisage a double relation of internality: Natures pervaded by the social, by the thousand and one sociotechnical interventions that are historically situated […] Societies pervaded by nature, in which social relations and cultural norms are structured and rigidified by mechanisms that organize metabolisms of matter and energy, and that govern the social uses of nature. Far from surrounding the social, the environment traverses it, and the history of societies, cultures and socio-political regimes cannot ignore the flows of matter, energy and information that frame them” (Bonneuil and Fressoz, 2016). [SOURCE: Page_21]

A few case studies have shown that some ways of farming contribute more to the global greenhouse gas emissions (Hemingway et al., 2023) or the nitrogen balance (Aubron et al., 2021; Moreau et al., 2012) than others. Plurality of forms of agriculture and livestock rearing and the social diversity has to be addressed to understand the root causes of the environmental negative externalities and to propose fairer guidelines. To take into account inequalities, we need to “bring class in” (Bernstein, 2021), but class is understood in this work in terms of relations (Wright, 1979). On the scale of a small agriculture region, the social diversity of farms constitutes those classes. We need to analyse their patterns of coexistence and the conditions of their reproduction. By coexistence, we take the side of the social organisation ethos of dominated and dominant fractions (Bourdieu, 2011), which in other words comes down to portraying the evolving power relations behind the use of resources and labour in a small territory. [SOURCE: Page_21]

Main research question Despite the global trends, the agrarian policies have not impacted the territories in a uniform way. India is so vast and diverse from many points of view – geomorphological, climate, social- that to carry out a fine-grain analysis of the transformations of agriculture, the scale of the small agricultural region, such as a group of villages, is more appropriate. My objective in this thesis, then, is to 1) analyse the transformations of agriculture in a small [SOURCE: Page_21]

21 [SOURCE: Page_21]

agricultural region in India, 2) understand the mechanisms of social differentiation at play, 3) evaluate the environmental and socio-economic consequences of those agrarian changes, 4) analyse the contribution of livestock in those transformations. This type of research necessarily implies a historical perspective, which is informative in two ways. First, from a purely descriptive perspective – but nonetheless essential- it enables us to describe changes and transitions and identify the mechanisms of those transitions. Second, it enables us to understand the current dynamics and configurations of territories and reasons for choices of crop or livestock production. Thirdly, the study of past processes is useful to consider alternatives and question their plausibility to build scenarios (Billen, 2016). For this, we chose to focus on a small agricultural region and to rely on a conceptual framework, which made possible to analyse agrarian transformations over time and which takes into account social diversity. [SOURCE: Page_22]

Conceptual frameworks and tools Some studies of agrarian transitions from a historical perspective focus on the changes of land use and matter and energy consumption. They are referred to under the umbrella-term of territorial metabolism or social metabolism (Fischer-Kowalski and Haberl, 2007; Haberl et al., 2016). Those studies usually encompass large scales of analysis (Bonaudo et al., 2021; Garnier et al., 2019; González de Molina et al., 2019; Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019; Le Noë et al., 2018; Marco et al., 2020) and are based on national and transnational agricultural statistics and archives such as the INSEE or FAO dataset. On the scale of smaller agricultural regions, retrieving data at farm-level becomes challenging, not to mention in India where the smallest scale of data in census is the one of the village and concerns only the type of land use, distribution of population among professional categories. The only diversity of farm types which can be found are types of farms by size. To depict the social diversity of farms in terms of access to factors of production and how they operate we had no choice but to rely on the data available in the field -the memory of farmers- and retrieve it through interviews and observations. To do so, comparative agriculture (Cochet, 2015) seemed to be the most appropriate and effective conceptual framework. Comparative agriculture has been widely used to evaluate socio-economic differentiation of farms on the scale of small regions or groups of villages. The approach has been commonly used to estimate gaps of income between production systems and the distribution of wealth created on-farm (Aubron et al., 2022, 2015, 2009; Hemingway et al., 2022; Palliere et al., 2018). Its use for environmental assessment has however only just started in being used for nitrogen balances (Aubron et al., 2021; Moreau et al., 2012) and greenhouse gas emissions (Hemingway et al., 2023). Those latter studies [SOURCE: Page_22]

22 [SOURCE: Page_22]

however focus on the current territorial configuration, and environmental assessment is not done over time. To better assess the environmental impacts of the agrarian dynamics, we have grafted on the comparative agriculture framework a metabolism approach, referred for now in its most absolute and strictest form: the quantification of flows of matter and energy. Those flows have been quantified at farm-level to compare types of farmers at a given moment in time, but also at a territorial level to illustrate the forms of coexistence and dependence. The time period of this study is naturally limited by the farmer’s memory: we could only go back as far as the 1950’s but this was enough to cover the post-independence agrarian policies of India. [SOURCE: Page_23]

The choice of the study area: Rapthadu mandal in Anantapur district To answer the research questions, we had to focus on a region with had undergone important agrarian transformations and where the role of livestock had been and/or still was important. We therefore aimed for an area with had been impacted by both the Green and the White Revolutions. Another criteria was the development of borewell irrigation, as borewell irrigation was shown to accelerate social differentiation over a common resource, groundwater, extracted though private investment (Birkenholtz, 2009; Taylor, 2013). [SOURCE: Page_23]

In India, I was hosted by the Indo-French Cell on Water Sciences based at the Indian Institute of Science, a university in Bangalore in the south of India (see location on Fig. 2). Given the immensity of India, I had to choose an agricultural study area with the criteria above and which was fairly accessible by road from Bangalore. My Phd research was part of the INRAE metaprogram IndiaBio which also funded my fieldwork in India. This research program focuses on the characterisation of the agroecological transitions at play in two Indian states (Andhra Pradesh and Sikkim). Those transitions have been launched in reaction to the dominant conventional model of agriculture which was brought forth by the Green revolution. Sikkim being in the Himalayan region of India and miles away of Bangalore we opted for a study area in Andhra Pradesh, the state neighbouring Karnataka State where Bangalore is located (Fig. 2). The Rythu Sadhikara Samastha (RySS) organisation, which coordinates the implementation of the agroecological transition in Andhra Pradesh, suggested focusing on the district of Anantapur. There, the transition from conventional agriculture to a more agroecological one was said to be under way and the area was one of the focal points of the agroecological movement, also known as the Zero-Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF). To study [SOURCE: Page_23]

23 [SOURCE: Page_23]

this transition, we had to select a mandal^3 which had been impacted by the Green Revolution. This was however not a difficult criterion given how widespread the Green revolution was. It was also important to find an area which had been targeted by the White revolution in order to study the evolution of the role of livestock and a particular its role in milk production and its importance in the farming activities. This criterion was less obvious as Anantapur, along with the neighbouring Kadapa district, were the districts with the lowest milk production density (daily production of milk per surface unit) in Andhra Pradesh, with a milk production density twice below the state average (NDDB, 2018, p. 63). The selling of milk was, compared to other places in India, quite low, and mostly concentrated in the mandals nearby the main cities of the district: Anantapur to the North and capital of the district (340 000 inhabitants) and Hindupur (200 000 inhabitants) to the South and neighbouring the Karnataka border (Fig. 2). Although Hindupur was much closer to Bangalore than Anantapur and thus much more practical, it had the disadvantage of having more canal irrigation and a less acute semi-aridity than Anantapur. We chose an area near Anantapur but which was not too close to the city so that it remained a rural area not encroached by the urban expansion. We finally chose to focus on the southern part of the mandal of Rapthadu, 30 to 40 km away from Anantapur, and 5 hours away from Bangalore by bus. Although the choice of the study area was strongly motivated by the presence of natural farming, the transition was partial and not systemic enough in the area to be relevant for my research questions. Despite the interviews I carried out initially with “natural farmers”, there will be no mention of this transition in the rest of the PhD manuscript. Rapthadu mandal however ticked the other boxes: it had been impacted by the Green Revolution and the White Revolution and irrigation today was done through borewell irrigation. It was also unexpectedly diverse regarding the livestock farming systems, which was an asset to analyse the roles of livestock in both social and environmental sustainability. The presence of large irrigated fruit plantations among small farms with rainfed groundnut, the partial development of borewell irrigation and the semi-arid climate conditions hinted that the area fitted the purpose of our research. Each village of this area could be considered as independent entities and the landscape [SOURCE: Page_24]

3 A mandal (also known as taluk or tehsil in other parts of India) is an administrative division in India corresponding to a group of villages in between the village level and the district level. [SOURCE: Page_24]

24 [SOURCE: Page_24]

variations of Rapthadu mandal could be found again at the level of each village. To simplify the process, we chose to model the functioning of an archetype village. [SOURCE: Page_25]

Location of main cities referred to in this study across Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh states and Karnataka-Andhra Pradesh border Source : Base map : google maps 2023 To enrich the analysis of the agrarian transformations and take into consideration the environmental question with regard to social diversity, we had to select biophysical objects such as nitrogen, carbon, energy, greenhouse gases, water. [SOURCE: Page_25]

The choice of biophysical objects -flows of energy and water- and refinement of the research question There would have been so many environmental indicators to study in this research work but due to the limited time we chose to focus this study on two indicators: energy and water. The first months of this PhD were impeded by the COVID context. Initially the fieldwork was supposed to begin in March 2021 but was pushed back to September 2021. We however used this time to explore the literature review on environmental assessments in the agricultural sector. During the months of waiting, we calculated the greenhouse gas emissions of the agriculture and livestock of a village in Gujarat state (North-West of India) based on a pre- existing typology of farms (Aubron et al., 2021, 2015). This study was published at a later date (Hemingway et al., 2023). Unfortunately, neither the type of flow (greenhouse gas emissions), 25 [SOURCE: Page_25]

nor the area of study (Gujarat state) were selected for this PhD research. In order to illustrate the changes of the agrarian system, we preferred flows that could be related to the production factors of the farmers which are land, water, capital and labour. Energy seemed to be the most relevant indicator because it enabled us to report the dependency on fossil energy, the changes in the use of both animal and human labour and also the food and feed production capacity of agriculture in terms of calories – even though a well-balanced diet is not just determined by calories! -. The estimation of the direct fossil energy consumption (diesel and electricity) could also be linked with the possession of fixed capital. Water is an important limiting factor in the area of study and was chosen as a second type of flow. A distinction could consequently be made between the terms of groundwater extraction, which require a certain amount of investment, either muscle power or direct fossil energy, and rainfed agricultural production. The choice of a study area where irrigation is mostly done via borewells is interesting because groundwater is a common water resource i.e. the groundwater table, but often used in an individual way through the private borewells. In the light of those indicators the research questions can be refined. Has fossil energy replaced muscle power? How have the shifts in energy patterns triggered by the agricultural revolutions changed the relations of production? And how has the efficiency of agriculture evolved accordingly? In the semi-arid area of Rapthadu mandal, how do farms coexist according to the groundwater resource? How has the territory evolved in terms of the use of water from the 1950’s up to today? Is the water being pumped at an unsustainable rate, i.e. is the groundwater table declining as it is in other areas of India? What is “too much” pumping in the study area and which type of farms consumed and control this water? [SOURCE: Page_26]

Structure of this PhD thesis My Phd thesis is organised into nine chapters. [SOURCE: Page_26]

Chapter one outlines the methodology behind my research. It presents the conceptual framework of comparative agriculture. It then successively explores how we carried out interviews and participant observation, which constitute the backbone of our fieldwork and more broadly this research work. It then explores how we modelled and characterised farm types in the 1950’s and today, and how we build the archetype village of this study. We then explain how we evaluate the farm types from an economic point of view, and how we quantified the flows of matter, energy and water flowing in, within and out of those farm types, and the indicators we chose to assess those flows. For this we found ourselves surrounded by a mosaic of intertwined personal narratives, archives dispersed in time and space and the landscape and [SOURCE: Page_26]

26 [SOURCE: Page_26]

agrarian practices that we could presently observe. We therefore explain how we found the clues that helped us turn the clock back to the 1950’s, how we made up for the patchy data to connect the story threads. [SOURCE: Page_27]

Chapter two provides a reading of the environmental setting of the study area by classifying and mapping the territory into landscape units. The underlying hypothesis is that those landscape units are a first material foundations of the processes of social differentiation: we assume here that nature has its own laws materialised under environmental constraints (soil, hydrological, topographical) which cannot be overcome by everyone. Some farmers will benefit from the “best” landscape units while others will be relegated to the unwanted landscape units. [SOURCE: Page_27]

Chapter three is the first chapter of a series of three which unravel the history of agriculture in the study area from the 1950’s to today. For each we describe the socio-economic differentiation pathways, practices and uses of natural resources. We illustrate those transformations by the representation of flows of energy and water in, within and out of the archetype village. We chose to simultaneously describe the agrarian transformations in parallel with the flow representation, because the social and environmental questions are inseparable, and that the combination of both approaches simultaneously is essential to understanding the process as a whole. Chapter three is the starting point of this historical analysis and describes the agrarian system in the 1950’s. Chapter four describes the changes which have happened in the 1980’s with the implementation of the Indira Gandhi Land Reform and the Yellow revolution, which aimed at boosting the oil sector and which concerned groundnut in the study area. Chapter five describes the changes from the 1990’s to today, mainly organised by the development of borewell irrigation during the “pump revolution”, the changes in dairy farming operated by the implementation of the White Revolution and the emergence of fruit cultivation. [SOURCE: Page_27]

Chapter six and seven explore the current agrarian dynamics at play in the study area from a economic, socio-technical and environmental perspective. Chapter six deals with the characterisation and the technical, economic and environmental evaluation of the cropping and livestock farming systems which are currently found in the study area. This analysis will be extended in Chapter seven at farm and territorial level, putting forward the relations of coexistence and interdependence between farms and the use and dependence on resources such as fossil energy and water. [SOURCE: Page_27]

27 [SOURCE: Page_27]

Chapter eight places the “industrialisation” of agriculture in the study area in a broader context by comparing it with the industrialisation of Western agriculture. It discusses the creation of a two-headed agriculture, where muscle power and fossil energy proceed together. We discuss the changes of energy efficiency and energy circularity in the territory, the changes in the role of livestock and suggests perspectives in the use of the groundwater table. Chapter nine concludes by discussing the methodological contribution made by this thesis to the integration of social diversity in environmental studies. It debates the conception of society among the variety of interpretation of metabolism. It concludes by questioning the connections between comparative agriculture and metabolism. [SOURCE: Page_28]

28 [SOURCE: Page_28]

CHAPTER 1: Methodology [SOURCE: Page_29]

In this chapter we unfold the conceptual framework we have used to analyse the transformations of agriculture in the area of study in light of the social diversity of the farms. We explain how we found the clues that helped us turn the clock back to the 1950’s. For this we found ourselves surrounded by a mosaic of intertwined personal narratives, archives dispersed in time and space, the landscape of the study area and the agrarian practices that we could presently observe. We explain how we compensated for patchy data to connect the story threads between the oral data of interviews and the written data of archives. To illustrate this story of agrarian change we relied on the representation of flows of matter, energy and water. Those flows were quantified on the basis of assumptions and calculations that are outlined in the final section of this chapter. [SOURCE: Page_29]

1. Comparative agriculture: the conceptual framework 1.1. Origin and overview of comparative agriculture Comparative agriculture is a framework of mixed methods aimed at understanding the functioning of agriculture in a region as a whole. As the name implies, it focuses on a particular sector of production of society: agriculture. In a similar way to other comparative disciplines e.g. comparative law, comparative politics, it involves the study of types of farms belonging to the same region, how they differ in their functioning, how they co-evolve and how they combine into a system. As agriculture varies around the globe, those comparisons between farm types can also be made at an upper level, between agricultural regions themselves situated in different social, cultural and environmental settings around the world. The aim is therefore to identify 1) trends and differences which eventually allow to better understand the how and the why of agriculture in the region itself (Aubron et al., 2023), but also 2) the evolutionary series which characterise the history of agriculture of those regions (Mazoyer and Roudart, 2006). The researcher in comparative agriculture progresses in his understanding of the transformations of agriculture by comparing types of farming. [SOURCE: Page_29]

Studies using the comparative agriculture framework are often referred to as ‘agrarian diagnostic analysis’, which – for the uninitiated- could imply any type of diagnosis at farm, herd, plot, territorial level. However, the agrarian diagnosis, in the comparative agriculture approach, refers to a very specific way of analysing agriculture. Comparative agriculture [SOURCE: Page_29]

29 [SOURCE: Page_29]

borrows conceptual and theoretical tools mainly from agronomy, geography, rural sociology, economy, history, anthropology and ethnology, but assembled in a way that makes it a fully- fledged approach. Although it was introduced more than half a century ago, at the end of the Second World War at the Institut national agronomique of Paris, little is known - beyond the French academic and rural development spheres- of this methodological framework. At the outset, comparative agriculture was conceived with the aim to design relevant rural development projects, and therefore propose practical and concrete solutions to hunger and malnutrition problems in the third world countries. It was thought and designed by René Dumont, French agronomist and first ecologist candidate in French presidential elections. He had initially trained as a tropical agronomist but then defined himself as an “agronomist of hunger” (Dufumier, 2002, p. 83). Throughout his many experiences in the ‘undeveloped’ countries, starting off with a first and transformative one in Vietnam, he became a strong advocate of the idea that rural development is first and foremost the matter of farmers, and not of civil servants (Dufumier, 2002, p. 83). From there, a new way of thinking emerged for designing rural development projects, with observation and understanding of farming practices at its core and with a central driving question: “why do farmers do what they do?”. This comprehensive way of looking at a territory and its practices merged to ensure practical, adapted and relevant solutions to rural development problems as Sigaut (1976) explains: “The problem is not to try out this « innovation » or the other, as one can blindly fumble for the right key. The problem is first to understand the keyhole, in other words the intern logic of the cropping systems. To achieve this, thorough analysis of current practices, based on precise and detailed observations, as objective as possible, and comparisons of those observations between them are required^4.” (Sigaut, 1976). [SOURCE: Page_30]

Comparative agriculture relies on the concept of the agrarian system (at territorial-level), production system (farm-level) and cropping and livestock farming systems (plot and herd level). [SOURCE: Page_30]

4 Own translation. Original text in French: « Le problème n’est pas d’essayer telle ou telle “innovation”, un peu à l’aveuglette, comme on essaye successivement les clés d’un trousseau pour trouver la bonne. Le problème est d’abord de comprendre la serrure, c’est-à-dire la logique interne des systèmes de culture qui existent. Cela exigera des analyses approfondies, basées sur des observations détaillées, précises et aussi objectives que possible des pratiques actuelles, et sur une très large comparaison de ces observations entre elles » (Sigaut, 1976). [SOURCE: Page_30]

30 [SOURCE: Page_30]

1.2. The keystone concepts Agriculture is not solely about the technical aspects of crop and livestock production; it is also a complex network of social relations. Bourdieu (1992) shows, for example, how in agrarian societies there are power dynamics which are governed by exchanges and practices between individuals and that there is a symbolic capital of social prestige, honour and recognition which is reflected in economic effects. Understanding agriculture is about analysing all the social production relations such as the right and access to land, how means of production are shared, how the savings available to acquire means of production are invested, what is the role of farmers in the relations of production area, and how the produce of labour is distributed (Kroll, 1992; in Cochet, 2015, p. 20). Agriculture can therefore be studied in many ways with some disciplines focusing on the plot (agronomy), others on the herd (zootechnics), the agricultural policies (economy), rural migration (sociology and geography). But once the complexity of agriculture is acknowledged, there is a practical problem: how is it possible to study all the “bits and pieces” of agriculture all at once? [SOURCE: Page_31]

1.2.1. The agrarian system In comparative agriculture, four key concepts are used to refer to three scales of analysis (Fig. 3) : the agrarian system at the village scale, the production system (PS) at the farm scale and the livestock farming system (LFS) at the scale of the animal herd and the cropping system (CS) at the scale of the plot (Cochet, 2015, 2012). [SOURCE: Page_31]

There is a need for an integrative concept which would simplify complexity but in return would help to better grasp the rationale behind. Agriculture as a whole and its evolution can be represented by the concept of the agrarian system, which is at the same time “(1) the characteristics of one or several agroecosystems; (2) a modus operandi, which itself is characterised by the farmers’ technical heritage (tools, knowledge, practices, know-how that have evolved over time); (3) the way the environment has been transformed by man over time; (4) the resulting landscape; (5) the relationships between the different agroecosystems that make up the environment; and (6) soil fertility renewal mechanisms.” (Cochet, 2012). Analysing agriculture in terms of an agrarian system would thus come down to “breaking it [the agrarian system] down into two principal subsystems, cultivated ecosystem and social productive system, studying the organization and the functioning of each of these subsystems, and studying their interrelations.” (Mazoyer, 1987; in Cochet, 2012). Although the integration of those multiple dimensions could be qualified as holistic (from the Greek “holos” meaning [SOURCE: Page_31]

31 [SOURCE: Page_31]

“entire” or “all”) because of the multiple entities it involves, we argue that the correct word would be systemic because there is a focus on the relations between entities. [SOURCE: Page_32]

Figure 3. Concepts used in comparative agriculture and related nested scales [SOURCE: Page_32]

Source: Adapted from Cochet (2015), p. 49 The agrarian system is viewed on the scale of a small region, which has to include a minimum number of farms in order to be able to study agricultural diversity, but has to be small enough to unravel local particularities. The scale of an agrarian system can therefore range from the one of a village (Aubron et al., 2021) or a group of villages (Bouëdron et al., 2019; Hemingway et al., 2022; Lacoste et al., 2018). Zooming out too much obscures the individual patterns of agrarian transformations, with the risk of certain sectors of activity concealing regional particularities (Renner et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_32]

The agrarian system is the result of an evolution: comparative agriculture is about understanding how farms co-evolved within the power dynamics -how some could gain importance while others couldn’t be renewed and eventually disappeared. History is thus seen, not as a succession of events but as an evolutive process, something which is inherited and passed on. The social strata of today are the results of a process of social differentiation which can be outlined in rough trajectories. Those pathways are modelled ones: each farm does not necessarily go through each step of the trajectory, as it is strewn with obstacles, but beneath the particularities there is a common process of evolution. The practices and the state of a type of [SOURCE: Page_32]

32 [SOURCE: Page_32]

farm at a given time is thus “historically constituted”. The choices of farmers are embedded in social, environmental, and economic conditions which determine and explain a given situation: the “motivation is not merely an individual attribute but is socially instituted in this pathway which generates particular opportunities and constraints, as well as guiding ideas and habits that ‘work’ within, and are partially created by, these pathways” (Van Hecken et al., 2019). It is for that reason that we will avoid talking about production “strategies” as the term can imply that choices are made within the purview of the farmer’s mindset and individual capabilities. [SOURCE: Page_33]

1.2.2. The production system The small agricultural region is constituted of a great number of farms which can be grouped into farm types, called here production systems. All the farms which can be related to a production system are based on a common trajectory and share a similar modus operandi and use a similar range of resources. The characterisation of a production system is based on the combination of both technical changes and changes of socio-economic conditions (Aubron et al., 2016; Fréguin-Gresh and Razafimahefa, 2016; Lacoste et al., 2018; Moreau et al., 2012). It thus differs from the farming system concept of the Anglo-Saxon Farming System Research which overlooks the social and historical aspects of the farm (Fresco, 1984; in Cochet, 2015, p. 22). The production systems are linked directly by selling and buying animal and human labour power, feed, food, manure and indirectly by the use of natural resources which can take forms of land and water grabs. In comparative agriculture, agriculture is examined from the vantage-point of labour. Labour is the source of wealth: the rhythm of production and labour bottlenecks dimension the agricultural production at farm-level ; and the transformation of agriculture is analysed in terms of labour productivity gains and losses. Inequalities are analysed in terms of how the wealth is distributed among the agents who have contributed to produce this wealth. The intertwinement of production systems forms the agrarian system. The production system is characterized by a range of viability (bounded by a minimum and a maximum surface or size of herd). The production system must be understood as a product of its natural and historical conditions. It is therefore much more than a mere scale of analysis, i.e. the farm. The notion of production system refers to a particular way of considering diversity as the product of a evolutive process. The production system is part of a “productive trajectory” where each step up this trajectory is made through an accumulation of surplus agricultural production and the investment of capital (Fig. 4). Along this trajectory, some production systems may not be able to make new investments and accumulate capital. Some of them [SOURCE: Page_33]

33 [SOURCE: Page_33]

cannot meet their essential needs any longer and may begin a downward spiral of impoverishment and eventually disappear. [SOURCE: Page_34]

Figure 4. The production system is historically constituted [SOURCE: Page_34]

1.2.3. The cropping and livestock farming systems Each production system is composed of interlinked cropping (scale of the plot) and livestock farming subsystems (scale of the herd) (see Fig. 3). At any given time, several production systems co-exist on the scale of a territory and are hence related by relations of dependencies. On the scale of a territory, we use the concept of the agrarian system which is simultaneously a group of interrelated production systems, a territory with biophysical characteristics (climate, soil, vegetation) but also a socio-economic ensemble made of social relations, capital and technical heritage (tools, knowledge, practices, know-how) which evolves with time (Cochet, 2012). At the scale of the plot or the herd, there are two types of subsystems. The cropping system is a set of plots cultivated in the same manner (Cochet and Devienne, 2006) i.e. with the same crop rotations and associations (commonly represented by a pie chart) and the same sequence of cultivation operations (commonly represented by a cropping calendar). Implicitly, plots belonging to the same cropping system have the same type of soil, are cultivated using the same type of tools (level of equipment) and the same type and quantity of inputs (fertilizer, water, seeds, plant protection) and produce a similar yield. The sequence of operations and the level of equipment leads to a certain amount of required workforce. In Anantapur for instance, rice can be grown today in irrigated conditions either on clayey soils once a year with a long fallow period or on loamy soils alternating with a cycle of groundnut and a shorter fallow period. Those two ways of growing rice differ in yields, water and fertiliser consumptions, labour intensity. They thus refer to two different cropping systems. [SOURCE: Page_34]

34 [SOURCE: Page_34]

Likewise, the livestock farming system is a concept which represents a logic of rearing animals and the organisation labour required to produce the animals and their related products (milk, meat, manure, leather, draught power). The animals can be separated into functional categories (the lactating mothers, the reproductive males, the young adults and the calves for instance) which have different feeding, herding, reproductive and health management practices. A livestock farming system is commonly represented by a flow chart diagram of the dynamic of a livestock farming system, with boxes representing a number of animals of a category at a given point in time and arrows representing the flows of animals which either grow from one stage to another, e.g. from calves to heifers, are sold or bought. The amount of products and the quantity of labour involved are commonly expressed in the base unit for the reproduction of the herd, which is usually the reproductive adult female and its progeny (AFEqU for Adult Female Equivalent Unit). In Figure 5 for instance, one adult female produces in average 0,45 calves and 0,01 heifers which are kept in the system i.e. not sold. The practices related to the ‘extraction’ of the animal products differ between the categories e.g. lactating females are milked, while cull cows are either slaughtered or sold. [SOURCE: Page_35]

Figure 5. Example of a flow chart diagram of the dynamic structure of the demography of a livestock farming system [SOURCE: Page_35]

The cropping and livestock rearing practices are identified and located over time and space and are illustrated by different types of calendar: feeding year planning showing the variation of feed rations over time and their quantities; forage or grazing calendars showing the areas used over the year; a calendar showing the timing of activities related to livestock rearing [SOURCE: Page_35]

35 [SOURCE: Page_35]

(parturition, weaning, milking, culling, grazing) or cultivation (sowing, weeding, harvesting, etc..); a labour calendar revealing the distribution of labour over the year with peak periods of work and lighter ones. Figure 6 gives an example of this last type of calendar, where the peak periods (March, April and December) correspond to the pruning and harvesting periods. [SOURCE: Page_36]

Figure 6. Example of labour calendar for one ha of grape vines The labour calendars provide useful indications for determining the technical limits of systems. Those limits are defined by the available manpower, the level of equipment e.g. milking machines, lorries to transport animals during transhumance, the size of the herd and the surface under cultivation. [SOURCE: Page_36]

2. To-ing and fro-ing from “reality” to the agrarian system 2.1. The sources of information and the tools to retrieve it To take into account social diversity, statistics were not enough. We had to retrieve this information through fieldwork. Comparative agriculture allows this, as it shares common ground with the fields of anthropology and ethnology for the importance of the notion of “immersion” in the field, with observation and in-depth interviews at its core : “Observation, listening, immersion in the environment, daily note-taking and absence of closed questionnaires, as well as through its duration, necessary contextualisation and non- delegation ” (Cochet, 2015, p. 94) are characteristics of the comparative agriculture fieldwork. And yet, the quantitative perspective it bears differentiates it from those social sciences approaches. [SOURCE: Page_36]

2.1.1. Fieldwork context One of the hallmarks of the comparative agriculture fieldwork is the immersion in both the social and the biophysical environment of the field. The aim is to understand how human beings make use of the environment and how the environment in return changes under the [SOURCE: Page_36]

36 [SOURCE: Page_36]

action of man. Fieldwork in India was split into two periods and was disrupted by the COVID pandemic^5. I spent on the whole 10 months in India, between the Indo-French Cell on Water Sciences at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore (state of Karnataka) and my study area in Anantapur district (state of Andhra Pradesh) (see location on Fig. 2). From October 2021 to February 2022, I undertook a first phase of fieldwork which consisted of a series of alternating ten to fifteen consecutive days of fieldwork in Anantapur district, followed by a short week of analysing, decanting, maturing, interpreting and reading at IISC. Initially, I had not intended to go back so frequently to Bangalore, but I morally needed those breaks out of Anantapur. At first, I struggled to blend into the field environment because of the straining context of the COVID outbreak and the general atmosphere of wariness. During those 15 day- stints in Anantapur, I rented a room in Anantapur. Eventually, those round-trips between Bangalore and Anantapur proved to be useful to take essential steps back on my research: I moved back and forth both physically from Anantapur to Bangalore and figuratively from oral data of interviews to written one of archives. My movement in space matched with the iterative refinement of my investigation, helping me to analyse, interpret, formulate and test new hypothesis (Cochet, 2015; O’Reilly, 2005; Peacock, 1987). The people I met often found my presence perplexing, especially given I was the only foreigner in the area, and a woman. I was however always accompanied by an interpreter as the vast majority of farmers did not speak English. The first contact was usually difficult, however eased by the presence of the interpreter. Nonetheless, once the conversation was fully engaged the interview usually went well and we were then introduced to another friend or relative, and were usually greeted with a friendly curiosity. We were however not spared by the cultural refusal to say “no” and consequently, some appointments were promised but not always honoured. I remember farmers leaving the interview without notice or not coming to an interview we had agreed on, an attitude which was hard to swallow at first, but that I managed with time to understand and accept. Even in conducting interviews, there were many trials and errors but the interviewing process gradually grew steadier. My second session of fieldwork lasted from May to September 2022. This time, fieldwork was far more positive: I managed to rent a room in a house with two Indian women who treated me like one of the family. The room was in the outskirts of Anantapur. In [SOURCE: Page_37]

5 This Phd thesis indeed began in December 2020 and the scheduled starting date of the fieldwork in India coincided with the outbreak of a ravaging wave of COVID-19 in India (March 2021). Given the necessary up- close personal interactions with farmers and field observations in comparative agriculture research, fieldwork could not be substituted with surveys entrusted to investigators, neither could the interviews could have been done remotely. The lockdown instated in response to the ravaging second wave of COVID-19 in India, followed by a complicated and restrictive visa regime, pushed the start of the fieldwork in India from March to September 2021. [SOURCE: Page_37]

37 [SOURCE: Page_37]

the villages, farmers had become used to my presence and were less reluctant to talk to the interpreter and myself. During this period, I extended my stays in Anantapur to three consecutive weeks instead of the previous one or two. [SOURCE: Page_38]

2.1.2. The interview and the observation The core of this research was the fieldwork which was structured mostly around interviews and field observations. A small part was also allotted to the standardised collection of samples and field measurements. All my interviews were semi-structured and looked more like conversations than formal questionings based on pre-set questions. The interviews were mostly individual ones, but we were sometimes joined by other people, passing by and curious about our presence here. Because I didn’t manage to rent a room directly in the villages I studied, I was not as culturally immerged in the rural every-day-life as an ethnographer or an anthropologist would have been while doing participant observation (Peneff, 2009; Spradley, 2016). Nevertheless, most of the interviews were done in an informal and spontaneous way, starting off with a question on a particular gesture or object as an opening gambit, and then pursued in the field or on the roadside. This way of approaching the field helped to avoid generating the artificial context of questioning which is often pointed out and criticized by many ethnographers (Olivier de Sardan, 2015b). My approach to people aimed at producing “in situ and contextualised knowledge ” from observations of everyday-life rural practices and also because it was based on repeated and prolonged interrelations with farmers fostered by relationships of trust (Olivier de Sardan, 2015b). The absence of closed and structured questions enabled to adapt my questionning to the respondent :“The best question is not the one given by the interview grid: it has to be found from what has just been said by the interviewee”6 (Kaufmann, 2001, p. 48). A balance had to be maintained between going with the flow of the conversation and not breaking dynamics of serendipity, and also redirecting the respondent when he or she diverted the interview to other topics. Serendipity is essential to interviewing in comparative agriculture because it allows new and unexpected insights and brings more reflexivity to the research (Pieke, 2000). The hypotheses of the research are constantly adapted and adjusted in an iterative process, with variable tailored to context instead of being pre-ordained before the interviews (Cochet and Devienne, 2006; Lacoste et al., 2018). The interviews were all done in Telugu language with an interpreter translating from Telugu to English. The length of the interviews varied from thirty minutes to two or three hours with an [SOURCE: Page_38]

6 Own translation. Original text in French : « La meilleure question n’est pas donnée par la grille : elle est à trouver à partir de ce qui vient d’être dit par l’informateur » (Kaufmann, 2001, p. 48) [SOURCE: Page_38]

38 [SOURCE: Page_38]

average around one hour and a half. The longest interview with one person was five hours. I carried out with my interpreter a total of 215 interviews. We also collected soil, water and manure samples. For the collection of samples, I was helped by my interpreter and also colleagues of the Indian institute of Science (Laurent Ruiz, Julien Amelin, Cassandre Aimon). I did not analyse the soil, water and manure analysis myself but this was done through Hemanth Moger (Indian Institute of Science) for the water samples, Dr Dharumarajan S. for soil samples and Dr Sumantha Bagchi for the manure samples.
