Some interviews were made at home, others on the village square or in the field. I always gave preference to individual interviews because I could then contextualise the data with the history of the respondent. However, when done on village squares the interview was often disrupted by people listening and joining in, drifting from an individual to a group interview. The group interview is often overlooked by anthropologists and ethnographers (Frey and Fontana, 1991) as it limits the interview to the pros and cons of an object or idea (Fontana and Frey, 2000). Those interviews, although not in the form that I had initially planned, provided useful information on the way people interacted and a glimpse on power relations. Ideally, interviews were made in the fields as it enabled us to relate words to objects, plants, animals and parts of the landscape. Our discussions were therefore corroborated by visual testimonies. The ‘village square’ was also a place of creativity where one of our questions led to a situation which was difficult to explain only with words – on past agricultural practices-. The intended individual interview was inadvertently transformed into an extraordinary reconstruction of a past agricultural scene where villagers passing by joined the scene playing the role of a farmer, or even a pair of bulls or mimicking an object. In every interview we supposed that “farmers, wherever they are in the world, “have good reasons to do what they do” and that, as a result, one must endeavour to find these reasons”(Cochet, 2015, p. 126). We aimed at understanding the causal relations, the reasons behind a motivation or a choice. To understand the functional relations we often asked farmers “how” they achieved something rather than “why”, as Katz (2002) indicates: “’How?’ is generally a better way to elicit responses useful for explanation because it invites a personally historicized, temporally formatted responses, while ‘why?’ authorizes responses formatted in the atemporal and impersonal categories of moral reason. […] Shifting the question to how […] turns the discussion toward ‘the long story’ that traces how networks of social relations and detailed processes of social interaction worked to shape the respondent’s present status. It is not uncommon for the researcher to experience a breakthrough toward an explanatory inquiry specifically by shifting the questions that guide the gathering of data from ‘why?’ will to ‘how?’”. In each of the interviews we had to deduce how objective were the words of the farmer. On countless occasions we were told that the reason behind choosing one crop or the other was that the farmer “liked” this crop. It was also sometimes difficult for me to figure out if the vocabulary used by the interpreter was the farmers’ or if it was already part of the interpreter’s own interpretation and understanding. There were therefore two translation processes, the actual translation of the interpreter himself from Telugu to English, but also the broader translation from the particular to the mechanism. “The only place to begin is with the particular, concrete, specific […]” then we move “to more 40 [SOURCE: Page_40]

and more general statements” and beginning “to make comparisons” (Spradley, 2016) in order to figure out the organisation rationale. The core of our fieldwork being the interview and the observation, this research is a fortiori marked with subjectivity. There are inherent biases to this type of fieldwork. One of them emerged from the translation from Telugu to English and the presence of the interpreter (Box 1). Another one occurred because of the up-close relationships we made with the inhabitants of the study area (Box 2). [SOURCE: Page_41]

Although I did learn some basics of Telugu language, my knowledge of the language was not enough to conduct an interview. But it enabled me to briefly introduce myself in Telugu -which often proved to be a good icebreaker- and pick up on some points that the interpreter sometimes forgot to translate, intentionally or not. The interpreter is indeed at the same time an invaluable gateway to the people of the study area but also a barrier because of his effect on the informant, the communicative process and on the translation itself (Phillips, 1959). The quality of the interview was extremely dependent on the interpreter’s “rapport, motivation, relation status and personal trust” (Phillips, 1959). This is especially true in an Indian context given the particular social hierarchy of casts. I had to change interpreters five times, either because they were not up to standard or because they were students and had found another more permanent and stable job. During my first stay in India, I worked with a local male interpreter from the Kuruba caste^7 (BC, the “caste of the shepherds”) who had never done any agricultural or pastoral work but who had studied agriculture at university. He produced accurate translations and the contact with members of the Kuruba caste was often facilitated. During my second stay, I worked for a short time with two male city dwellers who knew nothing of the rural world which had the advantage of limiting some cognitive biases but the disadvantage of making the interviews sometimes very tedious for the interviewee and myself as the conservation was interrupted by explanations of basic farming vocabulary. I could feel there was a certain distance between them and the farmers because they were foreigners like me but in a different way, as they came from the city and were seeing for the first time a heap of straw or a plough. My last interpreter, and the one with whom I worked the most, was a male interpreter from the Sugali Scheduled Tribe. I first feared that his lower social status and his geographic origin (he was from another district) would be the sand in the gears that would prevent gaining the interviewee’s trust. But he had a wide experience in the field and was very knowledgeable on farming as he had previously worked in villages to promote rural [SOURCE: Page_41]

7 The Hindu society is divided into castes. In 1921, the Indian government implemented a reservation system to set quotas at different percentages in education and employment for the historically disadvantaged groups. The main categories are OC (Other category) which have no reservation in employment and usually include the higher castes; SC (Scheduled caste) which include most of the Untouchables, i.e. the lower castes; ST (Scheduled Tribes) which were formally marginalised factions of the society who had no land and lived in the unwanted land; BC (Backward Caste), which are considered as economically and socially backward but not as stigmatised as the SC and ST. [SOURCE: Page_41]

41 [SOURCE: Page_41]

development projects. Most of all, he had excellent interpersonal skills, with a chameleon-like personality, capable of adapting to nearly every situation and people. Box 1. Biases of the ethnographic-like fieldwork: on working with an interpreter [SOURCE: Page_42]

Inevitably, we got caught up in the “cliques” (Olivier de Sardan, 2015) of the wealthier -and the most visible- castes, so much so that initially we thought that most of the farmers in the village had access to irrigation. We realised at a later stage that the village population was divided into neighbourhoods corresponding to each caste (the Reddy, the Kuruba, the Untouchables ..) and that every neighbourhood had its own square with a big tree, around which people, often elderly and with a majority of men, met to discuss or play games. Old people from the higher castes could easily be found on the Reddy or Kamma squares, waiting for the day to end, while the squares of the lower castes were often empty by 8 o’clock in the morning because the men and women had already gone to the fields and the elderly if not in the field, usually stayed at home or around the house. The people belonging to higher castes were much more visible and accessible, and it was therefore much easier to start a conversation with them. Again, if the interview had ‘gone well’ and that we had earned the interviewee’s trust, he or she would either introduce us to a friend or relative or give a name, and by successive contacts and linking we would progress in our interviews (Olivier de Sardan, 2015; Weber and Beaud, 2003), with the risk of staying within the same network or social group. Once we became aware of this bias, we purposefully went to the ‘empty’ village squares, walked up to the doorsteps and eventually managed to talk with the ‘invisible’ men and women. Anecdotally, we realised that most of the farmers were cultivating under rainfed conditions and that we had been previously ‘hostage’ (Olivier de Sardan, 2015) of the network of fruit growers who totally depend on irrigation. Box 2. Biases of the ethnographic-like fieldwork: on getting caught by the “cliques” [SOURCE: Page_42]

2.1.3. Crisscrossing the oral with the written data To put the puzzle together, the information from interviews was sometimes not enough or too vague. This was especially the case for the 1950’s. Yields and quantities of inputs could not be properly recalled by farmers and we had to gather other information. Likewise, we took a critical look at the data from archives, finding some values in censuses either too low or too high. But when the archival data seemed inconsistent with the recalled oral data, it was necessary to make hypotheses on why it appeared so. In some cases, the gaps between the archival and the oral data could be explained by the fact that censuses provide average values on a district scale and are not precise enough to take into account the variability of the [SOURCE: Page_42]

42 [SOURCE: Page_42]

production conditions i.e. land, implements. The collection of data on field by surveyors to make regional statistics can be a challenging task: cropping associations were so complex that determining their yield was bound to bear some inaccuracies, as Francis (1905), rightly points out: “No fixed system or custom exists regarding the mixing of crops. The variety of combinations is very large. […] It gives some trouble to those whose duty it is to make out the statistics of the area under the various corps, as they have to note the proportion borne by the rows of each plant to the total number of rows and thence calculate the area under each. The figures for pulses, which are mixed with other crops on no system, are perhaps seldom reliable” (Francis, 1905, p. 45). Finally, the archive does not allow to separate what had been believed from what had effectively happened (Lara-Millán et al., 2020). Descamps (2005) correctly questions the greater value given to the written archive data compared to the data provided by memory: “Any retrospective oral records seem at first glance relative and imperfect and characterised by its heterogeneity and discontinuity […]. The witness affected by any disorders related to ageing and by varying capacities of remembering, and being unequally motivated or interested by the autobiographic or thematic exercise […] but are the written records otherwise? They often come as discontinuous and patchy, dismembered, ordered in a certain way, sometimes interspersed with fake or suspect documents, unreadable or damaged. It takes a naïve or lazy historian to expect and require in all circumstances complete and uniform documents, well ordained and classed according to the criteria of our research, or to even hope to find all the documents and all the answers to the questions we ask ourselves!”(Descamps, 2005, p. 422)8. [SOURCE: Page_43]

We therefore had to juggle between various sources of information, in a similar way to the triangulation process explained by (Olivier de Sardan, 2015b) except that instead of crisscrossing different viewpoints and conflicting discourses we adjust the missing data with the available ones. We went back and forth between the oral data from retrospective interviews and what we could observe at present and could be transposed back into the past, to our own interpretation of the functioning of the agrarian system, and coming back to the written data. [SOURCE: Page_43]

8 Own translation. Original text: “Toute entreprise d’archives orales rétrospectives se présente d’emblée comme une entreprise marquée par la relativité et l’imperfection et tout fonds d’archives orales est avant tout caractérisé par son hétérogénéité et sa discontinuité […]. Témoins affectés par les troubles du vieillissement et par des capacités inégales de remémoration, inégalement motivés ou intéressés par l’exercice autobiographique ou thématique […] Mais en est-il autrement pour les fonds d’archives écrites qui nous parviennent parfois discontinus et lacunaires, déclassés ou reclassés, démembrés, triés, parfois semés de « faux » ou de documents suspects, illisibles ou endommagés. Il faudrait être un historien naïf ou paresseux pour exiger en tout circonstance des séries complètes et bien homogènes de documents, pour attendre des archives qu’elles soient triées et classées selon les critères de notre propre recherche ou de notre propre problématique, ou encore pour espérer trouver tous les documents et toutes les réponses aux questions que l’on se pose !” (Descamps, 2005, p. 422) [SOURCE: Page_43]

43 [SOURCE: Page_43]

We relied on censuses, village monographies^9, old reports and books from geographers during the colonial era which provided rich and detailed descriptions. We even relied on old photos and documentary video archives and also used the black and white video clips of musical classics, where rural life was a topic of predilection (Appendix 1). This helped to better visualise the rural scenes and objects of the olden days. The values we finally used were not averages but were chosen because they represented a coherent order of magnitude enabling comparisons between systems. In Appendix 2, we give an example of three ways of estimating the capacity of a leather bucket which was used in the 1950’s to irrigate: using the estimations directly provided by the farmers, using the dimensions visualised on a video archive and calculating the maximum volume covered by an animal skin. [SOURCE: Page_44]

2.1.4. The archetype The organisation of agriculture, at each point in time, is complex. To understand this complexity, the composite organisations have to be simplified into smaller organisational forms. This way of simplifying reality has already been widely used by the population ecology school (Greenwood and Hinings, 1993) and by researchers studying interactions between stakeholders in governance analysis (Celliers et al., 2023; Lammers, 1978; Weber, 1947). This is also the case for the comparative agriculture school, which uses the archetype tool to reduce variability and understand complexity (Lacoste et al. 2018). However, comparative agriculture has its own way of “uncovering the organizational pattern” (Greenwood and Hinings, 1993) and building archetypes. The comparative agriculture archetype is not extracted from an automated process of clustering algorithms with pre-defined variables (Celliers et al., 2023; Landais, 1998), but is built by human interpretation with variables defined a posteriori (Lacoste et al., 2018; Landais, 1998). [SOURCE: Page_44]

The archetype is, all in all, a representation of a group of individuals and does not exist per se. However, in the classification made by automated clustering the archetype is usually an average type evaluated by an average, a standard deviation, whereas the archetype in comparative agriculture is neither real nor an average (Aubron, Noël, and Lasseur 2016). In this sense, the archetype in comparative agriculture looks very much like the ideal-type of Weber (Weber, 1978, 1947). It ultimately provides an image of coherence and harmony (Mazoyer and Roudart, 1997), at the risk of over-simplifying somewhat (Cochet, 2015) and building spurious representations of a combination of gears running smoothly. This was a risk [SOURCE: Page_44]

9 We used the 1981 village monography Bhairavanitippa (Kalyandurg mandal, Anantapur district), a village 50 km away from our study (Gov. AP, 1981). [SOURCE: Page_44]

44 [SOURCE: Page_44]

that Pouillon had previously warned against before: “What is important is the difference, which has to be understood without yielding to temptation of reducing it.” (Pouillon, 1956)10. This can be avoided by focusing on comparing process rather than actual objects (Cochet, 2015). It is also a question of striking the right balance between focusing on minute differences and building too many types on the one hand, and restricting diversity too much on the other. [SOURCE: Page_45]

The archetypes in comparative agriculture are based on small samples – sometimes three interviews- but this does not prevent us from outlining key features, main factors of differentiation and from determining new research leads : “Working on small groups or samples does not prevent us from counting, or even from using more sophisticated formal investigative tools, and get tangible results. We recognise here the point of view of the founders of micro-history, who were far from refusing any form of quantification but rather advocated for experimentation and against cumbersome and routine tools: C. Ginzburg talked about an alternative between “ensuring a weak scientific status to achieve tangible results, or assume a strong status to achieve negligible results” (Ginzburg, 1980). Today methods which are well- adapted to the study of small groups […] have acquired a renowned scientific status, but the weight of the quantitative-qualitative divide often remains, which brings us to excuse the size of the samples. However, the article of J. Finez and C. Comet, as does the one of F. Eloire, E. Penalva-Icher and E. Lazega show well how it is possible to abstract mechanisms from the anecdote: this involves many measures, quantifications in the strict sense, as well as the identification of patterns (whose presence can be evidenced itself by quantitative tests) and by individual or group trajectories” (Lemercier and Ollivier, 2011)11 [SOURCE: Page_45]

Original text in French: « Ainsi, le fait de travailler sur de petits groupes ou échantillons n’empêche pas de compter, ni même d’utiliser des outils formels plus sophistiqués, et d’en tirer des résultats marquants. On retrouve là le point de vue de fondateurs de la micro-histoire, qui étaient loin de refuser toute quantification, mais plaidaient en faveur de l’expérimentation et contre les outils lourds et routiniers : C. Ginzburg parlait d’une alternative entre « assurer un statut scientifique faible pour arriver à des résultats marquants, ou assumer un statut fort pour arriver à des résultats négligeables » (Ginzburg, 1980 ; voir aussi Lepetit, 1989). Aujourd’hui, des méthodes particulièrement adaptées à l’étude de petits groupes […]ont acquis un statut scientifique reconnu, mais le poids du clivage quantitatif-qualitatif reste souvent, qui amène à s’excuser de la taille des échantillons. Lazega montrent bien comment on peut, tout en étudiant de petits groupes, sortir de l’anecdote pour abstraire des mécanismes : cela passe tant par des mesures, des quantifications au sens strict, que par la mise en évidence de formes (dont la présence peut être elle-même attestée par des tests quantitatifs) et par le récit de trajectoires individuelles ou de groupes ” (Lemercier and Ollivier, 2011) [SOURCE: Page_45]

2.2. The long and winding road of fieldwork and analysis (steps of the research) The results presented in this study are the product of ten months fieldwork, analysis and modelling in India, followed by additional months of analysis and modelling in France. They were built upon an agrarian diagnosis which followed the comparative agriculture framework and on the quantification of flows of matter, energy and water. In this section we unravel the successive steps, tools used and results along this lengthy process. Figure 7 presents a summary of those steps. [SOURCE: Page_46]

2.2.1. Landscape analysis The first steps in India were dedicated to the choice of the study area, based on the criteria explained in the introduction. We then started the agrarian diagnosis by an analysis of the landscape (step 1 on Fig. 7). Comparative agriculture is indeed grounded in the understanding of the environmental setting of the study area, which is achieved through landscape observations and complemented by the analysis of thematic maps (soil, vegetation, topography) and satellite images. The environment is analysed in such a way that it can be mapped as a combination of landscape units. Each of those units are homogeneous entities of the territory, with a biophysical characterisation of its own. Landscape units are used by man differently, eventually in complementarity with one another, by means of varying practices (Cochet, 2015, pp. 90–91).“Observing the landscape revealed practices; what could be seen suggested what was functional ”(Deffontaines, 1997; in Cochet, 2015, p. 90). This way of mapping the territory into landscape units assumes that nature has its own laws materialised under environmental constraints (soil, hydrological, topographical). This necessarily induces a first level of social differentiation: the farmers who will be able to benefit from the “best” units and those who have to deal with what is left and unwanted. The landscape analysis was made in situ, which meant that sometimes it was carried out with the help of locals who gave, for example information on soil properties or on the use of a particular type of plant. It was also enriched by observations made at a later stage during the fieldwork or unintentionally made en route from one place to another. [SOURCE: Page_46]

46 [SOURCE: Page_46]

Figure 7. Steps of the agrarian diagnosis and environmental assessment at farm-level [SOURCE: Page_47]

47 [SOURCE: Page_47]

2.2.2. Historical investigation and typology of production systems We then traced the history of the study area since the 1950’s by building trajectories of farms. This required piecing together information about livestock and farming practices from archives and from narratives of elderly farmers i.e. at least 70 years old. All the households were grouped together and not spread out amongst the landscape units. We fairly quickly found out that the village was divided into neighbourhoods each being attributed to a social group – the caste - (more information upcoming in Chapter 3). In order to take into account social diversity, we started by randomly selecting elders in each of the neighbourhoods. The interviews with those elders were centred on the evolution of the farm, from childhood up to present days. We followed each step of evolution: for instance, the stages of capitalisation such as investment capital, evolution of family labour, evolution of land size and changes in access to land. We linked events on a larger scale e.g. subsidies provided by the State and described how the farm had been impacted by those policies. At each point in time, we characterised the farm unit, identified the landscape units it relied on, and how those landscape units were used by those farms. This historical investigation led to the modelling of farm trajectories in the form of ramifications representing the differentiation of farms (step 2 on Fig. 7). The final branches in step 2 and 3 of Figure 7 represent a preliminary typology of the farms found at present in the study area. The farm types were therefore historically-constituted. [SOURCE: Page_48]

2.2.3. Quantification of flows of matter, labour, energy, water The next step was the step of characterisation of the typology of present farms. Younger farmers i.e., usually less than 70 years old and more than 30 years old, were selected according to a purposive sampling in each of the pre-defined farm types of the preliminary typology. Semi-directive interviews about the technical functioning of the farms were carried out with those younger farmers in order to provide a fine-grain characterisation of the farm types and generate the final typology of production system (step 4 on Fig. 7). This typology in comparative agriculture is therefore a simplified representation of reality based on a finite number of observed individuals. Step 5 was dedicated to the quantification of flows of matter and labour of those farm types, between the cropping systems, livestock farming systems and also the family labour. Labour was accounted for in a man-day unit. In this study we considered the family labour within the production system, therefore counting the flows of family labour on the crops of the farm as internal flows. The flows of labour from hired labour were therefore flows entering the production system. All the products which were produced and sold were flows of matter flowing out of the production system and all the products which were consumed [SOURCE: Page_48]

48 [SOURCE: Page_48]

by livestock e.g. straw produced on-farm or by family labour e.g. grains produced on-farm were internal flows of the production system. Step 6 (Fig. 7) dealt with the conversion of those flows of matter and labour into flows of water, energy and money for each of those production systems. The calculations and assumptions of those quantifications will be explained in the next section. [SOURCE: Page_49]

2.2.4. Building an archetype village We then upscaled this analysis at territorial level. The agrarian diagnosis was carried out on the scale of a group of villages (see study area on the left on Fig. 8), but representing the metabolism of the study area would have required too many interviews to be carried out by the interpreter and myself. Moreover, each of those villages was found to hold all the landscape units which were defined at step 1 (Fig. 7) of the agrarian diagnosis. This meant that the village could be considered as a proxy of the study area to represent the metabolism of the agrarian system. We identified three types of villages in the study area: the ones structured around a tank which is a man-made runoff water harvesting reservoir, the ones fed by perennial rivers and others which were neither near tanks nor rivers. We chose to represent an archetype village structured around a tank (right on Fig. 9), as they are emblematic of dryland areas of Southern India. The water of those tanks is used to irrigate fields downstream (Gunnell and Krishnamurthy, 2003; Landy, 2018). [SOURCE: Page_49]

49 [SOURCE: Page_49]

Figure 8. Map of the area of study and selection of a village amidst the group of villages We chose to represent an archetype village of intermediate size, neither too big nor too small, and set it at 1 000 hectares (ha). Using Google Earth satellite images, we estimated the tank surface at approximately 60 ha and the surface under construction (houses) at 10 ha for the current period. We had to define and aggregate the spatial heterogeneity of this archetype village i.e. establishing the proportions of each of the production systems and the related land use of the village in the 1950’s and today. This estimation had to be representative of the real villages of the study area. The censuses (Appendix 3) usually provided only the number of households per village, the proportion of broad social categories such as landowners and landless households, and the land use at the time where the census was set. They did not provide any information of the types of farms, and their number of animals, types of crops and cropped surfaces. Given the absence of data at farm-level in censuses, we had to determine this through retrospective interviews. For this, we focused on one “real” village, in order to refine our understanding of the village functioning and structure. This “real” village where the additional interviews were held had to be one of the villages structured around a tank. We opted for Cherlopalli village because 1) it was fairly accessible i.e. close to the highway and 2) of an intermediate size i.e. 1796 ha. The village of Bandameedapalli for instance is very close in [SOURCE: Page_50]

50 [SOURCE: Page_50]

terms of structure to Cherlopalli but is much larger (2 432 ha) and it would have been more difficult to grasp the overall structure. The data of interviews was crisscrossed with data from archives to obtain information on population density, number of landless and landowning households. However, as Cherlopalli is part of Maroor revenue village^12, very often the data in archives are given at the level of the revenue village, and not of the hamlets composing the revenue village. The data of Cherlopalli itself was often lacking. In those cases, we relied on the data of Bandameedapalli village. In conclusion, the archetype village was built upon a mix of data from both Cherlopalli and Bandameedapalli village which are very similar in terms of structure, but one is much bigger than the other. [SOURCE: Page_51]

Figure 9. Crisscrossing data between villages The population density is in line with the ones found in archives, at both time periods (Appendix 3). From there, we had to establish the proportion of the social categories which constitute the typology of the 1950’s (identified during the agrarian diagnosis, step 2 of Fig. 7). Appendix 3 provides information on how we used the data from censuses to build a first draft of the proportions of the production systems in the village in the 1950’s. The combination of archival data led to a first estimation of 5% of large holder farmers, 50% of smallholders, 5% of landless pastoralists and 45% of landless agricultural labourers. This first draft was set to the validation of elders who had previously belonged to each of the identified social categories. [SOURCE: Page_51]

We held discussions with those elders, and successively adjusted the model till it reached a consensus (Fig. 10). [SOURCE: Page_52]

Figure 10. Steps and tools used in the construction of the archetype village in the 1950’s We started those interviews by asking questions such as “At that time, how many households were similar to yours?” (adapting the “yours” to the social category of the respondent). Those interviews were semi-structured and the interviewees sometimes gave unexpected additional information or comments which helped refine the village structure and the description of its functioning. The elders were often not alone, either accompanied by their wife or by friends, which were usually from the same caste. Those interviews were carried out during the final stages of the fieldwork: people had got used to our presence and we had built up close relationships with some of the inhabitants. This facilitated the discussions and all the interviewees took this step of the work seriously, sometimes engaging in fierce debates with their spouses, relatives or friends on the accuracy of the number of households belonging to one category. Some of them even started counting down the households they considered as part of a category, giving family names which we had got familiar with by the time of the end of this fieldwork, and could identify with a family history and emplace in space. As each social category had a pre-set surface of cropped land and herd size, we estimated the land use of the archetype village and compared it with the land use estimates of real villages found in archives for validation. We relied on the same steps of the archetype village of 2022 except that we [SOURCE: Page_52]

52 [SOURCE: Page_52]

could also refine interpretation with what we could see at present whilst on the field and also on Google Earth satellite images. [SOURCE: Page_53]

Step 8 (Fig. 7) was dedicated to the representation of flows of matter and labour between production systems in the village. This meant identifying for instance the products produced and bought in the village and/or and the ones that were produced and exported out of the village. This template of flows of matter and labour at territorial level was the basis of the village energy and water balance drawn at step 9 (Fig. 7). [SOURCE: Page_53]

The quantification of flows of matter, energy, water was made both at farm-level (step 6) and village-level (step 9). The calculations and assumptions are outlined in the following section. [SOURCE: Page_53]

3. Flow quantification and indicators This section explains the methodology adopted in the processes of data sourcing and preparation used for the quantification of the different flows: matter and labour, energy, water and money. However, as it was difficult to find farm-gate prices for a specific year in the 1950’s, we compared economic performances of farms only for the current period (2022). In this section we will therefore explain the methodology used to calculate the flows of matter, labour, energy and water, and related indicators. The steps of the economic quantification will be explained when needed (Chapter 6 & 7). The economic analysis was taken from the comparative agriculture framework. The energy flows were mostly derived from pluri-energy analysis (Vigne et al., 2013b) and the water flows from the estimation of the water balance (Ritchie, 1998). [SOURCE: Page_53]

All the results, whether economic, energy or water-related, were given for a “normal” year, neither good nor bad. The purpose of our research was to compare situations over time and space and farm, crop and animal husbandry units at a given time (Delarue and Cochet, 2013). Data from interviews has some variability: farmers themselves gave approximate values (e.g. a yield of “10 or 15 bags of 100 kg of grain per ha”) and the value used in the model could not be more significant digits than the value it came from. The area of study is a semi-arid region with variable rainfall from year to year. The yields and prices were expected to more or less fluctuate, with some years better than others. Those variations have been evened out in order to be representative of a ‘normal” year. When the interannual variability was necessary to understand choices or the vulnerability of farmers, we presented cases with ‘good’ and ‘bad’ years. [SOURCE: Page_53]

53 [SOURCE: Page_53]

The results involved many calculations which were done using Microsoft Excel at cropping system, livestock farming system and production system level and Microsoft Access at village-level. [SOURCE: Page_54]

3.1. Flows of matter and labour We considered the family workforce as a sub-system of the production system, in order to differentiate the matter self-consumed by the household and the workforce expended by the active family workers and the draught animals owned by the family. We considered two to four amongst a total of five family members as active family workers in the 1950’s. Today, the majority of production systems are characterised by two active family members, the children all being enrolled at school and the elders working on the farm on particular occasions, mostly to take animals for grazing. [SOURCE: Page_54]

The production system is made of three sub-systems: the cropping system, the livestock farming system and the family members (see Fig. 11). Internal flows of matter circulate between those three components: flows of manure from the livestock farming system to the cropping system; flows of crop by-products (straw, grains, hay) from the cropping system to the livestock farming system; flows of food (any vegetables, grains, fruits) from the cropping system to the family members: flows of food (milk, rarely meat) from the livestock farming system to the family members. Flows of labour also structure the production system: human labour to crops and livestock and animal labour to crops. [SOURCE: Page_54]

Figure 11. Intra-unit consumption flows of matter and labour within the production system [SOURCE: Page_54]

54 [SOURCE: Page_54]

3.1.1. Flows of food To determine the internal flows and the imported flows of food i.e. flows of food consumed by the family workforce, we determined the household composition and the household diet. The household composition in the 1950’s was established based on Anantapur district census of 1951: the average household size at the time includes 5 members (Gov. India, 1951). We can confidently divide this household, based on the age pyramids in 1951 (Appendix 4) into 2 children and 3 adults. Based on interviews, we supposed that three adults are one adult man and his wife, and one of the parents either female or male. In 2022, we considered the same composition of household for today, based on our observations of household composition. The main difference between families in 1950’s and 2022 is the number of active workers. This has an impact on the overall management of activities and labour but did not change the number of mouths to be fed. For a same sex and age, we did not consider that the food intake varied whether the person worked in the field or not. We relied on studies of food diets in the state of Andhra Pradesh (Giri, 2006; Vijayaraghavan and Rao, 1998) for considering a yearly basic ration of 160 kg of cereals, 15 kg of pulses, 5 kg of oil, 42 kg of milk (or 43 L), 4 kg of sugar, 2 kg of leafy vegetables and 14 kg of other vegetables, 1,5 kg of fruits. We did not consider vegetables and fruits in the calorie intake as they have a low calorific value and are considered negligible for the estimation of the calorific energy. We adjusted those proportions so that they fit the daily energy requirements (Appendix 5). We took into account the gender and age of the family members but not the physical activity, thus making no distinction between an adult working on the farm and another adult doing any fieldwork. We considered a daily energy requirement of 2 100 kcal for an adult woman, 2 700 kcal for an adult man and 1 600 kcal for a child of more than 9 years old (40 kg weight) according to the Indian values of (Faizan and Rouster, 2023). Considering one adult man as the reference unit of one “adult equivalent unit”, one child corresponds in terms of calories to 0,55 adult equivalents and one adult woman to 0,78 adult equivalent. We understood the changes of food patterns from interviews and other studies (Appendix 5). Staple food changed from a millet-based diet in the 1950’s to a rice- based one in 2022. In the 1950’s, ragi mudde was a popular meal made of finger millet (Eleusine coracana) and a little bit of rice; rice was given as a daily wage to agricultural labourers in the 1950’s. Today rice and wheat flour (to make chapatis) make most of the meals. We have supposed a share of 75% of millets and 25% of rice in the cereals need in the 1950’s and a share of 75% of rice and 25% of wheat flour in the cereals need today. We also know that oil was almost entirely made out of groundnut in the 1950’s, and that today sunflower oil is [SOURCE: Page_55]

55 [SOURCE: Page_55]

also used (we supposed a share of 50-50% today). With all those assumptions we can establish the following basic rations (Fig. 12). Assumptions are outlined in Appendix 5. [SOURCE: Page_56]

Figure 12. Yearly household diet in kg of dry matter in the 1950’s and 2022 [SOURCE: Page_56]

3.1.2. Flows of feed The animals are fed on distributed fodder or directly grazed grass. The diets were estimated by calculated the following feed balance: [SOURCE: Page_56]

Total need dry weight = Grass intake dry weight + Distributed fodder intake dry weight Equation 1. Dry matter feed balance The total dry matter need was calculated taking into account the average annual weight of animals which varied according to breed, sex and age. We used the dry matter intake values per 100 kg of body weight estimated by Singhal et al. (2005) for dry animals, lactating animals and working bulls (Appendix 6). The distributed feed was estimated based on the declarations of farmers and on weighing measurements. Farmers usually didn’t talk in kilograms but in their own units corresponding to the containers they used to give feed. For instance, most of the distributed feed was given in a basket locally called “jalla”, which we weighed for all the different types of feed. Based on those units we asked the farmers how many jallas of each type of feed they gave per day. Those values differed according to the time of year e.g. more feed given during the dry season when the grass was scarce and drier, and according to the state of the animal e.g. lactating or not. The dry matter grass intake rate was calculated by deducting the dry matter intake from distributed feed from the total dry matter need. The flows of matter from grazed grass were considered as internal to the production system, despite the fact that the animals grazed on grass that was not necessarily on the land of the livestock owner. [SOURCE: Page_56]

56 [SOURCE: Page_56]

3.1.3. Flows of manure The amount of dung excreted by livestock depends on the animal species, the breed, the diet, the weight and size of the animal (Kaur et al., 2022). We estimated the weight of the animals in our study area through an interview with the veterinary local services and information in reports and scientific literature. We considered a daily excretion rate of 5% of the body weight for cattle and buffaloes, and 4% of body weight for sheep and goats (Avcioğlu and Türker, 2012). Dung is collected, mixed with household waste and shed waste, and the feed that has been left by the animals in the trough. Manure is kept in heaps for usually six months. During this time, volatilisation of nitrous oxide and ammonia occurs and the weight of the manure heap decreases more or less heavily depending on the meteorological parameters such as temperature or rainfall (Gupta et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2020). The manure is spread on fields to improve mineral soil fertility through the adding of nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus. Manure also acts as a soil texture improver through carbon and soil aggregates and can help the water retaining properties of a soil. Dung is also “lost” to the fields when animals are taken out for grazing. The amount of dung collected depends on different types of practices. They vary according to whether the animals are kept at night in the free stalls near the house or penned on fields, if the animals are taken out for grazing and in this latter case, if part of the dung is collected by the herdsman and taken back at the house. The description of the practices, the assumptions behind the calculations and results are outlined in Appendix 6. [SOURCE: Page_57]

3.1.4. Flows of labour We estimated and accounted the labour spent for all the cropping and livestock rearing activities, including the time spent to take care of animals on a standby basis. As important as it was for running the farm, labour spent for domestic chores was not accounted for because we did not analyse it enough to quantify it precisely. The amount of human labour is expressed in man days per animal or cropping unit (ha, adult male unit or adult female equivalent unit). We considered a full day of work of 7 hours. For instance, if a type of work requires 10 man- days per ha, it means that either one man can complete the work in 10 days, or that 10 men can complete the work in one day. The values for man days were determined by criss-crossing several interviews and in some cases by observations and timing of works under process. The amount of animal labour was expressed in a similar way, in animal days per ha. For example, a ha of groundnut can be sown in approximately 8 hours with two men and a pair of bulls. This comes down to approximately 2.3 man-days and 2.3 animal-days per ha sown. Values of man- days are given in the 2nd column of the tables of Appendix 7. [SOURCE: Page_57]

57 [SOURCE: Page_57]

3.2. Flows of energy Matter and labour circulate within the production system and are exchanged with the exterior (Fig. 11, previous section). The understanding of the circulation of energy and matter is key to understanding the functioning of a system (Mazoyer and Roudart, 2006, p. 47). We considered only three types of energy: the metabolic energy expended by humans and animals during farm work, the gross energy contained in biomass and the gross energy contained in fossil fuels directly or indirectly consumed. [SOURCE: Page_58]

We chose not to consider solar energy flows for several reasons. Firstly, our research focuses on the transformation of agriculture on one and only one territory unlike Vigne et al. (2013b) who compare four territories at different latitudes, with therefore varying daily extraterrestrial radiation. Secondly, the use of solar energy varies with the cultivated surface i.e. receiving the solar radiation. The changes in land use and access to land between production systems is much more telling by the clear and simple counting of land owned, than by representing the solar energy collected by a surface as suggested by Jones (1989). Finally, the daily extraterrestrial radiation varies depending on the season from 8 in winter to 10,5 KWh.m^2.day-1 in summer and the beginning of the monsoon (Allen et al., 1998). The difference of solar energy consumed would probably not even have been noticeable between rainfed crops (cultivated during the monsoon) and irrigated crops (cultivated in summer). The only nuance would have been between production systems with access to irrigation which grow crops two to three times a year, thus capturing much more solar energy, unlike the one for the production systems in rainfed conditions. [SOURCE: Page_58]

Figure 13 shows the flows of energy coming into the production system, circulating between the cropping system(s), the livestock farming system(s) and the household, and the flows of energy exiting the production system and which correspond to either sold products or labour energy expended when household members work on other people’s farms. Figure 14 shows the same type of flows but on the scale of the village. The circulating flows correspond to the matter and labour exchanged between farms within the village. The energy flows directly imported correspond to external supports of energy inputs which are required to achieve agricultural production. They may be of biological (gross energy of biomass), fossil (direct and indirect) or labour (hired labour or hired animal draught power for cultivation) origin. [SOURCE: Page_58]

58 [SOURCE: Page_58]

Figure 13. Energy flow diagram at farm-level [SOURCE: Page_59]

Figure 14. Energy flow diagram at territorial level [SOURCE: Page_59]

59 [SOURCE: Page_59]

Labour energy [SOURCE: Page_60]

The first type of energy flows is the muscular work by human labour or draught animals which we shall refer to as human labour energy and animal labour energy respectively. We counted this energy as the metabolic energy expended during farm work, from any effort during cultivation, grazing, milking and transport etc. Other studies accounted labour energy as the energy of food metabolized while working i.e. the fraction of the average diet corresponding to the actual work time (Aguilera et al., 2015; Galán et al., 2016; Tello et al., 2015). We preferred the first option because we could highlight better the work intensity and better appreciate the productivity gains with the use of draught animals compared to manual work in the 1950’s. The energy analysis as such provided additional information in the quantification of labour than the usual man-days estimated in comparative agriculture studies which de facto do not completely differentiate painstaking from lighter works, apart from the length of the work. Calculating labour energy also enabled us to include the work of animals and compare the role of animals in relation to humans in delivering muscle power. [SOURCE: Page_60]

For each type of work, we multiplied the amount of work (in man-days or animal-days) by an energy expenditure coefficient (in energy unit per time unit) (Eq. 2): [SOURCE: Page_60]

Energy human labour = Man-daysMD/ha x Energy coefficientkcal/min x 0.004184 x 420 in MJ.ha-1 or MJ.animal unit-1 (1 kcal = 0.004184 MJ ; 1 day of 7 hours = 420 minutes) Equation 2. Calculation of human labour energy The same was done for animal labour, by using different energy coefficients thus differentiating the types of work, and using animal-days as the unit representing the amount of work (Eq. 3): Energy animal labour = Animal-DaysAD/ha x Energy coefficientkcal/min x 0.004184 x 420 in MJ.ha-1 or MJ.animal unit-1 (1 kcal = 0.004184 MJ ; 1 day of 7 hours = 420 minutes) Equation 3. Calculation of animal labour energy The coefficients for energy costs of activities correspond to the number of calories burnt per time unit. They were retrieved from previously published studies of physiology which aimed at measuring the calories spent per time unit during effort. Those studies were first carried out at the end of the 19th century through the works of Wilbur Olin Atwater (Passmore and Durnin, 1955) and coefficients have been refined ever since. Most of the energy coefficients used for human labour energy in this study have been retrieved from the works of Vaz et al. (2005) who have compiled a prodigious amount of data from the energy spent from playing cards, dancing foxtrot and harvesting rice. [SOURCE: Page_60]

60 [SOURCE: Page_60]

In some cases, Vaz et al. (2005) presented several compiled values for a same type of work, extracted from different studies. Vigne (2012) recalculated the labour coefficients by classifying work activities from the easiest to the most difficult in order to identify levels of penibility. Because time on the field was limited, we chose to prioritise and give preference to the understanding of practices and process rather than carrying out closed-surveys aiming at classifying the painstaking degree of activities. To arbitrate between one coefficient or the other in the compilation of Vaz et al. (2005), we chose the values as follows. 1) When available, we chose a value from an Indian study. 2) If no Indian value was available, we calculated an average value out of all the display values, separating the values given for energy expended by men or women, when the type of work was gendered. Ploughing for example is an exclusively masculine activity. When there was no coefficient corresponding to a particular type of work, we used the value of the work that we judged closest to the one we sought to evaluate. For example, in the 1950’s, farmers used to incorporate green leaves in the ground before sowing rice (as depicted in the music clip in the film Thodi Kodallu -Appendix 1) by stepping and treading on the leaves after having flooded the fields. There was no value in the compilation of Vaz et al. (2005) for this type of work, as it was very specific. The way in which the green leaves were incorporated seemed closest to “walking in the mud” and we chose the corresponding energy coefficient. [SOURCE: Page_61]

For the energy labour of animals, we used previously calculated coefficients except for the energy expended when raising water from wells during irrigation which we recalculated ourselves (Appendix 2). All labour energy coefficients used in this study are compiled in Appendix 7. [SOURCE: Page_61]

Gross energy contained in biomass [SOURCE: Page_61]

The second type of energy flows is the gross energy (or gross calorific) content of biomass. Gross energy corresponds to the amount of heat released during its combustion under standard conditions and is conventionally measured with a bomb calorimeter. Biomass is the organic matter produced by or which constitutes living organisms (plant-based products such as straw, grains, leaves, and animal-based products such as milk, meat, manure, leather). All the energy coefficients for gross energy of biomass and dry matter content are compiled in Appendix 8. [SOURCE: Page_61]

61 [SOURCE: Page_61]

Gross energy contained in fossil fuels [SOURCE: Page_62]

The third type of energy flows are the flows of fossil energy, which correspond to the gross heat content of fossils fuels directly consumed on the farm (electricity, fuel) or indirectly to produce inputs (feed concentrates, fertilisers, plant protection inputs). For direct flows of fossil energy we used the energy coefficient from Indian studies (Sarkar et al., 2022), to take into account the specificity of India in terms of energy use and production. The energy consumed by agriculture in India comes from electricity (62%) and petroleum products (38%) and the majority of India’s electricity production is coal-based (86%) (TERI, 2021) (Appendix 9). We determined the fuel and electricity consumption of machinery (Appendix 10). The flows of indirect fossil energy were calculated using a Life Cycle Assessment approach. For feed concentrates for instance, we considered the energy expenditure of each component during the agricultural phase, then the transport of raw materials to the feed concentrates manufacturing unit, the fossil energy used during manufacture and then the transport to the study area. However, we did not consider the fossil energy used to produce the machines, buildings and drill borewells. We considered those flows negligible because they would have had to be spread throughout the lifespan of those fixed assets of capital. All the fossil energy coefficients for gross energy of biomass and dry matter content are compiled in Appendix 11. [SOURCE: Page_62]

Indicators [SOURCE: Page_62]

We chose to focus on various energy indicators. To compare the changes in production against the energy used and evaluate the changes of efficiency of the agriculture, we chose to rely on EROI (Energy Return on Investment) indicators. Energy efficiencies and EROIs are different terms, although they are sometimes used interchangeably. The EROI is the output of energy divided by the energy invested^13. When cultivating rice for example, the fossil energy used to run machines is invested to produce rice grains, and not converted i.e. diesel does not transform into rice grains. To compare the production of rice grains with the fossil energy used to grow rice, the EROI is relevant. Energy efficiency on the other hand implies a conversion of energy. For example, an animal consumes feed to produce meat or milk, the gross energy of feed is converted to animal edible products. We considered two types of EROIs. The first one [SOURCE: Page_62]

13 The EROI is actually commonly used to calculate the ratio between “the energy delivered by a particular fuel to society and the energy invested in the capture and delivery of this energy” (Hall et al., 2014). Studies have shown a declining EROI of fuels in relation with the decline in oil production of a well (Hall et al., 2014). This ratio will continue to decline because all the easily-accessible fossil fuel sources are becoming exhausted and more and more energy will be required to go deeper and refine the oil into oil readily usable by consumers. [SOURCE: Page_62]

62 [SOURCE: Page_62]

corresponds to the sum of energy being exported divided by the sum of energy invested (Galán et al., 2016) (Eq. 4): [SOURCE: Page_63]

𝐸𝑃𝑅𝑂𝐷𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 𝐸𝑅𝑂𝐼𝑒𝑥𝑡−𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 = 𝐸𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 [SOURCE: Page_63]

Equation 4. EROI with no account of internal flows At farm-level, the energy invested does not include the energy produced on farm and reinvested on the farm and at territorial level, it does not include the energy produced in the territory and used by other farms in the territory. Eimport is the net energy invested at farm or territorial level. However, this EROI is somewhat problematic for two reasons. The first one is that it mixes both energy invested and energy consumed. At the denominator Eimport includes both the energy of fossil fuel as well as the energy of muscular power of men and animal. Agreeing that a single energy efficiency indicator is not enough (Galán et al., 2016), we therefore chose to break down this EROI into some of its subcomponents: the study of labour being a focal point of this study, we chose to focus on the EROIs related to human labour (Eq. 5 and 6): [SOURCE: Page_63]

Energy productivity = (EProdexport + EProdconsumed)/worker or man-days Equation 5. Energy productivity of energy produced and exported or consumed, expressed per worker or man-days Energy productivityonly export = (EProdexport)/worker or man-days Equation 6. Energy productivity counting only the energy produced and exported, expressed per worker or man-days The second problem is that the EROIext-import (Eq. 4) does not include the flows of energy circulating in the farm or the territory. Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros (2019) argue that efficiency should take into account the energy reinvested in the system (what they call “self-refueling”), otherwise the EROI is overestimated. At territorial level we will also discuss the evolution of the energy efficiency using this indicator which we shall name EROIcircu (Eq. 7): [SOURCE: Page_63]

𝐸𝑃𝑅𝑂𝐷𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 + 𝐸𝑃𝑅𝑂𝐷𝑟𝑒𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝐸𝑅𝑂𝐼𝑐𝑖𝑟𝑐𝑢 = 𝐸𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 + 𝐸𝑃𝑅𝑂𝐷𝑟𝑒𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑 [SOURCE: Page_63]

Equation 7. Energy efficiency taking into account internal flows -from Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019- The purpose of this indicator is to compare systems functioning mostly on internal circulation of energy and others which function mostly on no energy reinvestment. However, to expressly refer to that, we will also use a circularity index at both farm and territorial scale. [SOURCE: Page_63]

63 [SOURCE: Page_63]

The circularity index is expressed as a percentage and corresponds to the energy circulating divided by the total energies imported, circulating and exported (those flows are identified on Fig. 14 for example at village-level) (Kleinpeter et al., 2023) (Eq. 8): [SOURCE: Page_64]

𝐸𝑐𝑖𝑟𝑐𝑢 𝐶𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑒𝑥 = 𝐸𝑖𝑛𝑚𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 + 𝐸𝑐𝑖𝑟𝑐𝑢 + 𝐸𝑃𝑅𝑂𝐷𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 [SOURCE: Page_64]

Equation 8. Energy circularity index (Kleinpeter et al., 2023) The last indicator we shall use is the indicator of energy self-sufficiency (Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019) which is the ratio between the energy produced and reinvested and total energy invested (Eq. 9): [SOURCE: Page_64]

𝐸𝑐𝑖𝑟𝑐𝑢 𝐸𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑓𝑠𝑢𝑓𝑓 = 𝐸𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡 + 𝐸𝑐𝑖𝑟𝑐𝑢 [SOURCE: Page_64]

Equation 9. Energy self-sufficiency index (Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019) This indicator seemed relevant with regard to our research questions. The study of evolution of inequalities is concomitant with the analysis of the evolution of the dependency of the systems on external sources of energy. [SOURCE: Page_64]

3.3. Flows of water In India, 84% of the pumped groundwater is said to be used for agriculture, 12% of industry and the remaining 4% for domestic use (Dhawan, 2017, p. 13). Crops and livestock consume water for their metabolism to run. The water consumed by crops is kept within the plants’ tissues, or “lost” to the atmosphere by evapotranspiration through their stomata. Animals loose water mainly through urine, faeces and evaporation from the body surface and respiratory tract (Stress, 1981). However, the water lost through urine and faeces is restored to the soil and is therefore not consumed per se but rather degraded. As for water evaporated from the body surface and respiratory tract, according to (Zhou et al., 2023), Holstein dairy cows loose water to the atmosphere by cutaneous evaporation at a rate of 20 to 30 litres of water per day for an ambient temperature of 25 to 35°C. This corresponds to 7 to 10 cubic metres per year, which is 200 to 273 times lower than what one ha of natural wild vegetation evapotranspires each year in Karnataka state (Hooge et al., 2022) ! We can therefore consider that the water evaporated by livestock is negligible compared to vegetation evapotranspiration. [SOURCE: Page_65]

Water is one of the means of production and is a limiting resource in Anantapur. Without any access to groundwater, farmers have to rely on the monsoon rains to cultivate, which limits both the length of the crop cycle and the types of crops grown. Farmers with access to groundwater or tank water can grow crops which require more water or grow also out of the monsoon season, thus multiplying crop cycles. [SOURCE: Page_65]

We estimated the water budget using a simplification of the FAO 56 method -single crop coefficient, Allen et al. (1998a)- and used the results to estimate the inflows and outflows of water at the scale of farms and then link farms at territorial level to analyse the changes of functioning of the watershed, which we assumed to correspond to the size of the village. [SOURCE: Page_65]

65 [SOURCE: Page_65]

3.3.1. Flows in the water balance and meterological data Given the small quantity of water consumed by livestock compared to vegetation (see above), we assumed water consumption from livestock and losses through transpiration to be negligible. We evaluated the water balance of cropped surfaces and grasslands whether grazed or not. The hydrologic cycle at village-level can be simplified as follow 1) the only input is precipitation (rain), 2) part of the rain water flows over the surface and is called surface run- off, 3) the other part of the rain water infiltrates into the soil 3) part of the soil water is lost to the atmosphere by vegetation transpiration and evaporation 4) when the soil compartment is full, the extra water percolate through the soil and the fissures of the hard rock aquifer to recharge the groundwater table, which can be pumped in borewells to irrigate some crops may (flow of pumped water). We chose not to take into account surface runoff. This means that the extra amount of water which has to be pumped is a conservative estimate. The flows of water we considered are rainfall, evapotranspiration, water recharge, pumped water (summarised in Fig. 15). We considered the groundwater table as unique, similar to a box with no-flow boundaries [SOURCE: Page_66]

Figure 15. Main flows of water at the scale of a cropping system [SOURCE: Page_66]

We retrieved the rainfall data from daily meteorological data from 1980 to 2020 -with a gap for the years 2016 and 201714- gathered at Anantapur meteorological station (ICAR, 2019). Given that the meteorological dataset did not provide dates prior to 1980, we faced a problem to estimate the water balance in the 1950’s. We analysed the trend of rainfall between 1980 and 2015 to see whether we could extrapolate from 1980 to the 1950’s. As data in 2016 and 2017 were also missing, we calculated the number of days of rain between 1980 and 2015, [SOURCE: Page_66]

14 This may be due a problem on the meteorological data which made it impossible to retrieve data on a series of days during 2016 and 2017. [SOURCE: Page_66]

66 [SOURCE: Page_66]

along with the regression equations and coefficients of determination (r²). In order to better identify years with many rainy days and years with few, we calculated a normalised index of annual number of rainy days. Its value for the year i is given by Equation 10: 𝑟 − 𝑟𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛 RIndexi= 𝑖 𝜎 [SOURCE: Page_67]

Equation 10. Normalised index of annual number of rainy days where ri is the number of rainy days in year i, rmean and 𝜎 are respectively the mean and the standard deviation of rainy days over the period 1980-2020. [SOURCE: Page_67]

There seems to be an upward tendency for both the amount of rainfall and the number of rainy days between 1980 and 2015 (growth rate of 2,55 for rainfall and 0,02 for the number of rainy days), but as the coefficient of determination are very low, we supposed that the climate conditions in the 1950’s could be considered as similar to those in 1980. [SOURCE: Page_67]

Figure 16. Rainfall variability in Anantapur, 1980-2015 Source: data retrieved from ICAR (2019) Water is transferred from soil or plants to the atmosphere by a process called evapotranspiration. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) is a measure of the ability of the atmosphere to remove water through evapotranspiration. It corresponds to the amount of water evaporated from a 2-inch cool-season grass surface, completely shading the ground, and never limited for water. It can be called atmospheric thirst or evaporative demand and integrates how hot, dry, sunny and windy the environment is (Penman, 1956; Robinson and Nielsen, 2015; Zomer et al., 2022). The plentiness of water is a condition which is rarely met, except perhaps over a lake when evaporation is close to the PET. In a desert, on the contrary, the only amount of water that can be evaporated is the water that has been brought by rain each year. Daily PET was not ready available in the ICAR database. We calculated it using the Penman-Monteith equation (Allen et al., 1998b) and the other parameters provided in the dataset : daily rainfall, (mm), temperature (°C), relative humidity -minimum and maximum- (%), wind speed (mph), [SOURCE: Page_67]

67 [SOURCE: Page_67]

sunshine hours (hours), evaporation (kPa) data (ICAR, 2019). The calculations and assumptions are contained in Appendix 12. [SOURCE: Page_68]

3.3.2. Water balance at plot and farm level Vegetation takes up water from the soil through its roots and uses this water to run its metabolism. Evapotranspiration combines two processes (Soutter et al., 2007): 1) a biophysical process known as transpiration which is the heart pump of vegetation, allowing the transport of nutrients within the plant, and occurring with a release of the water to the atmosphere through the plant’s stomata and 2) a physical process which corresponds to the evaporation of water from the soil. This depends on the evaporative demand (potential evapotranspiration) and on the capacity of soil to hold and transfer water. Evapotranspiration varies depending on whether all the requirements of the plant are met, between an Actual Evapotranspiration (AET) value where water is available in limited conditions and a Maximum Evapotranspiration value (conventionally named ETc but which we shall in this work name MaxET for easy readability). [SOURCE: Page_68]

If all the water that the plant needs is available, the vegetation evapotranspiration corresponds to the maximum evapotranspiration and depends on the potential evapotranspiration (PET) and on the architecture of the crop. The crop characteristics can be represented with a crop coefficient Kc which varies according to the stage of the crop (initial stage, development stage, mid stage and end stage) (Fig. 17). Crop coefficients are given in Appendix 12. [SOURCE: Page_68]

Figure 17. Variation of crop coefficients of groundnut from planting to harvest [SOURCE: Page_68]

Source: Crop coefficients from FAO (Allen et al., 1998b) The maximum crop evapotranspiration is calculated with the equation below (Eq. 11): [SOURCE: Page_68]

𝐸𝑇𝑐 = 𝑘𝑐 . 𝑃𝐸𝑇 [SOURCE: Page_68]

Equation 11. Maximum crop evapotranspiration ETc [SOURCE: Page_68]

68 [SOURCE: Page_68]

A crop coefficient (Kc) lies between 0 and 1,2 and varies according to the anatomy and height of the plant. It includes the evaporation from the soil and varies according to the development stage of the crop. During the initial stage, the seed has just sprouted and the canopy of the plant thus very limited: the crop evapotranspiration is similar to the soil evaporation. As the crop canopy develops and covers the soil surface, evaporation from the soil surface declines and the transpiration component of the evapotranspiration increases. Although some data (Allen et al., 1998b) provide a decomposed version of the crop coefficients (with two separate crop coefficients, one for vegetation evapotranspiration and one for soil evaporation), we will use the combined one as it is the one that is most frequently available in studies. We used kc values from the FAO database (Allen et al., 1998a) and also from other studies. The FAO kc database provides general kc values for crops grown in pure stands in an ideal controlled environment, implying that there is always sufficient water to avoid water stress. Our study area has a semi-arid climate, with very different conditions from the experimental conditions of the FAO studies. We favoured values from semi-arid areas, at best Indian, when they existed. All the values and references are outlined in Appendix 12. For the wild vegetation, we used the crop coefficients of Descheemaeker et al. (2011) who studied the evapotranspiration of a dry shrubland in Ethiopia. We assumed the vegetation in the study area to be similar. We adjusted the coefficients according to whether the grasslands were not grazed, grazed once a year or grazed several times a year. Box 3. Crop coefficients of cultivated crops and wild vegetation If the water is available in limiting conditions i.e. when the surfaces are rainfed, the actual evapotanspiration has to be adjusted from the maximum evapotranspiration, taking into account the amount of the rain and the water availability in the soil. The actual evapotranspiration is therefore either equal to the maximum crop evapotranspiration if there is enough water from rainfall or below and in that case the plant is under a more or less slight water stress (Fig. 18). [SOURCE: Page_69]

The vegetation evapotranspiration in this study is the actual evapotranspiration, which corresponds on the one hand to the maximum crop evapotranspiration (ETc) for irrigated crops and on the other hand to the actual crop evapotranspiration (AET) for all rainfed crops and wild vegetation. The rainfed surfaces (crops or wild vegetation) are by definition never irrigated and the rainwater is not always enough to fulfil the water needs of the vegetation. The irrigated [SOURCE: Page_69]

69 [SOURCE: Page_69]

crops in the vicinity of any groundwater pumping infrastructure are assumed to receive all the water they require. [SOURCE: Page_70]

Figure 18. Actual evapotranspiration (AET) and maximum evapotranspiration (MaxET) We also calculated in some cases the maximum crop evapotranspiration (MaxET) for all types of crops and surfaces in order to compare the gap between the vegetation evapotranspiration in water-limiting and non-water-limiting conditions. [SOURCE: Page_70]

Water pumped and water recharging the aquifer [SOURCE: Page_70]

The amount of water contained in the soil is represented by a box with a maximum water content (𝛥Swatermax), which depends on the water holding capacity (WHC) of the soil and the root depth (Rootdepth) (Eq. 12): [SOURCE: Page_70]

ΔS𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑥 = 𝑊𝐻𝐶 . 𝑅𝑜𝑜𝑡𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑡ℎ [SOURCE: Page_70]

Equation 12. Maximum amount of water held in the soil Water holding capacity [SOURCE: Page_70]

The soil acts like a sponge which if wetted, will retain water (gravity pushes water into the soil pores gradually) up to a certain amount where water will overflow. This is where the soil water content will be at field capacity (FC). The water content at field capacity thus depends on the soil structure and particle size distribution. Once the water is in the soil, it is held more or less on the surface of soil particles by hygroscopic forces. Not all the water in a soil can therefore be absorbed by plants using their roots. Under a certain point, called the wilting point (WP), the binding forces between water and soil particles are so tight that the [SOURCE: Page_70]

70 [SOURCE: Page_70]

plant can no longer remove the water from the soil. The plant starts to wilt and cannot regain turgor. The hygroscopic water is so tightly held in the soil that it cannot be removed except with very high temperatures. A clayey soil retains much more water than a sandy soil. The sandier the soil, the lower the wilting point is. Between the wilting point (WP) and the field capacity (FC), the plant can extract water from the soil and release it to the atmosphere via the plant’s stomata (evapotranspiration). The maximum amount of water that can be extracted from the soil by plants is termed the water holding capacity (WHC) expressed in mm of water per cm of soil (Ward and Trimble, 2003). We have estimated the WHC at 1,8 mm/cm of grey clayey soil and 1,7 mm/cm of red loamy soil, using the texture triangle of Jamagne et al. (1977) -given in Appendix 13- and on clay and silt percentages of soil samples we had analysed at the National Bureau of Soil Survey in Bangalore. [SOURCE: Page_71]

Root zone depth [SOURCE: Page_71]

As for the root zone depth, the more developed the root system is, the bigger is the water reservoir (WR) accessible to the plant. We used data from previous studies, mostly from (Dorenboos and Kassam, 1979) that we harmonised to have comparable root zone depth (values are given in Appendix section 12). [SOURCE: Page_71]

Before the rainy season starts the soil still contains some water. When the ground is left uncropped following harvest at the end of the monsoon season, grass does not grow again until the next rains and the kc for bare soil is usually 0.15 (Allen et al., 2005). Considering that evaporation in bare soil happens up to a depth of 15 cm, as mentioned in the Food and Agriculture Organization irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56 (FAO-56) (Allan et al., 1998), we chose a lower kc for bare soil in order to model a decline in the soil water content without emptying all the water in the soil. We chose a kc for bare soil of 0.01. [SOURCE: Page_71]

Once the rain starts, the soil “fills up” with water and the soil water content is adjusted daily. We considered that all the water above the maximum soil capacity permeates the rock materials beneath the surface and recharges the groundwater table. For irrigated crops, the flow of water pumped from the groundwater table was estimated as the water provided when the soil has been emptied of its water – and not as soon as the level of water has declined with irrigation increasing the water content to field capacity (Appendix 12). [SOURCE: Page_71]

For a given cropping system, some water may therefore recharge the groundwater table at some point in the crop cycle -for instance when the crop is grown during the monsoon season- and some water may be pumped at another point of the crop cycle, for instance when [SOURCE: Page_71]

71 [SOURCE: Page_71]

the crop is grown during the dry season. We estimated an annual net groundwater recharge which corresponds to the gross groundwater recharge minus the water provided by irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_72]

𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟 𝑅𝑒𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑒𝑡 = 𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟 𝑅𝑒𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑔𝑟𝑜𝑠𝑠 − 𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟 𝑃𝑢𝑚𝑝𝑒𝑑𝑔𝑟𝑜𝑠𝑠 [SOURCE: Page_72]

Equation 13. Net amount of water recharging the groundwater table This is the same on the scale of a farm, which may hold both rainfed and irrigated cropping systems. The net water recharge at farm-level may be positive if the flows of water recharging the groundwater table outweigh the flows of pumped water of irrigated crops. [SOURCE: Page_72]

The net recharge can be calculated at territorial level by aggregating all the net recharges of farms of the territory and the net recharge of areas neither grazed nor cropped. The net recharge at territorial level may be positive or negative giving an indication on the dynamic of utilisation of the groundwater resource. We will also evaluate the contribution of each farm and type of land use to the overall territorial net water recharge. [SOURCE: Page_72]

Conclusion of chapter 1: In chapter 1 we presented the origin and keystone concepts of the conceptual framework which we chose to carry out this study: comparative agriculture. We explained how we constructed the history of agriculture of the area, how we modelled and characterised farm types at both period and combined them at territorial level by building an archetype village. We present the diversity of tools we used: oral data from interviews, observations and archival data. We chose to focus on flows of energy and water. Flows of energy include flows of human and animal labour energy, gross energy of biomass, and direct and indirect fossil energy. Water flows were accounted for by calculating water balance at plot level and upscaling at farm and territorial level. [SOURCE: Page_73]

Rapthadu mandal is located on the Deccan plateau, which stretches between the Western Ghats and the Eastern ghats mountain ranges, in the southern part of the Indian peninsula. The first impression of Rapthadu mandal is one of a dry, hot, red and flat landscape. The vast wash pediment of red soils is in fact an expanse of slightly undulated plain with rocky residual hills here and there. The wash pediment is carved by non-perennial rivers forming saucer-shaped wash depressions. We rely on the terminology of Gunnell and Bourgeon (1997)15 for the characterisation of the geomorphology of the area (Fig. 20). The topographic variations do not exceed 20 to 30 metres, the highest point being approximately 410 meters. [SOURCE: Page_76]

Figure 20. Main geomorphological units of the study area Source : Gunnell and Bourgeon (1997) In this chapter, we first give an overview of the climate of Rapthadu mandal and its implication for farming. As part of the Deccan plateau, the area is characterised by a hard rock aquifer, rendering irrigation somewhat challenging. To understand the reason for existing of the geomorphological units presented in Figure 20, we rely on a broad geological history of the Deccan plateau. We then close this chapter by the presentation of the landscape units of the territory. [SOURCE: Page_76]
