1. A semi-arid region 1.1.1. The monsoon seasonal climate system Asia, and more specifically India, is characterised by a monsoon seasonal climate system. The monsoon is first and foremost a movement of air masses, originating from a difference of specific heat between water and land. Water has a higher specific heat than land, meaning that it takes more energy to heat water by one degree than with other substances such as soil. In other words, the sea temperature is much more conservative than the temperature of land. The difference of temperature between land and sea causes a difference of atmospheric pressure because the air that is heated expands i.e. higher pressure, whereas air that cools down contracts i.e. lower pressure. This pressure difference is equalised by winds, with air masses flowing from high to low pressure areas (Clift and Guedes, 2021; Erickson, 2014; Park, 2001; Philander, 2012; Woodward, 2009). [SOURCE: Page_77]

When temperatures start rising around the months of May-June, the land mass heats up rapidly, drawing humid air in from the surrounding ocean. Over the sea, the air is charged with the moisture from the evaporation of water from the ocean and the air masses cool down over the land and even more so if it expands over mountains. The hot wet monsoon winds are divided into two branches (Fig. 21, left), one from the Arabian sea to the west of India and the other from the Bay of Bengal to the East (Prasad, 2019; Rakhecha and Singh, 2010). The south western coast of India is home to the Western Ghats Mountain range, as high as 2 695 meters. The Arabian sea branch of the monsoon hits the Western Ghats and releases the moisture in the form of heavy rains at the highest altitudes. The Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon causes heavy rain in the North East of India which moves gradually to the west because of the deflection caused by the Himalaya Mountain range, resulting in rainfall in most of the northern part of the country. The movement of the air masses towards the north east tends towards an equalisation of the atmospheric pressure differences. The lower pressures are gradually replaced by higher pressures up to a point where the monsoon starts to lose its hold and the winds are reversed. This occurs around September and marks the end of the advancing south- west monsoon. The long rainy season is well depicted by the Indian author Kushwant Singh (1956): “The monsoon is not like ordinary rain which comes and goes. Once it is on, it stays for two months or more. Its advent is greeted with joy. […] While the monsoon lasts, the showers start and stop without warning. The clouds fly across, dropping their rain on the plains as it pleases them, till they reach the Himalayas. They climb up the mountainsides. Then the [SOURCE: Page_77]

77 [SOURCE: Page_77]

cold squeezes the last drops of water out of them.”. In October, the phenomenon is reversed: the land mass becomes cooler than the surrounding ocean and the pressure is higher over land than over the ocean. Cool dry air flows from the land out over the ocean, and collects moisture from the Bay of Bengal and releases it over the southern eastern part Indian Peninsula e.g. Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu (Prasad, 2019; Rakhecha and Singh, 2010). This corresponds to the North East Monsoon (Fig. 21, right). [SOURCE: Page_78]

Figure 21. The Indian monsoons Source : Basemap Google Earth 2023 [SOURCE: Page_78]

1.1.2. The game of water and chance: a thirsty and variable climate Anantapur is located in the state of Andhra Pradesh in the south eastern part of India, approximately 300 km away from the western Ghats and 250 km from the Eastern Coast. The central position of Anantapur, (Fig. 22), in the rain shadow of both monsoons, means that it receives meagre rainfall. Not all the moisture of the South-west monsoon is indeed released when it encounters the Western Ghats : the onshore winds continue to gradually pour the remaining moisture over the Indian Peninsula in a west to north east gradient over Maharashtra, Gujarat, parts of Madya Pradesh (Gunnell, 2000). The annual rainfall is 628 mm. The PET is 1 868 mm and exceeds by a factor of three the annual rainfall, making water a limiting factor. [SOURCE: Page_78]

78 [SOURCE: Page_78]

We discuss the reasons of the high PET and compare with other territories in Box 4. Anantapur has an Aridity Index^16 of 3.14 referring to a semi-arid climate. [SOURCE: Page_79]

Figure 22. Mean annual rainfall and climate classification across the Indian sub-continent [SOURCE: Page_79]

Source : Mean annual rainfall based on 0.5° x 0.5° grid data for 1971–2005 and climate classification (1971-2005) from (Raju et al., 2013) [SOURCE: Page_79]

The high value of Anantapur PET is explained by the location of Anantapur, in the northern hemisphere at the latitude of 14,68 degrees. The extraterrestrial radiation is fairly high because of the proximity to the Equator but the photoperiod varies very little throughout the year. Energy is available all year round in good quantities to evaporate liquid water. Relative air humidity is on average 55% which is much lower than in Bangalore (Bhimala et al., 2021) (see location on Fig. 22) but close to the one of Rajasthani areas (location on Fig. 22) (Singh, 1999). The drier the air, the bigger the quantity of water evaporated. The wind speed is also higher in summer: 15 miles per hour instead of the usual 7 mph (ICAR, 2019). This increases the evaporation of water in summer. The PET of Anantapur is higher than the one of Gundlupet (south of Karnataka state, see location Fig. 22). This means that for a same crop, the maximum crop evapotranspiration will be higher, and so will be by definition the water needs. Box 4. Discussions on the hight PET of Anantapur and comparisons with other territories [SOURCE: Page_79]

16 Aridity Index calculated as PET/rainfall (Budyko, 1974) [SOURCE: Page_79]

79 [SOURCE: Page_79]

Rainfall in Anantapur varies greatly from one year to another, with sixteen years below 75% of the average rainfall between 1980 and 2016 (see Fig. 16, Chapter 1), meaning that rainfed farming is a gamble for many farmers and that even the growth of natural grasses can be limited and compromised. Anantapur is known to experience drought once in every five years on average (Gopinath et al., 2013). The first rains usually occur around the 15th of May and the first 10 mm are usually reached around the 21st of May. However, the monsoon was the earliest in 2020 (first rains in April) and the latest in 2003 (first rains beginning of June and first 10 mm reached beginning of July). It is however the North-East monsoon that brings the most rain, i.e. 40% of the annual rainfall between September and November. The year can be decomposed into three seasons (Fig. 23): 1) a rainy season from May to November with relatively humid and warm weather, 2) a winter season from December to January characterised by a cooler and drier weather and 3) a summer season with low rainfall and warm weather. [SOURCE: Page_80]

2. Hidden, yet existing water 2.1. Groundwater trapped below in crystalline rocks: a difficult barrier to overcome In Anantapur, groundwater is trapped beneath the land surface in the hard rock aquifer. Those bedrocks are part of an ancient geological history: they were formed over 2,500 million- years ago at the transition between the Archean and the Proterozoic eons. This stratigraphical break can be seen from above (see the pink-grey discontinuity on Fig. 24) [SOURCE: Page_81]

Figure 24. Major soils and landforms in Anantapur and Bellary regions [SOURCE: Page_81]

Source: Satellite image from Google Earth Most of the Archean rocks are igneous or magmatic rocks and are therefore mainly composed of feldspars, quartz, olivines, pyroxens, amphiboles and micas. The Archean rocks can be found in many parts of the world (Canada, Australia, India, Russia, etc.) in the form of large blocks 100 to 1000 kilometres wide called cratons. In India, the Dharwar craton covers the state of Karnataka and parts of the states of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. During the course of a Proterozoic continental rifting, the Dharwar craton broke into pieces, forming blocks of granites (magmatic rocks) and gneisses (metamorphic rocks). The areas between those rocks i.e. orogenic belts were typical areas of high-pressure metamorphic assemblages such as gem stones. Andhra Pradesh was indeed home to the famous diamond mine of Kollur which produced many large diamonds called the Golconda diamonds, some of which composed [SOURCE: Page_81]

81 [SOURCE: Page_81]

the Jewels of the Nizams of Hyderabad state. Still during the Proterozoic eon, the gneisses and granites were degraded into sedimentary deposits. This process led to the formation of sedimentary basins such as the one of Cuddapah basin -one of the largest- located north-east of Anantapur district and composed of conglomerate, sandstone and shale. While most of the Archean rocks of the Dharwar craton are granites, there is a second type of rock: metamorphic rocks from mix of sedimentary rocks and basalts from the greenstone belts and visible on the satellite images (greenstone because of the green shade of chlorites, actinotes and amphiboles of the mafic rocks). [SOURCE: Page_82]

2.2. Remnants of the past water: the water behind the chemical and the mechanical weathering of the crystalline rocks With decreasing humidity from West (Western Ghats) to the East (Deccan) and increasing length of the dry season (top left of Fig. 25), the intensity of weathering of the bedrocks also decreases (see Fig. 25 – Weathering intensity). Geochemical weathering alters the fresh rocks into rotten rocks or saprolite. In the humid climates of the Western part of the gradient, the conversion to saprolite is fairly rapid and the saprolite layer is much thicker (several tens of metres) than to the east where because of a drier climate saprolitisation is not intense (Gunnell and Bourgeon, 1997). [SOURCE: Page_82]

Figure 25. Multilayer gradient modelling of a South Indian climosequence from West (Kerala) to East (Karnataka) and rainfall distribution over Southern Peninsular India NB: Red arrow on map showing distance between the Western Ghats and the study area Source: Multi gradient modelling, left (Gunnell, 2000) ; rainfall distribution (Das, 2021) [SOURCE: Page_82]

82 [SOURCE: Page_82]

In the study area (eastern part of the gradient), the crystalline bedrocks cannot usually be seen except on rare occasions where canals have been cut through the hard rock aquifer (Fig. 26). The un-weathered bedrock is covered by the saprolite layer (Fig. 26 and Fig. 27) (weathered upper part of the bedrock) which is much thinner than to the west (approximately 4 meters on the photo). [SOURCE: Page_83]

Figure 26. Alteration profile of the first meters of the hard rock aquifer in Anantapur Source: photo taken where the PABR right canal – top right- cuts through the hard rock aquifer [SOURCE: Page_83]

83 [SOURCE: Page_83]

Figure 27. Alteration profile of the hard rock aquifer Source: (Aoulou et al., 2021; from Wyns et al., 2004) Compared with the rich alluvial aquifers of the Indo-Gangetic Plains, hard rock aquifers are very different by structure and also by the underlying coping and adaptions mechanisms of farmers (Shah, 2012). The deep sandy alluvial formations of the Indo-Gangetic plain have an ample storage capacity of water which favoured the development of irrigation using shallow open wells during the colonial era. Hard rock aquifers on the contrary have a limited water storage capacity: beneath the saprolite, water can only be found in fractures. [SOURCE: Page_84]

To the West of the gradient, kaolinite-type clays prevail while to the East kaolinites are much less and overweighed by smectite-type clays which are, in addition, of reddish colour (Gunnell and Bourgeon, 1997). To the East the soil is of reddish colour and granular, as seen on Figure 26. The difference in soil composition is directly linked to the increase of the length of the dry season and the decrease of annual rainfall from West to East (Gunnell, 2000; Gunnell and Bourgeon, 1997). In case of water intermittently leaching into the bedrocks, the hydrolysis of the granite minerals (biotite, albite, feldspar) is partial. Partial hydrolysis occurs because of the non-carbonate nature of the parent material i.e. granitic crystalline rocks, and also the capacity of the parent material to release iron oxides. The partial alteration leads to the formation of 2:1 clays such as smectites. The oxidation of ferrous irons (from biotite) by dissolved oxygen releases insoluble ferric ions which gives the rocks a reddish and brownish colour. Under tropical humid climates, there is a higher-level of hydrolysis. The bonds between [SOURCE: Page_84]

84 [SOURCE: Page_84]

the clay minerals and the iron oxides get weaker and all the basic cations are washed away. The orthoclase feldspar KAlSi^3O$_8$ are hydrolised leading to the formation of 1:1 clays such as kaolinites, silica and potassium ions. To the west, there is high-level of hydrolysis due to higher rainfall and shorter dry season, which explains the thickness of the saprolite (weathered bedrock) and the importance of kaolinites ; to the east because of a longer drier season and a smaller amount of rainfall, the saprolite is thinner and smectites with iron oxides prevail. (Gunnell and Bourgeon, 1997). [SOURCE: Page_85]

2.3. Erosion and circulation of water Strangely enough, water is everywhere in the toponyms in Anantapur, as an Indian researcher and local stakeholder of rural development pointed out to me during my first visit to Anantapur: “There are more oceans and rivers in Anantapur than anywhere else in the world.” (personal communication, Y. V. Malla Reddy^17). Toponyms ending in -eru in telugu are plenty and refer to streams and rivers e.g. Kuderu mandal; toponyms ending in -kunta refer to a small tank e.g. Nambulipulikunta mandal, in -cheru for a medium-sized tank e.g. Kothacheruvu mandal or Cherlopalli village (cherlo being a synonym of cheru). Nerukuntlapalli village is the ‘village of small water bodies’, and Ramasagara village holds a very large tank, the name meaning “seas” in Telugu. [SOURCE: Page_85]

The climatic gradient also explains different landforms. To the West of the Deccan plateau where the climate is humid, the landscape is made of steeper slopes, convex hills and “demi-oranges” (see Fig. 28 A). The contrasts with the east is striking : the mean slope is less than 1% in the study area, and the landscape is made of coalescing concave wash pediments (see Fig. 28 B) on the eastern part (Gunnell and Bourgeon, 1997). [SOURCE: Page_85]

Figure 28. Convex hills (west) versus concave mantled pediments (east) [SOURCE: Page_85]

Source : (Gunnell and Bourgeon, 1997) [SOURCE: Page_85]

17 Personal communication with Y.V. Malla Reddy at Action Fraterna Ecology Centre in Anantapur (2021). [SOURCE: Page_85]

85 [SOURCE: Page_85]

The high slope to the west is due to the presence of the Western Ghats, formed from tectonic movements from the Eocen area to the Tertiary. The tectonic movements also gave way to the inclination towards the east of the Indian Peninsular plaque (Bourgeon, 1988; Radhakrishna, 1993). The pediment very gently slopes down to the East (not noticeable with the naked eye), giving the direction of the water flow when the river beds are not dry. The rivers flowing to the East are very different from the Western ones: “While the western face of the Sahyadri presents a youthful aspect, the Deccan plateau lying to the east, presents a different picture altogether, one of feature less senility. The land shows evidences of having been reduced to base level in an earlier cycle. A thick residual cap of soils, alluvia and laterites, is seen over the peneplaned surface. Major rivers and their tributaries follow sluggish, meandering courses. That such plain-lands are found at present at elevations of 500 to 1000 m above sea level only shows that the region as a whole had experienced repeated uplift which exposed the peneplaned surfaces of earlier cycles to new cycles of erosion […] The wide and almost senile valleys of the east- flowing rivers are on the whole graded almost to their heads, nearly in sight of the Arabian sea, and contrast very strikingly with the youthful gorge-like courses of the west-flowing streams. These latter have only 50 miles (80 km) in which to fall 2000 feet (610 m) or more to base-level.” (Radhakrishna, 1993). During the erosion of the bedrocks, silica was removed by the action of water. Because of the variations of settling velocities, sand particles accumulated in the river and steam beds, while silt and clay particles accumulated mostly in the wash depressions. [SOURCE: Page_86]

are separated by smaller irrigated fields: enclosed fruit plantations (top left on Fig. 29) (sweet lime and pomegranate mostly, but also grape vines and banana) of approximately 1 ha and fields of vegetables (right on Fig. 29, second from the top) (okra and tomato) of 0.5 to 1 ha. Many of those enclosed fruit plantations are located along the highway which crosses the study area to the East and which corresponds to the Bangalore-Hyderabad highway (left of the area shown on Fig. 29). Vegetables and fruit trees are irrigated using borewells. They are usually 50 to 200 metres deep and drilled in the fractured horizon of the aquifer, the layer below the saprolite. The fractured horizon has a low storage capacity but a high permeability. Although water is stored in much smaller quantities in the fractured layer than in the saprolite, it circulates at high speed within the cracks of the hard rocks. This implies that if the groundwater table is lower than the level of the saprolite, a borewell will be successful only if a fracture is intercepted while drilling, making the process a risky gamble. However, the permeability of the fractured horizon rapidly decreased with depth, because of a decrease in the number of fractures (Guihéneuf et al., 2014; Lachassagne et al., 2021). Statistically, the probability of increasing one’s chance of either finding water or having a better yield of a borewell in hard rock aquifers is low. [SOURCE: Page_89]

Approximately a third of the wash pediment is not cultivated and can be divided into two types of areas. The first type is a very open grass steppe (right Fig. 29, third from the top) with barely no rocks and consisting of grasslands dominated by C$_4$ plants, mostly Eragrostis and Digitaria species (Rao et al., 2017). There may be sparsed dwarf shrubs but they are very small in height, at most 50 cm. Based on the estimations of Floret et al. (1993, p. 30) in an African dryland, the absence of shrubs in this very open grass steppe could mean that those areas have previously been cultivated and not more than 10 years if the land was cleared manually, though perhaps a bit longer in case of mechanical clearing. The second assumption is, in analogy with other Indian semi-arid grasslands, that those open grass steppes have existed as natural ecosystems of their own for a very long time. Fossil evidence show signs of grasslands existence as far back as 60 million years ago, although at the time in limited quantities. Grasslands became dominant 5 to 8 million years ago when the uplift of the Tibetan plateau occurred which is thought to have induced the monsoon climate and the transition to a [SOURCE: Page_89]

89 [SOURCE: Page_89]

seasonal climate (Vanak et al., 2017). Some of those grasslands are enclosed with stone pillars and barbed wire (Fig. 31), indicating perhaps a forthcoming implantation of a fruit orchard. [SOURCE: Page_90]

Figure 31. Open grass steppe enclosed with stone pillars and barbed wires in the background The second type of area is a mixed acacia shrubland with many large rocks and natural grasses, with scattered or grouped spinescent shrubby trees (Fig. 32). Most of the shrubs and trees come from the legume family, which grants them nitrogen-fixing qualities: Acacia nilotica (Babul tree), Acacia sundra (Tottler willed), and Senna auriculata also known as Cassia auriculata (tangedu, Tanner’s cassia), Milletia pinnata (Karanja) and Azadirachta indica (neem tree). The leaves and pods of the acacias and Senna auriculata are also important fodder resources for livestock, especially sheep and goats, which very likely favours the dispersal of their seeds (Tiver et al., 2000). All those plants have in common their resistance to dry conditions through “escape, avoidance and tolerance” strategies to drought (Levitt, 1972), such as staggered germination or a tendency to shed their leaves. [SOURCE: Page_90]

Figure 32. Mixed acacia shrubland with large rocks [SOURCE: Page_90]

90 [SOURCE: Page_90]

Another important and useful plant is the milkweed Calotropis procera (Sodom apple tree), whose leaves enrich the soil in nitrogen (Varadarajan and Sanyasi Raju, 1956). Calotropis is a C$_3$ plant which has various coping mechanisms and physiological characteristics which helps the plants to survive dry conditions such as cuticular wax on the leaves and stems of the evergreen shrub Calotropis procera, a deep tap root system , and a modification of the shape and thickness of the leaves according to the degree of humidity and corresponding transpiration and metabolic adjustments (Batool et al., 2020; Hassan et al., 2015; Kaur et al., 2021; Pompelli et al., 2019). The plant is however not consumed by grazing animals (Suresh Kumar et al., 2013). The importance of large rocks suggests that those areas have never been cultivated. They are mostly located far from villages, around the basement of the rocky hills. [SOURCE: Page_91]

Both areas are grazed and browsed by sheep and goats. The dry matter productivity of grassy areas was estimated based on a compilation of studies of arid and semi-arid grasslands (Table 6): [SOURCE: Page_91]

have separated from the underlying granite layer. Shells of granite break loose forming concentric layers of highly decayed rock within weathered bedrock (saprolite). These concentric layers peel off (like the layers of a peeled onion), creating boulders within the saprolite which can be several metres large. Once those boulders have been pushed aside, opening new fields as shown on the bottom right photo on Figure 33, usually rainfed. [SOURCE: Page_92]

3.3. The wash depressions and rivers beds The study area is located in the Upper Pennar sub watershed (belong to the Pennar water shed) and is carved by non-perennial rivers and streams. Most of them are dry summer. They form three types of landscape units: the first one where water accumulates in small quantities in very shallow areas, where thick thorny shrubland develops; the second one where water accumulates in deeper depressions crossed by a man-made bund water forming what is called a tank ; the third one corresponds to rivers of 10 to 60 meters wide. [SOURCE: Page_92]

Some parts of the wash pediment have been very lightly carved forming shallow depressions where water regularly accumulates, which is favourable to the formation of sodic soils. Those areas are not cultivated and are covered by thick thorny bushes (Fig. 34), including the invasive weed Prosopis Juliflora, and umbrella-like trees, which are tolerant to saline and sodic conditions (Gupta and Gupta, 2015; Kaur et al., 2021; Shivanna, 2018). [SOURCE: Page_92]

92 [SOURCE: Page_92]

Figure 34. Thorny shrubland on sodic soils [SOURCE: Page_93]

Near to villages, rivers are occasionally crossed by check dams (small concrete dam) in order to store water during the monsoon (Fig. 35). Those rivers are between 10 and 60 meters wide. Some villages are located near those rivers e.g. Gantlaparthi village on Figure 9. Sand accumulates on the river bed and behind the check dams. Those check dams can be crossed by motorbike when the water is not too deep (maximum 1 to 2 feet deep) and women often wash clothes on the edges of the dam (as in background of Fig. 35). [SOURCE: Page_93]

93 [SOURCE: Page_93]

Figure 35. Check dam across the river between Yerragunta and Gandlaparti villages, full of water after heavy rains (November 2011) Streams meet and form a network which leads to deeper saucer-shaped wash depression where the runoff water is collected. The glacis slopes are the transition areas between the wash pediment and the wash depression and are composed of a thickened wedge of colluvium. Those wash depressions are crossed by a man-made bund (Fig. 36), where surface runoff is captured behind the bund. The overall device is called a tank. The first tank in the Deccan would have been built in 1 500 BC and its construction would have required much human skill and labour (Shah, 2008). The tank had several functions. By capturing the runoff water behind the bund, crops could be cultivated downstream of the bund in the lower bank (command area of Fig 36). Those crops were irrigated when needed and in appropriate quantities by opening sluices along the tank bund (adjustment of the supply of water). By retaining water, the tank bed is also a reservoir of accumulated erosion materials from the residual hills and the wash pediment interfluves, which can be scoured out to amend fields (Gunnell and Krishnamurthy, 2003). Even though there is no doubt that tanks are the work of great human ingenuity, their success was however limited by recurring problems of reservoir siltation. Their maintenance was based on a particular form of social organisation (Shah, 2008). In the 13th and 16th centuries several tanks were known to be deeply silted and despite much digging out of sediments, raising bund heights and building new sluices, they could not be used at optimal capacity (Morrison, 2015). Finally, those tanks favour the groundwater recharge (R.N.Adhikari et al., 2015). Till the 19th [SOURCE: Page_94]

94 [SOURCE: Page_94]

century tanks were the backbone of the agrarian economy because they enabled to maintain the groundwater table fairly high in order to lift water from wells below (Dikshit et al., 1993). [SOURCE: Page_95]

Figure 36. Tank structure [SOURCE: Page_95]

Figure 37. View of Cherlopalli tank: rice fields in the command area of the tank on the left, bund stretching in the middle and tank bed partially full of water on the right (taken in June 2022, beginning of the monsoon) Sir Dietrich Brandis, a German-British botanist who worked for the British Imperial Forestry Service in colonial India, describes tanks in Anantapur as an oasis in the middle of a desert-like landscape: “The Anantapur tank is a magnificent work, and the view from the bund very fine. On three sides the tank is surrounded by bare hills, which have a most desolate appearance. At this the most favourable time of the year, the country looks parched and much worse than the hills around Ajmere to which there is otherwise a certain resemblance. So much more pleasing is the contrast of the large extent of emerald green paddy-fields below the tank. There is apparently no waste of water, no swampy ground below the bund; only fields and channels. Two crops of rice in the year […]. On the bund there are some specimens of Acacia planifrons, the umbrella thorn of Madura and Tinnevelly, with horizontal branches. This tree is also cultivated near Bellary […]. Vast extents of waste lands, with here and there a poor [SOURCE: Page_95]

95 [SOURCE: Page_95]

crop of kulti (Dolichos biflorus) and arikata (Oplismenus Colous). On the hills nothing save shrubs of fleshy Euphorbia and few tufts of grass. This part of the Anantapur taluk is a dreary waste, with here and there an oasis of fields irrigated by tanks or wells. If it were not for the streams which come from the hills further south and which feed the Anantapur and Shinganamalla tanks, the country would be a complete desert.” (Brandis, 1883). Strictly speaking, the tank command area is only the extent of land irrigated by gravity from the water stored in the tank (Dikshit et al., 1993, p. 17), and therefore does not extend very far below the tank bund. However, what we have named tank command area here extends to the whole area of grey hydromorphic soils that stretches up to 2 kilometres away from the tank bund. The tank-beds (Fig. 36) are usually full of water-logged Prosopis juliflora (Fig. 34), a well-known invasive shrub in India (Subramaniyasharma et al., 2023). [SOURCE: Page_96]

The soils in the tank command area are dark-grey hydromorphic clay-rich soils, with a higher WHC than the red soils on the wash pediment -1.8 mm/cm- (see Table 5), which are the results of the accumulation of clays and silts in anoxic and waterlogging conditions. Those soils are often saline because of the water logging conditions which prevent the leaching of the salts imported by the irrigation water. [SOURCE: Page_96]

The tank command area is mostly cropped with small fields of rice (Fig. 38) (0.25 ha) and tiny plots of irrigated Napier grass of no more than 0.1 ha. [SOURCE: Page_96]

Figure 38. Rice fields in the tank command area [SOURCE: Page_96]

96 [SOURCE: Page_96]

Both crops are irrigated by borewells. Nearly half of the tank command area is encroached by Prosopis Juliflora, which grows well in sodic conditions (Singh et al., 1994). On the border of the tank command area, below the tank bund and at the level of the glacis foot slopes, there are a few remnants of large dug wells. They are a dozen metres deep (much shallower than the borewells). They have been dug in the saprolite, which is the weathered bedrock layer of the hard rock aquifer (Fig. 39). The saprolite is the result of the alteration of the mother rocks and can hold much more water than the layer of unweathered hard rocks because of a high porosity which can reach 30%, while the bedrock has a porosity lower than 2% (Heath, 1984; Sharp, 2014). The saprolite thus insures the capacitive function of the aquifer. However, the saprolite has a low permeability and water circulates slowly (Lachassagne et al., 2021; Maréchal et al., 2004). In Rapthadu mandal, the saprolite is fairly thin, 5 metres as shows on Fig. 26), and can reach up to 20 meters below the ground at the very maximum according to (Rao et al., 2006). Because the wells are dug in the brittle materials that constitute the saprolite, the wells are to be supported by a casing of paved stones in the upper part (see Fig. 40). [SOURCE: Page_97]

97 [SOURCE: Page_97]

Figure 39. The variation of hydraulic conductivity and porosity with depth in crystalline basement [SOURCE: Page_98]

Source: from Howard (in Chilton and Foster, 1995; Howard and Griffith, 2009) [SOURCE: Page_98]

Figure 40. Remnant of a large dug well in Yerragunta [SOURCE: Page_98]

98 [SOURCE: Page_98]

Another feature of the dug wells is that they have a very large diameter (10 metres diameter approximately) (Fig. 40). Because of the low permeability of the saprolite (like a sponge), water circulates slowly and the well is refilled accordingly. The large diameter of the wells thus enables to speed up the recharge. In summer the groundwater table may decline, which decreases the saturated thickness undermining the efficiency of the saprolite for conducting water (Chandra, 2018). In many areas in India, tanks were used alone to irrigate crops below them by gravity. Although irrigation was very limited in the 19th century in Anantapur district (20%), most of the irrigated land was irrigated using wells (42%, followed by tank irrigation 30% and river channel 28%) (Kumar, 2018, p. 50). Dam and river-channel irrigation prevailed in coastal Andhra districts (A and B on Fig. 41), while irrigated land under wells and tanks were mostly found in inland Andhra, in what was known as the “Ceded istricts^19” (C and D on Fig. 41). The Ceded districts correspond to the study area and some neighbouring districts. The importance of wells in the Ceded Districts is all the more striking that wells were more expensive in the Ceded Districts than in coastal Andhra Pradesh, because they had to be much deeper and required deep cutting through rocks (Kumar, 2018, p. 55). The presence of many dug wells near the tank command area is most certainly explained by the uncertain water storage capacity of tanks in the area where the rainfall is low and erratic. Vaguet and Vaguet (1992), studied an area in Telangana region, north of the area of study, and characterised by an even higher semi-aridity. This region depended only on tank irrigation and according to them, the absence of wells in Telangana region was an obstacle to its agricultural development. [SOURCE: Page_99]

19 The Ceded Districts are the districts of Anantapur (study area), Kadapa, Kurnool and Chittoor which were given by the monarchy of Hyderabad (Nizam of Hyderabad) to the East India Company in 1800. [SOURCE: Page_99]

99 [SOURCE: Page_99]

The city of Madras corresponds today to the city of Chennaï. [SOURCE: Page_100]

100 [SOURCE: Page_100]

Conclusion of chapter 2: The study area, located in the mandal of Rapthadu, Anantapur district is characterised by a semi-arid climate: rainfall is low and only available during the six months of the monsoon season. Located in the rain shadow of both monsoons, the area receives meagre rainfall. The area is flat but subtle topographic variations reveal three main landscape units. The wash pediment is a vast expanse of land of red loamy soils with variable size stones, from gravelly to stony in some areas. The wash pediment is composed of an open grass steppe, large fields of rainfed crops and a few irrigated plots of land, i.e. vegetables and fruit plantations. A few sparse rocky hills are located on the wash pediment, with mixed shrublands and large rocks. Those hills and boulders are residues of inselbergs, which have been fragmented by mechanical weathering. The large boulders and the shrubby vegetation make those areas impossible to cultivate as such but they can be grazed. Non-perennial rivers have carved the wash pediment forming saucer-shaped depressions called wash depressions. The soils of the wash depressions are of grey colour and hydromorphic nature. Some of those wash depressions are crossed by a man-made bund where surface runoff is captured behind the bund. This structure is called a tank. Below the tank, in the tank command area, rice and Napier grass are cultivated. The tank command area and the river edges are also partly encroached with an invasive shrub called Prosopis Juliflora. The area is also characterised by a crystalline hard rock aquifer, making groundwater difficult to extract. The landscape shows remnants of large dug wells, especially in the tank command areas. Those wells are a dozen of metres deep and dug in the saprolite, i.e. the weathered bedrock layer of the hard rock aquifer. The saprolite is made of altered mother rocks and its permeability is low: water circulates slowly and the wells refill at a slow pace. To optimise this recharge, those wells were dug with very large diameters. There are also borewells which are currently used. They are much deeper than the dug wells, 50 to 200 metres deep, and drilled in the layer below the saprolite in the fractured horizon of the aquifer. This layer has a low storage capacity but a high permeability: the water circulates at high speed within the fissures of the hard rocks. This means that a borewell is successful only if it encounters enough of those fractures. Drilling borewells in the hard rock aquifer is therefore a risky gamble. This is an environment with many constraints, the most obvious ones being 1) the low rainfall making rainfed cultivation possible only part of the year, 2) the presence of large [SOURCE: Page_101]

101 [SOURCE: Page_101]

boulders and thick shrubs making those areas uncultivable as such and 3) the hard rock aquifer which is a difficult barrier to overcome to extract groundwater. A historical analysis is now required to understand the landscape in the 1950’s and how the farmers of Rapthadu managed to adapt to those constraints when muscle power was the only source of mechanical energy. Chapter 3 to 5 unravel the evolution of the area since the 1950’s, showing how the agrarian system evolved and led to the landscape features which can currently be seen and described in this Chapter. [SOURCE: Page_102]

102 [SOURCE: Page_102]

CHAPTER 3: Harnessing animals and men in an environmentally constrained landscape (1950’s-1970’s) [SOURCE: Page_103]

The date and location of this figure is unknown but it seems to accurately depict agrarian scenes of the 1950’s, as told by elderly farmers. [SOURCE: Page_103]

103 [SOURCE: Page_103]

This chapter is the starting point of the historical analysis of this study. We chose to start the analysis of the socio-economic differentiation and metabolic evolution of the agrarian system from the 1950’s, just after the Independence of India from the British rule (1947) for two main reasons. As interviews with elders were at the core of this analysis, this limited the historical depth of this study to what could be recalled by those elders. The second reason is explained by the consideration of the agrarian policies which were implemented by the State and Central government of India to increase the production of the agricultural sector just after Independence. Those policies came into effect in the area of study from the 1970’s. In this chapter we describe the agrarian system in the 1950’s, as a departing point of this agrarian history. We examine the structure of the agrarian system in the 1950’s, based on the landscape structure which we have described in the previous chapter, and also the means of production which the social categories in the 1950’s had access to. At the onset of Independence, the inequalities in Indian society were strong. The agrarian society of Rapthadu was no exception. The agrarian system of the 1950’s was mostly shaped around social relations of production between land owning and landless categories. [SOURCE: Page_104]

1. Inequalities at the heart of the social and spatial organisation of the agrarian system 1.1. A spatial and social segregation The population densities of Rapthadu mandal in the 1950’s were of the lowest in rural India, ranging from 0.3 to 0.9 inhabitants per ha (Gov. India, 1986, 1951). The houses were grouped into villages or hamlets usually near tanks or rivers. Some villages were neither near tanks nor rivers, and were located along the Secunderabad-Bangalore Road, which was already a major road^21 in Anantapur district. The village caste system divided the population into categories of people with specific positions as well as the relations that shape them. The village was split into neighbourhoods, in order to separate the households belonging to different castes (Fig. 43). Those neighbourhoods were structured around a village square with usually a neem tree and a shrine. Those village squares are at the same time a place of relaxation (photo A on Fig. 43) where elderly people can be found having a nap or sitting, a place of worship (photo B on Fig. 43) or a place of leisure (photo C on Fig. 43 representing a game carved in stone). [SOURCE: Page_104]

21 The Secunderabad-bangalore metalled road is the former Bangalore-Hyderabad highway which can be seen today. Secunderabad is a twin city of Hyderabad. This road was one of the three main metalled roads in Anantapur district, already at the beginning of the 19th century (Francis, 1905, p. 74). [SOURCE: Page_104]

104 [SOURCE: Page_104]

Figure 43. Map of a village built on the edge of a tank [SOURCE: Page_105]

Figure 43 shows the location of the neighbourhood of each caste of the village of Cherlopalli. It shows the irrigated fields of the tank command area in green, the tank bed in blue separated from the irrigated fields by a tank bund (wash depression). The rest of the territory is made of rainfed fields and grasslands of the wash pediment, in orange. Photos are close-ups of the village squares. [SOURCE: Page_105]

The Indian caste-system was structured around the concept of purity. There was a line of pollution, under which impurity was absolute and to which the Untouchables belonged. The caste system was governed by certain principles: 1) there are different degrees of purity – or impurity, depending on the way we look at it-, even amongst Untouchable castes, building a hierarchy between castes, 2) membership to a caste is determined by birth and strict endogamy is practice (Jodhka, 2013). In the area of study, the dominant castes are the Reddys and the Kammas, while the Madigas make up most of the Untouchables. In between the higher castes and the Untouchables, there were the Kurubas and the Vaderra castes. Castes may be historically associated with a particular type of work: Madigas were associated with tannery and leather making – the fabric of the impure-, the Vaderra with all the works related to stone, the Kuruba with pastoralism. The Reddys were historically the land-owning aristocracy of the villages. The Kammas were the highest upper caste of the villages, although much less represented than the other categories, but with a high influence in both village life and political life. In informal grouped discussions I noticed, on several occasions, disagreements and diverging perceptions between Kamma and Reddy people about policies of chief ministers of Andhra Pradesh. Caste was indeed also a political framework, with Indian political parties [SOURCE: Page_105]

105 [SOURCE: Page_105]

sometimes attached to a particular caste. In Andhra Pradesh, the two main political parties were consensually established as the parties of the Kammas (TDP party – Telugu Desam Party-) and the Reddys (YSRCRP – Youth Labour and Farmer Congress Party-). Another caste, the Boyas, sometimes lived in single-caste villages such as Pesaragunta and Palavayi (location on Fig. 8 of Chapter 1). [SOURCE: Page_106]

The castes were grouped into broader categories: the Backward Castes -BC- (Vaderra and Kuruba), the Scheduled Castes – SC- (Untouchables), the Other Castes -OC- (Reddy and Kamma), the Scheduled Tribes -ST- (Boyas) (Fig. 44). This classification originates from a system of quotas implemented in 1921 by the British government in order to favour historically disadvantaged groups in civil servants’ jobs and education (SCs, STs and BCs). The positions in the administration and education were indeed mostly occupied by members of the upper castes (OC) and the other categories were left behind. Despite the implementation of quotas about a century ago, disparities persist and the reservation system was questioned again in the 1980’s. One of the main criticisms which was raised was that the policies and the quotas directed towards the historically disadvantaged groups, e.g. reserved seats in public sectors and schools, subsidies, only benefited the “creamy layers” of each of those categories (Jaffrelot, 2007). [SOURCE: Page_106]

Figure 44. Main castes in the study area found in rural areas The Kometis were the caste of the merchants, in charge of buying the agricultural production of farmers, and selling food. They have not been modelled in the archetype village as they were not involved the agricultural production itself but acted as brokers. [SOURCE: Page_106]

Despite the importance of the caste in the making of social hierarchies and relations between classes, this work aims to pull away from essentialist and deterministic views of social [SOURCE: Page_106]

106 [SOURCE: Page_106]

differentiation. The social categories are defined in this work by the access to the means of production – land, water, capital, labour- and the relations of coexistence and domination within the agrarian system. The social categories often include people of several castes. The pathways of differentiation were not straightforward. The pre-destined trajectories may have been diverted by individual pathways. The representativity of social categories of the archetype village is presented in Appendix 15. [SOURCE: Page_107]

1.2. The social categories with land 1.2.1. Smallhodler farmers: relying mostly on family muscle power In the 1950’s, the most represented social category in the area of study were smallholder farmers. They had not more than 2 ha of land and a very small herd: 1 pair of bulls and 2 dairy animals at the very most. Most of them belonged to the Reddy caste (OC category) but some of them also belonged to the Kamma caste (OC) and the Kuruba (BC) castes. In the villages located near the Bangalore-Secunderabad road (Ramanepalli, Golapalli, Maroor) and the ones near rivers (Gantlaparthi, Kothapalli), those smallholder farmers usually had only rainfed land on the wash pediment, which was enough to sustain only 1 pair of bulls. In the archetype village, emblematic of villages structured around a tank, the classic exemplar of the smallholder farmers -and the one we chose to model- had 2 ha of land, 1 pair of bulls and 1 buffalo. They represented 50% of the agricultural population of the archetype village. Most of their land (1.6 ha) was located on the wash pediment where they could only grow rainfed crops, but they could nonetheless grow irrigated crops on 0.4 ha in the wash depressions and glacis foot slopes. The surface under irrigated crops was limited by the labour capacity of bulls. Draft animals were indeed used to raise water from wells to irrigated crops and a pair could only irrigate at maximum 0.4 ha. Draft animals were also used for preparing land, as well as sowing, weeding, harvesting and post-harvesting operations. Irrigation was possible because the smallholder famers had a pair of bulls and the fields they owned in the wash depressions and glacis slopes were close to dug wells. They usually did not own those wells, but had access to them. On the rainfed lands (wash pediment), they grew a plethora of millets and pulses : foxtail millet (Setara italica in Latin, korra in Telugu), pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum in Latin, cambu in Telugu), little millet (Panicum sumatrense in Latin, sama in Telugu), kodo millet (Paspalum scrobiculatum in Latin, varadugu in Telugu), sorghum (Sorghum bicolor in Latin, jona in Telugu), horse gram (Macrotyloma uniflorum in Latin, ulavalu in Telugu), red gram or pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan in Latin, kandi), cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L., alasandalu), green gram or mung bean (Vigna radiata L., pesalu). They provided a healthy diet (see Box 5): finger millet [SOURCE: Page_107]

107 [SOURCE: Page_107]

grains are rich in methionine amino acids, millets have a high mineral content and low glycemic index, and pulses provided the necessary proteins. Millets demand less water and nutrients than other crops and have a drought tolerance physiology due to a reactive stomatal regulation (Winkel and Do, 1992).The pulses were cultivated either in rotation or associated with the millets. [SOURCE: Page_108]

Finger millet, also known as ragi, along with the rainfed millets and pulses, was the staple food at the time. Finger millet was used in the very popular ragi mudde also known as ragi ball (Fig. 45) which was mixed with rice. Apart from people belonging to the higher castes, rice was consumed in small quantities. The ragi mudde was accompanied by a preparation made of mixed pulses, called dahl. Women also collected the pods of tamarind trees (Fig. 45) to add to the local dhal. [SOURCE: Page_108]

Figure 45. A typical meal in the 1950’s: ragi mudde and pulse curry Source : Phadnis (2019) [SOURCE: Page_108]

Milk was also an important food. There were no cooperatives and no infrastructures for cold storage at the time. The milk was therefore not marketed and consumed either fresh from the cow or the buffalo’s udder, or processed at home into dairy products which were mostly curd and ghee (clarified butter) (see Fig. 46). The surplus milk, if any, was given to labourers as part of their wage. Buffalo milk was favoured to make curd and ghee (higher fat content -7.5%- than the milk of local dairy cows -5%- see Appendix 16). [SOURCE: Page_108]

Figure 46. Home-made main milk products throughout the milk processing chain Box 5. Food in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_108]

108 [SOURCE: Page_108]

The smallholder farmers relied mostly on family labour. Of the total annual 744 man- days required, 84% were provided by family labour. There were 3 active workers among the 5-member household. The peak labour periods were mostly triggered and driven by the land preparation, sowing and harvest of crops (May, September and January, see Fig. 47). With 3 family workers they managed to feed the household in milk, millets, pulses and even produce a small surplus which they sold to the Kometi merchants or gave as wages to agricultural labourers. Their low dependency on hired labour and their mostly household-orientated production is illustrated by a high circularity index (90%) and a high energy self-sufficiency index (98%) (Fig. 47). [SOURCE: Page_109]

109 [SOURCE: Page_109]

Figure 47. Structure and metabolic profile of smallholder farmers in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_110]

110 [SOURCE: Page_110]

1.2.1. Large holder farmers: relying on others A small portion of the agricultural population were farmers with very large expanses of land, from 25 to 100 ha. They belonged to the Kamma caste. They owned wells, mostly located in the tank command area or the glacis foot slopes. In the villages devoid of tanks, they had a few wells on the wash pediment. Their irrigated land was sown with finger millet and rice, and the rainfed areas were sown with the usual millets and pulses, and also groundnut. Their land was very large but not all was cultivated at the same time. A Kamma woman once told us “We had so much land I wouldn’t even be capable of telling you where it was exactly!” The rainfed crops were in rotation with fallow periods of 3 to 8 years depending on the size of the land. [SOURCE: Page_111]

In the model represented on Fig. 48, we defined an archetype of 1.5 ha of irrigated land in the tank command area and approximately 50 ha of land on the wash pediment with a 5-year fallow period. At the time, every landowner paid a tax on the land they cropped every year, a system inherited from the Ryotwari system implemented during the British colonial era (see Box 6). Because the tax was only paid on the actual cropped land, this meant that the large holder farmers only paid the tax on the land they had cropped, and not on the ley fallows. Nonetheless, everyone in the village knew which land was used by whom, even if under fallow and not officially owned i.e. if the tax had not been paid. “There weren’t any signs showing that this land belonged to this farmer or the other, but everyone knew which land belonged to whom, even if it wasn’t cropped” explained a farmer of a former large holder family from the Kamma caste. [SOURCE: Page_111]

Under British rule the Land settlement was introduced in 1793, therefore implementing three types of revenue collection systems: the Zamindari system (mostly in the states of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa and Varanasi), the Ryotwari system (in most of South India) and the Mahalwari system (north-west India). In the Zamindari system, the zamindars were landlords with full proprietary rights over land. Land was therefore owned by a land-owning class who decided on the land use, employed labour or rented out land to tenants. Sir Thomas Munro, one of the British administrators of India, introduced the Ryotwari system, which was implemented in most of South India (including the study area). In the Ryotwari system, the intermediaries are eliminated. Each farmer is recognised as a landowner, the Ryot. A tax was assessed based on the land which is not cropped, and not merely occupied. For this purpose, the British started making a land survey in each village in 1880, in order to assess and measure all the surfaces under [SOURCE: Page_111]

111 [SOURCE: Page_111]

cultivation. This survey was successively refined and rectified throughout the beginning of the 20th century. Based on this assessment, the British collected a land tax through collectors, called Karnam, which were from the Reddy caste (known as Reddy karnalus by old interviewees). After independence, this system continued as land tax but collecting was directly done by the State through the Revenue Office. Land titling was conditioned in the study area to the paying of the land tax “Government gave an official document called patta, which had particulars of assessment and area under the occupation of pattadar – holder of the patta- to each individual peasant. The pattadar could transfer, inhert and sell the land for which patta was given. The irony was that he was the owner of the land until he paid the land revenue mentioned in his patta. This drew a link between ownership right over land and the capabilities of paying the land tax.”(Kumar, 2018, p. 86). Box 6. A tax on cropped land and an implicit land ownership over ley fallows The key differences with the smallholder farmers were that 1) they rotated their rainfed crops with a 3 to 10-year fallow period, 2) they grew groundnut in addition to millets and pulses, 3) they had a much larger herd, with at least three pairs of bulls and half a dozen to a dozen dairy animals, 4) they depended mostly on hired labour. [SOURCE: Page_112]

The large holder farmers of the archetype village (Fig. 48) had 50 ha of land, of which 1.5 were located in the tank command area (wash depressions), the rest being on the wash pediment. The production unit was composed of only 2 family workers among the 5-member household. The family workers were usually the head of the family, involved only in ploughing and land preparing activities, along with one of his sons. They had much more land than the smallholder farmers, and because they relied mostly on hired labour (87% of the total annual labour requirements), they could crop more land each year. The total labour amount was three times more than the one of the smallholder production units. The labourers were hired on a daily basis or as permanent labourers who lived at their home. [SOURCE: Page_112]

112 [SOURCE: Page_112]

Figure 48. Structure and metabolic profile of the large holder farmers in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_113]

113 [SOURCE: Page_113]

With three pairs of bulls, they could cultivate approximately 1.5 ha of irrigated crops near wells, and also grow groundnut as a rainfed crop on the wash pediment, in addition to the usual millet and pulse crops. The variety of groundnut which was sown at the time was indeed a spreading variety which had to be harvested using a tremendous amount of animal power. The spreading variety -also known as the runner variety or Virginia type- was characterised by a crop cycle lasting approximately 140 to 155 days (5 months). Sowing was done during the month of July once the monsoon had started. This brought the harvest period to the month of December, a month after the last monsoons rains (Fig. 49). [SOURCE: Page_114]

Figure 49. Labour calendar of groundnut spreading variety in the 1950’s This meant that, by the time the crop had matured, there was no soil moisture left and the soil was rock hard. Plucking manually the groundnut pods out of the earth was therefore very hard and there was a high risk of leaving many of the pods in the ground. In order to ease the work and also ensure a decent harvest, farmers had to use three pairs of bulls simultaneously to have the necessary energy to lift the groundnut pods. In addition to those three pairs of bulls, four people were needed: 2 to stand on the wooden plank so that it would go deep enough and cut the soil below the groundnut pods, 1 to hold the device and also help to push the plank in the ground, and one person to lead the pair of bulls (see Fig. 50). Although groundnut was quite profitable at the time it was just technically impossible to harvest, and therefore to grow, without at least three pairs of bulls. [SOURCE: Page_114]

114 [SOURCE: Page_114]

Figure 50. Harvesting the groundnut spreading plants in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_115]

To facilitate the work of bulls, sand was also spread on the groundnut fields before sowing (Fig. 49) in order to smoothen the texture of the red loamy soils of the wash pediment (Appendix 17). This technical limit to groundnut cultivation was difficult to overcome. Even though there had been several attempts by the Indian government to develop groundnut cultivation in the area (see Box 7), its cultivation was limited to farmers with at least three pairs of bulls, which meant the minority. In the archetype village it covers only 10 to 15% of the annual village cropped surfaces. [SOURCE: Page_115]

Groundnut had indeed been introduced as far back as the 16th century. In 1913, India was a major provider of groundnut for France and 50% of the Indian groundnut production was destined for export (Dorin and Landy, 2002, p. 92). One of the main export outlets was indeed the soap industry (Daviron, 2019, p. 195). Just after World War I, the closing of mills in Marseille (France) and the spread of a disease on groundnut in India was a blow to the groundnut production and trade. It broke the groundnut development momentum at the beginning of the 20th century (Imperial Economic Committee, 1934). By the beginning of the 20th century there are barely no signs of groundnut in the agricultural statistics of Anantapur (Francis, 1905). During the 1930’s, groundnut cultivation again increased (Imperial Economic Committee, 1934) but still very few farmers cultivate it. Box 7. Attempts to develop groundnut in dryland South India [SOURCE: Page_115]

115 [SOURCE: Page_115]

The spreading variety was characterised by an indeterminate growth, which meant that flowering was continuous. The pods ripened at different stages. When the plant was harvested, some pods were immature. Despite those inconvenient, the groundnut had the advantage of having a high sale price and had a high production of biomass which was used to feed livestock. [SOURCE: Page_116]

1.2.2. The livestock of the landowning categories Both large and smallholders had bulls and dairy animals. The cattle and buffalo grazed all year-round. The smallholder farmers themselves took their animals out to graze but the large holder farmers hired labourers for this task. [SOURCE: Page_116]

All the livestock were fed on grazed grass as well as crop co-products (Fig. 51). The stems and leaves of the crops were collected and stacked up in heaps to feed the cattle and buffaloes. [SOURCE: Page_116]

Figure 51. Share of fodder, grass and grain concentrates in dry matter distributed or grazed throughout the year of livestock farming systems in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_116]

During the dry season, when the herbaceous vegetation was scarcer and more lignified, the share of dry matter from straw and hay in the diet of cattle and buffaloes was more important than during the monsoon season (Fig. 51) when grass was green and of good quality. The straw and hay were collected and kept with great care in large heaps. The farmers recall piling up straw and hay in a precise order with the external layer of the heap comprising of rice straw, in the middle was placed the groundnut hay, red gram and horse gram because of their higher nutritive value and the green fodder (finger millet and sorghum) was placed at the bottom of the heap, on the ground. At the top, the millet straw (foxtail and little millet) was placed. [SOURCE: Page_116]

116 [SOURCE: Page_116]

Although we found no photos to illustrate the heaps in the 1950’s, Figure 52 gives an idea of the size and shape of the heaps of straw at the time. Old farmers said the heaps were of similar size and shape, except that the material differed from the one today. [SOURCE: Page_117]

Horse gram grains were also given to bulls during the days when they worked in the fields. [SOURCE: Page_117]

Figure 52. A heap of rice and groundnut straw today [SOURCE: Page_117]

While most of the distributed fodder was given dry, the leaves and stems of finger millet were given as green fodder as finger millet fodder tended to dry quickly after harvest and become very coarse (B. V. S. Reddy et al., 2003). The irrigated crops were very important not only to produce rice and finger millet grains for humans, but also to produce feed for livestock: one ha of irrigated crops produced an equivalent amount of dry matter as a ha of rainfed groundnut, a productivity 4 times higher than all the other rainfed crops (Fig. 53). The irrigated crops were particularly valuable for the livestock of smallholder farmers, who could not grow groundnut with the means of production they had. [SOURCE: Page_117]

Figure 53. Yields of crops in dry matter in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_117]

The large holder farmers had local dairy cows while the smallholder farmers had buffaloes. Those production choices were explained by the types of crops they grew and the land that they [SOURCE: Page_117]

117 [SOURCE: Page_117]

could crop each year. The main advantage of buffaloes over local dairy cows was that, even though they could subsist on a mostly grass-based diet (Fig. 51). The buffaloes were also hardy breeds which could subsist on very low-quality feed. They were therefore preferred by smallholder farmers who produced less feed than large holder farmers. Large holder farmers preferred to rear local dairy cows because they produced more milk^22 than the buffaloes. The local cows had a higher proportion of distributed fodder in their diet (Fig. 51 and Fig. 54) and were more discriminating than the buffaloes, with a particular appetite for the nutritious groundnut hay (Fig. 54). The fodder intensification from millet and pulse rainfed crops to groundnut rainfed crops – allowed by the possession of three pairs of bulls- permitted a 4-fold increase of dry matter feed production per ha (Fig. 53). The large holder farmers could therefore swap the buffaloes for the local dairy cows, have a larger herd and in fine produce more milk and manure. [SOURCE: Page_118]

Figure 54. Diet of a local dairy cow (and progeny) in the 1950’s Cattle and buffalo rearing did not involve transhumance in summer. Straw and hay were consequently vital for the survival of the cattle throughout the summer season. In other arid and semi-arid areas of the world, it is common to find pastoral systems using transhumance to adapt to climate uncertainties (Krätli and Schareika, 2010; Scoones, 2020). Keeping cattle in this dryland area without migrating during the dry season was only possible with previously stored fodder. One of the reasons explaining the absence of transhumance was that if the herd had left the village for the 3 months in summer, at least 25% of the manure would have been lost. Manure was precious for crop cultivation and was collected from the stables and shed where the animals had been kept overnight. During day time, the smallholder farmers collected manure on roads, fields. When they used to take their animals out for grazing, they even carried the amount of dung they could carry back to their household. There dung was collected and mixed with feed refuse and household waste to make manure heaps (Appendix 6). Another [SOURCE: Page_118]

22 The local dairy cows produced in average 2.5 Liters of milk per day, with a maximum of 4 litres (Mulay, 1916) while the buffaloes produced around 1 liter per day (Epstein, 1962, p. 69). [SOURCE: Page_118]

118 [SOURCE: Page_118]

reason for the absence of transhumance could be related to the environment and lack of forests. In other dryland areas in the world, many iconic pastoral communities such as the Maasaï or the Fulani adapt to the harsh environment by relying on nomadism, semi-nomadism or transhumance (Hemingway et al., 2022; Scoones, 1995). In North West India, Lucas (2014) mentions a pastoral society with cattle who migrated from Saurashtra to Petlad area in Gujarat State. In south India, the Gollas were a community that used to migrate with their cattle. Rodgers (1991) formulates an interesting idea about the interaction between livestock and grasslands under a dry climate “The severe […] dry season typical of the Deccan and Western Ghats in peninsular India cannot produce a grass cover of sufficient palatability to maintain medium size herbivores. Browse becomes an essential part of the diet. Browse consist of palatable herbs, often legumes; shrubs such as ber (Zizyphus species), and fallen tree litter. These brows components, and grass standing crop, are more abundant in open wooded communities than under closed forest. The dense moist deciduous forest have little fodder at ground and shrub layer levels, and their carrying capacity for terrestrial mammals is low compared to open thorn bush and dry deciduous communities. It is perfectly feasible, therefore, to imagine pastoralist people in India’s forest.” (Rodgers, 1991). Looking at satellite images, it seems that many areas where cattle was managed in a transhumant way had forest: Saurashtra in Gujarat state (Lucas, 2014), but also Utnur, Kodekal and Kupgal in Karnataka state where archaeological evidence shows the former presence of forest cattle pens (Murty, 1993). The study area on the contrary had no forests. [SOURCE: Page_119]

Livestock was vital farming: it produced manure, milk and draft power for land preparation, sowing, irrigation, wedding, harvest and post-harvest operations. They were very-well looked after, some of the families keeping their animals in their own houses (Fig. 55). “We looked after them as family members” said a large holder farmer, showing proudly the room in where he used to keep his cows at night. [SOURCE: Page_119]

119 [SOURCE: Page_119]

Figure 55. An old stable in a house where livestock used to be kept [SOURCE: Page_120]

1.3. The landless social categories 1.3.1. Landless agricultural labourers An important portion of the society was landless and had only its muscle power to rely and depend on. These social categories had no other alternative but to earn a living from working on other people’s farms. They usually belonged to the Scheduled castes (SC) or the Scheduled Tribes (ST), some of them also belonged to the Kuruba caste (BC). They had no right and access to land. They worked on other people’s farms, either as permanent workers or daily labourers. When they were permanently engaged at a large holder farm, under a contract called gitam, they lived in the owner’s house and were involved in agricultural activities and daily household chores. The gitam labourers were therefore linked to the large holder farmers by relations of bonded labour (Breman, 1993). Because they were considered as impure, the Untouchables (SC) under a gitam contract were usually not allowed to feed or milk the animals. This work was done by gitam labourers who were not Untouchables, such as the Kurubas (BC), who were considered slightly purer. An old SC member remembered his father working under a gitam contract in the 1960’s (the interviewee was born in 1962): “My father worked for a [large holder farmer] under a gitam contract. He earned 100 to 150 Rupees per year. The farmer had 300 acres of land and he had many gitams! [people working under a gitam contract]. My father was fed at the home of his employer but we usually came back at our house once a week. He worked hard, sometimes all day till 10 pm. At the house of the employer, [SOURCE: Page_120]

120 [SOURCE: Page_120]

he had to pound grains, feed the animals and clean the house. In the day he used to work in the fields. My father used to tell me how tiring it was when they had to spread manure on the fields. The farmer has such a big land that sometimes the field was very far from the village. We had to fill bullock carts of manure and transport it to the field. My mother was not a gitam. She used to work in the field for 2 seers 23of grain per day. Myself, I used to take animals for grazing and was paid for that.” [SOURCE: Page_121]

Because of their “impurity”, some of the Untouchable agricultural labourers were considered in a dehumanised way, their only value being their labour. We were once told by a group of elderly Untouchables that they were not allowed to drink from the tin glasses from which the Indian people usually drank, as they would have soiled the glasses by touching them with their lips. We were told that a permanent labourer got injured once doing farm work. He couldn’t be healed and was left handicapped. Being of no use to the farm, he was not fed anymore and was left to die. [SOURCE: Page_121]

Women were usually not involved in a gitam contract, but engaged as daily labourers, working on different farms every day. They worked harvested and weeded crops. The weeding of groundnut with hand hoes and the transplanting of rice and finger millet was exclusively female tasks. Some of the men who worked as daily labourers collected the skins and hides of dead animals, which they could either sell directly to Anantapur market or process them into leather to use in the village. By collecting the hides of the dead cattle, they became their owner: “The carcass of the dead animal becomes the property of the village scavenger, although the animal when alive belonged to some ryot [landowner], and the income of the village scavenger depends considerably on the number of animals that die during the year. Unfortunately in many cases the village scavenger is not above increasing his income by the judicious use of poison and naturally chooses animals, for whose hides he will get a good value.” (Guthrie, 1934, p. 45). “When the market for skins is brisk, or in revenge for a slight injustice, mortality among the cattle is apt to rise material, and the suspicion is frequently voiced that this is due to poisoning.” (Fuchs, 1981, p. 196; in Rai, 2018). The hides of cattle were not renowned for their quality, as they came from animals who had died of old age or disease and were often branded (Guthrie, 1934, p. 47). They were therefore mostly used to make leather buckets and harnesses in the villages. The other pieces of skins and hides could be sold directly in Anantapur market [SOURCE: Page_121]

23 1 seer equals to approximately 1 kg. [SOURCE: Page_121]

121 [SOURCE: Page_121]

where they could be valued at 30-40 Rs. The leather processing practices are outlined in Box 8. [SOURCE: Page_122]

The collected skins and hides were first salted (step 1: salting) by hand in order to preserve them (approximately 50% of salt in relation to the skin weight). Bacterial growth usually begins approximately 2 hours after slaughter and bacteria can destroy the skin by putrefaction. If the salted skins and hides were not brought to the market but kept for leather goods in the village, they had then to be soaked in water to remove the salt and rehydrate them (step 2 : soaking). The hides and skins were then placed in an alkali solution made of lime (sunam) to remove the hairs from the epidermis (step 3: liming) – lime broke the disulphide bonds of the keratin molecules. The skins were left to soak in this solution for two weeks. Any remnants of hair could be removed by scraping them with a curved knife (Fig. 56) (step 4: fleshing). Scraping had to be done carefully, in order not to damage the skin. [SOURCE: Page_122]

Figure 56. Curved knife used for scraping the hides and skins [SOURCE: Page_122]

The skins and hides were soaked in a bath with pieces of bark of a local tree, Senna auriculata. The bark contained anthraquinones, which are molecules which have been used as dyes and pigments for centuries such as the cochineal carmine or the indanthrene blue. For this reason, the tree is also called the Tanner’s tree and the bark is known as the Aravam bark or tanner’s bark (Heyne, 1814; Ridgway, 1856). Box 8. Practices of leather manufacture in the villages More information on the leather trade in Madras Presidency are given in Appendix 18. [SOURCE: Page_122]

In the archetype village the agricultural labourers represented 40% of the agricultural population. There are no figures providing an overview of their structure because, having no land and no livestock, they do not constitute a production system per se. [SOURCE: Page_122]

1.3.2. Landless pastoralists A small percentage of the agricultural population were landless but also had a flock of sheep and goats to live on in addition to working on other people’s farms. In the archetype [SOURCE: Page_122]

122 [SOURCE: Page_122]

village they represented 5%, of the agricultural population. The pastoralists most often belonged to the Kuruba Caste (Backward Caste). Their flocks were fairly small, 20 to 40 adult females, mostly made up of ewes sheep but also with a few goats. While one of the family workers was looking after the herd in the day and keeping the sheep at night, the other members used to work on other people’s farms to supplement their income (Human labour arrow flowing out of the production system on Fig. 57). Those households went through the life cycle of Chayanov (1966), by which the family and the flock evolve in parallel. The family and the flock started out small: the head of the household started off by buying a few ewes with the money he and his family had earned from working on other peoples’ farms. Given the mortality and lambing rate at the time, the herd is expected to grow by approximately 5% each year (Appendix 19). This growth rate was very slow and did not allow for a substantial increase of the herd size over the course of the household life. [SOURCE: Page_123]

123 [SOURCE: Page_123]

Figure 57. Structure and metabolic profile of pastoralists in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_124]

124 [SOURCE: Page_124]

The flocks combined at the same time sheep but also a few goats. The diet was purely grass-based (Fig. 58). The goats could cross the shrubby and thorny areas more easily than sheep. They could therefore open the way for sheep when the flock was grazing and browsing in the mixed acacia shrublands of the rocky hills and patches of the wash pediment. Those areas bared many large rocks, and were for this reason, de facto never cultivated. They were however rich in fodder resources, from the natural grasses and the leaves and pods of all the Acacia species shrubs (Acacia nilotica -Babul tree-, Acacia sundra -Tottler willed-, Senna auriculata -Tanner’s cassia-). As sheep and goats were the only animals which could graze and browse those areas, pastoralists had the exclusive use of those areas. [SOURCE: Page_125]

Figure 58. Diet of an ewe (and progeny) in the 1950’s At night time the sheep were penned on the fallow lands of the cultivators, thus enabling a transfer of fertility from the shrubland areas with large rocks to the fallow lands. Access to grazing resources was partly ensured by networks of social relations with farmers. Pastoralist brought their flock to graze on farmer’s harvested fields at the end of the monsoon season and during winter, to graze on the millet stubble. The sheep were also penned at night on the farmer’s field all year round. The pastoralists were linked together by mutualistic exchange relationships. Night sheep penning was done collectively: 3 or 4 pastoralists grouped their flock together merging them into one group for the night. This decreases the workload for night surveillance, as 1 or 2 pastoralists could look after the whole combined flock. In the morning, flocks were separated and each pastoralist took his own flock to graze his own way. The combined flocks were called a manda (Fig. 59). [SOURCE: Page_125]

125 [SOURCE: Page_125]

Figure 59. Organisation of a manda (group of flocks) In summer, when grass resources were particularly low and of mediocre quality, priority was given to the animals of the smallholder and large holder farmers to graze on the village grasslands. The pastoralists had to take their sheep on a transhumance to Bellary, 200 km away from the area (see Chapter 2, Fig. 24 for Bellary location; see Table 7 for calendar). In Bellary the soils had a better water holding capacity than the red soils of Anantapur and could provide greener pastures. Sheep could also browse harvested crops in Bellary which were harvested slightly later than the crops in Anantapur. The deep black soils of Bellary region were called regur soils: “The richest in nutrients and most retentive, able to retain every drop of moisture within easy access of plant roots. A natural buffer against famine … [these soils] discourage both runoff and percolation; they can support a crop maturity even in drought, but they deprive the water table and discourage surface storage.” (Ludden, 2008). The access to fields in Bellary was based on the social relationships that the pastoralist had built with the farmers of Bellary over generations. “To go the Bellary, we had to know the people” said an old pastoralist during an interview. This negotiated access was transmitted from one generation to the other. [SOURCE: Page_126]
