Pastoralists used to sell their male sheep at Anantapur market. They also sold the raw skins of their dead animals or the sheep they occasionally slaughtered, to supply the leather industry. South India was historically an important hub for leather work (see box 9), especially in Tamil Nadu, the neighbouring state where the skins and hides collected in Andhra were conveyed. The sheep skins of Madras Presidency had a good reputation, and were expected to give excellent leather, with a tight and fine-grained texture. [SOURCE: Page_127]

Traces of leather manufacture in Tamil Nadu literature goes back as far as the year 500 BC (Ramalingam, 2016). In the 18th century, leather goods were produced in cities to meet the demand for leather shoes and saddles for generals and rajahs. During British colonisation the demand for raw hides and semi-tanned leather was high. At national level, 36% of the leather pieces and skins came from cattle, 6% from buffalo, 38% from goats and 11% from sheep (Das, 1936). Government tanneries were established and raw hides and semi-tanned leather was exported to England, which had the effect of increasing the price of remaining raw hides in the villages (Sujatha, 2002). While 76% of the total material was exported from Madras to the United Kingdom at the beginning of the 20th century, most of the material exported from Madras was in a half-manufactured state i.e. dressed skins and hides. Two major technical improvements strengthened the production and export of Indian leather: ➢    Strengthening of the vegetal tanning material: in 1847, tanneries started using myrabolan (type of plum tree) extract as a vegetal finishing tannage. Before that, skins were tanned using only the bark of Cassia Auriculata tree (avaram bark). When the skin was exposed to sunlight it was stained with patches of red colour. The myrobolan extract acted as a stabilizer and gave the leather of Madras Presidency a first-rate quality for which it was renowned internationally ➢    Introduction of chrome tanning: one of the effects of exports of raw hides and semi- tanned leather to England, was importing in return manufactured leather goods in India at low cost, which threatened the local Indian industry. In an attempt to strengthen the Indian leather industry weakened by foreign competition, the first chroming tanning factory was established in Madras in 1904 after experiments made at the chrome tanning department of the School of industrial Arts, backed up by superintendent Sir Alfred Chatterton and then sponsored by the states (Bhattacharya, 2018). The British commercial lobbies did not greet the chrome tanning technology with enthusiasm and tried to hold it back. Despite the states support for the development of chrome tanning, 43% of the hides and skins in India were still processed out of government tanneries -by village tanners- in 1950’s (Sujatha, 2002) At the beginning of the 20th century the Indian leather exports were dominated by Madras and Calcutta and 17 tanneries out of the total 22 in India were located in Madras (Ramalingam, 2017). During First World War, the number of tanneries in Tamil Nadu increased due to a large military demand of leather boots (Ramalingam, 2017). Given the growing demand for leather in India during [SOURCE: Page_127]

127 [SOURCE: Page_127]

the colonial era, an important labour market had to be created to meet demand. The skins and hides, considered as waste, were considered unclean: caste Hindus , i.e. non-Untouchables, could never touch their leathers shoes with their hands, or any part of the leather of the harness or saddlery, and they had to be touched with a cloth (Reddy, 2018, pp. 56–57). The skin and hides by-products could only be handled by people considered as having an inferior social status, which were mostly from the Scheduled Castes, typically Madigas, and Muslims. Even among the leather working class there is a social hierarchy with some only dealing with cattle and leaving the sheep and goats to even more inferior people (Rai, 2018, pp. 353–354). Box 9. Marketing chain and importance of the leather trade in South India in the first half of the 20th century The skins were bought by merchants at markets who then sold them to private and government local tanneries. Those tanneries were usually established near railway junctions to facilitate transport, such as the Guntakal junction between Bellary and Anantapur (Appendix 20). [SOURCE: Page_128]

The skins and hides were processed into leather which was then transported to the headquarters of companies in Madras city (today called Chennaï) ready for export to Europe (mainly the United Kingdom) and the USA (Fig. 60). In Anantapur city the leather value chain was mostly in the hands of the Muslim communities. [SOURCE: Page_128]

Figure 60. Overview of the leather value chain in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_128]

128 [SOURCE: Page_128]

2. Combining the extensive and the intensive in a composite landscape Smallholder and large holder farmers cultivated rainfed crops on the wash pediment and irrigated crops in the wash depressions (tank command area and glacis foot slopes). Irrigation on the wash pediment was possible when there was a well but those were quite rare on the wash pediment. Each crop was separated by long fallow periods, which had agronomic functions in the management of the ecosystem. Pastoralists were the only ones to use the mixed shrublands with large rocks. There are many avenues of inquiry to address the practices and the overall management of the agroecosystem in the 1950’s. We rely on the Latin terminology of ager and saltus to designate the cultivated land (temporarily or permanently) and the permanent grasslands respectively (Fig. 61). [SOURCE: Page_129]

Figure 61. Location of the saltus, irrigated and rainfed ager in the archetype village in the 1950’s N.B.: wash depressions enlarged for more visibility – should be smaller, total 4% of the territory- [SOURCE: Page_129]

2.1. Concentrating energies on the irrigated ager The irrigated ager was very limited: 5 to 10% of the area (Appendix 3). In the villages structured around a        tank (Bandameedapalli, Cherlopalli, Yerragunta, Pullalarevu, Gondireddypalli), gravity-fed irrigation from the tank was not enough to irrigate the crops throughout the season and irrigation was mostly done in the vicinity of wells. Those wells were [SOURCE: Page_129]

129 [SOURCE: Page_129]

nearly all located in the tank command area and the glacis foot slopes. In the villages near rivers (Gantlaparthi), the non-perennial characteristic of rivers did not allow a sufficient flow of water, and irrigation was also mostly made using wells nearby the river. In the villages neither near tanks nor rivers, a few wells were dug on the wash pediment. Finger millet and rice were the only irrigated crops. They were part of an intra-annual rotation and grown by both smallholder farmers and large holder farmers. [SOURCE: Page_130]

In the following section, we outline the specific practices behind the cultivation of irrigated crops. Growing irrigated crops required specific means of production and specific management of fertility, making the irrigated cropping system an “all-intensive” one. [SOURCE: Page_130]

2.1.1. Reaching out for water below using wells The irrigated cropping system was constituted of an interannual rotation starting with a first cycle of finger millet, followed by a second cycle of rice and ending with a fallow period corresponding to the dry season. In the tank command areas, water stored in the tank was partly let out through sluice gates on the tank bund called “tumas” (Fig. 62). However, given the low and erratic rainfall, the tanks were not full every year. Gravity fed irrigation from the tank water was only possible for the first fields downstream the tank bund and allowed irrigated cultivation for only three months. Irrigation was therefore mostly done by raising water from wells. This enabled a temporal correction, growing finger millet from June to August, and then a second cycle of rice throughout the rest of the monsoon season and part of winter, up to January. [SOURCE: Page_130]

Figure 62. Ruin of a tuma -tank sluice gate on the tank bund- overgrown with vegetation [SOURCE: Page_130]

130 [SOURCE: Page_130]

Water was lifted from wells by means of animal power to irrigate the finger millet and rice crops. The way of raising water from wells was called the kavili or kapile or mohte system (spellings vary). The wells were dug using the manpower of a particular category of workers. The wells were dug by groups of landless and livestock less people (agricultural labourers) of a particular caste, the Vadderru caste. In fact, the people belonging to the Vadderu caste were divided into two types, the Vadderu rathi who were in charge of digging wells and the Vadderru manthi who were in charge of carving stones. The existence of a skilled and specialised caste for digging wells suggests it was an important and difficult task: “We built enormous wells. The surface was very tough: ‘Omaya ! Omaya !’ [meaning in Telugu “oh my god!”] six people could dig two metres in one year but we didn’t work all year round. It cost seventy thousand Rs for a well four mutlu deep. [one mutlu is two metres].” remembered a 70-year old member of the Vadderru rathi community. The fact that an organised labour system was needed and developed contrasts with other areas in the world where the farmer himself dug the well alone. This is most certainly linked to the geological structure in which the well is carved and also the depth of the well. In Anantapur, wells were dug in the saprolite (weathered bedrock) by hand and the casing was made out of paved stones (see previous section 3.3 in Chapter 2), whereas in the Indo-Gangetic plains were made in the alluvial deposits. The Anantapur wells were also deeper (a dozen metres) than the ones in the Indo-Gangetic alluvial plains. [SOURCE: Page_131]

The water extraction device consisted of the well, which was slightly raised (1 to 2 metres) above the level of the plot to be irrigated. The water was contained in a leather bucket which had at the bottom a spout operated by a leather rope attached to the bullock yoke (Fig. 63). The top of the leather bucket was fastened by a second leather rope which ran over a pulley to the bullock yoke. The pulley was supported by two upright granite beams at the sides of the wells (see Fig. 64 B and C). The leather bucket was progressively raised as the pair of bulls went down the slope (see Fig. 63). When it reached the top of the well, the bucket emptied by itself because of the rope attached to the spout and the roller at the top of the well, thus saving the labour of one man (Michael, 2008) – only one person was required to drive the bulls-. The bulls turned round and started walking back up the slope which lowered the bucket again (see Fig. 63) and the process was repeated until the field was adequately irrigated. The glimpse of this agricultural scene can be viewed in the music clip of the film Gaali Medalu (1962) (Appendix 1). [SOURCE: Page_131]

131 [SOURCE: Page_131]

Figure 63. Structure of a kavili well [SOURCE: Page_132]

Source : adapted from (Singh, 1980, p. 191) [SOURCE: Page_132]

Figure 64. Remnants of a kavili well. A. Overall view of a kavili well. B. Granite structure at the top of the well. C. Granite structure at the top of the well, view from above Source: our own, May 2022 [SOURCE: Page_132]

132 [SOURCE: Page_132]

The leather buckets were made by the agricultural labourers who scavenged for dead animals in the village, collected the hides of cattle and made them into leather. We know from interviews that the biggest hides (those of buffaloes or bulls) were used to make the leather buckets. This indication was useful in determining the volume of a leather bucket (see Appendix 2). In order to prevent any leakages, one leather bucket was made out of one whole skin and not several pieces of leather stitched and patched together. [SOURCE: Page_133]

2.1.2. Renewing fertility and controlling weeds on the irrigated cropping systems The irrigated land in the tank command area was cultivated every year for two crop cycles. Much effort was spent to renew fertility. For both crop cycles, manure and tank silt was spread and mixed with the soil during the ploughing of the field. Silt was collected in summer when the tank bed was fairly dry and was transported by bullock cart to the field. The smallholder farmers dug out and transported the tank silt themselves while the large holder farmers used to assist each other in digging out tank soil. Cattle manure was spread out from the manure heaps to the fields. Smallholder farmers used to also collect every piece of manure and dung they could find, collecting them from roads and fields when animals were out for grazing and carrying it back home in baskets. Manure and silt were mixed with the soil while ploughing. This was done using a small ard (chena madaka in Telugu, chena meaning small). Small bunds were made to delimitate the nursery and the finger millet or rice field. The field and nursery were then flooded and farmers added extra organic matter in the form of green leaves. Those green leaves were collected from leguminous trees found on the wash pediment, such as the neem leaves (Azadirachta indica, neem tree), Milletia pinnata (Karanja) and Senna auriculata also known as Cassia auriculata (tangedu, Tanner’s cassia). Farmers also cut leaves of the milkweed Calotropis procera (Sodom apple tree), whose leaves enrich the soil in nitrogen (Varadarajan and Sanyasi Raju, 1956). The milky sap of the plant is known to have a strong proteolytic activity (Freitas et al., 2007) meaning it helps to breakdown proteins into smaller polypeptides or amino acids. Farmers said that the use of Calotropis procera leaves enabled them to ‘give heat’ (to use the farmers’ own words) to the nursery which could maybe related to the catalytic property of the plant’s sap. Figure 65 and 66 were taken 2022 even though this practice is now rarely made. Figure 65 shows a farmer cutting the leavers of Calotropis procera shrubs and Figure 66 shows a field covered in branches of neem. [SOURCE: Page_133]

133 [SOURCE: Page_133]

Figure 65. Farmer cutting leaves of the Calotropis procera weed with a machete [SOURCE: Page_134]

Figure 66. Branches of neem in a flooded field [SOURCE: Page_134]

134 [SOURCE: Page_134]

The green leaves were then mixed in the soil by puddling the fields. This was done using pair of bulls dragging a weighted harrow across the fields and labourers marching in the fields and incorporate the green leaves. The scene can be viewed in the film Thodi Kodallu (1957) (see Appendix 1). Green manure and cattle manure were complementary to maintain the structural stability of the soil. The soil microorganisms first gradually consumed the soil organic labile fractions of the green manure. From the decomposition of the vegetable debris, carbohydrate compounds were released and formed strong soil aggregates which improved the soil aggregate stability. However, when with time those organic compounds change into humic substances, those aggregates eroded (Chenu et al., 2000). It was thus the decomposition of manure, and its effect on the formation and stabilisation of soil macro aggregates which occurs in a more progressive and persistent way, which took over in the aggregate formation as shows the model of (Monnier, 1965) and confirmed by (Abiven et al., 2009). [SOURCE: Page_135]

Although the composition of tank soil varies from one tank to another, the soil analysis of Bandameedapalli tank soil revealed a high percentage of silt and clays (Table 5, Chapter 2). Adding tank soil to the irrigated fields enabled the farmers to change the texture of the soil, and enhance the water holding capacity of the soils, making them particularly well-suited for irrigated crops (James William Mollison, 1901; Joshi and Deoras, 1955). Adding tank soil was a way of increasing mineral fertilisation providing nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus elements (Joshi and Deoras, 1955; Mohammed et al., 2009), increasing organic matter (Adhinarayanan, 2017). Adding tank silt was proved to increase the portion of water stable aggregates in soil and also add extra nitrogen (Joshi and Deoras, 1955) [SOURCE: Page_135]

Nitrogen was also brought by non-symbiotic fixation of the finger millet root system. Despite its powerful root system with helps in capturing soil moisture (Lynch and Wojciechowski, 2015), finger millet does not tolerate drought (Ahmadi et al., 2002) and had to be grown in irrigated conditions. Its powerful root system helped sequester carbon (Lynch and Wojciechowski, 2015) and also enabled a decent fixation of nitrogen, through the presence of N$_2$-fixing soil bacteria in the root zone. The nitrogen-fixating bacteria functionned in non- symbiotic conditions and the nitrogen fixation activity was much lower than the common symbiotic nitrogen fixation of leguminous crops. However, the well-developed root biomass of finger millet made the quantity of nitrogen per soil surface unit noticeable (Weinhard et al., 1971). The cultivation of finger millet in first position therefore provided nitrogen for the second crop of rice. [SOURCE: Page_135]

135 [SOURCE: Page_135]

Ridges and furrows were made using a hand hoe for finger millet. Rice and finger millet seeds were first broadcasted in nurseries and then transplanted (see Appendix 21 for archive photo). Although labour-intensive, transplanting was more advantageous than direct seeding in terms of weed control. Once the crops had been transplanted, they were at least weeded twice, using a small hoe for the finger millet, and by hand in the flooded rice fields. The flooding of rice fields was also a cultural practice for weed control. [SOURCE: Page_136]

2.1.3. Irrigation: a labour-intensive activity “Everything […] was of the crudest and clumsiest.” (The Indian World, 1906, p. 429). It required a pair of bulls and ideally two men, one to lead the pair of bulls and one to help discharge the water. Accidents were frequent and the whole water extraction operation was an arduous and delicate task, which is underlined by the popular saying “Women give birth while men pull water from the kavili well”24 which puts childbirth delivery and water extraction on the same level of risks and energy spent. We estimated the carrying capacity of the leather bucket at 150 Litres and water yield of 1 to 2 L.s-1 which is low (see Appendix 2), but reasonable. The energy expended by one bull for irrigation is 2.5 MJ per hour of work (Appendix 2), which is the most-energy demanding task of the bulls. The water was enough to meet the water requirements of the finger millet and the rice and “so long as the little field was green the farmer and his household could live. […] But not every farm has a well, not every farmer has a team of bullocks to pull up water, nor men to help him. And where there were no wells the ground was baked to brick dust.” (The Indian World, 1906, p. 429). [SOURCE: Page_136]

In the model we considered a standard pair of bulls of the Hallikar type, but in fact there were two types of bulls in the 1950’s: the Hallikar bulls (Fig. 67) and the Ongole bulls- also know as the Nellore bulls- (Fig. 68). Hallikar bulls were bought at Anantapur market while Ongole bulls were reproduced on the farm. The animals of the Hallikar breeds were renowned for their strength and endurance, but the male Ongoles could deliver intense mechanic energy but for a shorter time period. The Ongole bulls were also important for the reproduction of the local dairy cows (which were of Ongole breed). [SOURCE: Page_136]

24 In telugu language ఆడదానికి పిల్ల గండం , మగనికి కవిలి గండం [SOURCE: Page_136]

136 [SOURCE: Page_136]

Figure 67. A pair of Hallikar bulls [SOURCE: Page_137]

Figure 68. An Ongole bull in Anantapur [SOURCE: Page_137]

The division of labour between the two breeds of bulls was clear: the Hallikar bulls were mainly used to raise water from wells and for transport and Ongole bulls were preferably used for any crop processing and tillage operations. The Hallikar bulls (also known as Mysore bulls) were renowned for their strength and endurance. (John Shortt, 1885) wrote: “The Mysore bulls are justly celebrated as draught cattle and for their spirit and power of endurance: they are active [SOURCE: Page_137]

137 [SOURCE: Page_137]

and quick in their paces, somewhat restive and fiery in disposition […] the cows milk fairly”(John Shortt, 1885, pp. 8–10). John Shortt (1885) writes a telling anecdote about the muscle power of the Hallikar bulls: they were so strong that 230 of them were sent with Bombay military troops to Afghanistan during the first Anglo-Afghan war (1839-1842) (John Shortt, 1885). The Hallikar bulls could not work more than 6 hours in a row, after which their strength and speed was reduced considerably (Campbell, 1990). The Ongole bulls however, are not known for their rapidity when working (Phaniraja and Panchasar, 2009) and have a lower horsepower (Alex et al., 2013). They are famous for their endurance and slow movements (Narendra Nath, 1993). Energy performances are summarized in Table 8. [SOURCE: Page_138]

Hallikar bull                            Ongole bull Horsepower              0.9 hp (Campbell, 1990).           (0.64 to 0.84 hp) (Alex et al., 2013). After 6 hours, strength and speed reduced by 75% (Campbell, 1990). Strength                          Speed                        Endurance, slow movements Table 8. Comparison of the energy performances of the Hallikar and Ongole bulls The Ongole bulls on the other hand have less strength but the Ongole cows had a higher milk yield. The Ongole bulls were also used for the reproduction of the cows of the large holder farmers which were local Desi cows (Ongole cows) and had good milk production: the Ongole breed“has also been long celebrated, not so much as draught cattle as for the milking qualities of the female, for which purpose cows are greatly esteemed and fetch large prices […] the cows are excellent milkers, some of them have been known to yield 12 kg of good rich milk in the 24 hours, and they rear a calf at the same time” (John Shortt, 1885, p. 18) [SOURCE: Page_138]

Hallikar bulls were therefore preferred for raising water which was an intense and tedious task (morning and night for irrigation) but requiring a lot of strength, whereas the Ongole bulls were used for less intense operations like soil tillage. [SOURCE: Page_138]

2.2. Composing with scattered resources on the wash pediment 2.2.1. Renewing soil fertility and controlling weeds The large holder farmers cultivated rained crops on the wash pediment following a rotation of groundnut, mixed pulses and millets and horsegram, each being separated by a period of between 3 and 10 years where land was left uncropped, depending on the surface of land possessed by the large holder farmer. Each portion of land of the large holder farmers on [SOURCE: Page_138]

138 [SOURCE: Page_138]

the wash pediment was therefore cultivated once every 4 or 11 years, during the monsoon season (Fig. 69) [SOURCE: Page_139]

Figure 69. Land use changes of the archetype village in 1950’s over seasons (monsoon, winter, summer) and over 6 years (with a 5-year fallow) [SOURCE: Page_139]

Although this land was not ploughed it was left to be grazed by animals each year. We have chosen to name this intermittent 5-year period of no cultivation a long ley fallow (see box 10, and Fig. 70), the duration of the long ley fallow being variable. We considered in our model a ley fallow of 5 years, meaning that large holder farmers cultivated a plot of land every 6 years^25. [SOURCE: Page_139]

25 The interannual rotation is the following: the large holder farmers cultivated groundnut on one of their fields of the wash pediment, left it uncropped for 5 years, then cultivated mixed pulses and millets, then uncropped for 5 years, followed again by groundnut, uncropped for 5 years, horse gram, uncropped for 5 years, back to groundnut, etc…. [SOURCE: Page_139]

139 [SOURCE: Page_139]

Which term can be used to name the fields, where vegetation is left to grow, between two crops? The debate is endless, and the terms used differ from one region to the other and from one time period to another (Morlon and Sigaut, 2008). (Ducourtieux, 2006, p. 20) put the finger on the origin of the debate : “The main difficulty is that there are two words to designate three different types of land: agricultural surfaces which are ploughed but not sown in order to rebuild fertility and control weeds between two crops; surfaces which have been cultivated, where natural vegetation is left to grow back and which should be cultivated again in a near future; surfaces which have been cultivated and which have been, a priori, abandoned”26. The Spanish use two terms, descanso for land being left fallow without any attention and barbecho for land left fallow after being ploughed (González de Molina, 2002). However, neither the descanso nor the barbecho are periods of “passivity”. They are essential periods in the crop rotation to renew the fertility of the soil and control weeds in order to prepare for the next crop (Godenzzi and Vengoa, 2014). The descanso may be translated in French by friche and the barbecho by jachère. In French, both the jachère and the friche are former cropped land (which are not cropped anymore), but in the first one the control of weeds and management of fertility is made by animals and in the second by vegetation regrowth (Bainville, 2021). Repeated tillage, ploughing and harrowing can be done in the jachère (jachère labourée) (Morlon and Sigaut, 2008) and/or it can be grazed by animals i.e. “jachère enherbée pâturée” ) (Morlon and Sigaut, 2008). The descanso, barbecho, jachère, or friche are all in fine necessary for cultivation, meaning that the real amount of land to produce crops is bigger than the actual cropped plot (González de Molina, 2002). In English there seems to be no distinction between the two types of areas, which can be loosely translated as “fallow land” (Bonneval, 1993). We found however a few references making a difference between the ley fallow^27 which is left to gradually become covered with herbaceous and shrubby vegetation in between two crops, and which can be grazed or not (Canarache et al., 2006, p. 486; Gregg, 1988); and the bare or clean or black fallow which is maintained free of herbaceous and shrubby vegetation by soil scarification (Canarache et al., 2006, p. 88). In the study area, the land was left uncropped for either the duration of the summer season, or for several years, allowing part of the vegetation to grow back. That land was however not ploughed. In this sense they were more like “Descanso” than “barbecho”. They were however always grazed, which makes them more like the French “jachère enherbée paturée” than a “friche”. The land in between two crops, unploughed but grazed, is called here ley fallows, either short (summer season) or long (several years). The land which is abandoned for economic reasons, and not agronomic ones, is land which is reverted to permanent grassland (named either “reverted land” or “permanent grassland” depending on the stage). Box 10. The fallow debate [SOURCE: Page_140]

26 Own translation. Original text in French: “La difficulté tient à l'usage de deux mots pour qualifier trois catégories différentes de terres : des surfaces agricoles labourées mais non ensemencées dans des techniques de restauration de la fertilité et de contrôle des adventices entre deux phases de culture ; des surfaces qui ont été cultivées, où croît une végétation spontanée et dont la remise en culture est prévue ; des surfaces qui ont été cultivées et qui sont, a priori, abandonnées. » (Ducourtieux, 2006, p. 20) 27 The ley fallow originally refers to planted grass but the definition has been broadened by (Ruthenberg, 1977), including natural fallow vegetation which he specifically refers as ‘unregulated’ ley. [SOURCE: Page_140]

140 [SOURCE: Page_140]

Figure 70. Crop cultivation, short ley fallow and long ley fallow periods according to the type of landscape unit and the social category The long ley fallow had several agronomic functions. It acted as a reservoir of feed for livestock. The consumption and digestion of vegetation by livestock created a “short-cut” for recycling the tropic elements into the soil in the form of excreta (Gachon et al., 1979). Digestion was concomitant with bacterial fermentation enhancing the one already occurring in the soil, thus leading to a “biological stimulation of the ecosystem” (Gachon et al., 1979; Landais et al., 1990). Weed growth was also stifled by grazing during seed or flower production of weeds. Sheep were penned at night after having grazed the mixed shrubland with large rocks during the day, thus ensuring a transfer of nutrients from the saltus to the ager. Leaving the land uncropped and unploughed for several years, allowed the farmers to enrich the upper soil by accumulated organic matter. Bhattacharyya et al. (2006, p. 46) estimated that the organic content of red soils in semi-arid conditions increased under grasslands from 0.56 % to 1.42% after a 9 year fallow period on the first 30 cm of soil. The rebuilding of the soil organic content allowed the restoration of the hydrological functions in the soil and facilitated water infiltration, and therefore a better utilisation of water by vegetation (Penning de Vries and Djiteye M.A., 1982; Pieri, 1989). Finally, both the rotation of millets with pulses and the ley fallows helped to eliminate the building-up of pests and prevented against the installation of specific weed species. The life cycle of pests such as thrips was broken by the ley fallow periods and the changes of crops, preventing damages on the groundnut crop (thrips are the vector insect of the rosette virus of groundnut). [SOURCE: Page_141]

141 [SOURCE: Page_141]

The short ley fallow of the smallholder farmers [SOURCE: Page_142]

Smallholder farmers however had only 2 ha of land, and could not afford to leave their land under ley fallow for more than the dry season. The short ley fallow of the dry season (Fig. 70) and the crop rotations facilitated to a certain extent in breaking the life cycle of pathogens and insects. But they had to rely on other ways to rebuild the fertility of the soil and control weeds. They fetched tank soil to enrich the land from time to time. They also collected all the manure they could, scraping every last bit from roads, fields, even carrying part of the dung their animals had deposited while grazing back to their manure heap. Those practices involved more digging work, collecting and spreading material per ha. [SOURCE: Page_142]

Both smallholder and large holder farmers ploughed their land several times during the first month before sowing their crops in line, making it possible to control weeds. [SOURCE: Page_142]

Ploughing and sowing in lines [SOURCE: Page_142]

During the month prior to sowing, the land was tilled once to three times using an ard plough. This enabled land to be prepared and remove weeds. The first ploughing was done during in the course of the month of May, before the start of the monsoon rains. This first scarification of the soil enabled the weeds to be exposed to the sunlight and be burnt, a practice called solarisation. Ploughing was repeated again one or two times till the monsoon rains arrived. The ard plough (madaka in Telugu) with which this was done, was made of wood except for a pointed iron piece which fixed at the edge of the share. The pointed iron share and the broader wooden wings are necessary in order to cut the hard and dry soil and press sidewards. The wood comes from the Babul tree (Acacia Nilotica), chosen for its mechanical properties which confer strength and toughness to the plough (ICFRE, n.d.). The wood has to have a high resistance against impact on tough soil and stones. [SOURCE: Page_142]

Although heavier ploughs made of iron existed at the time, the smaller wooden ploughs (chena madaka, chenna meaning small in Telugu) were more common for several reasons. The bulls were not strong enough for heavy ploughs: a bigger plough (pedda madaka, pedda meaning big in Telugu) of 104 kg (Brackenbury, 2000, p. 78) of similar structure as the one previously described, but of bigger format, was occasionally used to dig deeper but was so heavy that it had to be used with more than two pairs of bulls. In the grey hydromorphic soils, the big plough could never be used because of the higher resistance of the soil. The small ploughs provided a shallow tillage which is better adapted to the hard soils full of stones and the semi-arid climate. When the stones were too many under the soil at the level of the tillage [SOURCE: Page_142]

142 [SOURCE: Page_142]

depth, farmers modulated the tillage depth by placing a wooden circular shim (Fig. 71) between the yoke and the wooden draft-pole in order to lower the angle between the soil and the beam and reduce the tillage depth. [SOURCE: Page_143]

Figure 71. Structure of the ard plough and modulation of the tillage depth As for its suitability to the soil a British agricultural chemist writes at the beginning of the 19th century: “Even if properly used, a plough that goes deep may do harm where a native one would not, viz., by turning up inferior soil, and by brining lumps of limestone to the surface. Again, it is quite possible that, were deeper ploughing to be in vogue, the moisture, which, in the case of some soils, it is so necessary to retain, might be lost. The turning over of a furrow is not always an advantage in India; if the soil be at all stiff, the sun will rapidly bake the slice turned over; it will remain more like a brick than like soil, and will not readily pulverize again. This would not occur with the native plough, the action of which is more like that of a pointed stick running through the ground, just below the surface, say 2.5 to 3 inches [5 to 7.5 cm] deep, simply stirring and loosening it. For hard and sunbaked ground, such as is often met with, no action could be better adapted, and, in a trial at Meerut, I saw an English plough completely fail on such land. […] The fine tilth produced by a frequent ploughing with a native plough produces a surface which will absorb water better, if rain follows, than would that left by a furrow-turning plough. Against deeper ploughing it may also be said that there is so little manure to go on the land, that more would be lost if the soil were turned up to a greater depth” (Voelcker, 2010, pp. 219–220) [SOURCE: Page_143]

143 [SOURCE: Page_143]

All the rainfed crops were sown using an animal drawn seed-drill (Fig. 72). The standard draft seeder was composed of a hopper linked by seed tubes to 4 furrow openers that penetrated the soil. The seed tubes transported the seeds to the furrow. With this device seeds could be sown purely or mixed. It required at least 2 people, one to drive the pair of bulls, the other to put the seeds in the hopper. Sowing using animal traction had the advantage, compared to broadcasting, of facilitating intercultural weeding operations. [SOURCE: Page_144]

Figure 72. Structure of a draft seeder [SOURCE: Page_144]

In Appendix 21, we provide archive photos shot in the 1950’s in the Deccan area where sowing can be seen using bulls and the same draft seeder as drawn on Fig. 72. [SOURCE: Page_144]

Weeding in between the rows [SOURCE: Page_144]

Weeding was done for all rainfed crops using several separate scuffle hoes (danti in Telugu, plural, dantulus) (Fig. 73, A) manipulated each by one person or either a device made out of combined scuffles (regalaguntaka in Telugu) (see Fig. 73, C). Both implements were made of a scuffle hoe (danti), with a stirrup-shaped iron blade (Fig. 73, B and photo in Appendix 22) which cut of small weeds, broke up the crusty ground and therefore loosened the soil. The scuffle hoes (dantulus) were each manipulated by one person and each scuffle hoe was tied to a yoke and dragged by a pair of bulls (Fig. 74). The number of scuffle hoes used depended upon the availability of labourers and the size of the field. In Madakasira (south of Anantapur district, close to the Karnataka border), where groundnut fields were much smaller, I frequently saw 2 or 3 people handling scuffle hoes behind a pair of bulls. In Rapthadu mandal the fields 144 [SOURCE: Page_144]

were much larger and there always were four or five people handling the scuffle hoes. On the photo of Fig. 74, taken in Rapthadu, five people are seen holding a scuffle hoe and one man is leading the pair of bulls. The use of bulls was necessary to be able to do a push-pull motion in the loamy soil and help drag the scuffle hoes. The individual scuffle hoes had the advantage of being able to be swiveled round (Fig. 75): the person could therefore also cut weeds. This was impossible when using the combined scuffles device (Fig. 76) where weeding and hoeing was only possible in between rows. The latter device however had the advantage of saving on labour. This operation also enabled the soil to be loosened so that rain water could penetrate in the soil which is well-illustrated by the French saying “Hoeing once equals watering three times”. 28 [SOURCE: Page_145]

Figure 73. Implements for weeding and hoeing, especially groundnut [SOURCE: Page_145]

28 Original saying in French: “Un binage vaut trois arrosages.» [SOURCE: Page_145]

145 [SOURCE: Page_145]

Figure 74. Hoeing and weeding a groundnut field with five scuffle hoes each manipulated by a labourer, one of which is also driving the pair of bulls [SOURCE: Page_146]

Figure 75. Weeding and hoeing in between plants on the line and in between lines [SOURCE: Page_146]

146 [SOURCE: Page_146]

For groundnut, the use of ready-combined scuffles (Fig. 76), allowed to remove weeds in between rows without the need of extra labourers in addition to the person leading the bulls. However, the combined device did not allow weeding in between plants on the line, but only in between the rows. The combined scuffles could not be used on the millets and other pulse crops as their height was much higher. [SOURCE: Page_147]

Figure 76. Hoeing and weeding a groundnut field with one regalaguntaka (combined scuffles) handled by one man, this man leads also the pair of bulls [SOURCE: Page_147]

Apart from those devices, the groundnut spreading variety also had the particularity of acting like a weed suppressor (more competition with weeds) and weeding was only necessary twice because of the spreading structure. [SOURCE: Page_147]

147 [SOURCE: Page_147]

2.2.2. Making do with rain A wide range of millets and pulses were grown because of their suitability and hardiness to semi-arid conditions. They were usually cultivated as mixed crops except for horse gram which was planted at a much later stage than the other rainfed crops, once the rainy season was well underway. Horse gram (Macrotyloma uniflorum or Dolichos biflorus) was indeed considered as “the poor’s pulse” because it can be cultivated with no addition of inputs (Majumdar, 2011) and with not much water. The other rainfed crops were grown in more or less complex associations. Behind the complexity there was however a logic. Millets were always associated with pulses under many forms. Although the mixed crops may convey a spurious image of messy and randomly selected crops, choices were made between crops with different root depths and plant heights in order to limit competition between crops (Fig. 77). Foxtail millet and little millet for instance were never grown together on the same plot because they had the same root system. The wide range of crops made use of complementary soil horizons (various root depth) (Fig. 77) and had different crop duration cycles in order to spread out harvest periods (Fig. 78) [SOURCE: Page_148]

Figure 77. Root depth, structure and plant height of rainfed crops cultivated in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_148]

148 [SOURCE: Page_148]

In each of those arrangements of crop associations, the seeds were drilled in rows with several lines of a main crop alternating with a line of another crop, the ratio between the two could vary according the family needs. The border of the plot was usually sown with pearl millet, which acts as a pest-repellent. Pearl millet was a very high crop (as shows the figure in Appendix 21). [SOURCE: Page_149]

There were three main types of associations: [SOURCE: Page_149]

1) The main crop was a type of millet, often either foxtail millet or little millet. The alternating rows were usually sown with either purely red gram/pigeon pea or a mix of red gram, cowpea, green gram, sorghum, sesame, castor. Foxtail millet and little millet could never be grown simultaneously on the same plot as explained above. This cropping system was called a row intercropping system (because the crops are sown in lines and grown simultaneously) – middle case on Fig. 78. 2) Groundnut was sown simultaneously in between rows of red gram. After the harvest of groundnut (December), horse gram could be sown in between the rows of red gram which would then only be harvested later in January (left on Fig. 78). This is known as the relay intercropping system because a third crop (horse gram) was planted instead of the main crop (groundnut) before the harvest of crop grown on rows (red gram). 3) Another alternative was to sow in between lines of red gram lines of mixed crop (green gram, red gram, sorghum, sesame) making a mixed intercropping system (right on Fig. 78, and displayed on Fig. 79) [SOURCE: Page_149]

149 [SOURCE: Page_149]

Figure 78. Types of crop associations for rainfed crops in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_150]

Figure 79. The mixed crop system: association of millets and pulses in Anantapur [SOURCE: Page_150]

Source : (Tanaka and Watabe, 1981) The purpose of cultivating several crops at the same time on a plot of land was multiple. Associating crops created a buffer against interannual climate variability and pests. If one crop failed the others would probably stand and cover the ground. Mixing crops diminished the risk and uncertainty over a cropping season. Mixing crops demanded more labour than monocropping because harvests had to be done separately at different times (see Fig. 78) but the labour was spread along the crop cycle. The farmers were therefore less limited by the [SOURCE: Page_150]

150 [SOURCE: Page_150]

harvest peak period of each crop, which increased in fine the annual labour productivity. The yields were said to be higher than if the crops were grown separately. This could be because of improved fertility: “The whole system appears to be one designed to cover the land, and thereby to prevent the bareness and consequent loss to the soil which would result from the sun beating down upon it, and from the loss of moisture which it would incur. It is known also that the process of nitrification in soils is much more active when the latter lies fallow.” (Voelcker, 2010). [SOURCE: Page_151]

2.2.3. Crushing stones to extend the ager: only possible for the large holder farmers Some areas of the wash pediment were full of stones which could be removed by hand unlike the large rocks of the rocky hills. Large holder farmers had the capacity to cultivate on those areas as they could employ labour to remove and crush the small and medium-size stones. Elderly farmers from the lower castes (Vaderru caste) recall being employed by farmers to crush the biggest stones by hand. Some medium-size stones were remove using a gaddaparra, a kind of metal crowbar (Appendix 22 for photos of tools). Shrubs were chopped using a matchakati (a sort of knife) and one week after being cleared, the land was burnt. Trees and shrubs never grew back as the tree stumps were removed. It required approximately 30 man- days to clear out one ha of land. Stones then had to be removed. Of course, the quantity of labour depended on the quantity and size of stones but 60 man-days to destone a ha of land was a fairly good order of magnitude. [SOURCE: Page_151]

2.2.4. Turning the tide of erosion: using animal power for organic and mineral fertility transfers As seen in chapter 2, the environmental characteristics of the area can be summarised as a harsh semi-arid landscape made of scattered rocks and stones, shrubby vegetation and small topographic variations. Beneath the seeming flatness there are micro-variations of reliefs which shape three main landforms: small residual reliefs, large and relatively flat areas (wash pediment) and small pockets slightly carved by water within the wash pediment (wash depressions). The mixed shrubland with large rocks also had the role of being a mineral fertility reservoir and the departure point of a transfer of mineral fertility made possible because of the slopes. Under the long-term action of water, the rocky boulders had partially broken down into small rocks and stone (physical and biological weathering). Erosion played a key role in filling the run-off reservoirs with silt deposits and the stream channels with sand. The tank silt was collected by humans using shovels and transported by bullock carts and spread mostly on the [SOURCE: Page_151]

151 [SOURCE: Page_151]

irrigated crops by all types of farmers and sometimes on rainfed crops by the smallholder farmers. Sand was extracted by large holder farmers from river channels and exclusively spread on the rainfed lands before groundnut cultivation. The slopes, as small as they may appear, were of the utmost importance. (Fig. 80) [SOURCE: Page_152]

Figure 80. Transfer of mineral matter in the 1950’s from the saltus to the ager through erosion and then animal power [SOURCE: Page_152]

This was done during the summer season when the rivers were dry. Adding sand loosened the soil and facilitated the harvest of groundnut. Large holder farmers used to dig out sand from river channels using shovels, transport them to the field by bullock cart and spread the sand in the fields during the end of the summer season (around May, see Fig. 49). Digging was done using shovels and the work was all the more painstaking because of the high temperature of summer season. Considering a distance of 1 km between the riverbed and the field, we estimated that 2 men can dig up 1 bullock cart of sand (~ 250 kg) in one hour. At this rate we considered a maximum of four days were spent excavating sand. Not all the land cropped with groundnut was improved with sand each year. More details on this practice are given in Appendix 17. Apart from easing the harvest, loosening the soil texture using sand facilitated seed and fruit development of groundnut. The groundnut plant is “a wonderful laboratory”, to quote Auguste Chevalier in 1934. “It is at the same time a complex symbiotic association and an organism which is remarkably well-adapted to drought, and capable of retrieving from the soil all the necessary nutrients necessary for the plant’s development and propagation.” (Chevalier, 1934). Groundnut is a leguminous crop which has the particularity of having subterranean seeds and fruits (hypogea means in Greek “beneath the soil”). Those seeds are protected by a shell. After flowering, the fertilised ovules appear at the tip of a peg [SOURCE: Page_152]

152 [SOURCE: Page_152]

(gynophore^29), which is a pointed offshoot resembling a small stalk (see Fig. 81). The stalk elongates downwards from the intercalary meristems with a gravitropic growth (Moctezuma, 1999; Moctezuma and Feldman, 1998) until it penetrates the soil. The groundnut plant ‘sows’ therefore its own seed (geocarpy) (Smith, 1950). [SOURCE: Page_153]

Figure 81. Gravitropic growth of the groundnut gynophore Source: (Smith, 1950) Once the seed has penetrated the soil, the development of the seed in the pod requires well drained and aerated soils for the respiratory exchanges to occur. This is a why groundnut could not be cultivated in grey hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions, as the soil penetration of the gynophore would have been impossible. The respiratory exchanges would have been limited and the seed wouldn’t even have been capable of developing into a pod. Adding sand lowered the apparent density of the soil, making it easier to work and also facilitating the penetration of the gynophore in the soil and also increasing rain water infiltration and decreasing water runoff (Groenendyk et al., 2015; Solter, 1992). [SOURCE: Page_153]

2.3. Disparate efforts for disparate values of land: the irrigated-rainfed dichotomy The practices in the 1950’s were such that much more muscular energy and organic and mineral matter was concentrated on the land with access to irrigation than on the rainfed ones. In Figure 82, we represented the total quantity of human and animal labour, and the quantity of matter (manure, silt, sand, neem leaves, calotropis leaves) spread on the fields of each [SOURCE: Page_153]

29 Gynophore is the organ that carries the seeds into the soil. Etymologically it is composed of the stalk that supports the female organs of the flower -the gynoecium- (from the greek “gyno” the woman and “phore” which supports). [SOURCE: Page_153]

153 [SOURCE: Page_153]

cropping rotation i.e. thus taking into account the duration of the ley fallows. We chose to represent the quantity of matter and not the quantity of calorific energy of inputs in order to analyse the weight of tank soil, sand and other inputs. Calculations are presented in fresh weight quantity (Fig. 82). [SOURCE: Page_154]

Figure 82. Comparisons of irrigated and rainfed cropping systems in the 1950’s in terms of organic and mineral matter spread, labour energy spent and calories produced The labour energy of the irrigated cropping systems was much more important than the rainfed cropping systems because of the energy spent on lifting water from wells. The labour energy [SOURCE: Page_154]

154 [SOURCE: Page_154]

of the rainfed cropping systems of large holder farmers was lower than the one of smallholder farmers because it was diluted by the long ley fallows. Farmers put most of the organic and mineral matter they collected on the irrigated cropping systems. With irrigation, they could cultivate two crops every year, thus producing much more than on the rainfed land of the wash pediment. Even though the energy produced per ha was less for rainfed crops of large holder farmers, the large holder farmers had much more land than the smallholder farmers, making them, on the whole, bigger producers of food and feed than the smallholder farmers. The land tax was higher for irrigated land than for rainfed land. The values varied 30 from one village to another and one plot to another, but ranged in 196131 from 500 to 1 500 Rs per ha of rainfed land and 2 500 to 6 250 Rs per ha of irrigated land (Gov. India, 1964, p. 400) [SOURCE: Page_155]

3. The hidden cost of self-sufficiency and environmental sustainability 3.1. An agrarian system harnessed by flows of human and animal muscular energies… All the agricultural operations in Rapthadu mandal were made with man and animal power. The large holder farmers could cultivate large expanses of land because a large part of the population was landless and could work for them. Smallholder farmers relied mostly on the muscle power of their own family workers, but hired labour was required in peak periods. In the archetype village, the manpower of the landless categories i.e. agricultural labourers and pastoralists, was captured by the landowning categories (red arrows on Fig. 83). What is even more striking is that 91 GJ of human manpower was absorbed by the large holder farmers, which is 1.3 times more than what was captured by smallholder farmers even though there were only 8 large holder farms and 80 smallholder farms (see social diversity of the archetype village in Appendix 15). [SOURCE: Page_155]

Animal labour was so valuable for farming and the cost of maintaining livestock so high in terms of resources and time spent, that the cost of renting bulls was very high and this happened in very exceptional circumstances. In our model we therefore considered that bulls were never rented out to other farms in the 1950’s. The flows of animal labour (in brown on [SOURCE: Page_155]

India, 1964, p. 34) 31 We used the value of the 1961 census because no values per village in the study area were found in the 1951 census [SOURCE: Page_155]

155 [SOURCE: Page_155]

Fig. 83) are therefore contained within the boxes representing the social categories owning draft animals, i.e. smallholder farmers and large holder farmers. [SOURCE: Page_156]

Figure 83. Flow of human and animal muscular energy in the 1950’s in the archetype village N.B.: With 472 agricultural workers, the maximum human labour capacity is 11 328 man-days per month. With 208 bulls, the maximum animal labour capacity is 4 992 animal-days per month: PS : Production System [SOURCE: Page_156]

The distribution of labour throughout the year shows that livestock rearing required a constant amount of labour over the months of the year as animals were taken out for grazing all year round (Fig. 84, top). As for cropping operations, it was the irrigated crops that required the most man power throughout the year, from May to August for finger millet and from September to January for rice (sowing, transplanting, irrigating, weeding and harvesting). The post-harvest operations of rice i.e. threshing, winnowing, de-husking and storing rice straw, was done in February. Winnowing of instance, required a lot of time and was made using a flattened basket (Appendix 21 for archive photo). [SOURCE: Page_156]

156 [SOURCE: Page_156]

Figure 84. Monthly amount of man and animal labour in the 1950’s in the archetype village [SOURCE: Page_157]

Most of the cropping activities of the month of December were dedicated to the labour- intensive harvest of groundnut, and the months of January and February to the manual separation of the groundnut pods from the plant, using a V-shaped stick. Land preparation and sowing of rainfed millets and pulses had to be done mostly in June and July to benefit from the optimal sowing window regarding rainfall. The harvests were spread out from August (cow pea, green gram), September (little millet, foxtail millet), sorghum (October) till January for red gram and horse gram. There were no cropping activities during the months of March and May (dry season) except for sand excavation in April for groundnut cultivation. With a total of 472 family workers in the archetype village, this made a maximum working capacity of 11 328 man-days each month considering that people used to have at least one day rest per week. May, September, December and January were the busiest. Most of the animal power was used for irrigation (Fig. 85). The second irrigated crop cycle (rice), required more water to maintain the level of flooding than the first irrigated crop (finger millet). This can be seen from the bigger amount of animal-days from October to December for irrigated crops than from May to August (Fig. 84, bottom). The village bulls were working at full capacity from October to Decembre. If a farmer had required an extra pair of bulls to irrigate his crops, this would have been barely [SOURCE: Page_157]

157 [SOURCE: Page_157]

feasible. The cost of renting was sky high: in exceptional circumstances where the bulls were rented out for irrigation, the bull owners requested half of the gross product of the crop. [SOURCE: Page_158]

In the 1950’s, 75% of the total muscle power (animal and human) was spent on crop cultivation (Fig. 85). The village workers spent 44% of their labour energy on rearing livestock, while the rest (56%) was spent on crop cultivation. The type of cropping activities that required the most human labour are the harvesting and post-harvesting operations (43%), followed by irrigation (24%) and land preparation and sowing (21%). Draft animals contibuted to 55% of the muscle power spent on crop cultivation. Most of their labour energy was expended for lifting water from wells (72% of the total animal labour energy) and for harvesting and post-harvesting operations (35%). [SOURCE: Page_158]

Figure 85. Contribution of different types of agricultural work and type of muscle power to the total labour energy of the village in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_158]

158 [SOURCE: Page_158]

3.2. … which succeeds in feeding its productive forces … 3.2.1. Food self-sufficiency In the 1950’s, the productivity of agriculture was such that it was enough to provide most of the village inhabitant’s food, as the only imports came from sugar (Fig. 86). There was a small surplus of milk, pulses and rice which was exported out of the village (Fig. 86). Millets, pulses, milk and most of the oil is produced on the large holder and smallholder farms. Sugar (jaggery) was imported from neighbouring areas where sugar cane was grown, such as in Karnataka state. Labourers were often paid in kind, in bags of grains (approximately 2 kg per day of work) or milk. Groundnut was a cash crop and was mostly sold out of the village to oil mills in the district. Groundnut contributed to nearly half the exports of products from the village in terms of calories. [SOURCE: Page_159]

Figure 86. Flow of calorific energy of human food in the 1950’s All values expressed in GJ [SOURCE: Page_159]

159 [SOURCE: Page_159]

3.2.2. Feed self-sufficiency: the crop-by product- grass equilibrium … a fragile one Although there are many assumptions behind our calculations, we can assert with reasonable certainty that the grass produced during the monsoon was enough to sustain a population of 208 bulls, 80 buffaloes, 64 dairy cows and 240 ewes (and their progeny). All the livestock was managed in a rotational grazing system with a high mobility, where grasslands area, whether part of the ager or the saltus, were grazed only once a year. This enabled the preservation of grass shoot meristems and avoidance of overgrazing. Once the monsoon season was over, although the remaining grass was sufficient in quantity to sustain the livestock population, it was more lignified and therefore not adequate in quality. Straw and hay were very important for cattle and buffaloes to live through the summer season (March to May). During those three months, pastoralists used to practice transhumance by foot to Bellary area, 200 km away from the village, as show the imported flow of calorific energy from grazed Bellary grass (Fig. 87) [SOURCE: Page_160]

Figure 87. Flows of gross energy of animal feed in the village in the 1950’s All values expressed in GJ [SOURCE: Page_160]

160 [SOURCE: Page_160]

3.2.2.1. A fragile equilibrium The feeding of animals was however highly dependent on rainfall, as most of the dry matter comes from grazed grass and rainfed crop-by products. There were most certainly years where the crop yields were low and where straw and hay were not produced in sufficient quantity to decently sustain the livestock population. Animals were in those years probably underfed. There was no mention of destocking (selling animals) in interviews. Some farmers had to take their livestock a little further afield than they were usually accustomed to. Taking animals to graze became more arduous. Farmers could be compelled to walk long distances from the village houses, as recalled by an old farmer: “If we didn’t have enough land for our cattle [meaning, “if we didn’t have enough straw”] we used to take the cows grazing close to the mountains, cut grass from grazing lands or from other farmers land”. [SOURCE: Page_161]

3.3. A sustainable use of the groundwater 3.3.1. A majority of grazed surfaces and rainfed crops Fig. 88 shows the trivial result that rainfed crops contribute to a positive water recharge and irrigated crops to a negative water recharge. As explained in Chapter 1, we used for the water balance daily data from 1985 to today. The high interannual variability of rainfall induces a variation in the amount of water recharged by rainfed surfaces (see bar errors on Fig. 88). We can therefore not conclude that groundnut for instance had a higher net recharge than millets. What is less intuitive is the positive effect of grazing and rainfed cultivation on the water recharge compared with ungrazed native vegetation (Fig. 88). For grazing, this could seem counter-intuitive but is confirmed by other studies (Bremer et al., 2001). This was explained by the fact that if biomass was grazed then the leaf area index of vegetation was brought down, therefore inducing less evapotranspiration. We assumed that the stimulated regrowth of grass after being grazed was limited, because the rains of the monsoon are not sufficient to prevent water stress on the grasslands. For rainfed crops, the weeding operations enabled the removal of the weed biomass and evapotranspiration only occurred from the harvested crops. In Australia, it was shown that the clearing of forest increased water recharge (Eberbach, 2003). [SOURCE: Page_161]

161 [SOURCE: Page_161]

Figure 88. Net recharge of groundwater table at cropping system level in the 1950’s In the 1950’s, 66% of the archetype village surfaces were grazed and 23% were cropped, with a majority of rainfed crops (82% of the cropped area). The only land use which had a negative net recharge (Fig. 88), i.e. pumped water, was the cultivation of irrigated crops. They were grown on very small surfaces, only 18% of the cropped area -i.e. 4% of the total village area!-, their surface being limited by the access to a well and the available animal power. The surfaces which were neither grazed nor cropped have a positive net recharge but close to zero (Fig. 88). This is because natural vegetation absorbed most of the rain and evapotranspired large amounts of water, meaning a low net recharge. 66% of the archetype village surfaces were grazed once a year. Those areas had the highest positive net recharge because grazing reduces evapotranspiration therefore favouring groundwater recharge. [SOURCE: Page_162]

3.3.2. All the production systems are net rechargers of the groundwater table Given the predominance of rainfed crops over irrigated crops on the scale of each production system and the importance of grazing to sustain livestock, it was therefore not surprising to see that all the production systems in the 1950’s were positive net rechargers (Fig. 89). While both smallholder and large holder farmers irrigated crops on a small portion of land (0.4 ha for smallholder farmers and 1.2 ha for large holder farmers), the predominance of rainfed crops implies that the positive recharge from land under rainfed crops outweighs the negative recharge of the land under irrigated crops (Fig. 88). The recharge of the cropped area of large holder farmers was 19 times higher than that of the small holder farmers because 1) [SOURCE: Page_162]

162 [SOURCE: Page_162]

the cropped area was 5 times higher and 2) because of differences in the net recharge among rainfed crops. For instance, groundnut had a higher net recharge than mixed pulses and millets (see Fig. 88). For all the production systems, the grazed surfaces, either from the fallows of the ager or from the saltus, played the most important role in the total net groundwater recharge at farm-level (Fig. 90). [SOURCE: Page_163]

Figure 89. Net recharge of groundwater table at farm-level in the 1950’s [SOURCE: Page_163]

3.3.3. The role of grazing livestock systems in the groundwater recharge On a territorial scale the net recharge was a fortiori positive, as shows figure 90, i.e. a total recharge of 2 947 601 m^3 (Fig. 90). All the production systems contributed positively to the village recharge (Fig. 91). However, most was contributed by the smallholder farmers (left on Fig. 90) as they outnumbered the large holder farmers and the pastoralists. Looking at the net recharge per type of land use (right on Fig. 90), it was the grazed surfaces which recharged the most (89% of the net recharge). Grazed grass played a major role in the livestock diet in the 1950’s and the role of livestock in the groundwater recharge was therefore predominant, for all production systems. [SOURCE: Page_163]

164 [SOURCE: Page_164]

Conclusion of chapter 3 In the 1950’s the society of the agrarian system of Rapthadu was class-structured, organised around landowners, and more particularly large holder farmers who owned vast stretches of land and reared large herds of cattle. They organised labour and had the access to the irrigated land and the means to extract groundwater. The landless categories had limited means of acquiring and accumulating wealth. The functioning of the agrarian system was based on those strong social inequalities where landowners controlled human and animal power and in return, forms of redistributive mechanisms maintained this society, mostly under the form of flows of gross energy of food and feed to maintain human labour and livestock. Despite the multiple constraints of the environment, mostly materialised by rocks and water scarcity, the functioning of the agrarian system was such that it succeeded in feeding its inhabitants -and even produced a small surplus which was exported out of the village- (Fig. 91). The agricultural population composed with the scattered resources, implementing practices which enabled them to optimise the use of rain, concentrating energies on areas and spreading it in others, and even going against the natural course of erosion. The village was almost totally autonomous, showed by a circularity index of 84% and a self-sufficiency index of 98% (Fig. 91)– except for the grassland’s pastoralists used in Bellary in summer- (Fig. 91) and groundwater was used in a sustainable way. The value of land was higher for irrigated areas than for rainfed ones: the access to irrigated land was limited, one had to have the means of production to dig a dug well i.e. capture the labour power to dig the dug well, have draft animals to lift water from wells. [SOURCE: Page_165]

CHAPTER 4: The land reform and the groundnut revolution (1970’s – 1980’s) [SOURCE: Page_167]

Figure 92. Mural painting in Anantapur – a farmer and his wife sowing groundnut- [SOURCE: Page_167]

167 [SOURCE: Page_167]

In the 1950’s, an important part of the agricultural population was landless. In the archetype village, they represented 45% of the agricultural population. Soon after Independence (1947), the Indian Central government handed to the State governments the role of implementing land reforms in order to reduce those inequalities of access to land (Pouchepadass, 2006). We did not find any values for Anantapur district nor Andhra Pradesh state, but estimations on the scale of the whole country suggest that one third of the Indian agricultural population was landless (Kumar, 1962), a value slightly lower than the one in the archetype village. According to Kumar (1962), the number of landless households had increased during the British rule, because of the establishment of a tax system which created situations of debt and the eviction of people from their land for non-payment. In the wake of independence, one of the main problems of Indian agriculture was the strong inequalities of access to land (Russell, 1952). India was also known for its famines (Klein, 1984), the one in 1943 which struck the State of Bengal led to the death of 4 million people ; not to mention the partition of India and Pakistan where India lost part of the irrigated and fertile lands of West Punjab (Dorin and Landy, 2009, p. 54). After Independence, the food situation was fragile and the Indian government established strong political choices to increase the agricultural productivity. Those policies started having an impact in Anantapur from the 1970’s onwards, starting off with a land reform and followed by a series of agricultural policies aiming at increasing food production. [SOURCE: Page_168]

1. Access to irrigation without draft animals: the gravity-fed irrigation systems in the villages near rivers 1.1. The Upper Pennar dam-reservoir project (from 1959) In the Deccan area, the British had already designed many dam-reservoirs in order to provide a better access to irrigation for farmers and supply household and industries with water. After Independence, a series of five-year plans were launched in order to renew old irrigation systems or build new dams. Much effort and hope were placed on those irrigation schemes. The first prime minister following independence, Jawaharlal Nehru proclaimed those dams as the “temples of modern India” (Dorin and Landy, 2002). In the Upper Pennar watershed, the construction of a dam 30 km north-west of the study area started in 1950. This project had most probably been designed during the colonial era -as the first five-year plan was only launched in 1951-. It was initially intended to be finished within three years but was completed in 1958. [SOURCE: Page_168]

168 [SOURCE: Page_168]

Its cost was about 15 million Rs (Reddy, 1971). This was a medium irrigation scheme^33, which irrigated 3 878 ha according to archives (Reddy, 1971). It consisted of a dam across the Pennar river, (Fig. 93) approximately 30 km of main canal and 2 distributaries. Those distributaries fed either already existing tanks in the region or directly fed rivers near to villages (the villages and tanks which benefitted from the project are given in Appendix 23). The project allowed the storage of excess monsoon flows of water, thus cushioning the seasonal variations of the river flow and ensuring water availability for more than one crop cycle in a year. Some villages in the study area, which were located nearby a non-perennial river, such as Gantlaparthi, were positively impacted by the project. [SOURCE: Page_169]

Figure 93. Peruru dam and the river -view showing check dam- separating Gantlaparthi and Kothapalli villages which are connected to the dam 30 km away [SOURCE: Page_169]

1.2. Access to irrigation for the farmers owning land near the river This project benefited smallholder farmers who had only rainfed land^34 (no wells) near the river. Without access to irrigation, the production of dry matter on 2 ha of land was just enough to feed one pair of bulls, but not enough to rear a dairy cow or a buffalo. With the implementation of the irrigated perimeter, those farmers with land near the river, could now grow two cycles of irrigated crops (finger millet and rice) during monsoon and winter, which [SOURCE: Page_169]

33 Irrigation schemes were classed into three according to the cost (classification before 1978) and the cultivable command area (cca) i.e. the irrigated perimeter (classification after 1978). The major irrigation schemes cost more than 50 million Rupees (Rs) and had more than 10 000 ha cca, medium cost between 1 and 50 million or had 2000 to 10 000 ha of cca and minor (less than 2 000 ha, and cost less than 1 million) (Meinzen-Dick and Svendsen, 1991). 34 The smallholder type described in chapter 3 had 1 pair of bulls, 1 buffalo, 0.4 ha of irrigated land in tank command areas and 1.6 ha of rainfed land on the wash pediment. The smallholder farmers we refer to here have not been described in chapter 3 because they were not part of the archetype village. [SOURCE: Page_169]

169 [SOURCE: Page_169]

enabled them to increase their feed and food production per ha (see chapter 3), and eventually rear a dairy animal. [SOURCE: Page_170]

The irrigated crops were irrigated by gravity channel which were dug from the river to the field. A check dam (Fig. 94) was built across the river in order to maintain the flow of water. A few meters upstream from the check dam a large canal was dug, which then branched off into several individual trenches that each farmer dug to irrigate their own field (Fig. 94). [SOURCE: Page_170]

Figure 94. Structure of an irrigated perimeter fed by rivers A few farmers had dug wells on the wash pediment but those cases were rare (most of the wells were found in the tank command area of villages with tanks). With the Upper Pennar project, the villages near to rivers therefore had an irrigated perimeter supplied by the river. Unlike the dug wells, the gravity-fed irrigation from rivers implied a collective management of the river water. Each individual trench (small canal on fig. 94) could be opened in turn, in order for everyone to have his share of water. The big canal (fig. 94) was regularly silted and had to be cleaned for the flow of water to circulate. The irrigated perimeters were organised around several committees (one for each big canal branching from the river) – in Gantlaparthi there were two committees-. Each committee member had to clean the canal, otherwise the members of the committee would be fined. Those fines were given at the temple by the fine collector, thus ensuring an economy around temples of the village, on which the many Hindu celebrations were funded. [SOURCE: Page_170]

Compared with irrigation from the kavili wells, there was no need for draft animals to irrigate the crops. Draft animals were only required to prepare the land and for post-harvest operations. Irrigation was made by opening the trench with a small hoe (parra in Telugu) and [SOURCE: Page_170]

170 [SOURCE: Page_170]

required only human labour. As it required only opening one or two trenches -the fields were small- family labour was often enough to irrigate the fields. The labour energy per ha was considerably reduced with the gravity-fed irrigation compared to the kavili irrigation system, for the same yields. The fields were however small, as the flow of water had to be divided amongst the members of the committee. Farmers who had land far from the river and out of reach of the irrigated perimeter could not benefit from the project. [SOURCE: Page_171]

2. Land to the landless: the Indira Gandhi land reform (1970’s onwards) Land reforms were impelled after independence at State level at different times according to the States : in Kerala it was launched in 1959, in Karnataka in 1974 and in West Bengal 1977 for instance (Dorin and Landy, 2009, p. 26). In Andhra Pradesh the Land Reform was initiated in 1973 and was called by farmers in the study area the “Indira Land Reform” as Indira Gandhi was prime minister at that time (1966-1977). Even though it started in 1973, it was a long process set up in successive waves. [SOURCE: Page_171]

2.1. Limiting the size of large holder farms and a reduced long ley fallow The large holder farmers, who had 25 to 100 ha of land were also impacted by the reform, as ceiling limits in land holdings were fixed through the Land Ceiling Act. In theory, the ceiling on land holdings was 10 ha for land with access to irrigation and 131 ha for rainfed lands (Chattopadhyay, 1973). According to interviews, the size of land holdings was limited to 26 ha. The large holder farmers preferably got rid of the worst land they had, which was the land far from wells and which had the most rocks. Nonetheless, the reduction of the size of the land holdings meant a reduction in the years of ley fallow. Assuming a land ceiling of 26 ha, [SOURCE: Page_171]
