2.2. Land to the tillers and subsidies for bulls: the case of agricultural labourers and pastoralists The surplus land taken from large holder farmers was given to the landless social categories which were the former pastoralists and agricultural labourers, most of them belonging to the Backward (Kurubas, Vaderras), Scheduled Castes (Untouchables) and Scheduled Tribes (Boyas). The distributed land was therefore rainfed land, and for some with many stones and boulders. The villages near rivers (Gantlaparthi, Kothapalli) had previously benefitted from the Upper Pennar dam project and were considered as part of government irrigation projects. In those villages, landless categories received 1 ha of land. All the other villages, i.e. near tanks or near the Bangalore-Secunderabad road, were not under the command of government irrigation projects. There landless categories received 2 ha of land. It is however unclear whether all the landless people received land. Although it was often mentioned that all the landless households received land, there are several reasons, outlined in Box 11 that cast doubt over this assertion. [SOURCE: Page_172]

In interviews, we were told that there is today at maximum 10 landless households in each village of the study area. However, there is no guarantee that this number could not have been bigger just after the first wave of land distribution processes. Those hypothetical landless people which were left behind, could have migrated to cities for better living opportunities and could therefore today not be found. Statistics in Anantapur show an increase in both rural and urban population and a migration to cities from the rural Anantapur areas to Anantapur city. Nevertheless, we could not determine whether those migrants were landless people or not. One thing is certain: today there are very few landless households in the villages. The land distribution process still remains partly unexplained as, despite the laws of the land reform, some interviewees explained that land was not given in a regulated and normalised process but through clientelist practices. Proximity and good acquaintance with high caste families favoured access to land. Those people with power were people from the Reddy caste, who worked as tax collectors and were close to the government (the Reddy karnalus) and also people from the Kamma caste, some of them being involved in politics. Box 11. The grey areas of the land repartition: migration and power relations [SOURCE: Page_172]

172 [SOURCE: Page_172]

Another component of the Indira Gandhi reforms, and which is absent from archives and scientific literature but which was important in the study area, was the improvement in the means of production through the subsidies to invest in a pair of bulls. This policy was often raised in interviews with former SC and ST landless agricultural labourers. Although we found no trace of it in archives, the program was sometimes named “Great Camp” by interviewees. [SOURCE: Page_173]

The new landowners who did not receive a subsidy to buy a pair of bulls had to borrow a pair for soil tillage and weeding operations to grow their rainfed crops. The population of bulls had increased since the 1950’s and the tillage and weeding operations were much shorter and temporary than the irrigation operations, where bulls were needed on a quasi-daily basis and for much of the duration of the day. In those conditions, renting bulls was affordable. The new landowners with no bulls however had to work on other people’s farms to supplement their income. As they didn’t have irrigated land, the 3 family workers still had time available to work on other people’s farms^35. From their labour they could also be paid in kind, like this farmer from the Scheduled Caste who was paid in manure: “Under Indira Gandhi [the land reform] I received 2,5 acres of land [1 ha – the interviewee lived in Gantlaparthi, a village which benefited from the Upper Pennar project] on eranella [rainfed land, red soil]. I used to grow foxtail millet, little millet and finger millet for my family. I used to work for people who had cattle. They were from OC community [Reddy or Kamma caste]. I got manure from them so I could manure my field. In exchange for labour the landlords from OC community also lent me their cattle for a few days so I could plough my field.”. [SOURCE: Page_173]

2.3. The limited access to irrigation of the new landowners All the new landowners only had land in rainfed conditions. The land was located on the wash pediment. For those who had bulls from the Indira Gandhi subsidies, crop by-products of millets and pulses were few and it was difficult to maintain the bulls. As discussed in chapter 3 the co-products per ha of rainfed millets and pulses were much lower than the co-products of a ha of irrigated finger millet and rice. The bulls were often underfed. To have a decent amount of straw to feed livestock and potentially hope to rear a buffalo for the household milk needs, access to irrigation was necessary. Share-cropping contracts (locally named kaulu contracts) emerged between the farmers with solely rainfed land and with farmers who had wells on the [SOURCE: Page_173]

35 We should remember that 65% of the total man-days spent on crops in the smallholder farms of the 1950’s was spent on irrigated crops even though irrigated crops accounted for only one fifth of the cropped land [SOURCE: Page_173]

173 [SOURCE: Page_173]

wash pediment. The latter were mostly large holder farmers. In those contracts, the well-owner gave access to the land in the vicinity of his well to the farmer with rainfed land for the duration of the crop cycle. While the share cropper tilled, cultivated and harvested the land with his own man and animal power and also provided all the inputs i.e. manure and seeds, the harvest was shared equally between the sharecropper and the well-owner (Fig. 95). In this way, the sharecropper could grow enough food for himself and his family, and also better feed his bulls with finger millet and rice straw. However, the loss of 50% of the gross product made it difficult to accumulate capital. The well-owner on the other hand had straw, finger millet and rice grains without paying any hired labour nor involving any family labour in the process, nor using manure from his heap. [SOURCE: Page_174]

Figure 95. The “kaulu” sharecropping contract between irrigating and non-irrigating farmers In some rare cases, new landowners invested in the excavation of a dug well on the wash pediment. This however required huge investment in terms of labour, and therefore in economic terms too. It could be achieved by borrowing money from wealthier farmers or -and this was only the case for pastoralists with land- decapitalise part of the ovine herd. “To dig my well I had to borrow money from a Reddy family [supposedly a smallholder farm with irrigated land, a pair of bulls and a buffalo or a large holder farm]. I paid my debt off after 10 years!” said a former agricultural labourer who had received land. Digging wells was usually possible closer to the wash depressions. In parts of the wash pediment and near the rocky hills however, wells could be dug but they were usually not as effective as the ones close to the wash depressions. As explained in chapter 2, the wells were dug in the saprolite layer, i.e. the weathered bedrock layer of the hard rock aquifer. The saprolite has a high porosity, therefore [SOURCE: Page_174]

174 [SOURCE: Page_174]

containing a lot of water, but its hydraulic conductivity -or permeability- is low: water circulates slowly (chapter 2, Fig. 39). A good well was therefore one where the saprolite was thick to optimise the well’s recharge, and this was the case near the wash depressions. [SOURCE: Page_175]

With the Land Reform, the cropped land on the wash pediment increased and the ley fallow shortened (Fig. 96). Most of the land on the wash pediment remained however rainfed (Fig. 96). [SOURCE: Page_175]

Figure 96. Evolution of the land use of the archetype village between the 1950’s and the 1980’s with the effect of the Land Reform [SOURCE: Page_175]

175 [SOURCE: Page_175]

Apart from the land reform, India launched several agrarian policies to boost the agricultural production of the country. [SOURCE: Page_176]

3. Groundnut for all: the Yellow revolution (mid 1980’s) Those agrarian policies were named revolutions because the technological changes involved were considered as revolutionary developments in science (Pearse, 1974) but do not refer to the uprising of part of the population. Each revolution focused on boosting the production of a particular food product: the Green Revolution targeted the production of rice and wheat, the Yellow Revolution of oil seeds and the White revolution of milk. Even though the Indian central government first launched the Green Revolution, then the White Revolution, and finally the Yellow revolution (Dorin, 1998; Dorin and Landy, 2002), there was a time lag between the moment when those agricultural revolutions were politically impelled at country-level and the moment when they were implemented at state level. There is also often a gap between the more or less canonical chronology of implementation at state-level and the moment where the technologies were truly adopted locally. Even though the Yellow Revolution was politically launched twenty years after the Green Revolution (Dorin, 1998), it is the Yellow Revolution that first impacted the study area. In this chapter we therefore deal with the Yellow Revolution, and the Green and White revolutions being discussed in the next chapters. [SOURCE: Page_176]

3.1. Context of implementation of the Yellow Revolution In 1984, Rajiv Gandhi replaces Indira Gandhi as Prime Minister. His advisor Sam Pitroda proposes the implementation of five “technological missions”. One of those, the Technical Mission on Oil Seeds (TMO) was launched in 1986 as part of the Yellow Revolution (oil crops). The aim of the Yellow Revolution, also known as Operation Golden Flow, was to substitute the importation of vegetable oil which had become too costly (Dorin, 1998). During the 1970’s, several droughts impeded the production of oil crops which increased the domestic price of oil. First helped by food aid supplies from the United States (soya oil producer), India increased the volume of imports of oil in an attempt to stabilise prices, but in vain. In 1981- 1982, the import of vegetable oil was the second biggest expense after crude oil (Dorin and Landy, 2002, p. 93). The TMO was therefore firstly characterised by high customs duty and minimum guaranteed prices on oil (Reddy, 2009; Reddy and Bantilan, 2011). It was also characterised by the deployment of a new variety of groundnut. The National Oilseeds Development Project (NODP) was launched in 1984-85 as part of the TMO. The aim was to increase the production of groundnut (Gulati, 1988). To achieve this, a change of biological material was needed, as the groundnut spreading variety used in the 1950’s could only be [SOURCE: Page_176]

176 [SOURCE: Page_176]

cultivated by farmers with at least three pairs of bull. The accessibility of the spreading variety was therefore highly limited (see chapter 3). [SOURCE: Page_177]

3.2. A new variety of groundnut: the erect groundnut variety The flagship of the Yellow revolution was, at least in Anantapur district, the introduction of a new variety of groundnut with a shorter cycle and an erect growth habit -instead of a spreading one- and a sequential arrangement of the vegetative and reproductive axes (Fig. 97) [SOURCE: Page_177]

Figure 97. Spreading and erect varieties of groundnut [SOURCE: Page_177]

Source: (IBPGR, ICRISAT, 1985) The erect growth habit enabled the farmers to grasp the whole plant by hand and can therefore easily be plucked out of the earth, without the help of bulls. However, the decisive and notable change was within the crop duration cycle, which was reduced from 130-150 days to 110-120 days. This brought the harvest time approximately 20 days forward, during the course of November instead of December, when the soil was still moist from the finishing rains (Fig. 98). The harvest of groundnut was eased and could be done by hand. Bulls were no longer needed. [SOURCE: Page_177]

177 [SOURCE: Page_177]

Figure 98. Labour calendar of the spreading groundnut variety in the 1950’s and the erect variety introduced in the 1980’s, both in rainfed conditions The erect variety possessed another characteristic, which was of use at the time only to the farmers with access to irrigation on the wash pediment. Even though the land on the wash depressions was irrigated, the grey hydromorphic soils made groundnut cultivation impossible in the wash depressions (see chapter 3). The former spreading variety was characterised by a seed dormancy of more than four months, which enabled the seeds to survive the unfavourable conditions of the winter and summer seasons (Ntare et al., 2008, p. 17). The genetic changes were made in the aim of suppressing seed dormancy and elaborating a high-yielding variety in conditions of irrigation. This was however not of much use so long as the conditions of production remained mostly rainfed (Rao, 2004), which was the case in the study area. Groundnut could indeed be cultivated only on the red loamy soils of the wash pediment, and those areas were in the vast majority under rainfed conditions. Nonetheless, this was only use in the 1980’s by the very few farmers who had wells on the wash pediment. Those farmers were large holder farmers who were already cultivating groundnut in the 1950’s. With the suppression of seed dormancy, it was therefore possible for them to re-seed groundnut a few weeks after its harvest and grow groundnut twice a year, in irrigated conditions using the few wells they had on the wash pediment. [SOURCE: Page_178]

All the elderly farmers we interviewed agreed that the new variety produced either the same number or less pods than the older one, and also less hay. The decline in pod yields was also [SOURCE: Page_178]

178 [SOURCE: Page_178]

confirmed by the study of Talawar (2004) and also by a village monography 30 km away from the study area which provides yields of the two varieties in 1985 (Gov. AP, 1981). The statistics in Andhra Pradesh state also show a yield that has remained fairly constant, but a groundnut pod production which has increased, therefore driven by a 1-5-fold increase of the area under groundnut (Fig. 99). [SOURCE: Page_179]

Figure 99. Evolution of the area under groundnut, production and yield in Andhra Pradesh state from 1980 to 1996 [SOURCE: Page_179]

Source: data from Talawar (2004) The harvest of the spreading variety required 56 man-days per ha and 9 animal-days. The harvest of the new variety now required no animal labour, but it still required a lot of human labour, i.e. 25 man-days per ha (Table 10). There was also no need of digging and transporting sand anymore which reduced the amount of labour for the amendment of the crop (Table 10). However, because of the grouped plant structured of the erect type, the weed suppressing function found in the spreading variety was no longer ensured and farmers had to weed three times instead of two thus increasing the labour for weeding (Table 10). [SOURCE: Page_179]

3.3. The bunch variety: a boon for some farmers and a first step towards the abandonment of draft animals for large holder farmers With the land reform and the subsidies on bulls, the former smallholder farmers, the pastoralists and most of the agricultural labourers (of the 1950’s) now had land and a pair of bulls. Most of their land was on the wash pediment. For this mass of farmers with one pair of bulls, the question of the adoption of the new variety, despite the labour productivity remaining constant, is not even raised. They could not grow the spreading variety before anyway because they only had one pair of bulls. The development of the new variety was a boon for them as they could swap their rainfed millets and pulses on the wash pediment with the new groundnut variety. In 1985, groundnut was paid 5 Rs a kilo, while millets and pulse grains were paid 1.5 to 3 Rs/kg (Gov. AP, 1981). The new groundnut variety had a higher yield and a better price than the millets and pulses. As both crops required the same inputs (manure and eventually tank silt spread every year in a different part of the rainfed land) the valued added was multiplied at least by three^36. The shift from millets and other pulses to groundnut also allowed to produce more feed for their animals (Fig. 101). [SOURCE: Page_181]

Figure 101. Dry matter yields of the rainfed crops cultivated in the 1980’s The adoption of the erect variety was unanimous, even for the large holder farmers who were already cultivating groundnut in the 1950’s. The change of variety occurred even though the physical labour productivity did not improve much (Fig. 99). The very slight increase in the physical labour productivity is however not enough to explain the adoption of the new variety. There are several hypotheses. By switching to the new variety, the number of bulls could be reduced by three, which either allowed feeding more dairy animals and/or the increase of the proportion of straw and hay in the diet of the animals, thus securing the feed of livestock in the dry season. In both cases, the shift from the spreading to the erect variety was the beginning of [SOURCE: Page_181]

36 For millets and pulses, yields range from 0.5 to 1 ton FW/ha with a price of 1.5 to 3 Rs/kg in 1985, thus at best a gross product of 3 000 Rs/ha. For the erect groundnut variety, the yield was approximately 2 tons FW/ha with a price of 5 Rs/kg, thus a gross product of 10 000 Rs/ha. [SOURCE: Page_181]

181 [SOURCE: Page_181]

a progressive abandonment of draft animals. The second reason was that it became possible to cultivate groundnut in irrigated conditions, useful only in the few areas close to wells on the wash pediment. Those areas mostly belonged to the large holder farmers. The third reason was that less man-days were required: for large holder farmers who mostly depended on hired labour, it also meant less wages to pay out. The last reason was that there were supposedly more incentives from the government seed distribution centres to develop the bunch variety. The groundnuts of the bunch variety had the same oil content as the spreading one but had less fibres which increased its gustative qualities. We know for instance that the new variety was subsidised but the amount of the subsidy is not known. However, as groundnut could be re- seeded from one year to another, there are uncertainties on the importance of this factor in the switch of varieties. [SOURCE: Page_182]

182 [SOURCE: Page_182]

Conclusion of chapter 4: The distribution of land during the land reform was a step towards the reduction of inequalities. However, the distribution process was not as smooth at it could appear as some landless households may have been left behind as the distribution of land was favoured by privileged relations with large holder farmers who had more political power. Access to irrigation was also very limited given the investment capacity it required to dig a well. Many landless households who received land were given land which was also full of rocks, limiting the areas under cultivation (Fig. 102). Crops were sown using animal traction around those boulders. Interdependencies between farms remained: the new smallholder farmers still supplemented their income by working on other farms. A new form of interdependency emerged with the establishment of sharecropping contracts over the access to irrigated land close to dug wells (Fig. 102). [SOURCE: Page_183]

Figure 102. Social diversity at the end of the 1980’s within the landscape -example of the archetype village- [SOURCE: Page_183]

The deployment of the Yellow Revolution made groundnut accessible to everyone who had land and a pair of bulls. Farmers could therefore grow a crop which could be sold at a higher price than millet and other pulse crops. The adoption of groundnut by all social categories with land entailed a progressive decline of rainfed millets which were replaced by [SOURCE: Page_183]

183 [SOURCE: Page_183]

groundnut. Little by little, groundnut became the major rainfed crop in the area. In the absence of statistical data on village or Rapthadu mandal level, Figure 103 shows the evolution of the proportion of crops in the entire Anantapur district. Despite the disparities among mandals of Anantapur district, it shows the increase of groundnut cultivation during the 1980’s and the 1990’s. The population of draft animals increased with the land reform and the subsidies on bulls. However, the Yellow revolution meant that three pairs of bulls per farm for crop cultivation was no longer necessary: the first stepping stone towards the abandonment of draft animals was in place. [SOURCE: Page_184]

CHAPTER 5: From muscle power to engine power (1990’s to today) [SOURCE: Page_185]

185 [SOURCE: Page_185]

1. The Green and the pump revolution: not for all… In the previous chapter we identified four types of farms with access to irrigation. Two types already had access since the 1950’s. Those were the large holder farmers and smallholder farmers of the 1950’s. The other two irrigating categories were more recent. They were composed of landless categories in the 1950’s who had received land during the Land Reform and managed to irrigate crops either through sharecropping contracts on land near wells or, for the case of pastoralists, by selling their sheep to dig a well. Water was lifted using the draft power of bulls. [SOURCE: Page_186]

Soon after the Yellow revolution, strong government incentives were carried out to boost agricultural production in the area, through the development of irrigation. Technical innovations were implemented, backed up by massive subsidies from the Central and State governments, in order to increase labour productivity. High-yielding varieties, synthetic fertilisers and the development of borewell irrigation were the key ingredients of the green revolution (Dorin and Landy, 2009; Hazell, 2009). The new irrigation technologies were part of a more specific revolution called the “pump revolution” (Shah, 2009). [SOURCE: Page_186]

Although the Green revolution had begun in the 1960’s in India and had been designed before the Yellow revolution, it became effective at different periods in the different states. In Anantapur the Green revolution and the pump revolution reached the rural areas soon after the Yellow revolution, towards the end of the 1980’s and the beginning of the 1990’s. [SOURCE: Page_186]

1.1. Releasing considerable technical and financial needs to increase labour productivity Public investments, both at Central and State level, were considerable to unravel the Green and pump revolution. India built synthetic fertiliser factories such as the Sindri Fertiliser company in the north eastern district Jarkhand – the coal capital of India- which was inaugurated in 1952 (Gov. India, 1961). The research centres developed high-yielding varieties and the Central and state governments decided to subsidise massively the agricultural sector as shown by the importance of subsidies in the agricultural budget of India in 1994-1995 (Alloua, [SOURCE: Page_186]

186 [SOURCE: Page_186]

1996, p. 81) (Fig. 105). 48 per cent of those subsidies were spent on ensuring access to electricity (Fig. 105). [SOURCE: Page_187]

Figure 105. Orientations of the agricultural budget of India in 1994-1995 and share of subsidies Source : Alloua (1996, p. 81) The access to food was improved by the implementation of Minium Support Prices (MSP) on food products and also the establishment of the Public Distribution System (PDS) in the 1950’s. In the PDS, staple food such as sugar, rice and wheat was bought by the government at a guaranteed price and redistributed at subsidised price i.e. the CIP (Central Issue Price) (Dorin and Landy, 2002, p. 72). Those food items could be purchased in local “Fair Price Shops” by the households who held a ration card. The system is still used today. In Andhra Pradesh, since 1982, the price of rice in Fair Price Shops has been fixed at 2 Rs per kg (Dorin and Landy, 2002, p. 133). [SOURCE: Page_187]

1.2. Diesel and electric surface pumps: a short-lived development of silk rearing for large holder and irrigating smallholder farmers After the oil shock of 1980, diesel subsidies multiplied throughout India, but this was not uniform over all states (Madhusudan et al., 2018, p. 20). Andhra Pradesh seemed to be one of those forgotten states but the households who could afford to buy diesel engine pump sets did so towards the end of the 1980’s. Given the tremendous amount of animal power irrigation required, the use of diesel pumps alleviated the workload of bulls. Draft animals were still used for transport, ploughing, weeding and harvesting. Despite this, the modality of refilling wells remained the same: the slow infiltration of water through the saprolite continued to limit the size of the irrigated fields. Those diesel pumps were surface pumps, which could not pump below a depth of 10 metres. An extra 5 metres could be gained by fixing the pump on a platform [SOURCE: Page_187]

187 [SOURCE: Page_187]

5 metres below the ground on the well paved wall (Fig. 106). Beyond this depth, water could no longer be pumped. [SOURCE: Page_188]

Figure 106. Pumping water: from animal power to diesel and electric surface pumps (1990’s) [SOURCE: Page_188]

During the beginning of the 1980’s, state policies modified the cropping patterns in the irrigated areas of the wash depressions. The Andhra Pradesh state government implemented a policy to increase the production of silk. The sericulture sector was structured by the creation of the Central Silk Board, the construction of silk mills and hand loaming units. Across India, the policy succeeded in multiplying the raw silk production by three between the 1980’s and 2000 (Narasaiah, 2003; R.k.datta, 2007). The production was mostly concentrated in the Southern states of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. In Andhra Pradesh, strong incentives were set by the State from the mid 1980’s to develop in rural areas the rearing of silk worms. Those incentives were incorporated under the Andhra Pradesh Silkworm Seed and Cocoon Act which was launched in 1983. The Silk Board Centre provided large subsidies on silk worm eggs, i.e. only 25 percent of sale price was charged. The eggs were purchased by the irrigating farmers of the area in Chintamani (Karnataka state) and Kadiri (Anantapur district) Silk Board Centres. They were of a new type of breed made from the crossing between bivoltine and multivoltine silkworms. Voltinism is the term indicating the number of generations of an organism in a year. Silk worms are usually either univoltines, bivoltines or multivoltines. The bivoltine breeds produce two generations per year, consumes less biomass than the univoltine but with a lower quality of cocoons (less weight and silk filaments). The local silk worm breeds were therefore replaced by the new cross bred silk worms. These silk [SOURCE: Page_188]

188 [SOURCE: Page_188]

worms were reared in small houses or sheds, the construction of which was subsidised by the State Government. Nonetheless, silk worms were fed on mulberry, a woody 10-year perennial plant which could only be grown in irrigated conditions. All the non-irrigating farmers could therefore not engage in silk worm rearing. They continued growing rainfed crops, rearing sheep for the pastoralists and work on the farms of the large holder farmers. [SOURCE: Page_189]

By the late 1980’s, the price of raw silk had overtaken the price of rice (Fig. 107) and all the farmers who had irrigated land started cultivating mulberry to engage in silk worm rearing, instead of cultivating finger millet and rice. [SOURCE: Page_189]

Figure 107. Evolution of the monthly wholesale price index of two products from irrigated cropping systems in Anantapur from 1982 to 1999 (Base year: 1981-1982= base 100) [SOURCE: Page_189]

Source: Data from (Gov. India, 2022a) Mulberry was grown mostly near the wash depressions as this was where most of the dug wells were, because of the higher width of the saprolite layer. It was grown on 0.4 to 0.8-ha patches of land, a size limited by the slow recharge of dug wells through the saprolite. Rearing silk worms was labour-intensive work, for they had to be tended with much care. They were kept in sheds and had to be fed daily with mulberry leaves (Fig. 108, right) which were picked and chopped manually. “It was so tiring, I remember feeding them three times a day, and I even had to get up at night twice to feed them again” said an elderly woman from an irrigating smallholder farm who used to rear silk worms. Once the cocoons were ready, they had to be sorted out manually (Fig. 108, left). In the large holder farms, all this work was carried out by hired labour from the non-irrigating smallholder farmer categories. It was practically a full- [SOURCE: Page_189]

189 [SOURCE: Page_189]

time job and one active worker of those non-irrigating households was engaged on a daily basis on the large holder farms. [SOURCE: Page_190]

Smallholder farmers with access to irrigation also started growing mulberry and rearing silk worms. They did most of the mulberry cropping cultivation and the feeding of the worms by themselves, thus occupying a large part of their labour calendar throughout the year. The cocoons were then sold in Dharmavaram (in Anantapur district, 10 km away from the study area), where silk sarees were handloomed. Dharmavaram silk sarees were famous -and still are- for the broad solid-coloured borders and a particular weaving technique called reku (R G, 2014). According to interviews, farmers could expect approximately 1 125 kg of cocoons per ha of mulberry which was well above the 280 kg average cocoon production in India in 1968 (The Wealth of India, 1973). [SOURCE: Page_190]

Figure 108. Sorting cocoons (left) and a shed with mulberry leaves (right) Source: photo taken in September 2021 in a village in Karnataka State between Mysore and Bangalore A few pastoralists also sold part of their sheep to dig a well, cultivate mulberry and rear silk worms: “With the land we got from the land reform, we had an additional income from crops. We improved the herd from 20 sheep to 60 with the income from crops. A sheep cost half a rupee at that time. Because we were looking after the sheep, we had to employ labour for agriculture practices. But 1 acre [0,40 ha] of the land we had was close to the village and water supply [wash depressions] so when people started growing mulberry we dug a well there and grew mulberry too! We had to borrow money from the Reddys and sell sheep. My son also used to work for them [people from the Reddy caste]. We had debts of 2 to 5 Rs every month. [SOURCE: Page_190]

190 [SOURCE: Page_190]

At some point we even had to sell some land. It took us 10 years to pay back our well. This was 40 years ago [1980 approximately]” said a pastoralist from the Kuruba caste. [SOURCE: Page_191]

As explained in chapter 4, most of the land which was distributed during the Land Reform came from the ley fallows of the large holder farmers. With the Land Reform the ley fallows were shortened. This, combined with the progressive simplification of crop rotations on the wash pediment due to the replacements of millets and pulses by groundnut, must have had major impacts on the fertility of the agrarian system and the development of pathogens. However, we did not find any evidence of problems of fertility management in our interviews and this point therefore remains unsolved. On the other hand, we know that the cycle of pathogens were no longer broken by long crop rotations and the number of pests, and especially thrips, increased on groundnut. In the 1990’s, farmers started buying pesticides to reduce the impact of thrips on groundnut. We know that the consumption of pesticides in India was high in the 1990’s -at the highest level between 1990 and 2012- (Devi et al., 2017). Among all the Indian States the consumption of pesticide per ha was the highest in Andhra Pradesh in 1992, alone accounting for 18 per cent of the total pesticide use in India (Chand and Birthal, 1997). The increased use of pesticides impacted the rearing of silkworms. Bivoltin hybrids were on the whole more sensitive to both diseases and pesticides than the former local breeds. On top of this, a fall in the price of silk around 1992 (Fig. 107) jeopardised the future of silk rearing in the study area. The price of silk in India fell due to Chinese competition (Historical developments in weaving machinery, 1992). [SOURCE: Page_191]

The 1990’s were also marked by rainfall deficit (see Fig. 16, chapter 1, section 3.3), which also compromised the production of mulberry, as it required irrigation all-year round. As mulberry was a 10-year crop, most of the farmers didn’t plant mulberry a second time. With this cumulation of drawbacks, mulberry crop, along with silk rearing, faded away throughout the 1990’s and rice cultivation took over again in the wash depressions. [SOURCE: Page_191]

By 1991, all the villages in the study area had access to electricity (Gov. India, 1991). This was the result of a massive rural electrification program launched since the 1960’s by the government of India. Priority in the extension of electricity had been given to farmers over households (Banerjee et al., 2014, p. 37) as this was considered a condition of agricultural development. The government encouraged farmers to purchase electric surface pumps through low electricity tariffs and subsidised electric pumps (Banerjee et al., 2014, p. 38). The diesel [SOURCE: Page_191]

191 [SOURCE: Page_191]

pumps were replaced by electric ones. The new electric pumps were however still surface pumps. [SOURCE: Page_192]

1.3. Transcending the physical limits of muscle power with borewells and submersible pumps: a cutting-edge technology The development of irrigation during the Green Revolution was put into effect through a specific revolution called the “pump revolution” (Shah, 2009). The former constraints on irrigation were lifted by the drilling of borewells and the use of submersible pumps. [SOURCE: Page_192]

The borewells were much deeper than the dug wells. They were between 25 and 100 metres deep (Fig. 109). The drilling process required much energy and cutting-edge technology to be able to break the natural barrier of rocks of the fractured horizon (Fig. 27, chapter 2). The method used was a hydraulic rotary boring method, which was useful to penetrate the hard rock formations. The hydraulic drilling machines relied on the Down the Hole Hammer (DTH) method, which was a drilling technique commonly found in hard rock aquifers areas. The method consisted in the use of a high-powered air compressor to rotate a drilling rod (hollow part of the drill stem) and also generate a hammering action on the drill bit. The tip of the rock drill was in contact with the ground while drilling and usually tipped with a diamond rotating head. [SOURCE: Page_192]

The surface pumps could however not extract the water of the borewells as they could not lift water below approximately 10 meters. The drilling of borewells was concomitant with the replacement of the surface pumps by electric submersible pumps (Fig. 109). A submersible pump, is a pump that by definition can be submerged in water to pump water. This was a very important factor because it meant that the constraint of the maximum height suction capacity of surface pump cavitation was lifted. Those submersible pumps also suffered less from cavitation, a phenomenon which was frequent in the former surface pumps, when the flow of water was not regular and the pressure not maintained. The submersible pumps could lift water at deeper depths by pushing water up to the surface. The first submersible pumps were single- staged ones but multiple stage pumps were later developed. Each stage consisted of a driven impeller and a diffuser which pushed the water to the next stage of the pump. At each stage, the pressure increased and the depth of water lifting was increased even more with the multiplication of stages. In dug wells, surface pumps used to lift the water which had accumulated in the dug well through the saprolite. In borewells the water which was pumped was the water surrounding the borewell and contained in fractures. The borewells did not [SOURCE: Page_192]

192 [SOURCE: Page_192]

recharge themselves through the saprolite as the dug wells used to do, and the size of the irrigated surfaces could be increased. [SOURCE: Page_193]

Figure 109. Pumping water deeper: from animal power to submersible pumps (1990’s) [SOURCE: Page_193]

Drilling borewells was a very costly process, which could not be engaged by all farmers. The first borewells were bored in the pre-existing dug wells which were mostly in the wash depressions. The cost for drilling depended on the depth of the borewell. According to Kovvali et al. (1997), a borewell in Anantapur cost in 1991 on average 33 750 Rupees (Rs). This was a considerable amount of money given that the average annual income of households living from agriculture was 7 046 Rs in 1981 according to a survey in a nearby village of Anantapur district (Gov. AP, 1981, p. 34). At country-level, Chand (2015) estimated the average annual income of an Indian household engaged in farming at 22 603 Rs in 1983 and 27 147 Rs in 1993. The cost of a borewell was all the more important that the percentage of borewell failure in the area was high. Those failures are explained by the structure of the aquifer. As explained in chapter 2, borewells are drilled in the fractured horizon of the aquifer and a borewell is successful only if it intercepts enough micro-fractures, in order to yield enough water: “In India, the rights in groundwater belong to the landowner as groundwater is attached to the land property. There is no limitation on the volume of groundwater extraction by a landowner. Since, land ownership is a pre-requisite to ownership of groundwater, it is difficult to assign ‘open access’ nature to groundwater resource. Though landowners own groundwater de jure, this right is limited by the huge investment necessary to tap the groundwater by construction-drilling of irrigation well(s) and high well failure probability, which makes a selected few among them to [SOURCE: Page_193]

193 [SOURCE: Page_193]

have access to groundwater.” (Vasudevan and Mysore, 1997). In the Deccan plateau, borewell failure was estimated at 40% (Vasudevan and Mysore, 1997) while Raizada et al. (2018) estimated at 51 to 77% in Netranahalli (Chitradurga district, neighbouring Anantapur district to the West). Considering the drilling process as a random experiment with two sets of outcomes, “successful drilling” or “failed drilling”, we estimated that a farmer would have to drill approximately 6, 10 and 24 times assuming a borewell failure of 40, 60 and 80 per cent respectively (Appendix 24). Once the farmers had engaged money by drilling the first meters of a borewell they usually pursued drilling deeper thinking that the deeper they drilled the better chance they had to find water. Similarly, to a gambler who continues gambling after losing, the farmer will in most cases spend a bit more money to drill a few more meters rather than stop drilling and face the fact that he has wasted money to drill the first unsuccessful meters. In psychology it is called the “escalation of commitment” and the “sunk cost fallacy” in economics and business management (Marechal, 2010). [SOURCE: Page_194]

1.3.1. The already-irrigating farmers adopt high-yielding rice varieties in the wash depressions Drilling a borewell was therefore very costly and was only possible for farmers who could afford to gamble for water. These were the ones who had accumulate sufficient capital. This was the case of the irrigating social categories who had prospered during the short era of sericulture. The large holder farmers also had been growing large areas of groundnut since the 1950’s, which also helped them to accumulate more capital. A descendant of large holder farmers proudly exclaimed: “Before, all my family members used to cultivate altogether 130 acres [52 ha] of land and out of those 130 acres, 100 acres [40 ha] was groundnut!”. Even though drilling borewells was a huge expense in absolute terms, the large holder farmers were the ones with the highest financial capacity to attempt several drillings, with a greater chance of getting a successful borewell. The smallholder farmers, although not as wealthy as the large holder famers given their smaller land holding size, were still much better-off than the non- irrigating farmers. Both the large holder famers and the irrigating smallholder farmers started drilling in the previously dug wells, and were usually successful after 1 or 2 attempts. There are two hypotheses which could explain the low borewell failure. First, it was the start of drilling in the area and the groundwater table was still fairly high. Secondly, the first borewells were drilled in the previous dug wells which were mostly located in the wash depressions and glacis slope, where the weathering of the bedrock was the most acute and the groundwater table the shallowest. [SOURCE: Page_194]

194 [SOURCE: Page_194]

Under those new borewells in the wash depressions, farmers grew the high-yielding rice varieties provided by the Green Revolution. Those varieties were grown in flooded conditions as was the former variety. The new varieties were characterised by their non- sensitivity to photoperiod, had a shorter crop cycle than the old variety, and could therefore be cultivated twice a year. They progressively replaced the finger millet crop. The variety sown during the first cycle (monsoon season) was usually the BPT 5204 variety (also known as Samba Mahsuri) and had a long cycle of 150 days (Fig. 110). The variety in the second cycle (winter and beginning of summer) was usually a shorter cycle (120 days) locally called Aruna (Fig. 110). [SOURCE: Page_195]

Figure 110. Evolution of rice cultivation and energy use (1950’s – 1990’s) [SOURCE: Page_195]

195 [SOURCE: Page_195]

The new varieties had a higher grain to straw ratio, meaning a higher partitioning of biomass for grains rather than straw. The old variety was comparatively taller and produced more straw than grain, with a grain to straw ratio of 0.6. The new variety could produce twice as many grains than the older one but the grain to straw ratio was 0.9. The production of biomass was therefore more favourable to man in this high-yielding strain. The increased biomass production was however conditioned upon the application of fertilisers, such as urea, which was subsidised. The organic inputs (neem, calotropis leaves) were replaced by chemical inputs (Fig. 110) which require much less work: it was no longer necessary to walk long distances to cut neem branches and calotropis shrubs and mixed them in the soil by walking in the muddy fields with bulls. Urea in solid form could be spread by hand over the fields. Rice crops were irrigated with borewells using submersible pumps (Fig. 110), which compared to the surface pumps, enabled to merge the previously small irrigated fields around borewells into one larger field of 1 to 1.5 ha. [SOURCE: Page_196]

In the state of Andhra Pradesh, the introduction of high-yielding rice varieties enabled to increase yields, even though the actual cropped area under rice remained fairly constant (Fig. 111). [SOURCE: Page_196]

Figure 111. Evolution of the surface under rice and rice yield in three states of south India, including Andhra Pradesh Source : Kumar (2019) [SOURCE: Page_196]

196 [SOURCE: Page_196]

1.3.2. Beginning of vegetable cultivation on the wash pediment for irrigating categories Some of the non-irrigating smallholder farmers tried to drill borewells. As they had inherited their land during the land reform, those drilling attempts were made on the wash pediment^37. Those non-irrigating social categories had gathered much less capital than the irrigating categories of the 1950’s. They had been landless for a long time and had only started cultivating groundnut for a very short period, namely less than 10 years. Apart from pastoralists, most of them still relied heavily on the income they had earned from working on other people’s farms. They were therefore financially disadvantaged. The classic case was the one of non-irrigating farmers borrowing money from the wealthier farmers, who were the large holder farmers. The large holder farmers applied huge annual interest rates, 24%! Those non- irrigating farmers who were trying their luck became heavily indebted as evidenced by this farmer: “I drilled 40 borewells but didn’t manage to get any water… I had so much debt… I borrowed money from other villagers or from banks. To repay my debt I eventually had to sell four ha of land near the highway [where the value of land today is higher] to a real estate company in Anantapur”. He was a farmer from the Reddy caste living in Ramanepalli, a village near the highway, on the wash pediment and a long way from any tank. [SOURCE: Page_197]

Despite large holder farmers lending them money, the non-irrigating smallholders had an additional disadvantage linked to where their land was located. As they had received land from the Land Reform, their land was usually on the wash pediment, and not in the wash depressions. On the wash pediment, the groundwater table was comparatively lower than in the wash depressions and required supposedly deeper borewells. They were also part of a second wave of farmers trying to drill borewells, and the groundwater table may also have started to go down. This is a mere supposition because data on the evolution of the groundwater table in the area was not accessible. Foster (2012) documented the decline of the groundwater table in a district of Andhra Pradesh (Fig. 112). Although the magnitude and the temporality of the decline of the groundwater level of Fig. 112 cannot be related to the one in the study area, the trend of the groundwater level is still informative. [SOURCE: Page_197]

37 As a reminder land was distributed mostly on the wash pediment during the Indira Gandhi Land Reforms (from the former ley fallows of the large holder farmers) [SOURCE: Page_197]

197 [SOURCE: Page_197]

Figure 112. The decline of the groundwater level in Nalgonda district of Andhra Pradesh state [SOURCE: Page_198]

Source : Foster (2012) The lucky farmers who managed to drill borewells after one or two attempts joined the ranks of the irrigating farmers. They started cultivating vegetables such as tomatoes, beans and chilies. Although there was no minimum guaranteed price on vegetables, the prices were higher than for rice. Vegetable cultivation was possible on the red loamy soils of the wash pediment but not on the grey hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions. The vegetables were grown on the wash pediment under furrow irrigation. The irrigation process was more labour-intensive than the flood irrigation practiced in rice fields. Although the lifting of water only required turning the pump on, furrow irrigation required a lot of work. Farmers had to dig furrows and ridges after preparing land and before planting. They also had to dig perpendicularly to the furrows field channels, which received the water flow from the pump. Every time they irrigated the crops, they had to open the access between the field channel and the furrows destined to be irrigated. According to the yield of the water flow, only alternate furrows were opened, rather than every furrow. During the next irrigation, the previously closed furrows were opened and irrigated (see Fig. 113). [SOURCE: Page_198]

198 [SOURCE: Page_198]

Figure 113. Alternate furrow irrigation 1.3.3. The non-irrigating farmers in the blind spot of borewell irrigation The other pastoralists and the other social categories were less fortunate. Most of them didn’t manage to drill borewells successfully, or didn’t even try drilling one. In the villages near rivers, the smallholder farmers couldn’t even try drilling a borewell. They had only received 1 ha of land during the land reform as their village was a beneficiary of a government irrigation project (see chapter 4). Their agricultural production and the wage they had earned from working on other farms did therefore not consist of a sufficient capital to even attempt to drill a borewell. They continued to grow groundnut in rainfed conditions and to work on other farms. [SOURCE: Page_199]

2. Pursuing the moto-mechanisation and putting a bow on draft animals 2.1. Moto-mechanising land preparation, harvest and post-harvest operations Moto-mechanisation was pursued throughout the 1990’s and the 2000’s, and concerned mostly the land preparation, harvest and post-harvesting operations of crop cultivation. [SOURCE: Page_199]

2.1.1. Tractors and combine harvesters in the wash depressions The land preparation and harvest of rice was considerably eased by the use of tractors with cage wheels and combine harvesters. Although this happened at the same time as the development of borewell irrigation in the wash depressions and the change of rice variety, we have chosen to deal with this part of moto-mechanisation separately in order to identify which technical changes were associated with which gains in labour productivity. [SOURCE: Page_199]

199 [SOURCE: Page_199]

In the 1950’s, rice fields were previously ploughed with a small ard. Green manure and cattle manure was then mixed into the soil by men and animals puddling the fields with their feet and hooves respectively. In the course of the 1990’s, large holder farmers invested in the first tractors. These tractors were at the time four-wheeled tractors of small size, from 20 to 30 hp. They were mostly used for ploughing and puddling the grey hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions. The large holder farmers bought these tractors using bank loans or benefitting from rare subsidies given during the first two mandates of Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu (1995-2004). Chandrababu Naidu belonged to the Telugu Desam Party, the party which had close links with the Kamma caste. We supposed that the affiliation to the Kamma caste of most large holder farmers facilitated the access to those subsidies, which were, in addition, very limited in number. In rice fields, the tractors were equipped with iron cage wheels (Fig. 114) which deeply mulched the soil in flooded conditions, therefore economising on power previously expended by humans and animals. While puddling and ploughing requires 23 man- days and 31 animal-days per ha, land preparation using tractors with cage wheels reduced the labour to 3 man-days per ha. The investment in tractors was however not wide spread and most of the irrigating smallholder farmers didn’t invest in tractors at the time. They either continued using their bulls or rented the tractors of the large holder farmers until they invested themselves in one. [SOURCE: Page_200]

Figure 114. A tractor with cage wheels attached to the tractor rim [SOURCE: Page_200]

200 [SOURCE: Page_200]

Harvest and post-harvest operations were facilitated by the use of combine harvester (Fig. 115): with this machine, the reaping, threshing and winnowing of the rice was done in a single process. Not a single joule of animal power was henceforth spent, and the only human joules were the one of the driver sitting on the combine harvester. The combine harvester reduced the labour harvesting and threshing by approximately 50 hours^38. However, this came at the expense of partial damage to rice straw compared to when rice was harvested annually cutting straw with a sickle. With the combine harvester, straw was left lying on the field but part of it was damaged during the process. Straw still had to be collected by human labour and stacked in heaps. [SOURCE: Page_201]

Figure 115. Combine harverster for rice type standard TSC-513, Amaravathi brand [SOURCE: Page_201]

Paddy rice was de-husked and polished in rice mills built in neighbouring villages, such as in Dharmavaram and Bandameedapalli. No farmer invested in combine harvester: those machines were much too costly^39 and only of use for the harvest of rice, which covered small surfaces in the area of study. By comparison, tractors could be used for land preparation of all crops. Farmers rented combine harvesters from nearby cities, probably Anantapur although the origin and the entity renting those combine harvesters remains unclear. They hired farmers from Punjab state (2 300 km from Anantapur) to drive the combine harvesters and harvest rice. [SOURCE: Page_201]

38 Before the combine harvester, the harvesting and threshing of rice required 50.2 man-days and 8.5 animal-days per ha. This was reduced to 0.36 man-days per ha with the combine harvester (calculated based on interviews). [SOURCE: Page_201]

39 We didn’t find values for the 1990’s but prices indicate an average price three times higher for combine harvesters (around 30 000 Rupees) than for tractors (7 000 to 10 000 Rupees) in 2015 (Madhusudan et al., 2018). [SOURCE: Page_201]

201 [SOURCE: Page_201]

Punjab was indeed one of the flagship States for rice and wheat production, where moto- mechanisation was much more thorough than in Andhra Pradesh State^40 (Madhusudan et al., 2018). Those Punjabi drivers harvested rice in their State (Punjab) in October, then followed the rice harvest in Andhra Pradesh in December-January then swung northwards up to Telangana which they reached in March, before coming back to Punjab. [SOURCE: Page_202]

The pursuit of moto-mechanisation enabled a further increase of labour productivity. On the whole, the labour productivity of rice was multiplied by 6 since the 1950’s. (Fig. 116). [SOURCE: Page_202]

Figure 116. Evolution of rice cultivation from 1950’s to today 2.1.1. Higher-powered tractors with PTO: moto-mechanisation of sowing and post-harvesting operations of groundnut In the 2000’s, the large holder farmers who had already invested in small tractors upgraded to higher-powered tractors of 30 to 60 hp. Those tractors could pull heavier implements such as 5-shank subsoilers (Appendix 22 for photo) and cultivators. But they could also transmit power to machines through their PTO (power take-off). With PTO, farmers could use automatic seed drills (Fig. 117) to sow groundnut and groundnut threshers (Fig. 118) to thresh groundnut. Groundnut is the only crop for which sowing can be moto-mechanised, as most of the vegetables were bought as small plants from local nurseries and rice was broadcasted. Being [SOURCE: Page_202]

40 By way of comparison, 20% of Indian tractors were found in Punjab state in 1982, while there were only 4% in Andhra Pradesh (Madhusudan et al., 2018, p. 8) [SOURCE: Page_202]

202 [SOURCE: Page_202]

the rainfed crop by default (even the irrigating farmers have part of their land under rainfed conditions where they grow groundnut), a few large holder farmers invested in seed drills. The investment was worthwhile as they could also rent the seed drill and groundnut threshers out to other farmers cultivating groundnut. [SOURCE: Page_203]

Figure 117. Automatic seed drill using the tractor PTO [SOURCE: Page_203]

Figure 118. Groundnut thresher operated by Power Take-Off [SOURCE: Page_203]

203 [SOURCE: Page_203]

2.1.1. Smallholder farmers growing rainfed groundnut where stone boulders remain: an impossible moto-mechanisation of land preparation and sowing operations Although more and more farmers used tractors and the associated implements, this was impossible where land had a high boulder density. Those boulders could not be removed with the power availability of tractors at the time. Backhoe loaders of higher horsepower, 75 hp, and excavators of 133 hp were required but these were unaffordable for all the non-irrigating farmers who had received rocky land on the wash pediment. They continued growing groundnut in rainfed conditions but keeping bulls to sow the seeds and prepare the land. In this way, groundnut seeds could be sown around boulders. [SOURCE: Page_204]

2.2. Sparing drop of water to irrigate more surfaces on the wash pediment 2.2.1. Drip irrigation of vegetables and sprinkler irrigation of groundnut Further drilling and pumping were encouraged by flat-rate electricity for irrigation. This was implemented under the mandate of Rajasekhar Reddy (YSR party) as Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh (2004-2009). With this new policy, electricity was available at the paltry sum of a few cents of Rs for six hours a day. The hours shifted every day or week and each village of the mandal had its own schedule. This is still in effect today where farmers are informed of the daily changes on a WhatsApp group. Under the mandate of Rajasekhar Reddy, a 90% subsidy was made available for the drip irrigation system. [SOURCE: Page_204]

The drip irrigation technique increased the pressure of the distribution of water and used less water per surface unit. A crop irrigated using the furrow irrigation system used approximately 40 mm/day of irrigation. With the drip irrigation technique, this value was reduced from 5 to 15 mm/day. If the yield of the borewell was too low, furrow irrigation was impossible, but with the water saving techniques of drip irrigation, irrigation could be carried out using less water. Those techniques were also less labour-intensive as they required only turning on the pump and the ball valves to create a manual shutoff in a section of the irrigation system. Closing and opening irrigation channels which was formerly carried out in the furrow irrigation system was no longer required, thus saving on labour (Table 11). [SOURCE: Page_204]

204 [SOURCE: Page_204]

However, the farms adopting those techniques did not consume less water. The use of sprinklers and a drip irrigation system in fact enabled the farmers to increase the surface under irrigation, a phenomenon known under the name of “rebound effect” (Venot et al., 2014). The smallholder farmers who had drilled borewells on the wash pediment increased their irrigated surface and vegetables had more importance in the groundnut-vegetable rotation. [SOURCE: Page_205]

2.2.2. Increasing the productivity of groundnut with sprinkler irrigation for farmers cultivating vegetables in rotation with groundnut Under Rajashekkar Reddy, 50 percent subsidies for the sprinkler irrigation system were also given. This system could be used on groundnut. For the smallholder farmers already irrigating on the wash pediment, they could fully irrigate their cropping system by successively using the drip irrigation system on vegetables and the sprinkler irrigation system on groundnut. Sprinklers used approximately 25 to 30 mm/day, a value in between the furrow irrigation (40 mm/day approximately) and the drip (5 to 15 mm/day). Sprinklers require more labour than the drip system as they have to be moved regularly to irrigate the whole field (Table 12). [SOURCE: Page_205]
