In those groundnut/vegetable cropping rotations, groundnut could be grown either in rainfed conditions or in irrigated conditions using sprinklers. In rainfed conditions, groundnut was sown in single lines (orsala in Telugu). In irrigated conditions, water could be supplied during the monsoon to fill the potential gaps in case of dry spell. The risks linked to climate were therefore controlled, except in the case of excess rains which could be particularly damageable at the end of the crop cycle – but this, was another problem. When groundnut was irrigated it was sown in crossed-row lines (irsala) (Fig. 119), thus increasing the seed density. This increased the land productivity of the groundnut crops compared to the rainfed conditions, but it demanded more labour. With crossed-row lines, weeding could not be done using bulls and the related implements, i.e. combine scuffles (regalaguntaka) and scuffle hoes (dantulus) (Fig. 120). [SOURCE: Page_206]

Figure 119. Sowing groundnut in crossed rows step by step (A : part of the plot which has not been sown yet ; B part of the plot which has been sown in crossed-rows ; C part of the plot which has been sown and levelled with a blade harrow) [SOURCE: Page_206]

206 [SOURCE: Page_206]

Figure 120. Groundnut sown in single lines and crossed-row lines [SOURCE: Page_207]

Some large holder farmers also started growing groundnut in irrigated conditions twice a year. With irrigation, good groundnut yields were ensured. As groundnut was a crop which benefitted from a Minium Guaranteed Price, profits were guaranteed. On the other hand, the income of farmers growing vegetables was much more uncertain as the volatility of vegetables, especially tomatoes, was very high. [SOURCE: Page_207]

Figure 121 presents the evolution of groundnut cultivation and its impact on land and labour productivity and energy consumption. We chose to represent only an annual cropping sequence, meaning that the interannual ley fallows in the 1950’s are not represented. [SOURCE: Page_207]

207 [SOURCE: Page_207]

Figure 121. The evolution of the cultivation of groundnut (1950’s – 2022) [SOURCE: Page_208]

208 [SOURCE: Page_208]

2.1. The White Revolution: structuration of the dairy sector and more inputs for higher milk production At the end of the 1990’s, the White Revolution was launched in the study area. This policy aimed at boosting the dairy sector by developing a network of dairy cooperatives and by structuring the dairy value chain (Dervillé et al., 2023). In the study area, this policy mainly consisted of building cooperative dairy collection centres, making crossbred dairy cows (Holstein Friesian or Jersey) and buffaloes available at subsidised prices and providing animal feed concentrates through the dairy collection centres. Two types of farmers benefited from the White Revolution. [SOURCE: Page_209]

The first type of farmers were the irrigating smallholder farmers with land in the wash depressions. Some of them already had local dairy cows and they replaced them with cross bred cows. They could make this change by changing the fodder calendar: they integrated Napier grass, an irrigated forage crop, in a three-year crop rotation with the rice which they were already growing on the hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions and glacis slopes. Napier grass was indeed a condition for the adoption of crossbred dairy cows. As Napier grass was irrigated, rearing cross bred dairy cows was only possible for the farmers with borewells. Those farmers usually bought between 2 or 3 cross bred cows (some farmers also bought hybrid buffaloes but this was less common). One cross-bred Holstein Friesian cow required approximately 0.03 ha of Napier Grass, which is cut every 1.5 months and cultivated for three years. Every day Napier grass was cut by hand, transported to the cow shed and chopped in a chaff cutter (Appendix 22 for photo). They were also fed on rice straw, groundnut hay, and manufactured feed concentrate which was made available at the dairy milk collection centres in each village. Those dairy animals were never taken out for grazing. As those crossbred dairy cow could withstand heat, they were kept in a shed with a ventilation system made of ceiling fan. This was particularly important in summer when the temperatures were too high. The crossbred cows produced twice as much milk as the local dairy cows fed on grass and groundnut hay in the 1950’s (Fig. 122). [SOURCE: Page_209]

Other farmers with only rainfed land also benefitted from the structuration of the dairy value chain. Although, because of lack of borewells, they could not rear cross bred cows or buffaloes, they could sell the milk of their local dairy cows to the village distribution centres. They also gave feed concentrate to their local cows. As they could not grow Napier, they cut wild grasses on field edges and along road sides. They also continued to herd their cows on grasslands, but only during the monsoon season. In summer, they gave them rice straw and [SOURCE: Page_209]

209 [SOURCE: Page_209]

groundnut hay. The milk production of those local dairy cows was increased compared to the one in the 1950’s when there was no feed concentrate and less dry fodder. Despite this, the milk champions were the crossbred dairy animals. Rearing local dairy cows was labour-intensive, mostly because of grazing and cutting grasses but it provided a regular income for the farmers who could, since the implementation of the dairy collection centres, sell the milk daily to the cooperatives. [SOURCE: Page_210]

Figure 122. Evolution of the diet and the milk production of a local dairy cow in the 1950’s and the dairy cattle today after changes from the Yellow, White and Green revolution [SOURCE: Page_210]

The White revolution also included the development of veterinary services in the villages and artificial insemination programs (Nair, 1985). Before the selling of bulls, the local dairy cows were reproduced with uncastrated bulls. With artificial insemination, reproduction [SOURCE: Page_210]

210 [SOURCE: Page_210]

was made at the local veterinary centres for both local dairy cows and buffaloes which were already present in some farms and also for the crossbred cows. The government dairy cooperatives, such as the Heritage cooperative, were rapidly replaced by private dairy companies (Dodla, Gayathri, Thirumala), whose competition was fierce. [SOURCE: Page_211]

2.2. Abandoning draft animals, an evolution which benefits pastoralists 2.2.1. Droughts: selling the superfluous draft animals The end of the 1990’s and the beginning of the 2000 were marked by repeated years with low rainfall (see chapter 1, Fig. 16), where the groundwater recharge was therefore lower than during other years. To illustrate this, we calculated the yearly net recharge of rainfed groundnut using the daily meteorological data of Anantapur since 1980 (Fig. 123). It shows a lower net recharge in 1999, 2000, 2002, 2003 and 2004. [SOURCE: Page_211]

Figure 123. Estimation of the variation of the net groundwater recharge of a rainfed groundnut crop between 1980 and 2019 With the increase in irrigated surfaces with the pump revolution, the level of the groundwater table also decreased, although the magnitude is not known. With the decline in the groundwater table due to the increase in irrigated surface and the lower rainfall, the first years of the 21st century were marked by drought which impacted farmers in various ways. In villages near tanks or near the highway, some farmers could not irrigate anymore because their borewells were not deep enough. The farmers with deeper borewells sold water to the ones who had no longer water in their own borewells by transporting the water in plastic water storage drums by tractor. This also happened in 2016 when another drought occurred. According to an interview one tank was sold for 800 Rs in 2016. Six families emigrated from Bandameedapalli (village near tank) to Gantlaparthi (village near river) because water was still available in the Gantlaparthi borewells. In the villages near rivers, water from borewells could still be extracted but the river had dried up for this first time since the Upper Pennar project. [SOURCE: Page_211]

211 [SOURCE: Page_211]

Due to low rainfall, grass resources were also under water stress and farmers had to go further and further away from the village to find grazing resources. It must also not be forgotten that since the 1950’s the draft animal population had increased, with the subsidies on bulls which accompanied the Land Reform. With the previous processes of moto-mechanisation of irrigation, land preparation, harvest and post-harvesting operations, the function of draft animals was reduced considerably and the selling of bulls had been pending for several years. Some farmers had already started selling their bulls but the drought at the beginning of the 21st century lead the rest of the farmers to sell them, even the most reluctant farmers who had not invested in tractors and borewells. [SOURCE: Page_212]

By the beginning of the 21st century, bulls were only of use for the non-irrigating farmers who had too many stone boulders on their land and also for crop weeding by all the farmers growing groundnut in rainfed conditions. The decline in the bull population went therefore hand in hand with the emergence of a production system composed of the few farmers who kept their pairs of bulls but who started to sell the animal workforce on all the other farms requiring bulls to weed their groundnut. Although those farmers with bulls were very few, they were key production systems for all the farms growing rainfed groundnut, which were the majority of the agricultural population. To feed those bulls, those farmers also started renting small areas under borewells from irrigating categories. Those land rents are done just for the duration of the crop and cost approximately 20 000 Rs/ha. The farmers with bulls rent half a ha of irrigated land to grow rice and produce rice straw to feed their bulls with. [SOURCE: Page_212]

2.2.2. Redirecting the flows of groundnut hay With, on the one hand, farmers selling draft animals, and on the other hand, production of groundnut hay maintained at the same level as when the bulls were there, there was a surplus of groundnut hay. The surplus of groundnut hay (Fig. 124) was bought by pastoralists during the summer season. This enabled them to stop going on a transhumance to Bellary in summer. To endure the dry season, groundnut hay replaced the Bellary pastures and crop stubble. The use of groundnut hay in summer was a first step in intensification of the pastoral sheep farming system (Fig. 124). At the same time, the use of medicine decreased considerably the mortality of sheep. With a higher growth rate and feed available to maintain the flock, the sheep population increased more rapidly from the end of the 1990’s. [SOURCE: Page_212]

212 [SOURCE: Page_212]

Figure 124. A truck hidden by a huge heap of groundnut hay Source: Photo taken by Cassandre Aimon in August 2022 [SOURCE: Page_213]

Figure 125. Evolution of the diet and production of the pastoral sheep farming systems from 1950’s to the beginning of the 21st century [SOURCE: Page_213]

213 [SOURCE: Page_213]

3. Closing and opening new areas 3.1. Enclosing areas on the wash pediment: fruit plantations and the race to pump water deeper and deeper 3.1.1. Drilling deeper borewells to plant fruit plantations: the small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming The farmers already growing irrigated crops on the wash pediment, i.e. irrigating smallholder farmers and large holder farmers, had a higher investment capacity than the non- irrigating categories. From the beginning of the 2000’s, they started growing fruit plantations, mostly sweet lime, pomegranate, banana and grapes vines. The fruit trees require water all year round. They are perennial plantations of 15 to 20 years (except for banana which is grown for three years in rotation with rice) and are costly to put in place: cost of the trees, manure, chemical fertilisers and drip irrigation system. Those farmers already had medium-depth borewells but with the possibility of borewells not working because of a seasonal decline in the groundwater table, there was a risk to lose the fruit plantations. This entailed that the farmers engaging in fruit plantations had to drill deeper, and therefore more costly borewells (Fig. 126). This enabled the farmers to secure their access to groundwater all year round and not lose their access to irrigation in case of drought. Those borewells had a depth between 150 and 200 metres (Fig. 126). They were more expensive because of the increased depth (Appendix 24) and were only affordable to the wealthier farmers. [SOURCE: Page_214]

Figure 126. Drilling deep borewells for fruit plantations [SOURCE: Page_214]

214 [SOURCE: Page_214]

The smallholder farmers who already had a medium-depth borewell and were already growing rice in the wash depressions and groundnut and vegetables on the wash pediment, tried to drill a deep borewell. If it was successful, they could irrigate a small fruit plantation, one ha at the maximum. The rest of their land was left rainfed and they continued growing groundnut. Those new small-scale fruit growers kept their dairy crossbred cows most of them had. The dairy cows were fed with Napier Grass grown on tiny patches of land near their borewell, and also on the groundnut hay they produced on their rainfed land. The fruit plantations were irrigated and manure was valuable to help the soil retain more water. Those plantations were irrigated using the drip irrigation system. With the PTO of tractors, fertilisers were directly distributed through the drip irrigation system (Fig. 127). [SOURCE: Page_215]

Figure 127. Fertigation: application of fertilisers in water tanks through the irrigation system using the tractor Power Take-Off [SOURCE: Page_215]

Those fruit plantations remained highly demanding in labour. For pruning and harvesting fruit trees, small-scale fruit growers and large-scale fruit growers hired batches of labour from outside the village. Those labourers were usually from landless categories or non- irrigating categories from other villages in Anantapur district. The daily labour wages were higher (500 Rs) than the ones of hired labour from the village (250 to 300 Rs), as they sometimes came from villages 30 or 40-km way from the study area. [SOURCE: Page_215]

215 [SOURCE: Page_215]

The small-scale fruit growers were also assisted financially in their investment by State and Central policies. From 2014-2015, fruit plantation was also highly encouraged by the Central and State government as shows the implementation of the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH). This scheme aimed at developing the production of fruits and vegetables in India by setting up fruit tree nurseries, subsidising fruit plants and drip irrigation systems. The subsidies were allocated by both Central and the State Government at 60 and 40% respectively (Gov. India, 2022b). Andhra Pradesh was a focal point of this scheme as the aim was to make this State the “fruit bowl” of South India. [SOURCE: Page_216]

3.1.2. Expansion of fruit plantations: the large-scale fruit growers The large holder farmers also started planting large fruit plantations. They could drill many deep borewells on their land, and gradually converted all their land into large fruit plantations. They abandoned the dairy animals they had, as they no longer needed them to generate an income. Those fruit plantations were enclosed and therefore were not accessible to grazing animals. To replace the fertility transfers and recycling formerly ensured by livestock and to improve the water retention properties of the soil, they had to buy manure to put at the base of the fruit trees (Fig. 128). [SOURCE: Page_216]

Figure 128. Manure at the base of sweet lime trees [SOURCE: Page_216]

Manure was insufficient in the village to meet the needs of the fruit plantations: many categories had abandoned livestock by now and manure was rarely sold in between farms of the village. The large-scale fruit growers had the financial capacity to buy large quantities of [SOURCE: Page_216]

216 [SOURCE: Page_216]

manure. As the quantities were huge, 25 tons of fresh manure per ha, they had to buy it from large dairy farms which were found in the neighbouring district of Nandyal (Andhra Pradesh), 200-km away from the village. Buying manure was therefore very costly, from both the cost of the matter and the transport. [SOURCE: Page_217]

Little by little, the number of fruit plantations grew. Large-scale farmers planted 6 ha or more on the wash pediment, especially along the Bangalore-Anantapur highway as shows the evolution between 2014 and 2023 of Fig. 129. As the large plantations were located on the highway, the fruits can be easily dispatched to wholesale fruit markets when harvested. [SOURCE: Page_217]

Most of the large-scale fruit growers now have large plantations of grape vines, pomegranate trees or sweet lime trees. Those fruit trees were irrigated using drip irrigation. Due to continuous irrigation, a salt crust tended to form on the red soils where fruit trees are grown. To address this salinisation problem, large-scale fruit growers rented trucks and backhoe loaders to excavate tank soil from neighbouring villages and applied the tank soil at the base of the fruit trees. Although access to tank soil was possible to all, the means to extract it were only affordable for the large-scale fruit growers. The renting of backhoe loaders and excavators were indeed very costly. With the large fruit plantations, there was a return to tank soil excavation^41 , but this time only made by the one category: the large-scale fruit growers. [SOURCE: Page_217]

The large-scale fruit growers also had land in the wash depressions, on which they used to cultivate rice. The income from fruit plantations being much higher than the income from the rice, they stopped cultivating their land in the wash depressions. Those areas were abandoned and reverted to shrubland, especially the invasive species of shrub called Prosopis Juliflora and also the invasive weed Parthenium hysterophus^42, which develops well in the grey hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions. The short dry season was not even enough to break the development cycle of the weed as it also tolerates moisture stress (Kohli and Rani, 1994). On the wash pediment, the continuous irrigation in the fruit plantations also favours the development of the Parthenium hysterophus weed, which has good tolerance of saline conditions (Hegde and Patil, 1982) created by continuous irrigation. With continuous irrigation the cycle of development of the weed is never broken. To remove this weed, large-scale fruit growers also started to use glyphosate-based herbicides. [SOURCE: Page_217]

41 In the 1950’s, all the farmers with bulls used to excavate tank silt using human and animal power. Those transfers stopped with the development of groundnut. 42 The Parthenium hysterophus weed is also locally called the Congress grass, as it is an invasive grass which was introduced when India was ruled by the Congress party. [SOURCE: Page_217]

217 [SOURCE: Page_217]

Figure 129. Fruit plantations (in light green) along the Bangalore-Anantapur highway [SOURCE: Page_218]

Source: satellite image from Google Earth, 2014 and mars 2023 [SOURCE: Page_218]

218 [SOURCE: Page_218]

From the 2010’s, investors also started planting fruit orchards on the wash pediment. These investors were of two types. Some of them were related to the study area as they were descendants of large holder farmers who had land on the wash pediment. They had grown up in Anantapur city, but with the lucrative development of fruit plantation, they decided to use the land of their ancestors to grow fruit plantations on the wash pediment. The second type of investors had no connections with the area. They were people who were born and raised in cities such as Anantapur and Bangalore. They started to buy or rent land to plant fruit plantations, especially along the Bangalore-Anantapur highway. If those investors rented land, they usually chose already borewell-drilled land as they preferred not to take the risk of having a failed borewell. Some of that land even already had fruit plantations in place. However, the land rent of those already drilled areas was sky-high: in 2022, the price of renting one ha including a borewell and a fruit plantation in, along the Bangalore-Anantapur highway, was 250 000 Rs per year. [SOURCE: Page_219]

With more and more borewells being drilled in the wash pediment, especially concentrated near the Bangalore-Anantapur highway, the risk of too close borewells was to create a cone of depression (Fig. 130). When borewells are drilled in close proximity, a competition between the two starts, with the deeper borewells lowering the level of water of the neighbouring shallower borewells (Fig. 130). Although the level of the groundwater rises again after pumping has stopped (Maréchal et al., 2002), a strategy is to deepen borewells to chase declining levels of groundwater (Shah, 2012). The wealthier irrigating farmers would invest in drilling borewells deeper and deeper in a desperate race with their neighbour to capture the remaining groundwater (Blakeslee et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_219]

Figure 130. Cone of depression from pumping one borehole at a given flow rate (Qp) Source : (Charpentier, 2020) [SOURCE: Page_219]

219 [SOURCE: Page_219]

3.1.3. Pushing stones around the rocky hills: releasing new cultivable areas with fossil energy Some of the new small-scale fruit growers had many boulders on part of their rainfed land. This was also the case for large-scale fruit growers, who had planted most of their land with fruit trees, but some parts remained covered with boulders sporadically. With the income from fruit plantations, those farmers had become wealthier and could rent backhoe loaders (Fig. 131), locally known under the name of their brand, “JCB’s”. Those backhoe loaders had a higher power (75 hp) than the local tractors and could be used to remove most of the big boulders. However, the bigger boulders had to be removed with even higher-powered machinery, excavators of 133 hp. They were even more costly to rent (Table 13). In addition to the renting of backhoe loaders and excavators, farmers also had to hire labour from the village to remove the small and medium-size stones. New cultivable areas were released (Fig. 132). [SOURCE: Page_220]

220 [SOURCE: Page_220]

Figure 132. Pushing stones on the wash pediment 3.2. Migration and opening new grazing lands: intensification of sheep farming systems 3.2.1. A high demand for mutton: emergence of sheep fattening systems In the area, the sheep population has increased since the 1950’s. In the archetype village there are more herds today than in the 1950’s and each herd is larger than in the 1950’s. The quantity of sheep meat produced and consumed has increased since 1961 on country-level (Fig. 133). The production has remained mostly orientated towards internal consumption, the share of exports being still very low (Fig. 133). [SOURCE: Page_221]

Figure 133. Production of sheep meat produced and consumed in India or exported since 1961 and average consumption per capita Production: C. Hemingway; Data source: FAOSTAT [SOURCE: Page_221]

221 [SOURCE: Page_221]

We know from interviews with butchers that the price of sheep meat has heavily increased over the last decades, entailed by an increase of the consumption of mutton (Fig. 133), therefore favouring a flourishing of butcher’s shops in Anantapur city. Although mutton has always been a luxury for rural population (John Shortt, 1885, p. 94), there has been an increasing demand from the growing Indian urban middle-class. Mutton was consumed in Hindu and Muslim festivals (Bakrid, Sankharati, Dasara…). The Hindu religion advocating vegetarians, the Brahmins -one of the most abiding and pure caste- usually do not cook meat at home. The development of festivities (weddings, engagements, baby shower and birthday parties) in cities such as Anantapur took place in specially designed wedding halls and western-style hotels was associated with a shift in food preparation which was previously done mostly home and now prepared and served by caterers (Cwiertka and Walraven, 2002, p. 51). Perhaps this new configuration reinforced the importance of mutton for festivities which also increased its value over the last decades. Imports of mutton have always been low (FAOSTAT) but this might change with the new free trade agreement between and Australia (ECTA, Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement) which has decided to suppress the 30% tariff on Indian imports of Australian lamb (Gov. of Australia, 2022; Gray, 2023). With the increase in the price of mutton, some non-irrigating farmers started to buy batches of 20 to 30 male lambs from pastoralists in the village or from the livestock market in Anantapur (Fig. 134). Those lambs were bought at three months old, and fattened till they were four months. They were then sold either to other village inhabitants for celebrations or to town-based butchers. Those butchers usually came directly to the village to buy the fattened lambs in batches. The lambs were fed on grasslands, groundnut hay and feed concentrate such as groundnut and chickpea cake, which were bought from shops in Anantapur. Unlike the pastoral sheep farming system, male lambs were kept at night in a small enclosure next to the house. Night droppings could therefore be collected and sold. [SOURCE: Page_222]

222 [SOURCE: Page_222]

Figure 134. Selling sheep at Anantapur livestock market [SOURCE: Page_223]

3.2.2. Intensification of the pastoral sheep farming system: benefitting from abandoned areas of the wash pediment and sowing horse gram forage With the increase in sheep population on the one hand, and the shrinking grazing land from the shortening of ley fallows and the apparition of fruit enclosures on the other, fodder resources for grazing animals became scarcer. At the same time as the development of fruit plantations on the wash pediment and the abandonment of land in the wash depressions, another dynamic emerged which freed some areas on the wash pediment (Fig. 135). This was linked to the migration of some large holder farmers who had not planted fruit plantations. Indeed, there were two types of descendants of large holder farmers. Both types had land on the wash depressions and the wash pediment but in different proportions. Most of those who had more land on the wash pediment than on the wash depressions engaged in fruit plantations. Some of the others, with most of their land in the wash depressions, and a smaller part on the wash pediment, left the area and the agricultural sector from the end of the beginning of the 2000’s to work in the banking, software or real estate sectors in cities such as Anantapur, Hyderabad, [SOURCE: Page_223]

223 [SOURCE: Page_223]

Bangalore or sometimes even Chennaï. Their land on the wash pediment was therefore abandoned and they made valuable pockets of grazing land for the sheep. In the wash depressions, their abandoned land was progressively encroached by the Prosopis Juliflora weed. [SOURCE: Page_224]

Figure 135. Two concomitant dynamics from the 2000’s: closing and opening areas on the wash pediment and abandoning the wash depressions [SOURCE: Page_224]

In the wash pediment, those areas were valuable grazing areas for the sheep of the pastoralists. The population of sheep indeed had increased since the 1950’s and grazing areas decreased because of the shortening of ley fallows and also the closing of areas from enclosed fruit plantations. With some descendants of large holder farmers leaving for the cities, the sheep could graze their abandoned land. The grazing of those areas also prevented them being reverted to shrubland. [SOURCE: Page_224]

That abandoned land was mostly grazed in the monsoon season. But in the winter season, when the rain had stopped, grazing resources were still scarce. During the course of the 2010’s, the tension between the mutton demand on the one hand, and the available fodder resources on the other, was such that pastoralists started to sow horse gram forage to feed their sheep in the winter season (from January to March). Horse gram was sown on the rainfed land of pastoralists (Fig. 136). Some pastoralists with large herds, in order to sow a few more has of horse gram, also rented land from large holder farmers who had left. With horse gram forage, new fodder resources were provided from the months of January to March, thus easing the tensions of the availability of fodder resources. In summer, the pastoralists continued to buy groundnut hay from non-irrigating farmers. Horse gram was a nutritive forage resource and adding horse gram in winter increased the level of nutrition. This decreased the seasonality of breeding even more, as ovarian cycles were maintained for a longer period than in the pastoral sheep farming [SOURCE: Page_224]

224 [SOURCE: Page_224]

systems of the 1950’s-1990’s, when sheep were entirely fed on grazed grass and on-field crop residues. The above reasons, along with the use of medicine to cure sheep, explained a higher reproduction rate and growth of herds. However, the feed intake was still very low and the animals were still sold at a young age. The body weight of the adult animals was very low compared to other countries (35 kg at most for rams). [SOURCE: Page_225]

Figure 136. Evolution of the diet and production of the pastoral sheep farming systems from 1950’s to today [SOURCE: Page_225]

225 [SOURCE: Page_225]

3.2.3. The disappearance of the leather value chain Pastoralists used to also sell the skin of dead animals to Anantapur market to merchants working in the leather value chain (see chapter 3). Since the British colonisation, India had been an exporter of mostly raw hides and semi-tanned leather (Sujatha, 2002). Exports of hides and skins had considerably increased between 1862 and 1902 and 76% of the total material was exported to the UK in the beginning of the 20Th century in a half-manufactured state i.e. dressed skins and hides (Appendix 18) (Chatterton, 1982, p. 10). Under the government of Narendra Modi (since 2014), a campaign named “Make in India” was launched to refocus and relocalise the transformation of leather in India. The program “Make in India” mainly consisted of 1) levying an export duty only on raw hides, skins, and wet-blue leather, 2) establishing a duty-free import of raw material and 3) instating a customs duty on the import of finished leather products. [SOURCE: Page_226]

On the other hand, there were other policies which went in the opposite directions and put a blow to the leather industry. In 2017, the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi introduced a ban prohibiting the trade of cattle for slaughter. This also included buffaloes which were formerly used for leather, and also meat. Much of the leather sector work in India was informal and carried out by the Muslim community. Under the government of Narendra Modi -Hindu nationalist government-, some of those illegal abattoirs were closed down, and only licensed abattoirs were allowed. The ban and the closing down of abattoirs is believed to have cut off a major part of the country’s leather industry supply chain. Although this should have made the prices of leather go up, it was difficult to get more information on this politically delicate and touchy issue. We know from interviews with pastoralists and merchants that the price of skins and hides has decreased. For pastoralists, it was no longer worth selling the skin to Anantapur. We also know that the number of merchants in Anantapur city involved in the leather trade has sharply declined and those who are still in activity buy the skins from butchers. [SOURCE: Page_226]

226 [SOURCE: Page_226]

Conclusion of chapter 5: Since the 1990’s, the Green Revolution and the pump revolution have succeeded in making it possible to extract groundwater deeper and deeper. With the access to fossil fuels to extract water and prepare land, the population of draft animals has gradually declined. With the drip irrigation system, irrigated surfaces also increased. The Green Revolution was also a fertile ground for the implementation of the White Revolution and a new dairy livestock farming system emerged composed of crossbred dairy cows fed on irrigated fodder and feed concentrates. From the 2000’s, the wealthier categories, already engaged in irrigation, started to plant fruit trees. Today investors are starting to come to the area in order to extend the area under fruit plantations. Until approximately 2010, the borewell drilling tendency was rather towards a substitution of types of irrigation (dug wells under the kavili system replaced by borewells with electric submersible pumps). From the 2010’s the areas under borewell irrigation have increased (Fig. 137). However, this development of borewell irrigation was still limited in the area, compared to other areas in India. Today only 15% of the surface of the archetype village is irrigated. The development of the dairy farming systems was not as important as in other areas in India because it was based on access to irrigation which was already not as widespread as in other areas of India (Lucas, 2014). Most of the farmers still cultivate groundnut in rainfed conditions. With the decreasing of ley fallows, the grazing areas for sheep have declined. With the increase in sheep population, the grazing intensity on those grasslands has increased, with areas grazed three times during the monsoon season instead of only once in the 1950’s. The pastoralists have managed to find ways of intensifying their sheep farming systems, despite the grazing resources becoming scarcer. In summer, they have started to buy the surplus groundnut hay which was formerly given to bulls. They have started sowing horse gram forage which is grazed during the winter. They have also benefited from the migration of some descendants of large holder farmers, as new grazing pockets of land were released on the wash pediment. [SOURCE: Page_227]

CHAPTER 6: Every drop counts: sweat, diesel, rain and groundwater [SOURCE: Page_229]

229 [SOURCE: Page_229]

In this chapter we present an overview of the cropping (scale of the plot) and livestock farming systems (scale of the herd) which compose the agrarian system in 2022. We analyse those cropping and livestock farming systems in economic terms (value added, labour productivity) and in metabolic terms (energy and water consumption). [SOURCE: Page_230]

1.    Valuing labour and land 1.1. Crop and livestock diversity of the village in 2022 Behind the general dryness and flatness of the village, there is a diversity of land use and cropping systems. Occasional patches of lush green from the irrigated crops break the brown, pale green and reddish shades of the red soils and rainfed crops. Approximately 60% of the land in the archetype village is under cultivation. Nearly three quarters of the cropped area is under rainfed crops, chiefly represented by groundnut. The remaining quarter of the cropped area corresponds to irrigated crops: fruit plantations, rice, vegetables in rotation with groundnut or Napier Grass. About 40% of the area is permanently grazed. Long ley fallow have disappeared and short-ley fallows in dry season remain in non-irrigated cropping systems. 2% of the land, located in the tank command area has been abandoned by cropping activities and is never grazed. Those abandoned areas in the wash depressions are encroached with the Prosopis Juliflora invasive weed. The livestock population is very diverse but mostly dominated by sheep. Most of the dairy animals are crossbred cows and the population of bulls has declined to 5 pairs since the 1950’s (Fig. 139). [SOURCE: Page_230]

Figure 139. Land use, type of crops and livestock population in the archetype village in 2022 [SOURCE: Page_230]

230 [SOURCE: Page_230]

1.2. A diversity of cropping and livestock farming systems based on unequal access to factors of production and agroecological potentialities The choices of crops and livestock by the farmers are not mere matter of likings and tastes of the farmers. The agricultural orientations are the result of both the history and agroecological potentialities of the landscape units: the agrarian history of the area has shown how difficult drilling borewells and removing stone boulders is (chapters 3 to 5). The access to factors of production determines the use of these landscape units, the most noteworthy being here the access to land and access to capital to drill borewells. Table 14 presents an overview of the types of land associated with each main landscape unit and Figure 140 gives the location in space. [SOURCE: Page_231]

Landscape unit           Main characteristics            Type of land use Rocky hills              Stone boulders and shrubs       Grazing areas for sheep and goats Wash pediment            Red loamy soils with open Perennial irrigated cropping systems (fruit grass steppe, a few rocks may plantations); annual irrigated cropping be found here and there         systems    (vegetables,   groundnut, rice); rainfed crops (groundnut, red gram, grazed horse gram); grazing areas for sheep, goats, bulls and dairy animals Wash       depressions Grey hydromorphic soils           Abandonned land (overrun by Prosopis and glacis slopes                                        Juliflora) ; Rice fields which may be in rotation with Napier grass Table 14. Localisation of the types of land use within the main landscape units Most of the crops are exclusively orientated towards food production except for rice and groundnut which provide both feed (groundnut hay, rice straw) and food. Napier grass and horse gram are the only forage crops, i.e. only grown and used for livestock. In this chapter we will see how the cropping and livestock orientations are mostly explained by the type of land, access to irrigation, labour availability and investment capacity. [SOURCE: Page_231]

N.B.: wash depressions enlarged for more clarity – should be smaller, total 4% of the territory In order to provide a synthetic overview of the diversity and potentialities of the cropping and livestock rearing practices, we chose to model contrasted choices. For instance, even though grape vines are grown on a tiny portion of the village territory, i.e. 1% of the cropped area (Fig. 139), modelling this system is informative as it represents the climax of investment in terms of agricultural development. As a reminder, the cropping system is a set of plots cultivated in the same way (Cochet and Devienne, 2006) i.e. with the same crop rotations and associations and the same sequence of cultivation operations (chapter 1). Cropping systems can be classed in three broad families: rainfed cropping systems, the annual irrigated cropping systems and the perennial irrigated cropping systems (Fig. 139). The livestock farming systems are less widespread in the production systems: owning livestock is no longer a sine qua none condition for farming. Livestock has been abandoned by some, and adopted by others. The livestock farming systems of today are more specialised than in the past, each of them producing not more than two of the following products: milk, manure, draft power, meat. The reliance on grasslands varies from one livestock farming system to another, with one no-grazing system, i.e. the crossbred dairy farming system, and a continuum of more or less grass-based livestock farming systems (Table 15). The domestic animals are reared with very diverse means of production: organisation of labour, workload and fixed capital (Table 15). As explained in [SOURCE: Page_232]

232 [SOURCE: Page_232]

chapter 1, we rely on the livestock farming system concept which is defined by 1) the type and breed of animals, 2) the size of the herd, 3) a succession of tasks requiring a particular type of labour organisation and a number of workers, 4) a type of feed. The livestock farming systems provide a range of products (milk, meat, manure, draft power) quantified by a yield and price, for a particular level of production. Leather is no longer a product as it was previously. All the livestock farming systems are based on family labour or mutualised labour in the case of the pastoral sheep farming system. Labour is no longer hired to rear livestock, as the large holder farmers used to in the 1950’s (see chapter 3). We identified six main types of livestock farming systems in the study area: [SOURCE: Page_233]

1.3. Economic assumptions and indications on calculations The creation of wealth from cropping and livestock activities is quantified at farm and herd level through three main economic indicators: gross product, value added, labour productivity. Apart from the physical labour productivity, those economic indicators were not used in the chapters dedicated to the history of the area, as there was no economic analysis carried out for the 1950’s period. Those indicators were not explained in chapter 1 (Methodology) and will be explained in this chapter. This chapter focuses on the technical and economic results of each cropping and livestock farming systems, i.e. at plot and herd level. As yields and prices fluctuate, we relied on values representative of a ‘normal’ year, neither especially good nor especially bad. Except when the interannual variability is necessary to understand choices or the vulnerability of farmers, we present cases in ‘normal’ years. [SOURCE: Page_234]

Gross product (GP) is the annual value produced from cropping and livestock-related activities. The production values were calibrated on local product prices, thereby providing for self- consumed products (by family labour and animals) a price that farmers would have to pay for the product if they had not produced it. The product prices are farm-gate prices collected during interviews with farmers and are valid for the year 2022 (Appendix 25). [SOURCE: Page_234]

The gross product includes both products sold and self-consumed, as it represents was has been produced through the agricultural labour process. The gross product of crops, GPcrops, is a function of crop yield (kg/ha) (Eq. 14). Yields include any food (grains, pulses, fruits and vegetables) and feed products (straw, hay, fodder). As food and feed prices vary throughout the year, we chose for each cropping season the average price (Rs/kg) at sales time. GPlivestock is a function of the Animal Equivalent Unit (AEqU), which is either a female and its progeny or an adult male for livestock farming system with only males (such as pairs of bulls). GP livestock accounting relies on the estimation of the animal-products sold or consumed by humans e.g. milk, meat, or re-used on farm e.g. manure, or outsourced to other farms e.g. draught power. For all the products except draught power, it is a function of animal yield (kg or liters/animal) (Eq. 15) [SOURCE: Page_234]

GPcrops = ∑𝑖 𝑌𝑖𝑒𝑙𝑑𝑐𝑟𝑜𝑝 𝑖 . 𝑆𝑎𝑙𝑒 𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒𝑐𝑟𝑜𝑝 𝑖 [SOURCE: Page_234]

Equation 14. Calculation of the gross product from crops GPlivestock = ∑𝑖 𝑌𝑖𝑒𝑙𝑑𝑎𝑛𝑖𝑚𝑎𝑙 𝑖 . 𝑆𝑎𝑙𝑒 𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑑𝑢𝑐𝑡 𝑖 [SOURCE: Page_234]

Equation 15. Calculation of the gross product from livestock [SOURCE: Page_234]

234 [SOURCE: Page_234]

The gross value added (GVA) corresponds to the gross product minus the intermediary costs (IC) (Eq. 16). Intermediary costs (IC) are goods and services used as inputs in the production process (Table 16). [SOURCE: Page_235]

GVA = GP - IC expressed in Rs/ha for cropping systems, and in Rs/AEqU43 for livestock farming systems Equation 16. Gross value added Intermediary costs Livestock farming system                                      Veterinary costs, Feed Cropping system                    Fertilisers, seeds, crop protection products, electricity for pumping water for irrigation, fuel to make any engines run Table 16. List of intermediary costs for cropping and livestock farming systems The net value added (NVA) takes into account the wear and tear of the equipment and buildings, i.e. the depreciation of fixed assets (DEP). Strictly speaking, the depreciation of fixed assets can only be estimated at farm-level because some equipment, is used both for cropping and livestock rearing activities^44. In this chapter we will only consider the gross value added at the scale of the cropping system and livestock farming system. [SOURCE: Page_235]

Based on the gross value added, we will calculate two types of labour productivity indicators. Labour productivity indicators will be calculated in this chapter based on the gross value added. Daily physical labour productivity is the quantity of a product (in kg or litres) per time unit, typically man-days (Eq. 17). [SOURCE: Page_235]

𝑸𝒖𝒂𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒕𝒚 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒅𝒖𝒄𝒕 Labourprod-phys = 𝐌𝐚𝐧−𝐃𝐚𝐲𝐬 [SOURCE: Page_235]

Equation 17. Economic labour productivity [SOURCE: Page_235]

Daily economic labour productivity is the value added per number of man-days. It measures the daily output for a cropping system or livestock farming system (Eq. 18): [SOURCE: Page_235]

𝑮𝑽𝑨 Labourprod-eco = 𝐌𝐚𝐧−𝐃𝐚𝐲𝐬 [SOURCE: Page_235]

Equation 18. Economic labour productivity [SOURCE: Page_235]

43 AEqU: Animal Equivalent Unit, e.g. an adult cow or an adult ewe, and their progeny, or a bull. 44 A tractor for instance is used to plough a rice field which will be at the same time a cropping system but also produce straw which is an input of a livestock farming system. [SOURCE: Page_235]

235 [SOURCE: Page_235]

2. An archipelago of irrigated crops in an ocean of rainfed vegetation Most of the cropped area is under rainfed crops: 42% of the village archetype is under rainfed crops, dominated by groundnut, while only 15% of the area is cropped with irrigated crops (Fig. 139). [SOURCE: Page_236]

2.1. An ocean of rainfed crops 2.1.1. Rainfed groundnut: betting on the rain Groundnut is the main crop of the area. Except for pastoralists who can grow horse gram on their rainfed land, groundnut is the default option for farmers who have no borewells. It is grown either as a monocrop or associated with rows of red gram. It is mostly grown in rainfed conditions. A small portion of the groundnut pods is kept for household consumption (approximately 80 kgs) and for sowing the next crop. The rest is sold to middlemen. [SOURCE: Page_236]

Drought stress severely affects the growth of root and the flowering which makes the cultivation of groundnut in rainfed conditions a real gamble. Pod yields can vary from 1 to 3 tons per ha approximately (Fig. 141) according to the rain variability. 2.5 to 3 tonnes of groundnut hay can be expected per ha, which is sold to farmers with livestock when the farm has no livestock itself. Too much rain may also occur at the end of the cycle in November, which can also damage both the groundnut pods and the groundnut hay. [SOURCE: Page_236]

Figure 141. Variability of groundnut pod yields Land preparation, sowing and threshing are usually moto-mechanised, but weeding and harvesting is either manual or done using both animal and human muscle power and represents a heavy workload (Fig. 142). Farmers apply pesticides four times in the crop cycle against thrips and the vector insects transmitting the groundnut rosette virus. Pesticides are applied with PTO (Power Take-Off) sprayers connected to tractors or backpack sprayers. The types of pesticides vary, from insecticides against larvae (such as Chloranthraniliprole-based insecticides) to those targeting full-grown insects, usually pyrethroid pesticides. [SOURCE: Page_236]

236 [SOURCE: Page_236]

Figure 142. Labour calendar for rainfed groundnut [SOURCE: Page_237]

2.1.2. Horsegram pasture-cropping system: taking zero risks Horsegram is sown on rainfed land towards the end of the monsoon, around October. The only expenses are seeds, the renting of the cultivator to prepare land and an automatic tractor-drawn seed drill. No weeding is done and the crop is directly grazed by sheep in January and February. It is therefore a low-cost and low-labour crop but which can only serve the purpose of feeding sheep. [SOURCE: Page_237]

2.1.3. Red gram: a highly moto-mechanised cropping system The farmers with only rainfed land and no livestock usually grow groundnut in rainfed conditions. However, a few of them, who have a part-time job such as running a tea shop or working at the dairy collection centre, grow mono-cropped red gram, also known as pigeon pea or Tur. All the cultivation operations are moto-mechanised, as show the very low amount of man-days per ha on Figure 143, i.e. less than 1 man-day per ha every month. Red gram is a leguminous crop and has the capacity to fix nitrogen. It does not require any fertilisers but pesticides are necessary against pod borers. The plant adapts well to the red soils of the wash pediment even when they are pebbly. The variety is the flavus variety with yellow flowers. It is sown at the beginning of the monsoon (June-July) and harvested in winter (January- February) (Fig. 143). It is a drought-tolerant crop with a deep root system which improves the soil. It is a key ingredient of the local dahl, a lentil soup. Andhra Pradesh has launched subsidy schemes for promoting red gram cultivation and the seeds are sold at a guaranteed price of 55 ₹ per kg. The cultivation of this crop is appealing as it requires no hired labour: it is mostly moto-mechanised, even for weeding. As the plants are sown with wider space between rows than groundnut, it allows a tractor to pass between the rows with a blade harrow. Manual [SOURCE: Page_237]

237 [SOURCE: Page_237]

weeding at the foot of the crops may also be carried out by family workers but it can be done progressively and over a longer period, unlike groundnut. The crop is harvested using a harvesting machine. However, yields are usually low because of damage caused by pests. The crop does not provide any by-products for cattle and buffalo. Leaves can however be browsed by sheep and goats after the harvest. [SOURCE: Page_238]

Figure 143. Labour calendar for red gram The irrigated crops are in minority compared to the rainfed crops. They are explained in the following sections. We begin with the annual irrigated crops. [SOURCE: Page_238]

2.2. Islets of irrigated groundnut, vegetables and rice (wash pediment) 2.2.1. The rice cropping systems: rice grain and paddy straw Rice is grown on small patches of land, either in rotation with groundnut on the red loamy soils of the wash pediment, or once a year on the grey hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions. The only farms growing rice on the wash pediment (in rotation with groundnut) are the ones that have livestock and need the rice straw to feed their animals. The only farms growing rice in the wash depressions are farms with dairy farming or farms having much land in the wash depressions. The latter are descendants of large holder farmers of the 1950’s. They have no livestock, grow rice in the wash depressions and rainfed groundnut on the wash pediment. [SOURCE: Page_238]

For farms producing rice, part of the rice grain is kept for family consumption and the rest is sold. The technical itinerary of rice on the red loamy soils is different from when it is cultivated in the tank command area. The main differences are summarised in the table below (Table 17). In the wash depressions, rice is grown either in rotation with Napier Grass (farms with dairy farming) or with one or two rice crop cycles in rotation with a ley fallow during summer (farms with no livestock). On the wash pediment, rice is grown in rotation with groundnut (Table 17). [SOURCE: Page_238]

238 [SOURCE: Page_238]

Cropping systems                 Rice/groundnut                     Rice/rice/ley fallow (1 year) or rice/ley fallow (1 year) or rice/Napier grass (3 years) Landscape unit                   Wash pediment                                     Wash depressions -red loamy soils-                         (tank command area, glacis slopes) -grey hydromorphic soils- [SOURCE: Page_239]

Land preparation        Tilling with cage wheels (3 times)                   Tilling with cage wheels (twice) Fertilisation        Fertilisation + : rotation with groundnut:   Fertilisation +++ (no crop rotation with leguminous no fertilisation before transplanting        crop) DAP before transplanting; after transplanting: higher quantity of DAP, urea and ammonium sulphate Irrigation need                        +++                                                  ++ More evaporation                                    Less evaporation from red soils which have a water           from grey hydromorphic soils which have a higher holding capacity of 1.7 mm/cm                    water holding capacity: 1.8 mm/cm) Expected yield                 4.9 tonnes/ha (grain)                               3.7 tonnes/ha (grain) (in FW)                        5.4 tonnes/ha (straw)                               4 tonnes/ha (straw) Table 17. Major differences in the technical cropping itineraries of rice either cultivated on the wash pediment or in the tank command area The variety of rice which is usually grown is the BPT 5205 variety (also known as Samba Mahsuri). The rice grains are pregerminated by soaking them in water for one day then exposed to heat the next day. The sprouts are broadcasted by male workers in a nursery where urea has been spread beforehand. The nursery is flooded with water for 5 days, then drained for 1 day, then flooded again continuously up to 4 to 5 cm for 10 days after the seeds have started raising. In the meantime, cattle or buffalo manure is spread on the flooded rice fields if the farm has some. Then, the field is tilled twice or thrice (depending on the type of cropping system, see Table 17) using cage wheels and a high-powered tractor (60 hp). By doing so, the action of the cage wheels break the clods of the soil which is turned into mud. This helps to partially eliminate the Parthenium weed which are rife on those type of soils. The puddling with cage wheels is the operation that consumes the most direct fossil energy (i.e. from fuel and electricity) (Fig. 144), even more than irrigation. In between the tillage operations, the field is left flooded for three days in order to limit the growth of the weeds. Land is levelled using a plan-like wooden beam which is either pulled by man or by tractor. [SOURCE: Page_239]

239 [SOURCE: Page_239]

Figure 144. Human labour and fossil energy consumption monthly calendar of rice cultivation: example of the rice/ley fallow cropping system in the wash depressions [SOURCE: Page_240]

There is a clear labour division in the rice cropping operations. Transplanting tasks are exclusively done by women (Fig. 145) whereas preparing land and harvesting is done by men. Transplanting from the nursery to the field is done after 45 days. Transplanting is the task which requires the most labour in the cycle, i.e. 45 man-days/ha (Fig. 144). Despite this, it is more advantageous than direct seeding in terms of weed control. The rice sprouts are pulled out with high speed and dexterity^45 by female labourers and then tied in bundles (Fig. 145). The men are then in charge of gathering the bundles and throwing them in the field. The women then detach the bundles and transplant the rice sprouts. The farmers spread DAP (diammonium phosphate) after transplanting to increase the number of productive panicles and bring phosphorus to rice (tilling stage). The vegetative growth ends when the tilling stage ends and the panicle formation stage starts. These are keys moments in the crop cycle, as they determine the number of the future grains and the needs in nutrients are high. After 30 days, urea is applied to favour grain filling and panicle weight. No fertilisers are spread during the reproductive phase. At the beginning of flowering (beginning of the final phase, the ripening phase) ammonium sulphate (NH₄)₂SO₄ is given. Even though ammonium sulphate is more expensive than urea, it is more suitable because the soil is alkaline and ammonium sulphate acidifies the [SOURCE: Page_240]

45 Having myself tried to transplant rice I realised that pulling the rice sprouts demands a lot of skill in order to adequately place the fingers and thumb and to use the right force so as to pull out the sprout without separating it from its root. [SOURCE: Page_240]

240 [SOURCE: Page_240]

soil. Punjabi labourers are hired to drive the combine harvesters for harvesting and threshing (see chapter 5). Farmers then manually gather the straw left on the field and stack them in large heaps. [SOURCE: Page_241]

Figure 145. Pulling out rice sprouts and tying them in bundles ready for transplanting [SOURCE: Page_241]

In the wash depressions, the soils are of hydromorphic nature and only two types of crops can be grown: rice and Napier grass. Technically speaking, two cycles of rice can be grown per year but today most farmers only grow one crop of rice and leave the land fallow for the rest of the year. Yields are much lower than when rice is grown on the wash pediment in rotation with groundnut (Table 17). The succession of operations are the same as when it is grown in the wash pediment, except for a few differences mentioned in Table 17, e.g. land is tilled three times instead of two. Today the possibilities of cultivation in the wash depressions are reduced, i.e. only rice or Napier Grass. Rice yields are low (table 17) with high intermediary costs, and rice cultivation is labour-demanding for transplanting and weeding (Fig. 144). The other option is to grow Napier grass, a three-year crop cultivated in rotation with one cycle of rice. As Napier grass is a forage crop (only intended to feed livestock) we have integrated it to the corresponding livestock farming system and it will be dealt with at a later stage. The wash depressions, by the narrow range of cropping options, have become the trivia areas of the agrarian system. [SOURCE: Page_241]

241 [SOURCE: Page_241]

2.2.2. Maximising groundnut production and guaranteeing high yields with irrigation (groundnut in rotation with rice or vegetables) When farmers have borewells of medium-depth on the wash pediment or the glacis slopes they can rotate vegetables or rice with groundnut grown in irrigated conditions. When groundnut is irrigated, it is usually using sprinklers. Groundnut can be irrigated during the rainy season, therefore allowing the farmer to add just the right amount of water in case the rainfall is too low. Groundnut can also be grown in summer in irrigated conditions. In both cases, yields are much higher than in rainfed conditions (see Fig. 141). With the connection to a borewell the risks of crop failure due to rainfall variability falls to zero and the groundnut is sown in double criss-cross lines. Because of the criss-crossed lines, weeding of groundnut cannot be done using bulls and the related implements (scuffle hoes) and all the weeding has to be done manually. In irrigated conditions, the groundnut land productivity increases but the amount of man-days also does. Figure 121 (chapter 5, section 2.2) shows, with irrigation, an increase in the physical labour productivity considering both pods and hay, and an increase in the land productivity. [SOURCE: Page_242]

2.2.3. Vegetables: gambling for prices The major vegetable crops are tomato and okra, which are both essential ingredients of Indian cooking. Occasionally chilli, beans and guar (also known as cluster bean) are grown, but those crops will neither be explained nor modelled here. Vegetables are grown in rotation with groundnut in irrigated conditions. They are never grown on the grey hydromorphic soils of the tank command area because they require well drained soils. They are grown on the red loamy soils of the wash pediment, and occasionally on the glacis slopes. The only moto-mechanised operation is the preparation of land before sowing. This operation is carried out using a 5-shank subsoiler to improve the soil structure and the water holding capacity, and to eliminate weeds by soil solarisation. Then a cultivator is used to crumble any soil clods and to remove dry weeds or stubble from the previous crop. A 1-row ridger coupled to a tractor is used to make ridges on which the tomato plants are planted. Manure is applied if the farm has livestock, otherwise cattle manure is never applied and sheep are penned at night in the fields prior to planting the vegetables at a rate of 2 500 Rs/ha. This is a only a small part of the intermediary costs of the vegetable cropping system, a cost which is largely affordable as the whole intermediate consumption on the vegetable crops is 118 295 Rs per ha. The farmers buy the plants from local village nurseries. The usual practice is to leave the tomatoes flat on the ground and not to attach the plants to stakes. This is explained by the cost of stakes and of labour to install the stakes, but also because the tomato varieties in the area have a determinate growth habit and [SOURCE: Page_242]

242 [SOURCE: Page_242]

stakes are not necessary. The red loamy soils of the wash pediment drain well and the semi- arid climate and its related high evapotranspiration are all factors which limit decay of tomatoes. Weed control is made manually by hoeing (using a hand hoe). We did not see any removal of suckers. Harvest is made every 4 days once the fruits are at turning stage. The prices of tomato are extremely volatile, ranging from 3 to 100 ₹ per kg according to interviews but from 6 to 20 ₹ per kg according to the press (Rahul M., 2021). The price can vary so suddenly from one day to the other that it is not uncommon to see harvested tomatoes being thrown away in fields or on road-sides, and left to rot. Despite the high volatility, the crop still attracts farmers with access to irrigation and who either have dairy livestock as an additional income or who grow okra on the other part of their land: the stable income from milk or from okra backs up the risks of loss of the tomatoes, and if the tomato price is high, the crop can be very profitable. A farmer told us in an interview that: “If the price of tomatoes is of 100 ₹ per box of 15 kg [6 ₹ per kg] I can pay back my investment”. The tomatoes are sold at the wholesale tomato market in Anantapur (mandi) and then exported to Bangalore, Chennai and Hyderabad. [SOURCE: Page_243]

The other main type of vegetables is okra. The variety of okra which is cultivated has cream-coloured flowers. The plants are about 1.5 meters high. Okra is an irrigated crop which can be cultivated every season of the year on well-drained soils. It is rotated with groundnut (Fig. 146). Land is prepared using a subsoiler, and a cultivator. Low ridges and furrows are made. The field is irrigated by the drip irrigation system and then the seeds are sown in line by women along the drip irrigation tubes. The labour calendar of the okra-groundnut cropping system is presented in Figure 146. [SOURCE: Page_243]

Figure 146. Labour calendar for okra in rotation with groundnut Farmers first remove weeds on rows using a one-row disc ridger pulled by bulls or by tractor. Then female labourers use a small hand hoe to uproot weeds on the ridge (Fig. 147). [SOURCE: Page_243]

243 [SOURCE: Page_243]

Farmers use DAP pellets which they spread by hand on the crops for first fertilisation. The rest is done by fertirrigation, matching a diaphragm pump to tractor PTO shaft speed to inject fertilisers in the irrigation water. Harvest starts 40 to 50 days after seedling and is spread out over 80 days. Fruits are harvested every 2 days in the morning. They are carried by autorickshaw or small truck from the field to the Bangalore-Hyderabad highway which passes via Anantapur. They are bought by merchants and transported directly to Bangalore in the beginning of the afternoon on the same day as the harvest, and transported directly to Bangalore. Fertilisers are also applied during harvest time to prevent the fruits from becoming too fibrous. At the end of the harvest, sheep can graze the remaining leaves. Prices also vary, from 10 to 50 ₹ per kg, but the variation is not as high as tomatoes. [SOURCE: Page_244]

Figure 147. Removing weeds on the ridge using hand hoes. Weeds in rows have been previously removed using a one-row disc ridger 2.3. Islands of irrigated fruit plantations on the wash pediment On the red loamy soils of the wash pediment, islets of irrigated fruit plantations are grown in the middle of a vast expanse of rainfed crops and natural vegetation, made of grasslands and a few patches of mixed shrubs and rocks. Those fruit plantations are perennial cropping systems, planted for a maximum of 15 to 20 years. The fruit trees are first characterised by an unproductive juvenile phase during which the fruit production is not enough to be commercialised. Then comes a transition adult phase characterised by low but increasing yields. The adult phase corresponds to the stage when the yields are at a plateau. The fruit trees are removed soon after the yields start declining, initiating the last phase of the [SOURCE: Page_244]

244 [SOURCE: Page_244]

plantation. All four types of fruit plantations are irrigated with deep borewells. Table 18 presents the main characteristics of the fruit cropping systems. [SOURCE: Page_245]
