General characteristics^46 of the fruit tree cropping systems 2.3.1. Banana, sweet lime, pomegranate and grapes: upward gradation of investment and wealth Out of all the fruit trees, banana is the one that has the shortest crop duration. It is grown for three years, in rotation with a rice crop cycle. It is generally grown on the red loamy soils of the wash pediment. It is irrigated with a drip irrigation system. After the first year, stakes have to be fixed to tether the banana plants and maintain them upright (Fig. 148) [SOURCE: Page_245]

Figure 148. Stakes supporting banana trees Source: photo taken near Gantlaparthi [SOURCE: Page_245]

46 As fruit plantations are removed once the yields start declining, the duration of the fruit tree plantations include the juvenile, transitional adult and adult phase with plateau yield. In order to overcome differences in yields between production phases and compare those perennial cropping systems with annual cropping systems, the indicators are average indicators weighted by the mean economic life of the plantation [SOURCE: Page_245]

245 [SOURCE: Page_245]

The three other types of fruit plantations have a longer duration, approximately 15 to 20 years. Sweet lime plantations require, with pomegranate, the lowest capital investment (Fig. 149). Sweet lime is the only fruit plantation which can provide an income to farmers during the juvenile unproductive phase of sweet lime trees: this is because groundnut is sown in between rows of sweet lime trees (Fig. 150) for the first two years of plantation. The sweet lime fruits are sold from the 4th year. Pruning is done once a year, in order to shape trees and eliminate the excess branches. Flowering is induced by water-stress. [SOURCE: Page_246]

Figure 149. Cost of plants, fertilisers, and capital to plant a fruit plantation [SOURCE: Page_246]

Figure 150. Groundnut in between sweet lime rows [SOURCE: Page_246]

The pomegranate orchards are planted with a high density, i.e. 1 000 plants per ha. The high density and the large quantities of inputs allow a high production of 19 tonnes of fruits (fresh weight) per ha (Table 18). The advantage of the pomegranate trees is that the fruits can [SOURCE: Page_246]

246 [SOURCE: Page_246]

be harvested after one year, allowing a fairly quick return on investment. Pomegranate trees can also withstand long drought periods. Pruning is made once a year in order to eliminate suckers and to thin out the tree to gain enough light for fructification. Because of the higher density of pomegranate trees compared to the sweet lime plantations, the pruning operations are more labour-demanding. Pomegranate trees can flower all year round in the south and centre of India. In order to have a synchronised flowering, chemical flowering inducers are used to provoke leaf senescence. [SOURCE: Page_247]

However, the sensitivity of the fruit trees to insects and fungi is high. There is a high risk of anthracnose disease which can completely destroy a crop if no preventive and curative measures are taken. Anthracnose is caused by a fungus, Glomerella cingulata, which develops mostly around leaf punctures made by insects and favoured by humid conditions. From flowering (August-September) to harvest (January) fungicide and insecticide are sprayed every week during the first two months and a half, then every two weeks till one month before harvest. The trees are sprayed on the whole 13 times. The application of fungicides and insecticide is a condition for pomegranate cultivation. If it is not carried out, the infection of the trees can lead to the removal of the entire fruit plantation, as experienced by several farmers we interviewed. Pomegranate fruits can also split due to nutrient deficiencies or excessive irrigation. Chemicals are also applied when cracks appear in other to prevent attacks from bacteria and fungi. [SOURCE: Page_247]

Grape vines are the least well represented perennial fruit cropping systems in the area but their cultivation are the peak of investment of all fruit cropping systems. India is the 6th country in the world with the highest grape yield (21 tonnes/ha), way ahead of France (59th country with the highest yield), Spain (61st) which produces approximately around 6 tonnes of grapes per ha. India ranks also 11 in the cropped surface under grapes while Spain, France and Italy are the three countries with the largest surface under grapes. India is also the 9 th biggest exporter of grapes (data from FAOStat). Although there is a mild growth of wine estates in India (especially in the Maharashtra and Karnataka states) the vast majority of the wine is for the growing urban India middle-class and the exports are almost non-existent^47. Most of the production in India is orientated towards table grapes, hence more than 85% of the production is orientated towards seedless varieties (Government of India, 2021) e.g. Thompson seedless, Manik Chaman. This is also the case for the grapes grown in Anantapur. There, the ruling grape [SOURCE: Page_247]

47 Personal communication with the manager of the Big Banyan tree wine estate manager, Karnataka state. [SOURCE: Page_247]

247 [SOURCE: Page_247]

variety are the Manik Chaman and Dilkhush varieties. The grape vines are irrigated using the drip irrigation system. They require a high investment with variations according to the tree density and the type of growing system, e.g. cost of fruit plants, drip irrigation system, starting dose of fertilisers when the trees are planted. Despite the heavy cost of installation of a grape wine, the market prices are high (we considered an average price of 45 Rs/kg (Appendix 25) although prices usually fluctuate between 12 and 50 Rs/kg). The high yields, 30 tonnes per ha (Table 17), are obtained because of particular growing practices: 1) grapes are trained on a pergola structure (Fig. 151), 2) pruning is made twice a year and 3) a high dose of fertilisers are applied. [SOURCE: Page_248]

Figure 151. Grape vines grown on a pergola structure [SOURCE: Page_248]

The vines are grown on a flat-roofed pergola structure, which is very expensive because it is built with stone pillars and barbed wire (Fig. 151). This growing technique favours the production of large quantities of grapes with a lower level of sugar and tannin, which is particularly suited for the production of table grapes but not wine grapes. The fruit-bearing shoots are spread out at 360 ° to provide a full coverage. The pergola structure can support important biomass production and optimise the reception of solar radiation. The dense shade [SOURCE: Page_248]

248 [SOURCE: Page_248]

of the pergola limits the growth of weeds between rows which enables to allocate practically all the water of the soil to the vines        (Carbonneau and Rotunno, 2000). In semi-arid Mediterranean areas, vines are usually trained in gobelets because it limits the foliar surface, and subsequently limits evapotranspiration and the use of water (Santos et al., 2020). In those areas vines are mostly destined for wine production. The pergola structure in the area provides considerable yields but is less adapted to the climatic conditions and vines have to be irrigated. Aubert (1972) observes irrigated vines under pergola structure in India as early as the 1970’s. The pergola system can also be found elsewhere in the world, for other reasons than the ones in Anantapur: it is found in the North of Italy, especially on the Po plain, where humidity is higher than in the southern part of the country (Carbonneau, 2013; Tirone, 1970). [SOURCE: Page_249]

Vines are pruned twice a year. A first pruning called back cutting initiates the beginning of a new production cycle. It is done around April or May, just before the beginning of the monsoon. The plant is totally trimmed and the shoots are pruned to one or two buds. The aim of back cutting is to start a new vegetative cycle. Vines are pruned a second time for fructification, towards the end of the monsoon season (around November and December) and this pruning is called forward pruning or winter pruning. The aim is to prepare fructification and optimise yields by stimulating the growth of vegetation from latent buds. The non-fruiting shoots are cut back and the tip of the fruiting shoots (bearing fruits) are cut (Fig. 152). Harvest is done approximately 100 days after the forward pruning, around March or April. [SOURCE: Page_249]

Figure 152. Application of a pruning wound protectant (in pink) after back cutting (left); removed shoots (right) put to the side of the plot [SOURCE: Page_249]

249 [SOURCE: Page_249]

2.3.2. Weeding and fertilisation of fruit plantations The fruit plantations are irrigated all year round using the drip irrigation system, which favours the growth of weeds. During the monsoon season and the winter season, weeding is made approximately once a month. During summer, weeding is made every month to every two months. Most of the weeding is made using a tractor drawn blade harrow in between rows as well as manual weeding with a hand hoe on rows. Glyphosate, a broad-spectrum systemic herbicide, is also used around tree trunks three times a year as a substitute for mechanical weed control, which saves labour charges. Rotavators can also be used to control weeds in between rows: rotavators are much more expensive than blade harrows^48. They are more efficient in cutting and pounding weeds, and they can also cut thick tall grasses (Fig. 153). However, there may be risks of damaging superficial root systems such as those of pomegranate trees. Rotavators are mostly used in sweet lime plantations (Fig. 153). [SOURCE: Page_250]

Figure 153. Weeding in between rows of sweet lime using a power tiller rotavator [SOURCE: Page_250]

Fruit trees require large quantities of fertilisers. For example, 20 to 30 kg of manure (fresh weight) is applied per vine and pomegranate plant (Fig. 154). Sheep are rarely allowed to graze in the tree plantations. Sheep manure is considered by the farmers as a “hot manure” with a higher fertilising value but with the risk of burning plants. Bovine manure is imported and acts mostly as a soil improver : it is applied in large quantities at the foot of each fruit tree, which increases the soil water retention and the weight percentage of soil aggregates (Darwish et al., 1995). The production of manure in the village is not enough to meet the needs of the fruit plantations and manure is imported in large quantities from the north of Andhra Pradesh [SOURCE: Page_250]

48 The cost or a rotavator is about 100 000 Rs in 2022, while for a blade harrow it is between 20 000 and 25 000 Rs. [SOURCE: Page_250]

250 [SOURCE: Page_250]

(Nandyal district), as far as 200 km from Anantapur. Heavy doses of chemical fertilisers -NPK (nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) and DAP (diammonium phosphate)- are also applied either directly in the drip irrigation system (fertirrigation) or spread in solid form. [SOURCE: Page_251]

Figure 154. Applying manure at the foot of each vine We estimated the dose of nitrogen per ha of the fruit plantations (Fig. 155) with the nitrogen and dry matter rate assumptions provided in appendix 26. Manure is applied to improve the water retainment capacity of the soil, which is essential in this semi-arid climate. As shows Figure 155, manure is also useful in providing nitrogen, especially for the pomegranate and sweet lime plantations, where manure accounts for more than three quarters of the nitrogen inputs. [SOURCE: Page_251]

Figure 155. Approximate annual doses of nitrogen applied to perennial fruit cropping systems [SOURCE: Page_251]

2.3.3. Marketing of fruits: the power of the middlemen There are three two main marketing channels for fruits in the study area: the fruits are purchased either directly by the corporate buyers (Happy Banana company for banana for [SOURCE: Page_251]

251 [SOURCE: Page_251]

instance) or by middlemen. In the latter case, the middlemen pay for the transport and most of the harvesting expenses. Otherwise, the farmer has to transport the fruit himself to the fruit wholesale market in Anantapur and has to bear the cost of harvest and transport. The choice between one option or the other is determined by the quantity of harvested products. When the fruits have been picked at the field, the farmer does not know yet the selling price of the crop: there are strong market fluctuations and the price is determined daily by auction at the fruit wholesale market. In the case of sweet lime for instance, if the farmer has less than 2 to 3 tonnes of fruits to sell, the buyers usually refuse to come at the farm, as the small harvest is not worth transporting (because of a partly empty vehicle). The farmer has to manage the harvest and transport of the fruits to the wholesale market. They usually pay an autorickshaw driver to transport fruits, which are of smaller capacity than the usual Bolero-type trucks. At the wholesale market, the prices fluctuate day by day and are fixed by daily auction between the middlemen and the buyers. The farmer is either present during auction or is informed on the phone of the price. He can either accept the price or refuse and postpone the selling to the next day. This is possible for sweet lime as the fruit can keep, but not for perishable fruits. Anantapur fruit wholesale market is the biggest government authorised sweet lime market of Andhra Pradesh. In average 100 to 600 tonnes of sweet lime arrive at the market each day, while it reaches 1 000 tonnes per day in peak time^49. The whole season last 8 months with a first season from March to May, a second one from June to August and a last season from December to January. [SOURCE: Page_252]

Many expenses are deducted in between the field and the wholesale market. Those expenses include mostly the commission taken by the middlemen and the labour charges for harvesting, which are shared between the farmer and the buyer if the buyer purchases the fruits directly at the orchard. The farmer gets 51 to 56% of the gross product of the crop (more details in Appendix 27). While the farmer earns slightly more if he transports the fruits himself to the market he will spend more time transporting and negotiating prices at the wholesale market. He will also have to bear market fluctuations at the wholesale market. [SOURCE: Page_252]

2.3.4. The invisible labourers for harvesting and loading fruits The harvest and the loading of fruits at the wholesale market is done by a specific type of labour (Fig. 156). The labourers who are employed to harvest fruits or load them at the fruit wholesale market come from rural villages of Anantapur district. They are usually landless and livestock [SOURCE: Page_252]

49 Personal communication with middlemen from Anantapur fruit wholesale market [SOURCE: Page_252]

252 [SOURCE: Page_252]

less. We spoked with a batch of labourers from Singalamala mandal (25 km away from Anantapur), all belonging to the Scheduled caste. While most of them were landless, a few had land but which was not suitable for cultivation. They were a mix of men and women, some of them teenagers (one of them started working as fruit harvester and loader at 13 years old) and which had dropped out of school. They work for the whole eight months season loading sweet lime at Anantapur wholesale market. During the remaining four months they work as labourers on farms in their village. They work six days a week with Sunday as leave-day. They only work in one wholesale fruit market. Every middlemen at the market has his own batch of loaders. Each loader loads between 1.5 to 2.5 tonnes of sweet lime each day (depending on low or high season). They get paid at the end of each day approximately 300 Rs/female worker and 500 Rs/male worker, but they have to pay their own transport from their village to Anantapur, meaning a net salary of 360 Rs per day of work per person. The same batch of workers is usually employed one year after the other. [SOURCE: Page_253]

Figure 156. Labourers loading sweet lime at Anantapur wholesale fruit market [SOURCE: Page_253]

253 [SOURCE: Page_253]

3. An array of livestock farming systems relying on heterogenous resources and labour 3.1. The sheep and goat livestock farming systems 3.1.1. The pastoral sheep farming system: using all the rainfed land and family labour to rear livestock The animals of this livestock farming system are mainly ewes and their progeny, two or three rams and also a few goats. As the proportion of goats is very low (5% of the herd approximately) we chose to call this system the pastoral sheep farming system, for better clarity. [SOURCE: Page_254]

The sheep and goats are reared for meat purposes. The breeds are referred as “non- descriptive” by the local veterinary services, but they have strong resemblances with local Deccani sheep breed. The sheep are small-sized animals, weighing approximately 30 kg live weight for the adult ewes, and requiring approximately 1 kg of dry matter per day. The diet of the sheep is grass-based during the monsoon season. In winter, sheep graze on horse gram fodder (Fig. 157). One ha of horse gram forage is required for 25 to 30 ewes and their progeny (Appendix 28). Pastoralists have to own land to be able to sow horse gram, or have to rent when they have a larger herd. In summer, the flock is mostly fed with groundnut hay because grass availability and palatability are low (Fig. 157). [SOURCE: Page_254]

Figure 157. Feed calendar of the sheep pastoral system There are always a few goats in the flock, which are herded together with the sheep. On the rocky hills and on field edges, vegetation may be shrubby and thorny and be a barrier to sheep who do not browse and are selective grazers. Goats, however, are browsers, with a shallower groove dividing the left and right side of the upper lip. They can also eat at chest level or higher, standing on their back legs. They can therefore easily overcome the thorny and rocky barriers. [SOURCE: Page_254]

254 [SOURCE: Page_254]

Sheep graze close to the ground and have a deeper groove divide. As they are also a gregarious species, they will follow the goats who can cross the shrubby and spiny trails. [SOURCE: Page_255]

Male lambs are sold at 4 months old. Two to three reproductive rams are kept for the whole batch of ewes for reproduction purposes. Ewes lamb for the first time when they are around two years old. The reproductive males are always kept with the female during day time while grazing and also at night in sheep pens. Anantapur is fairly close to the Equator (latitude + 14°) which means that the seasonal variations in photoperiod are much smaller than in other countries, such as in European ones. As sexual activity is expressed in response to photoperiod cues in small ruminants, sheep reproduction and lambing happens all year round, with however a higher rate during the monsoon season. Lambing is not a burden of work for pastoralists as ewes give birth without help, sometimes even while they are grazing during the day. In this case the pastoralist carries the newborn lamb by its front legs for the rest of the day (Fig. 158) or swings it over his shoulders. [SOURCE: Page_255]

Figure 158. A pastoralist carrying a newborn lamb with fresh umbilical cord and still dripping with blood [SOURCE: Page_255]

We considered a rate of three lambing every four years, i.e. a lambing interval of 16 months, taking into account a pregnancy of 5 months, the post-partum anoestrus period and fertile mating period. This is a fairly fast-paced reproduction system. We considered one or two lambs born per ewe lambing. Ewes are usually culled from the flock after approximately two lambings [SOURCE: Page_255]

255 [SOURCE: Page_255]

when they are four years old. Some may be kept longer, up to a maximum of seven years old, in which case they can be bargained at a price of 5 000 Rs per head. [SOURCE: Page_256]

Although the selling of the male lambs is very lucrative, there are heavy expenses in medicine and groundnut hay to feed the sheep in the dry season. Sheep are regularly infected by diseases. We estimated the total cost of the curative and preventive treatments at approximately 1 000 Rs per ewe annually. This corresponds to approximately 30 per cent of the intermediary costs. The main diseases affecting the sheep are the following as given in Table 19. [SOURCE: Page_256]

Disease            Main characteristics Bluetongue         Very frequent (50% of the herd infected every year). High fever, salivation, swelling disease Pulpy     kidney   Usually occurs during the monsoon season. In Telugu it has two names : motchudiamandu (enterotoxaemia)   meaning grazing or chetoku meaning “snapping fingers”. Enterotoxaemia is indeed a disease which causes rapid death. It is due to the development of anaerobic bacteria in the gut. Those bacteria synthetise toxins which cause the internal poisoning of the animal. The animals continue grazing without showing any abnormal signs even though infected. This makes the disease non detectable. The animals suddenly fall and die: the death is so quick and unexpected that it said that they die in a “snapping of fingers”. Prophylactic measures are taken to reduce the risks of infection. Haemorrhagic       Respiratory infection usually found on buffaloes but which can also infect sheep and goats. septicaemia Ovine rinderpest   Clinically characterised by constant gastroenteritis Table 19. Main diseases of sheep and goats Lambs less than 2 months old do not follow the rest of the herd during the day as they can not walk long distances. They are kept in huts for the first two months, (Fig. 159) during the day to provide them with shade -trees are sparse in this area- especially during the scorching summer days. As the sheep are penned on previously harvested fields, the ground is usually bare (Fig. 159). They are given medicine three times a month, to prevent them from eating the earth when in the huts. [SOURCE: Page_256]

256 [SOURCE: Page_256]

Figure 159. Lamb huts [SOURCE: Page_257]

The herd is penned at night on the wash pediment, usually on a farmer’s field (Fig. 160), following the same modalities as in the 1950’s, i.e. a collective night penning with other flocks (see chapter 3, Fig. 59, section 1.3). This means that the sheep droppings are never collected. With this practice a fertility transfer is made from the grazed areas during the day to the fields at night. Farmers paying pastoralists to pen their sheep at night on their fields are usually the ones who have no livestock. More information will be given at farm-level in the next chapter. The pastoralists use barbed wire to pen their sheep at night and they change location every two days during the monsoon season and every ten days in summer. [SOURCE: Page_257]

Figure 160. A flock of sheep next to the area where they were previously penned the night before [SOURCE: Page_257]

257 [SOURCE: Page_257]

On Figure 160, sheep are out of the area where they were penned the night before (with barbed- wire fencing) – photo taken early morning before the flock is taken out for grazing. Lamb huts are seen in the background 3.1.2. The lamb fattening system: a temporary supplemental income Some of the farmers depending only on rainfed groundnut cultivation may rear a batch of male lambs, buying them at three months old and fattening them for four months old. They then sell them to either other village inhabitants for celebrations or to town-based butchers. Those butchers usually come directly to the village to buy the fattened lambs in batches. The male lambs are bought at 6 000 Rs per head approximately. Buying a dozen of them represents a fairly big investment. Farmers usually borrow money from other inhabitants at a monthly interest rate of 2%, i.e. an annual interest rate of 24%. Farmers therefore usually don’t buy more than 30 male lambs. Those farmers fatten lamb for 4 months, occasionally or on a continuous basis, buying another batch after selling the previous one. There is therefore a maximum of three batches of 20 to 30 male lambs per year. The male lambs are herded on grasslands all year round, but never on horse gram fields as the farmers who fatten lambs also grow rainfed groundnut on the totality of their land. The lambs are however fed on groundnut hay, groundnut and chickpea cake, in monsoon, winter and summer alike. Groundnut hay is bought in the village but the feed concentrates are bought in shops in Anantapur city. Unlike in the pastoral sheep farming system, male lambs are kept at night in a small enclosure next to the house. Night droppings can therefore be collected and sold. [SOURCE: Page_258]

3.1.3. The goat farming system: the alternative of the landless Farms with only one small herd of goats (10 to 30 goats and progeny) are very rare in the village, three at most. Goat owners are either landless people or former sheep pastoralists who, by the hazards of life, had to sell their flock of sheep to pay heavy bills due to an accident or life-changing disease. Conversely, rearing goats is usually a transitory stage before returning to sheep rearing again. For those reasons, we did not proceed to the economic and metabolic quantification of this system, and will only describe their functioning and origin. As goats are browsers, they can accept low standards of feed, from wild shrubby and thorny vegetation. The grazing distances of goats are therefore shorter than the ones travelled by the sheep herds. In the same way as the pastoral sheep farming system, the goats may be herded on sown horse gram fields in January and February, but which are sown on leased land as the farmers rearing goats are landless. The goats are also given groundnut hay in summer. The kids are fed with tree leaves, which are harvested green with a long-handled sickle locally called chikulu (see Fig. 161). Female and male are taking out for grazing together. [SOURCE: Page_258]

258 [SOURCE: Page_258]

Figure 161. A goat pastoralist with his chikulu (long-handled sickle) [SOURCE: Page_259]

Unlike in the pastoral sheep farming system, the goats are kept at night in a pen adjoining the house (Fig. 162). The sheep goat droppings are collected when the herd is gathered at night and are sold to other farms. [SOURCE: Page_259]

The goats are not milked, the milk being exclusively kept for kid growth: “We do not milk goats, it would be like stealing the milk of the kids.” a goat pastoralist once told us. The male kids are sold between 3 and 4 months old and the goats culled after giving birth approximately five times. They are sold in Anantapur. In order to cut back on feeding spending (groundnut hay), some males are sometimes sold at an even younger age, in the beginning of the summer. The goats reach sexual maturity a bit later than the ewes, with a first kidding at three years old. They usually give birth to two kids at a time. The goats are often infected by [SOURCE: Page_259]

259 [SOURCE: Page_259]

the bluetongue disease which can lead to the death of animals and/or hinder reproduction efficiency. We once met a pastoralist who had lost half his herd in one go. If the reproductive goat dies, new females are bought in Anantapur market to build the herd up again. [SOURCE: Page_260]

Figure 162. Keeping the goats in a pen adjoining the house [SOURCE: Page_260]

3.1.4. Selling meat Despite the ban on cattle slaughter (Chapter 5, section 3.2.3, and Appendix 29 for map of animal slaughter legislation according to States in India), Andhra Pradesh is one of the biggest state producers of meat in India (Appendix 29), mostly because of the rearing of sheep. The sheep population in the study area and also in India has increased since the 1950’s along with the demand in mutton (see section 3 in chapter 5). In Anantapur city, butcher’s shops have flourished over the last 20 years. The butchers are usually Muslims. They buy the sheep directly in the village farms or at Anantapur livestock market which was created in 1992. For every animal sold at the market a tax of 30 Rs/sheep and 100 Rs/cattle is applied. The market is divided into section (poultry section, cock fighting section, cattle and buffalo section, ovine and caprine section). In Anantapur livestock market, the farmers selling sheep came from all over Anantapur district, and also from Bellary area (district bordering Anantapur district to the North-East. They were either sheep fatteners with rainfed crops, pastoralists or even merchants [SOURCE: Page_260]

260 [SOURCE: Page_260]

who were buying animals in the village and selling them at a higher price at the market. We met a merchant who had bought a pair of old bulls in the village and was selling it back at the market, with a profit of 500 Rs per head. Some farmers only sold 1 to 3 sheep while others sold whole lorries of 30 to 50 sheep and goats. We also met a buyer from Nizamabad (Telangana state, 550 km away from Anantapur) who had come to buy rams for a Muslim festival. He had been coming to Anantapur for the last 15 years because of the highly-rated quality of Anantapur sheep meat. Another buyer bought a whole lorry of female kids which he was intending to sell in Tamil Nadu where a government scheme provides 5 goats and sheep for free for female widows. [SOURCE: Page_261]

Figure 163 presents the share of net value added of sheep between the pastoralists, the butchers and the wetskin merchants, taking the bone, fat and meat ratios in sheep of Sen et al. (2004) and the skin weight of Joseph et Nithya (2009). The butchers fetch the animals directly at the farm in the village or at the livestock market in Anantapur. Half of the net value is kept by pastoralists. The rest is taken by butchers. The wetskin merchants buy the skin at very low prices (20 Rs per skin) [SOURCE: Page_261]

Figure 163. Share of the net value added of sheep along the value chain in 2022 per animal Production: C. Hemingway; Data source: interviews 3.2. The bull farming system, a niche in the economy of the agrarian system Animal power has gradually decreased but it has been retained in particular niches where operations could either not be motorised or where the benefits of animal work still outweigh the advantages of motorisation. The first case is illustrated by the groundnut weeding and hoeing operation which cannot be done with tractor drawn implements. Where groundnut is sown in single lines (rainfed conditions), the use of the bullock-drawn implements (separate or [SOURCE: Page_261]

261 [SOURCE: Page_261]

combined scuffle hoes) is more advantageous than employing labourers to remove weeds with hand hoes. The second case occurs when the configuration of the terrain does not allow the passage of a tractor. This is the case when the field is too stony or when the field is a long narrow plot: the configuration of the plot is such that it is difficult to turn the tractor around at the end of a row when weeding between rows of vegetables or making ridges using a one-row disc ridger. For those reasons, the bull farming systems are few but remain indispensable for specific operations. The local bull farming system is typically composed of a pair of Hallikar bulls which are bought from Anantapur market, ready-trained and at around 2 or 3 years old. They are sold after approximately 4 years of work on farm. They are fed on rice straw, groundnut hay, rice bran, and also on horse gram grain during the days where they work on fields. Rice straw and groundnut hay are bought in the village while rice bran and horse gram grain are bought in shops in Anantapur. Bulls are also taken out for grazing during the monsoon. [SOURCE: Page_262]

The bulls provide manure and muscular power which is used on-farm or outsourced to other farms. The type of operations varies in price and duration. It was difficult to estimate precisely the gross product from animal traction solely from farmers statements as the animal power outsourced to other farms depends on the demand. It can therefore vary from one year to another according to the crops sown. We proceeded in two ways. We first asked each farmer owning a pair of bulls how much he charged for each operation and how much he roughly earned per month and per year by selling animal power. Secondly, we identified the peak periods of work. We then estimated the gross product from animal traction on village scale by aggregating the animal labour demand for crops for each month of the year. We divided the monthly demand by the number of pairs of bulls remaining the archetype village, i.e. 5. Peak periods are in August and September when weeds are removed from rainfed groundnut fields (Fig. 164). This way of estimating the income concurred with farmers’ statements. [SOURCE: Page_262]

Figure 164. Labour monthly calendar of a pair of bulls [SOURCE: Page_262]

N.B.: one pair of bulls can work maximum 60 animal-days per month [SOURCE: Page_262]

262 [SOURCE: Page_262]

Most of their work consists of weeding rainfed groundnut, especially with separate scuffle hoes. Sowing groundnut using bulls is increasingly rare in the archetype village today, apart from the farmers owning bulls and sowing their own groundnut fields (Table 20). 3.3. The dairy farming livestock farming systems 3.3.1. The Holstein Friesian crossbred dairy farming system of farms with acces to irrigation The most widespread form of livestock farming system of medium-sized farms with access to irrigation is composed of 1 to 6 Holstein Friesian (HF) cross-bred cows and their progeny. They produce between 1 700 and 1800 Liters of milk per lactation. The main products of this crossbred livestock farming system are milk and manure. Cows start calving at 2 years old. The cows are culled when they are 7 to 8 years old, which corresponds to approximately 4 calvings. Beyond this limit, milk production tends to decline. Male calves are sold as soon as 263 [SOURCE: Page_263]

possible, as they are of no use on the farm and represent a cost for feeding. They are usually sold at 1 month old. [SOURCE: Page_264]

Feed and water are brought to the cow at the trough. Cows are never untethered and are never taken out to graze. All their dung is carefully collected and conveyed to the manure heap. They are kept in basic concrete sheds with corrugated roof sheeting. The sheds are usually opened on the sides to allow maximum ventilation and equipped with ceiling fans for increased rate of cooling. The ceiling fans are turned on day and night during summer and only during day time in winter and the monsoon season. The cows are fed with groundnut hay, rice straw, rice bran, broken rice and also green Napier fodder which is cultivated on small patches of irrigated land. One cow and her progeny requires approximately 0.01 ha of Napier Grass annually. During lactation they are also given daily 1 kg of feed concentrate which is bought from the local dairy branches at the village milk collection centres. The feed concentrate is made from different raw materials (groundnut cake, maize grain, rice bran, etc.) and manufactured in factories belonging to each private dairy company. [SOURCE: Page_264]

Figure 165. Feed calendar of crossbred dairy cows The working time is mostly devoted to milking, collecting dung, washing animals and feeding, which includes Napier cultivation, cutting and transporting from the field to the shed (Fig. 166). As Napier grass is never sold nor bought, we could not provide a price per kg of Napier grass. We modelled it as an integral part of the dairy livestock farming system, with cost of inputs (mostly urea, manure for fertilisation, consumption of water, electricity for raising water from borewells, fuel for ploughing the land, and also the drip irrigation system) and amount of labour for cultivation and cutting as part the livestock farming system. The variety used for Napier grass is usually the coven variety (Co$_1$) or super napier. The crop is planted in rotation with rice on the grey hydromorphic soils of the wash depressions and sometimes on the glacis slopes. After preparing the land with a tractor drawn 5-shank subsoiler and a tiller, the drip system is put in place. The field is flooded and Napier grass cuttings are planted (Fig. 167). Farmers cut stems from neighbouring fields, which are distributed by [SOURCE: Page_264]

264 [SOURCE: Page_264]

farmers for free. The crop is irrigated all year round and after each cutting, the crop is hand- weeded and urea is broadcasted. Napier is kept for three years, and is cut every month and a half. We estimated the yield at 125 tonnes of fodder, in fresh weight (Appendix 28). [SOURCE: Page_265]

The cows reproduce via artificial insemination, which is carried out at the local veterinary centre (Fig. 168). The dairy farmers try to keep the herd reproducing on a 12-month calving interval. The signs of heat are usually seen 2 months after calving but the accuracy of heat detection is quite poor and it usually takes approximately 2 to 3 attempts to have a cow pregnant. The calving interval is therefore usually of 16 months. The cows are milked up to the 7th month of pregnancy. Veterinary costs include the cost of artificial insemination and the purchase of prophylactic medicine. [SOURCE: Page_265]

3.5.1. The buffalo dairy farming system of farms with access to irrigation The buffalo dairy farming system is composed of 1 to 6 buffaloes from the river type buffalo, i.e. domestic buffalo Bubalus bubalis, and usually from the crossbred Murrah breed. [SOURCE: Page_267]

They are fed with Napier grass, groundnut hay, rice straw but less feed concentrates than the HF crossbred cows. They are on the other hand taken out for grazing during the rainy season and they are hardier than the HF crossbred cows. Medicine expenses are therefore rare. The age at first calving for buffaloes is later than for the HF cows: 3,5 years instead of 2 for the HF cows. Because of a higher fat content of buffalo milk, the milk is sold at a higher price than cow milk (52 Rs per litre instead of 30) (Appendix 16). During the first lactations the fat content of the milk is usually lower and increases with the age of the buffalo. Because of the higher fat content, buffalo milk is preferred for household consumption (for making curd for instance). [SOURCE: Page_267]

The tolerance of buffaloes to heat stress is low because of difficulties to increase cutaneous evaporation in those conditions (Moran, 1973). They are regularly taken out to tanks to swim (Fig. 169) or are splashed and sprinkled with water every day in summer or once every 3 or 7 days in winter. [SOURCE: Page_267]

Figure 169. An Indian farmer taking her buffaloes and calves to cool down in a tank Compared to cows, it takes twice as much time to milk one buffalo because of the slower milk ejection reflex and the harder teat sphincter muscle (Borghese et al., 2007). Based on observations and interviews, we counted 10 minutes to milk one cow and 20 minutes for a [SOURCE: Page_267]

267 [SOURCE: Page_267]

buffalo. The efficiency of the milk ejection from the udder can be enhanced by the presence of the suckling calf (Borghese et al., 2007), a technique which is widely used in the area. We met a farmer once who had a calf who had died; he had the calf stuffed and used it to stimulate milk ejection from the mother (Fig. 170). [SOURCE: Page_268]

Figure 170. Stuffed calf (top right) overlooking the female buffaloes [SOURCE: Page_268]

The main form of buffalo rearing is carried out by farms with no access to irrigation (and therefore no Napier Grass). This form of livestock rearing is developed in the next section. It is the form which was modelled in the archetype village. [SOURCE: Page_268]

3.6.1. The buffalo and local dairy cow farming system of rainfed farms In the case of farms with no access to irrigation, farmers who have livestock rear 1 to 3 buffaloes or local cows (Ongole breed) to produce milk. They are the local breeds, i.e. neither the HF crossbred cows nor the crossbred Murrah buffaloes. These local dairy animals are taken out for grazing and also fed on harvested forage weeds (Fig. 171 and Fig. 172). This is any type of grass or weed taken out by man which can be found on fields, road-sides, and grazing lands (see Fig. 171). Those weeds can also be found in between the rows of fruits trees in fruit enclosures, when the fruit plantation owner gives access to the farmer with livestock. The grass is usually plucked out by hand, whereas the Napier grass has to be cut with a sharp knife or sickle. The large bundles are then carried to the cow shed by motorbike. Feed concentrates are [SOURCE: Page_268]

268 [SOURCE: Page_268]

given in smaller quantities than for the HF crossbred cows (Fig. 172) and are limited to rice bran. Local cows and buffaloes yield approximately 950 and 1 150 Liters of milk per lactation. The price of buffalo milk is however higher than the cow milk due to a higher fat content (Appendix 16). [SOURCE: Page_269]

Figure 171. Taking out a buffalo for grazing (left) and bundle of forage weeds (right) [SOURCE: Page_269]

Figure 172. Feed calendar of local dairy cows in dry matter 3.6.1. Selling milk Cow milk has a lower fat content than buffalo milk and the price per litre is therefore lower (Appendix 16). The milk is sold at dairy collection centres based in the village. The transport of milk from the village to the dairy factory benefits from a particularly well- organised transport network which succeeds in collecting fresh milk twice a day (early morning and evening) from the village dairy collection centres to the dairy factories in Anantapur. The transport is based on a multitude of milk transporters who collect the milk daily from the villages and who are paid by the dairy factories. Each household sell each day tiny volumes of milk every day: on the 4th and 5th of September 2022, we recorded on average 3,87 Liters of milk brought per household at the dairy cooperative, with a minimum at 0.49 Liters and the biggest volume at 15,45 Liters! (data collected from Dodla milk collection centre in Maruru village, see Appendix 16). There are usually 2 or 3 dairy collection centres in each village and [SOURCE: Page_269]

269 [SOURCE: Page_269]

for each there is collector that can fit all the milk cans in one rickshaw and bring them to the dairy factory in Anantapur. The Andhra Pradesh prohibition of cow slaughter and animal preservation act of 1997 stipulates than the slaughtering of cows is entirely prohibited bur the slaughter of bulls and bullock is authorised only if the animal is not economical or not likely to (GOI, 2022) (Appendix 29). Information on the fate of sold cattle (cull cows and male calves) was difficult to get. We know that they were sold, but to whom remains mysterious. However, we did see during our visit to Anantapur cattle market, a section at the back where old-aged animals were attached -and even a few animals that had died at the market kept- away from prying eyes. We were not allowed to take any photos and conversation with middlemen or farmers could not be engaged in this part of the market. [SOURCE: Page_270]

4. Economic and environmental performances of cropping and livestock farming systems 4.1. Irrigation is the main goal: economic performances of cropping systems The rainfed cropping systems are the cropping systems which produce the lowest wealth, i.e. gross value added (Fig. 173). When access to irrigation is provided, land productivity increases notably, despite heavier intermediary costs. This is even more so for fruit plantations, which have a land productivity two to four times higher than vegetable cropping systems. The land productivity of the rice cropping system on the wash pediment is slightly higher that of the vegetable cropping systems. Prices of vegetables, especially tomato, vary considerably, with potentially much higher gross value added than the rice cropping systems. The rice cropping system in the wash depressions is the exception, as it has a land productivity close to that of rainfed cropping systems. This is indicative of the loss of importance of the wash depressions, which were in the 1950’s the crux of the agrarian system and are now its trivia areas. [SOURCE: Page_270]

Figure 173. Land productivity of cropping systems [SOURCE: Page_270]

270 [SOURCE: Page_270]

The economic labour productivity shows similar conclusions (Fig. 174). The labour productivity of fruit plantations is still the highest, especially for pomegranate and citrus. The labour productivity of grapes is lower than the one of citrus and pomegranate, mostly because of the increased amount of labour for the two yearly prunings of grapes. [SOURCE: Page_271]

Figure 174. Economic labour productivity of cropping systems Those results show that irrigation, on the wash pediment induces an increase in economic performances, with fruit plantations being the holy grail, therefore justifying why some farmers incur debt to drill borewells. Grapes and pomegranate have a similar land productivity (Fig. 173), but the labour productivity of pomegranate is higher (Fig. 174). Some farmers prefer growing grapes instead of pomegranate, because pomegranate trees have a high risk of anthracnose disease which can completely destroy the plantation crop if no preventive and curative measures are taken (see section 2.3). [SOURCE: Page_271]

4.2. Livestock of the poor? Economic performances of livestock farming systems We included the Napier Grass and horse gram cropping systems as part of the livestock farming system as they are destined exclusively to animal feed. The pastoral sheep farming system provides the highest gross value added of all livestock farming systems per herd (Fig. 175), at the expense of a huge amount of labour: pastoralists have to work day (grazing) and night (night surveillance of the herd). This is showed by the low labour productivity, which is not very far above the wage of a daily labourer (Fig. 175). [SOURCE: Page_271]

Sheep fattening is effective in providing punctual boost of wealth (Fig. 175). It is also the only farming system which requires an investment large enough to make farmers contract a loan -apart from borewells of course which are indispensable for rearing crossbred dairy [SOURCE: Page_271]

271 [SOURCE: Page_271]

cows-. The investment made by sheep fatteners is made for a short duration, i.e. the 4 months of the fattening period. [SOURCE: Page_272]

Figure 175. Economic performances of livestock farming systems In the archetype village, there are today only 7 local dairy cows, 12 buffaloes, while there are 124 HF crossbred cows. The farmers rearing dairy animals choose the type of animals according to whether their land is irrigated or not. If they have a borewell, then they rear crossbred HF cows. The HF crossbred dairy farming system is the only system which requires irrigated land directly on farm for growing Napier grass, which out rules de facto all the farmers with no borewells. As land is rented on an annual or a crop cycle basis, land is never rented to grow Napier grass which is a 3-year crop. Among dairy farming systems, the HF dairy farming system has the highest labour productivity (Fig. 175) because it is a non-grazing system. The workload is much less than in grazing farming systems. Nearly half of the gross product is absorbed by intermediary costs of feed (Fig. 175). This includes feed concentrates, straw, hay and the cost cultivation of Napier. All the other dairy livestock farming systems, namely with buffaloes and local dairy cows, have the lowest labour productivity -with the pastoral sheep farming system-, not much so much more than the daily wage of labourers. The gross value added of the buffalo dairy farming system is slightly higher than the one of local dairy cows because buffalo milk is sold at a higher price because of a more important fat content (Appendix 16). [SOURCE: Page_272]

272 [SOURCE: Page_272]

Bulls have a higher gross value added per herd than HF crossbred dairy farming systems (Fig. 175) but a similar labour productivity to the HF crossbred dairy farming system. The gross product from bulls is maintained high because of a high demand for weeding crops, especially groundnut. However, the amount of labour for rearing those bulls is higher than for HF cows, because the bulls are taken out for grazing and also because of the workload for selling the animal force on other farms. [SOURCE: Page_273]

The comparison of economic performances of livestock and cropping farming system shows major differences between the system with access to irrigation and the ones which are rainfed. It shows also major differences in the workload, thus influencing the labour productivity. The final section of this chapter outlines the environmental performances of the crop and livestock farming systems, linked to the consumption of fossil energy and their role in the groundwater recharge. [SOURCE: Page_273]

The comparison of the gross value added of irrigated cropping systems and livestock farming systems requiring access to irrigation also shows that the gross value added per ha of fruit plantations (Fig. 173) is at least equal to the gross value added generated by 12 HF crossbred dairy cows (Fig. 175). [SOURCE: Page_273]

4.3. Producing agricultural products at what environmental price? The Green and pump revolution have created perennial cropping systems which have an annual evapotranspiration three times higher than rainfall (Fig. 176). These correspond to the fruit plantations and the irrigated Napier Grass grown for cross bred cows.Those cropping systems therefore have the most negative net groundwater recharge, ranging from -1 000 to 1 500 mm. The other irrigated cropping systems have a lower evapotranspiration because they are not irrigated all year round, i.e. there are periods of ley fallows in between the crop cycles. They still have a negative groundwater recharge, similar to that of the irrigated cropping systems of the 1950’s, i.e. the finger millet and rice cropping system. Today, grasslands are grazed more intensively than in the 1950’s, i.e. three times instead of once. This brings down slightly the evapotranspiration of grasslands and contributes to a higher net groundwater recharge (Fig. 176). The highest net groundwater recharge per ha comes from grazing areas including natural vegetation and horse gram. [SOURCE: Page_273]

273 [SOURCE: Page_273]

Figure 176. Actual evapotranspiration and net recharge of cropping systems in 2022 and 1950’s The ranking of the cropping systems in terms of fossil energy consumption is however different (Fig. 177). The indirect fossil energy from synthetic fertilisers is the heighest in all cropping systems except in most of the fruit cropping systems, where the indirect fossil energy from herbicide, insectide and fungicide are more important (Fig. 177). The pomegranate cropping systems has a high share of indirect fossil energy from fungicide due to the preventive measures against anthracnose disease. The indirect fossil energy from manure is important in all fruit cropping systems because three quarters of the fossil energy consumption is due to the transport of manure, which is bought 200-KM away from the village. Regarding the direct fossil energy consumptions: the cultivation of rice has the highest fossil energy consumption mostly because of the considerable amount of direct fossil energy from fuel usage while preparing the field with cage wheels and the use of a combine harvester for harvesting rice [SOURCE: Page_274]

274 [SOURCE: Page_274]

crops. The highest consumption of fossil energy related to electricity is found in the perennial cropping systems because of continuous irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_275]

Figure 177. Fossil energy consumption of cropping systems The pump revolution was a fertile ground for the White Revolution : today the majority of dairy animals are crossbred cows, which have to be fed on irrigated fodder. The importance of grass in the diet of animals has overall recoiled. We calculated the net water recharge per livestock farming system (Fig. 178): we considered the water recharge per surface of grasslands grazed, and per quantity of rice straw, Napier grass, groundnut hay and horsegram fodder fed to the animals. It comes as no surprise that the crossbred dairy farming system is the livestock farming system which indirectly extracts the most groundwater, especially because of the daily intake of Napier Grass which is a perennial irrigated crop. The HF crossbred dairy farming systems not only is a net extractor of the groundwater, but also relies on feed concentrates, which are produced out of the territory with products which have also potentially extracted groundwater. [SOURCE: Page_275]

275 [SOURCE: Page_275]

All the other livestock farming systems contribute postively to the groundwater recharge. The grazed grass outweighs the negative recharge related to the production of rice straw in all livestock farming system. The sheep fattening system has a small net water recharge because the feed intake is much lower than in the other systems : the male lambs are between 3 and 7 months old, with a small body weight and therefore lower feed intake than adult ewes and rams. By comparison, the pastoral sheep system includes animals throughout their life span, from birth to death, with a therefore higher live weight and higher dry matter intake at adult age. [SOURCE: Page_276]

Figure 178. Net water recharge of livestock farming systems There are major differences in fossil energy consumption between the livestock farming systems (Fig. 179). Today all the livestock farming systems are dependent on fossil energy, either electricity or diesel. The crossbred dairy farming systems have the highest fossil energy consumption, mainly speared by the ventilation those crossbred cows require. The consumption of fossil energy to produce feed, apart from the manufactured feed concentrates given to HF cows, is also very important. This includes the diesel used by machines, electricity used to pump water from borewells, and any chemical fertilisers, pesticide, herbicide to grow straw and hay. The pastoral sheep farming system for instance has a high fossil energy consumption mostly because of the direct and indirect fossil energy consumed for growing groundnut hay. [SOURCE: Page_276]

Figure 179. Fossil energy consumption of livestock farming systems [SOURCE: Page_276]

276 [SOURCE: Page_276]

Conclusion of chapter 6: The economic quantification at plot and herd level is a potent tool to analyse the choices of agricultural production. The quantification of flows of water and energy allows to understand the environmental sustainability of the cropping and livestock farming systems, linked to the dependency to imported inputs and the use of groundwater. The choices of production are mostly driven by the access to irrigation and the organisation of labour. Irrigation on the wash pediment generates higher wealth than rainfed systems, with a capitalisation trajectory which culminates with fruit plantations. This explains why, despite the constraint of the environment, farmers incur debt to drill borewells. The analysis also reveals an inversion of the value of land since the 1950’s. In the 1950’s, the wash depressions where the crux of the agrarian system because they were the only areas where crops could be irrigated. All the energies (gross, human labour and animal labour) were concentrated in the wash depressions (chapter 3). Conversely the wash pediment could only be used to grow rainfed crops, with comparatively much lower productivity. Today those constraints have been partially lifted by the use of fossil energy: some borewells have been drilled and stone boulders removed on the wash pediment. Providing the access to capital is ensured, the range of possibilities is wide on the wash pediment, whereas it is restrained on the wash depressions: only rice and Napier can be grown, with either low value added and low labour productivity for rice, or of only use to livestock for Napier Grass. Today, the link between the creation of wealth and the environmental performances is not straightforward. The dichotomy between irrigated and rainfed cropping systems is clear in terms of wealth created and contribution to the recharge of the groundwater table. However, the environmental analysis shows a high consumption of fossil energy for all cropping systems, first and foremost due to the production and transport of synthetic fertilisers, followed by the indirect fossil energy from manure, and the direct fossil energy from on-farm diesel and electricity consumption. The perennial irrigated fruit plantations have the highest gross value added and labour productivity per ha but are also the cropping systems which pump the most groundwater and consume the most fossil energy -except for sweet lime plantations-. The rice cropping systems in the wash depressions have a high fossil energy consumption (synthetic fertilisers, electricity to run the pumps for irrigation, and fuel used to prepare the flooded land of rice crops and harvest the rice) and also the lowest gross value added and labour productivity per ha, making rice a lose-lose cropping system both in economic and environmental terms. Rainfed groundnut, which makes most of the cropped [SOURCE: Page_277]

277 [SOURCE: Page_277]

land today, has a low gross value added and a low labour productivity but has a positive net recharge. The fossil energy consumed from rainfed groundnut cultivation is still high, because of the consumption of fuel for land preparation and post-harvest operations, and from the consumption of synthetic fertilisers. As for the livestock farming systems, the pastoral sheep farming system has the highest gross value added but the lowest labour productivity. Rearing sheep in a pastoral way is lucrative, but at the expense of a huge workload from day-grazing and night- surveillance of the herd. The pastoral sheep farming system has, with the other grazing systems, the highest net water recharge, because of the role of grazing in the groundwater recharge. The role of grazing areas in the groundwater recharge is even higher in 2022 than in the 1950’s because of a higher grazing intensity. At the other end of the spectrum, the HF crossbred dairy cows have the highest labour productivity, but also consume the most fossil energy and the most groundwater, linked to the importance of feed concentrate and irrigated Napier Grass in their diet. [SOURCE: Page_278]

278 [SOURCE: Page_278]

CHAPTER 7: Living from agriculture? analysis of the economic, social and environmental sustainability of farming [SOURCE: Page_279]

Figure 180. Wondering on the prospects of a life as farmers: a little farmer’s girl in a truck while her parents are harvesting vegetables [SOURCE: Page_279]

In this chapter we analyse the agriculture on the scale of the farms and the territory. We look at the current diversity of farms and question whether farming can provide a decent income for farmers. We then evaluate the socio-economic inequalities in between farms through the comparison of agricultural incomes. Through the analysis of the net water recharge and the energy consumption and production at farm and territorial level we analyse the new social relations of production built upon interdependences of flows of water and energy. [SOURCE: Page_280]

1. Types of farms and economic indicators at farm-level 1.1. The economic analysis of production systems 1.1.1. Net value added and depreciation of fixed assets As mentioned in the previous chapter we deduced the annual depreciation of fixed capital (DEP) from the gross value added to obtain the net value added. The net value added can be calculated at farm level as some fixed assets may serve both cropping and livestock rearing purposes (Eq. 19): [SOURCE: Page_280]

NVA = GVA - DEP Equation 19. Net value added The annual depreciation is the wear and tear of fixed capital, examples of them are provided in Table 21. The annual depreciation for each equipment is given in Appendix 30. Borewells, once they are drilled do not wear out (apart from the pump which has to be changed, the borewell structure doesn’t) and we had to estimate the depreciation in another way, detailed also in Appendix 24. [SOURCE: Page_280]

Examples of fixed capital assets 1.1.2. Agricultural income From the net value added calculated at plot and herd level, we calculated the household income earned from agricultural activities. The annual household agricultural income (AI) is what remains in a household’s budget for consumption, investment or capitalisation over an average year. The wealth created during the agricultural process (NVA) is shared between the entities who have contributed to its production (Cochet, 2015): part of the NVA is given to the [SOURCE: Page_280]

280 [SOURCE: Page_280]

hired labour as wages, another part is given to landowners for the land which is rented, another part corresponds to the annual interests paid back for contracted loans (Eq. 20): [SOURCE: Page_281]

AI = NVA – Wages – Land rent – Paid back interests Equation 20. Agricultural income The agricultural income of the household is divided by the number of family workers, hereby giving the agricultural income per family worker of the production system. [SOURCE: Page_281]

Drilling borewells represents a high investment, especially because farmers have to make several attempts because of a high borewell failure (Appendix 24). In most cases, farmers borrow money either from banks if they are well-off, or from other wealthier villagers. In the model we considered that all the farmers which had drilled borewells had contracted loans from the wealthier villagers (usually being the large-scale fruit growers). In this case, the monthly interest rate is of 2% (annual interest rate of 24%). Large-scale fruit growers are able to drill their borewells either with their own money or by borrowing money at banks where the annual interest rate is lower, i.e. 12%. The loan is usually paid back in 30 months (2,5 years), but with different rates (Table 22). We considered in this economic analysis that farmers with a borewell still had an ongoing loan. Table 22 presents the cost of drilling of one borewell and the annual interests when loans are contracted through villagers or banks. [SOURCE: Page_281]

absolute minimum income in the area to cover basic needs (food need, health, hygiene, schooling and housing) during an average year. We carried out four household interviews to evaluate the food, hygiene and housing expenses, relying on a 24-hour dietary recall to gather information on the food and beverages consumed by the households in the past 24 hours. We managed to establish the composition of 4 typical meals in the area of study: rice and rasam, rice with groundnut chutney, rice with dahl and rice with vegetable curry (Appendix 31). We consider 2 meals per day (minimum subsistence) most of them based on rice except 2 meals in the week based on chapatis (made of wheat flour). The village inhabitants eat meat very rarely, and when they do it is usually chicken. Mutton is kept for special occasions in villages (weddings for instance). For rice we used the price of 2 Rs/kg as we considered that the rice, if not produced on the farm, would be bought at the local Fair Price Shop for the households who hold a ration card. This subsidised price has been implemented with the PDS (Public Distribution System) in the 1950’s where staple food (sugar, rice, wheat) is bought by the government and redistributed at subsidised price (Dorin and Landy, 2002, p. 72). In Andhra Pradesh, since 1982 the price of rice in Fair Price Shops has been fixed at 2 Rs/kg (Dorin and Landy, 2002, p. 133). We then added expenses for hygiene expenses (toothpaste, soap, cleaning products, etc.), clothes, electricity, gas, drinking water, health expenses (medicine). School fees and housing fees were considered nil as we assumed that children went to government schools where school uniforms and schooling materials are given for free. We also considered that the poorer families had a free government house. We came to total of 59 121 Rs/year/household. As we considered in most cases 2 family workers this comes down to 29 560 Rs/year/family worker^50 for him or her and their dependants. The assumptions taken to calculate the survival threshold are given in Appendix 31. [SOURCE: Page_282]

1.2. A typology of farmers steeped in history The agrarian history which was traced back from the chapters 3 to 5 shows that one of the key determinants of the socio-economic differentiation of farms was the access to groundwater, and also access to livestock. In the 1950’s, the large holder farmers and the smallholder farmers had access to the irrigable land in the tank command area, had the investment capacity to dig wells and also the necessary animal power to extract the water from those wells. The irrigated surface was directly proportional to the number of bulls. It also [SOURCE: Page_282]

[SOURCE: Page_282]

282 [SOURCE: Page_282]

required at least three pairs of bulls to engage in groundnut cultivation on the wash pediment. Sheep farming enabled pastoralists to have another income, in addition to working on farms. Agricultural labourers had no livestock and no land and they had only their muscle power to earn a living. With the agrarian land reform and the Yellow revolution the cards were partially reshuffled. With the pump revolution, the importance of draft animals and of the land in the wash depressions was highly diminished. Borewell irrigation was, and still is, a matter of capacity of investment for making several attempts to drill successful and increasingly deeper borewells. Irrigated areas shifted from the tank command areas to the wash pediments and the diversity of irrigated cropping systems increases, e.g. rice, vegetables, fruits. Input-intensive dairy farming systems with crossbred dairy cows is today only an option for the farmers who have access to irrigation. The rest of the farmers either relies solely on rainfed groundnut cultivation and on a secondary job either as agricultural labourer on working outside of the agricultural sector. [SOURCE: Page_283]

The village population density is today of 1.4 inhabitants per ha and the social categories are mostly represented by farmers with rainfed groundnut (with or without livestock), making 51% of the agricultural population of the archetype village. Pastoralists represent 11% of the farms. The farmers with full or partial access to irrigation remains a minority -38%-. All the social categories can be found in Table 23. The surface is generally not a determining factor except for the large-scale fruit growers who usually have a cropped land at least two to three times bigger than the rest of the farms. [SOURCE: Page_283]

1.2.1. The farms in the blind spot of irrigation 1.2.1.1. Non-irrigating farmers growing only rainfed groundnut, with no livestock and selling human labour power The farmers who were landless in the 1950’s and received 2 ha of land during the Land Reform. The ones who did not manage to drill a successful borewell (either because they didn’t have the financial capacity to attempt it, or the borewell they drilled had failed) grow groundnut in rainfed conditions on their whole land. They are mostly families belonging to the SC or BC castes. Those farms usually do not have livestock and they are composed of 2 family workers. [SOURCE: Page_285]

Groundnut cultivation requires hired labour, especially for the weeding and harvesting operations. In theory there are two options to do the weeding of rainfed groundnut, either carrying it out only with human labour which remove weeds with a hand hoe, or carrying it out with both human labour and animal labour and using scuffle hoes. As a reminder, production of groundnut fluctuates considerably with rainfall variability (T. Y. Reddy et al., 2003). Weeding not only elimites weeds but also allows to loosen the soil to enable rain water and the groundnut peg to penetrate in the soil (see chapter 3, section 2.2.4). Pegging in the soil is tugor dependent (Boote and Ketring, 1990). Weeding has to be done as quickly as possible in order to absorb as much rain as possible. If the field is hoed using only human labour (with hand hoes), then it requires 22.5 man-days per ha (Table 24). With bulls the work is faster and also less costly in terms of wages (Table 24). If farmers decide to do the weeding themselves, i.e. only family labour (last column in Table 24), then the maximum surface two family workers can cultivate would be between 0.1 and 0.6 ha, depending if we consider a time-lapse for weeding of 2 or 7 days. Weeding with bulls is therefore much more interesting financially and allows to go at a faster pace. [SOURCE: Page_285]

285 [SOURCE: Page_285]

Table 24. Comparisons of the labour and wages for weeding groundnut depending on if animals are used in addition to human labour Bull owners are paid per surface, while hired labour holding scuffle hoes are paid on a daily basis. Figure 181 shows the time spent and wages spent by the farmer owning the groundnut field in the case of a 2 hectare field. It shows that the lowest amount of wages spent by the farmer are when 2 labourers holding scuffle hoes and the bull owner weed the groundnut field, i.e. a total of 3 workers. However, with 3 workers, the time spent weeding is also the highest, i.e. 2 days of work. It is in the interest of the owner of the bulls to work as fast as possible in order to be hired by as many groundnut farmers as possible, and therefore increase its gross product from selling animal workforce. The negociation between the bull owner and the farmer is much in favour with the bull owner as 1) the groundnut growers absolutely need the bull owners to accelerate the weeding of groundnut (see previous paragraph) and 2) the bull availability in the village is low. The bull owners therefore have the power of negociating a duration of weeding as low as possible, i.e. 1 day instead of 2 (Fig. 181). In this configuration, the number of workers holding scuffle hoes has to be increased. The maximum is six, including the bull owner, as above this value the width of weeding would be too wide to transmit the traction force of the bulls (Fig. 181). Figure 181 shows that within this condition of 1 day of weeding, it is less costly of the groundnut grower to have a total of 5 workers instead of 6. We therefore see that in rainfed conditions, it is necessary to carry out the weeding of groundnut with bulls, and that hiring labour is necessary. In the case of a 2-ha land, the optimal number of workers is 5 as seen on the photo of Fig. 181. This value changes with the size of the plot. [SOURCE: Page_286]

Figure 181. The trade-off between the value of wages and time spent weeding 2 has of rainfed groundnut The harvest of groundnut is done entirely manually, by plucking on the groundnut plants by hand. It takes 50 man-days to harvest two ha of groundnut. Once the pods are mature, the risks of a late harvest are attacks from insects and fungi which can severely damage the crop. By waiting too long after the end of the dry season, the soil may become hard and impede the harvest. Again, hiring labour is necessary to harvest groundnut. The farmers relying only on rainfed groundnut are also the ones that work on other farms as labourers. [SOURCE: Page_287]

The agricultural income of those farmers is low, and they have to supplement their agricultural income by either working as daily labourers on other people’s farms (as show the red arrow of human labour flowing out of the production system on Fig. 183) or by having a part-time job, such as owning a small local retail-store (Fig. 182), owning a tea shop, managing the nearby milk collecting centre, transporting milk cans from the milk collection centre to the dairy factory headquarters in Anantapur. Those agents are paid 1 Rs/liter of milk transported, in addition to the transport charges. The farms living only on rainfed groundnut cultivation have no fixed capital apart from small implements such as hand hoes. The depreciation of assets is therefore zero. Approximately one third of the wealth created is left to hired labour (Fig. 183). As they have no livestock, the circularity and self-sufficiency indexes are close to zero (Fig. 183). As they have only rainfed crops, their net recharge is positive (Fig. 183). Most of the imported energy comes from the indirect fossil energy of fertilisers and pesticides used on [SOURCE: Page_287]

287 [SOURCE: Page_287]

groundnut (Fig. 183). The export most of what they produce, groundnut pods and groundnut hay for farmers owning livestock and not growing groundnut, such as pastoralists. [SOURCE: Page_288]

289 [SOURCE: Page_289]

1.2.1.2. Farmers cultivating rainfed groundnut and having a pair of bulls This production system is a variant of the previous production system. The farmers belonging to this production system grow groundnut in rainfed conditions on their 2 ha of land. They inherited those 2 ha during the Land Reform, and have kept a pair of bulls because most of their land still has many stones. They never managed to drill a borewell. In order to produce rice straw for their bulls, they rent 0.25 ha of irrigated land on the wash pediment which is in the vicinity of a borewell. They grow one cycle of rice on this land, which they only rent for the cropping season. The 2 family workers usually don’t work on other people’s farm as rearing bulls is labour demanding (mostly from grazing). The selling of draft power (Fig. 184) represents 58% of their gross product. Given the tiny surface under irrigation (0.25 ha of rented land) they are net rechargers of the groundwater table. They have an EROI above 1. Compared with the previous production system they have an additional entering flow of fossil energy and calorific energy corresponding to the rice bran and horse gram the farmers give to bulls on the days when they work on fields (Fig. 185). [SOURCE: Page_290]

Figure 184. A bull owner with his bulls, sowing groundnut with the farmer owning the field [SOURCE: Page_290]
