1.2.1.3. Farmers with access to irrigation in the wash depressions Those farmers are descendants of the large holder farmers who had a lot of land in the tank command area (they are mostly from the higher caste, Kamma caste). They have 1.6 to 4.8 ha of land, one third being located in the tank command area are cultivated with rice and the rest being on the wash pediment with no borewells. On the wash pediment they only grow groundnut in rainfed conditions. They have no machinery (tractors and implements) and only have 1 or 2 borewells (medium-depth) in the tank command area. They have no livestock. They are usually elderly farmers who have remained in the village but whose children don’t live in the village anymore and work out of the agricultural sector. As they have no livestock their circularity index is low (Fig. 186). They have an EROI above 1, explained by their specialisation in products with a higher energy content (groundnut, rice) than fruits and vegetables (Fig. 186). [SOURCE: Page_292]

Compared with their ancestors (large holder farmers in the 1950’s) who had a total of 51 ha and 8 ha of cropped land each year (Fig. 48, section 1.2.1, chapter 3), the workload is much lower (164 man-days instead of 2 083 man-days) because they have less land, no livestock and the land preparation, irrigation and harvest of rice is moto-mechanised. 87% of the man-days came from hired labour in the 1950’s (Fig. 48, section 1.2.1, chapter 3), and the rice and groundnut growers rely on hired labour at 74% (Fig. 186). The amount of energy produced and exported per worker for the rice and groundnut growers today is similar (105 GJ/worker) to what was produced and exported per family worker of large holder farmers in the 1950’s (180 GJ/ha). [SOURCE: Page_292]

292 [SOURCE: Page_292]

Figure 186. Structure and economic and environmental performances of rice and groundnut growers [SOURCE: Page_293]

293 [SOURCE: Page_293]

1.2.1.4. Pastoralists The vast majority of farms belonging to this production system are from the Kuruba caste. From all our interviewees, one was from the Reddy caste. Each farm owns 2 ha of land, inherited from the Land Reform, and which has remained rainfed ever since, either because of borewell failure or because those farmers didn’t even try drilling a borewell. They have 40 to 90 ewes and their progeny, which makes 60 to 150 heads. All their work is done by family workers. At night, they pen together their sheep with other flock to mutualise the work load of night surveillance, as pastoralists were already doing in the 1950’s. The size of their flock depends on the number of family workers and the feed production capacity. At least two labourers are required to manage a herd: one for taking the animals out to graze, and another person to assist, carry out household chores such as preparing the meals for the pastoralists who watch over the sheep at night, and even to help while administrating medicine to the animals. Pastoralists told us that the maximum flock size that a man could look after alone was 150 sheep. In Madakasira (south of Anantapur district), this limit is much lower because the surface under cultivation is much denser. In Anantapur, fields are much larger than in Madakasira and the cropped surface is overall less in Anantapur. The level of surveillance while grazing is therefore less in Anantapur. However, this limit is much lower than in some areas in France, where dogs are trained as “living fences” and guide the flocks. Although there are a few stray dogs roaming around the flocks and camps at night, the purpose of those dogs is rather to protect the herd from any thefts at night time and to protect the pastoralists sleeping at the camp. During the day, the dogs are not of much use and the flocks are entirely guided by the pastoralists who throw stones after sheep and goats lagging behind. The second factor that conditions the size of the herd is the feed production capacity. Pastoralists own 2 ha of land, inherited from the Land Reform. In winter, sheep graze on horse gram forage (Fig. 187). One ha of horse gram forage is required for approximately 30 ewes and their progeny. Figure 188 models a farm of 2 ha of land, with 50 to 60 ewes and progeny. For larger herds, pastoralists have to rent additional land to sow more horse gram, at a cost of 2 500Rs/ha per cropping season. The flows of grazed horse gram and grazed grass are internal flows of calorific energy of the production system (Fig. 188). The flow of human family labour on crops is very low as it is only required to prepare land and sow horse gram (Fig.188). In summer groundnut hay is bought, represented by the entering flow of caloric energy of animal feed and the indirect fossil energy linked to the production of the groundnut hay (Fig. 188). [SOURCE: Page_294]

294 [SOURCE: Page_294]

Figure 187. Sheep grazing in a field of horsegram [SOURCE: Page_295]

The only fixed capital pastoralists have is composed of barbed wire for fencing sheep at night, a charpoy bed (Indian traditional bed) for the man watching over the herd at night and 1 to 5 huts (pilala guddu) to keep lambs during the day while the rest of the herd is out grazing (Fig. 188). Compared to the pastoralists in the 1950’s (Fig. 57, section 1.3.2 of chapter 3), the circularity and self-sufficiency indexes have not evolved substantially. The total workload has also remained approximately the same. However, the energy produced and exported per family worker has increased from 1.6 GJ to 4 GJ/family worker (Fig. 188). The net water recharge has doubled because of a larger-size flock and a higher grazing intensity than in the 1950’s. [SOURCE: Page_295]

The access to resources is ensured by the access to land (cultivated with horsegram) but also through strong networks of social relations. We have identified three types of social relationships: networks with farmers and networks with other pastoralists which already existed in the 1950’s, and kin networks which have emerged since the beginning of borewell irrigation. Networks with farmers are still in place: pastoralists bring their flock to graze on the harvested field of farmers, mainly the okra fields and the horsegram fields. Pastoralists can also pen their sheep at night on the fields of livestock-less farmers before they are sown. Pastoralists may also have access to fruit plantation enclosures, to graze on the grass in between the rows of fruits, but this is quite rare and only once the fruits have been harvested. Networks with other pastoralists take the form of mutualistic exchange relationships. The animals of the different flocks are penned all year round together (see chapter 3) at night on fields, which represents a significant workload as at least one person is required day and night to look after the herd. The workload for the herd surveillance is mutualised as 5 to 8 herds, each belonging to a separate pastoralist family, are penned together at night. This is represented by the flow of [SOURCE: Page_295]

295 [SOURCE: Page_295]

human labour entering the production system on Fig. 187. One group is called a manda, and is composed of approximately 1 000 sheep and 5 to 8 herds. Two people have to sleep overnight with the herd, along with dogs to watch over and keep any potential thieves away (the study area is far of any forest or conservancy area and there are no animal predators). In the morning, the herds are separated as each pastoralists herds his flock his own way. One person can look after a herd of maximum 150 sheep but two people are required preferably. There are many prophylactic medicine to be given to the sheep (see section chapter 6). The workload for vaccinating the animals is also mutualised as medicine is given early morning before grazing in an assembly-line method, where 1 person fetches the sheep from the enclosure, another one retrieves it, another one immobilises it, another one has the medicine bottle and the last person administers the medicine. In this way, 10 sheep are vaccinated in 2 minutes (from observation). Medicine is bought for the whole manda, which is also a way of reducing costs. Mutualisation is also advantageous for negotiating access to harvested fields (red gram, usually where the leaves are nutritive, but also okra fields). The price is usually 2 500 ₹ per ha although if the field is not harvested it can mount up to 7 500 ₹ per ha. However, if the farmer requests pastoralists to pen their sheep at night on his field to fertilise his land, penning is free of charge and a mutual agreement is made between the pastoralist and the farmer. Since the 1950’s, with the advent of borewell irrigation, new social relationships have emerged based on kin networks. In the families of pastoralists, mostly Kuruba caste families, some members managed to drill borewells. In this case those former pastoralists abandoned sheep rearing to devote themselves fully to crop cultivation (usually small fruit plantations with dairy farming). The other family members continued to rear sheep in a pastoral way using their rainfed land to sow horsegram. The members who have continued pastoralism often have preferential access on the ley fallow land of the brothers who have abandoned pastoralism, to access the grass of the ley fallows and the grass in the fruit plantations. They also have preferential access to pen their flock at night on their brother’s land. From the perspective of the brothers who have abandoned pastoralism, it ensures either a fertility transfer or a recycling of biomass. All those social relationships are an integral part of the functioning of this production system. This social capital (Bourdieu, 1980; Scoones, 1998) represented by the networks with farmers and pastoralists is still as important as it was in the 1950’s. In the 1950’s those networks were also necessary for the summer transhumance to Bellary (see Chapter 3). [SOURCE: Page_296]

296 [SOURCE: Page_296]

Figure 188. Structure, economic performance and metabolic profile of pastoralists in 2022 [SOURCE: Page_297]

297 [SOURCE: Page_297]

1.2.2. The farms with access to irrigation on the wash pediment There are four production systems with access to irrigated land on the wash pediment: the large-scale fruit growers, the small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming and the vegetables growers with or without dairy farming. [SOURCE: Page_298]

1.2.2.1. Vegetable growers, with or without dairy farming Farmers which have received land during the Land Reform on the wash pediment and who have managed to drill a medium-depth borewell, usually grow vegetables, okra or tomato (Chapter 6) and have no livestock. They grow vegetables in rotation with groundnut. Farmers who descend from smallholder farmers (therefore having both land in the wash depressions and on the wash pediment) and who have also managed to drill a medium-depth borewell, grow vegetables and also rear crossbred dairy cows. The soils of their land in the wash depressions are indeed of hydromorphic nature, allowing only rice and Napier Grass cultivation (chapter 6). Those armers grow Napier Grass in rotation with rice on their land in the wash depressions, in order to feed the 1 to 3 crossbred dairy cows they have. The farms growing vegetables on the wash pediment and who do not have livestock, could also have grown Napier grass on their irrigated land on the wash pediment and reared dairy cows. However, both the land productivity and the labour productivity of the vegetable cropping system are higher than the one of crossbred dairy farming system^51 (chapter 6). When irrigation is possible on the wash pediment by means of a medium-depth borewell, farmers usually live only on the cultivation of vegetables. When they have land also on the wash pediment where only rice and Napier grass can be grown, they rear dairy cows in addition to the cultivation of vegetables. [SOURCE: Page_298]

Figure 189 illustrates the functioning of the vegetable growers with no livestock. They have 2 ha of land on the wash pediment, inherited from the land reform. This production system is composed of 2 family workers who are fully engaged in cultivation, i.e. 68% of the total human labour is carried out by family workers (Fig. 189). With one medium-depth borewell they can irrigate approximately 1.2 ha of land at a time, the rest being cropped with rainfed groundnut or left fallow. The whole land is covered by the okra-groundnut-fallow rotation presented in chapter 6. They usually prefer to grow okra as the price is a bit less volatile than the one of tomatoes. They can get a regular income from okra cultivation throughout the 80 days harvest period of each okra cycle. Okra can be cultivated both during the monsoon and in [SOURCE: Page_298]

51 Okra-groundnut cropping system: labour productivity approximately 852 Rs/man-days and land productivity approximately 200 000 Rs/ha ; Crossbred dairy livestock farming system : labour productivity approximately 600 Rs/man-days; value added generated by 2 HF cows approximately 100 000 Rs. [SOURCE: Page_298]

298 [SOURCE: Page_298]

summer (chapter 6). When okra is grown on the maximum irrigated surface, i.e. 1.2 ha of land, the two family workers are engaged full time as shows the labour calendar on Fig. 188 during the months of March to May. During the monsoon the land is partially cropped with okra and the other part with rainfed groundnut. 32% of the total human labour is carried out by hired labour, mostly for groundnut when it comes to weeding and harvesting the crop. The family workers of this production system rarely work on other people’s farms, except in December when they have finished harvesting their own crops (Fig. 189). The main flow entering the farm is the flow of fossil energy to produce chemicals which is composed at 90% of chemical fertilisers. As they have no livestock, they usually pay pastoralists to pen their sheep at night before sowing their fields (see imported flow of calorific energy of sheep droppings on Fig. 189). Their circularity and self-sufficiency indexes are close to zero as they have no livestock: the only internal flow correspond to the human family labour energy (Fig. 189). [SOURCE: Page_299]

299 [SOURCE: Page_299]

Figure 189. Structure, economic performance and metabolic profile of the vegetable growers with no livestock [SOURCE: Page_300]

300 [SOURCE: Page_300]

1.2.2.2. The small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming The small-scale fruit growers are either farmers who received 2 ha of land during the Land Reform and which have managed to engage in borewell irrigation, or descendants of smallholder farmers of the 1950’s. In the latter case, they already had land before the Land Reform. They usually have 2 ha of land, mostly located on the wash pediment. They may have, at maximum, 3 ha of land, if they cultivate also part of the land of one of their brother’s, who has left the village to work in other activity sectors. [SOURCE: Page_301]

They have only managed to drill 1 deep borewell and only part of their land is therefore irrigated. They also rear crossbred dairy cows. Most of the irrigated land is cropped with fruit trees and a small part is kept to grow Napier grass to feed the 1 to 3 crossbred Holstein Friesian cows. The crossbred dairy cows contribute to only 20% of the gross product but provide the necessary manure to apply at the base of the fruit trees (internal flow on Fig. 190). The farmers usually start by planting sweet lime as illustrated on Fig. 190. Sweet lime is indeed the most affordable fruit tree out of the four found in the area (sweet lime, pomegranate, banana and grapes) (see chapter 6). The rest of the land is under rainfed groundnut, which the hay is used to feed livestock (internal flow on Fig. 190). The flows of manure from the livestock farming system to the fruit plantations, and the groundnut hay and Napier grass induce important internal flows, therefore maintain the circularity index at 38% and the self-sufficiency index at 55%. Those values are however lower than the ones of the smallholder farmers of the 1950’s (Fig. 47, section 1.2.1 of chapter 3), where circularity was 90% and the self-sufficiency index 98%. The only imported flow of energy of smallholder farmers in the 1950’s was from hired labour. Today, the inflows of energy of small-scale fruit growers are much more important and of different nature: the calorific energy of feed concentrate for the cross bred cows and the fossil energy for electricity for the ventilation of the cows, for producing chemicals and feed concentrate (Fig. 190). The flows of fossil energy of chemicals are composed at 90% by the fossil energy consumed to produce synthetic fertilisers. The farm exports fruits, groundnut and also milk to the dairy collection centres. Even though 57% of the land is rainfed, the rest is cultivated with perennial irrigated crops which require water all year round, therefore tipping the net recharge below zero (Fig. 190). This production system is based on 52% of hired labour on crop cultivation. The labour spent on livestock rearing is 100% family labour. [SOURCE: Page_301]

301 [SOURCE: Page_301]

Figure 190. Structure, economic performance and metabolic profile of the small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming, the case of sweet lime [SOURCE: Page_302]

302 [SOURCE: Page_302]

In practice, the trend of those farms is to drill a second deep borewell in order to increase the irrigated surface and therefore reduce the surface under rainfed groundnut. Figure 191 shows the evolution of agricultural income for a pomegranate grower, in the case where the farm has one borewell (full line) or two (dotted line). The conversion of additional land to irrigating land enables farmers to increase their income for the same cropped surface per worker. [SOURCE: Page_303]

Figure 191. The role of borewells in the increase of the agricultural income of production systems If all the land is converted to irrigated land and fruit plantations, the farm has a higher income, and produces less groundnut hay. The crossbred cows are gradually sold out and farmers start importing manure from outside the village. The small-scale fruit growers eventually abandon livestock and grow only fruit plantations, therefore becoming large-scale fruit growers. [SOURCE: Page_303]

1.2.2.3. The large-scale fruit growers The large-scale fruit growers are either descendants of the large holder farmers of the 1950’s or investors from out of the study area and who have bought or rented land on the wash pediment, especially along the Bangalore-Anantapur highway. Fig. 192 represents a large-scale fruit grower descending from large holder farmers of the 1950’s, i.e. no land rent. They own between 2 to 8 ha of land located on the wash pediment. This land has been fully destoned and fully put under borewell irrigation. They have no livestock. All their land is under perennial crops, which are usually grape vines and pomegranate trees, which have the highest value added per ha (see chapter 6). Although not the majority, a few large-scale fruit growers choose to plant mango orchards, but this cropping system wasn’t modelled in this study. It is still worth mentioning that mangoes, can be grown in irrigated conditions by the large-scale fruit growers in order to provide a wide variety of mangoes off-season, therefore benefiting from very high prices to sell mangos all over India, from Bangalore, Hyderabad, to Delhi. The large-scale fruit [SOURCE: Page_303]

303 [SOURCE: Page_303]

growers have 2 to 6 deep borewells depending on the surface they possess. We considered one family worker for this production system as the head of family is usually the only one implicated in farm operations and in the farm management. Other family members and relatives usually work in the banking or software sectors in cities such as Anantapur, Hyderabad, Bangalore or sometimes even Chennaï. The wife usually stays at home but never works in the fields. Those farms rely on at 97% on hired labour for planting, weeding at the bottom of plants, pruning and harvesting fruits. All other operations are moto-mechanised. The family worker carries out the tractor-operated operations such as weeding between fruit tree rows with the blade harrow and spraying chemicals using a tractor mounted sprayer (PTO). He also sets off the drip irrigation system once or twice a week and buys the fertilisers and manure. The large- scale growers are fully equipped with a tractor, a tank sprayer and a subsoiler. All their surface is under borewell irrigation and they grow irrigated perennial crops: they therefore have a negative groundwater recharge and are therefore net extractors of the groundwater table (Fig. 192). They also import a lot of cattle manure 200-km away from Anantapur, which represent an inflow of indirect fossil energy to produce and transport the manure, and also a flow of calorific energy (Fig. 192). Manure is bought in large quantities, approximately 25 tonnes FW per ha, to be spread at the base of fruit trees to improve the water retention in soil (see chapter 6) and the flow of calorific energy corresponds to nearly 90% of the imported flow in the production system. The second most important inflow is the indirect fossil energy consumed to produce chemicals used on the fruit plantations: 34% correspond to the manufacture of fungicide, 49% for herbicide and 13% for synthetic fertilisers, the rest being consumed for the manufacture of insecticides and growth regulators. Pomegranate is indeed a crop which is very sensitive to diseases and fungi. The large-scale fruit growers also spray herbicides to control weeds. This production system functions in a very linear way with the circularity and self- sufficiency indexes close to 0. The only internal flow is the flow of human family labour on crops. The EROIS are below 1, meaning that more energy is imported than what is produced and sold. Fruits have indeed a low dry matter content (see Appendix 8) and the calorific energy produced per ha is therefore lower than for groundnut for instance. The large-scale fruit growers have the financial capacity to drill more borewells and deeper ones. In the hard rock aquifer areas (study area), tube wells interfere which results in competitive deepening of wells. In alluvial aquifers on the other hand, there is no interference and the depletion of the water table aquifer imply that the wells dry up and have to be abandoned (Shah, 2012). The large-scale fruit growers have the capacity to therefore capture the groundwater which can be chased down from neighbouring cones of depressions. 304 [SOURCE: Page_304]

Figure 192. Structure, economic performance and metabolic profile of the large-scale fruit growers [SOURCE: Page_305]

305 [SOURCE: Page_305]

2. Reshaping socio-economic patterns 2.1. Hiring labour to increase family earnings The large-scale fruit growers and the small-scale fruit growers have the highest net value added at farm level and the highest labour productivity (net value added divided by man-days). The labour productivity is far above the daily wage of hired labour (Fig. 193). Hiring labour is thus highly profitable. The key determinant of the growth of net value added is the access to irrigation, and especially to deep borewell irrigation to be able to grow fruit trees. Owning livestock is not a game-changer, except for pastoralists (Fig. 193). They have the second highest net value added per farm but their daily labour productivity is comparable to the ones of the other non-irrigating categories. The non-irrigating categories with no livestock and the rice growers in the wash depressions have the lowest net value added for all production systems (Fig. 193). The farmers growing vegetables and rearing dairy animals have a net value added similar to the ones of small-scale sweet lime growers but their labour productivity is comparatively much less. The net value added of vegetables growers with dairy farming is higher than for the vegetable growers without livestock because of the income from dairy farming and the higher income of tomatoes compared to okra. However, given the volatility of tomato prices, the net value added of the vegetables growers with livestock is highly variable. [SOURCE: Page_306]

Figure 193. Net value added and labour productivity at farm-level [SOURCE: Page_306]

All the production systems rely on hired labour (Fig. 194). For all production systems hired labour represents more than half of the total labour, except for the non-irrigating farmers who [SOURCE: Page_306]

306 [SOURCE: Page_306]

have livestock, i.e. bulls or dairy farming or sheep. The hired labour of pastoralists is not hired per se but corresponds to the reciprocal sharing of labour among pastoralists for night surveillance. The importance of hired labour is one of the characteristics of the patronal farming model. The analysis of the gross margin (wages deducted from the value added) divided by the number of man-days of family work shows that hiring labourers is a way of increasing the earning, especially for farms with irrigation (Fig. 195). This also the case of farmers cultivating rainfed groundnut (Fig. 195). As seen in the previous section, hiring labour is more interesting for rainfed groundnut cultivation than only relying on family labour. [SOURCE: Page_307]

Figure 195. Gross margin of production systems [SOURCE: Page_307]

307 [SOURCE: Page_307]

Most of the hired labour is hired for the weeding and harvesting operations. The weeding of groundnut and vegetables is mostly done by women (Fig. 196) who are paid less per day of work than men, 250 Rs instead of 300 Rs per day. The pruning and harvesting of fruit trees are done by external labour from out of the village. They are paid 500 Rs per day. They are hired in batches by the middlemen who buy the fruits. 2.2. Agricultural incomes: same old story or a changing trend of income inequality? Figure 197 shows for each production system the range of agricultural income per family worker as a function of the surface cropped per family worker of a household. It is compared with the survival threshold per family worker calculated in section 1.1.3 of this chapter and detailed in Appendix 31. [SOURCE: Page_308]

The large-scale fruit growers stand out from all the production systems, with an agricultural income 10 times more than the others. They earn between 45 000 to 90 000 euros annually per worker. This is because they grow fruit plantations on a large area, the size of their holding ranging from 4 to 8 ha of land. [SOURCE: Page_308]

The other agricultural holdings are characterised by a cropped surface of 1 to 2 ha, and have an annual agricultural income ranging from 300 euros annually (survival threshold) to 6 800 euros annually (pomegranate growers with dairy farming). The small-scale fruit growers have the second highest income (after the large-scale fruit growers), especially the ones who grow pomegranate. Nonetheless, pomegranate is a risky crop, very sensitive to diseases and some of the farmers we interviewed had already lost their whole plantation due to insufficient chemical [SOURCE: Page_308]

308 [SOURCE: Page_308]

treatments. The vegetable growers also have a good income, at least 4 times higher than the survival threshold. The volatility of tomato prices is backed up by the stable income from dairy farming (vegetable growers with dairy farming). Borewell irrigation is however not accessible to everyone. The surface under irrigation in the archetype village is still very low, i.e. 15%. A high investment capacity is required to be able to drill borewells several times because of a high percentage of borewell failure. [SOURCE: Page_309]

Most of the production systems today have no access to irrigation. 40% of the households live only from rainfed groundnut. They earn between 17 000 and 41 300 Rs per worker annually, namely between 200 and 470 euros. Their income is at the level of the survival threshold for a surface of 1 ha (Fig. 197), but below the national rural poverty line^52. They have to work on other people’s farm as daily labourers to increase their income. 5 households with no access to irrigation rear bulls in addition to groundnut cultivation. This enables them to have an income much higher than the farmers living only on rainfed groundnut (Fig. 197). 11% of the households belong to the categories of the pastoralists. They have only rainfed land, but sheep rearing enables them to get an income similar to the small-scale fruit growers cultivating sweet lime trees. [SOURCE: Page_309]

Figure 197. Agricultural income of production systems in 2022 Borewell irrigation, albeit uncertain, has been, for the ones who have managed to drill a successful borewell, a major socio-economic elevator. Today, part of the small-scale fruit [SOURCE: Page_309]

52 As a reminder the national rural poverty line is 42 300 per family worker (section 1.1.3). [SOURCE: Page_309]

309 [SOURCE: Page_309]

growers are descendants of landless pastoral categories of the 1950’s. They sold their flock of sheep to drill borewells on the land on the wash pediment which they got from the Land Reform. When the borewells were successful they gradually, they managed to engage first in vegetable cultivation. With the white revolution they started dairy farming by buying crossbred cows. They then managed to drill a deep borewell which enabled them to plant small fruit plantations. Today they are small-scale fruit growers and their situation is much different from their brothers who did not manage to drill borewells successfully who have continued rearing sheep. Both types of farmers usually belong to the Kuruba caste (BC, former pastoralists category), but the ones who have had access to irrigation have abandoned sheep rearing. They belong today to the same production system than smallholder farmers of the 1950’s who could drill borewells more easily on the wash pediment because of previously accumulated capital from rice and finger millet cultivation in the wash depressions. The former pastoralists who are now small-scale fruit growers can be considered in this sense as “nouveaux riches”. [SOURCE: Page_310]

The farmers with rainfed groundnut and irrigated rice in the tank command area have also a low income, close to the ones of farmers with rainfed groundnut, because the rice cropping system of the wash depression has the lowest land productivity of all. However, those farmers do not live purely from agriculture. They are descendants of the large holder farmers who used to control land in the tank command area today grow rice in the wash depressions and groundnut in rainfed conditions on the wash pediment. A major part of those descendants has migrated to the cities to work in other sectors than agriculture. This rural exodus of the ex- rich farmers of the village started in the 1990’s with the loss of value of the land of the wash depressions, which was in the 1950’s the crux of the agrarian system. Some farmers have stayed in the village or come back punctually to the village to grow rice for the whole family and then go back to the cities for the dry season. They are usually elderly farmers, maintaining the land of their family to grow rice for the family. Their relatives who are working in other activity sectors sustain them with their income. [SOURCE: Page_310]

2.3. Livestock of the rich or livestock of the poor? The role of livestock in wealth production Table 25 presents the contribution of livestock to the production of wealth, i.e. the gross value added at the scale of the production system. Dairy farming represents less than 25% of the gross value added for farms with access to irrigation. For farmers with only rainfed agriculture, livestock has a higher contribution, from 30 to 54 % for farmers rearing bulls for instance. For sake of simplification, we have not represented on the previous graphs the [SOURCE: Page_310]

310 [SOURCE: Page_310]

production system structured around rainfed groundnut cultivation and dairy farming of buffaloes (1 to 2), but the agricultural income of those farmers is similar to the one of the farmers growing rainfed groundnut and rearing bulls. For those non-irrigating categories with dairy farming, the contribution of dairy farming to the gross value added is 62 %. Livestock can contribute to more than 50 % of the gross value added but only for farmers with only rainfed land. When access to irrigation is possible, the contribution of livestock to the wealth produced is less and livestock tends to be gradually abandoned with the increase of irrigated surfaces and the drilling of deeper borewells for fruit plantations. [SOURCE: Page_311]

3. The coexistence of production systems and dependencies within the agrarian system 3.1. Living in the interstices: the critical situation of pastoralists Today there are more sheep in the village than in the 1950’s: there are more pastoralists (from 10 to 30 households) and the size of the flock per household has also increased. We know that the maximum flock size that a man can look after alone is 150 sheep (see chapter 6). The size of the flocks in the area vary, the smallest start at around 40 ewes and progeny (approximately 60 heads) and the maximum is 90 ewes and progeny (150 heads). Today an ewe and her progeny requires approximately 0.3 ha of grasslands per year. Today, we know that all the areas which are not cropped nor encroached by Prosopis Juliflora, are grazed by the sheep of the pastoralists. There are 30 pastoralists in the archetype village today (Appendix 15) and the farm type used to model flows is composed of 42 ewes and progeny. This is much [SOURCE: Page_311]

below that the maximum flock size of 90 ewes and progeny. As a consequence, the growth of the sheep population has not been as important as it could have been. The decline of the cattle and buffalo population has strongly benefitted the sheep because with the decline in cattle population, there was more grasslands available for sheep and more groundnut hay to give them in summer. At both time periods the sheep and goats were constrained by the availability of fodder resources. In the 1950’s, the most problematic season for the pastoralists was summer when the grasses were dry and of poor quality. They had to migrate to Bellary. During the monsoon and winter there was enough grass and the grazing areas were only grazed once a year. Today, the sheep are fed with groundnut hay in summer. Nearly half of the groundnut hay produced in the village is sold to the pastoralists who do not grow groundnut but need it to feed their sheep in summer (Fig. 198). The rest of the groundnut hay is exported out of the village as the other categories with livestock produce their own groundnut hay (Fig. 198). [SOURCE: Page_312]

Figure 198. Flows of gross energy of animal feed in the archetype village in 2022 All values expressed in GJ However, the cropped surface increased by 2 or 3 times since the 1950’s, with a disappearance of the ley fallows which were a reservoir of natural fodder. The enclosed fruit plantations are also additional lost grazing areas, which are inaccessible to pastoralists throughout the year. This has made fodder resources scarcer during the monsoon and winter. In winter, pastoralists take their herd to graze on horse gram forage. On the other hand, the scarcity of fodder resources during the monsoon are not compensated by other types of feed. [SOURCE: Page_312]

312 [SOURCE: Page_312]

In 2022, the scarcity of fodder resources is therefore mostly encountered during the monsoon season. [SOURCE: Page_313]

The other production systems rely less on grass resources than the sheep. They depend mostly on straw, hay and also irrigated fodder. The production systems with crossbred dairy cows have no pale-green arrows circulating with the production system (i.e. natural grazed grass) but it has been replaced by a vivid green arrows representing the flows of Napier Grass produced on-farm in irrigated conditions. All the feed concentrate flows, the fossil energy to manufacture the concentrate and the calorific energy of the feed, are flows entering the village and going towards the categories with dairy farming. A thin arrow goes to the non-irrigating farmers with bulls (Fig. 198) as they have to buy horse gram grain and rice bran for their bulls when they are at work. The production of rice straw in the village is low and a small quantity has to be imported to feed livestock (Fig. 198). [SOURCE: Page_313]

3.2. Living from what others are missing: needing the water of the non-irrigating categories In the 1950’s, all the farms contributed positively to the groundwater recharge as each farm had less than a quarter of their cropped surface irrigated. The surface under irrigation was limited by the number of bulls. On the scale of the farms, the flows of water infiltrating and recharging the groundwater table outweighed the water being pumped for irrigation of finger millet and rice. Since the pump revolution, water is no longer raised by animal power but by electric pumps. With one borewell approximately 1.2 ha of land can be irrigated all year round. Perennial irrigated cropping systems have emerged such as fruit plantations and Napier grass cropping systems. As a consequence, some farms have become net extractors of the groundnut table such as the large-scale fruit growers, the small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming and the rice and groundnut growers with no livestock (Fig. 199). The other production systems still are net rechargers of the groundwater table (Fig. 199). Henceforth, the pumping-extracting balance is now done between farms, and not within a farm as it was in the 1950’s. The farms in 2022 with have a positive net recharge compensate fully or partly the water extraction of farms with a negative net recharge. [SOURCE: Page_313]

313 [SOURCE: Page_313]

Figure 199. Net water recharge of production systems in 2022 [SOURCE: Page_314]

At the scale of the village the net water recharge is still positive despite more water being pumped than in the 1950’s (Fig. 200). This means that the volume of water recharging the groundwater table still outweighs the water which is extracted for irrigation. The use of groundwater has not reached yet a limit over which there would be more water being pumped than recharged and where the groundwater table would start declining, as it is doing so in other areas in India (Baccar et al., 2023). The irrigated surfaces have increased slightly (from 4 to 15% of the territory) but the increased volume of pumped water has been compensated by 1) rainfed cropping areas which have increased and 2) grazing areas which have declined but area grazed with a higher intensity than in the 1950’s. A new form of dependency has therefore emerged. The pastoralists and the farmers growing groundnut in rainfed conditions are the major contributors to the groundwater recharge which in return enables the farmers with fruit orchards and growing vegetables to exist. Figure 199 shows that the water extracted by 1 farm belonging to the large-scale fruit growers’ category can be compensated by the water recharged by either 1 to 2 farmers belonging to the pastoralists category or approximately 10 farms belonging to the category of farmers with rainfed groundnut and no livestock. [SOURCE: Page_314]

3.3. Importing food, manure and fossil energy In 2022, apart from rice and groundnut, most of the food is produced out of the village and imported in the village. The poorer categories which don’t produce rice grains have access to rice through the Public Distribution system (Fig. 201). Sugar, wheat flour for making chapatis and sunflower oil is also bought in the local shops (Fig. 201). All the categories, except the large-scale fruit growers grow and export groundnut in the village (Fig. 202). They all keep are small part of the groundnut pods for household consumption, i.e. approximately 80 kg. Most of the non-irrigating farmers grow groundnut mixed with rows of redgram. All the categories which do not produce red gram import it in small quantities to make the dahl-based meal (Fig. 202). [SOURCE: Page_315]

This corresponds to the selling of culled cows and male calves to middlemen (Fig. 203). Today the quantity of manure collected on the territory has declined because of a smaller livestock population. Synthetic fertilisers cannot replace manure entirely: apart from the small inputs of nitrogen, manure is essential for carbon, improving soil texture and retaining water in the soil. Manure is still extremely valuable and is never sold between farms. Farms who do not have livestock anymore, such as the vegetables growers with no livestock, pay pastoralists to pen their flock at night on their fields. The sheep and goat dropping is directly deposited on field during night penning. Those flows were however not calculated and are represented by a dashed line on Figure 204. Manure is indispensable for the irrigated fruit trees in improving soil water retention. The farms growing small fruit plantations use the manure produced by their own HF crossbred cows. The large-scale fruit growers have no livestock and buy large quantities of manure, approximately 25 tonnes fresh weight per ha of [SOURCE: Page_317]

317 [SOURCE: Page_317]

fruit plantations which corresponds to a cost of 100 000 Rs^53. This is two to three times what the most represented category earns annually, i.e. the farmers with only rainfed groundnut. The other farms usually use the manure they produce for the ones who have cattle or buffaloes, while the others rely on their interactions with pastoralists to fertilise their land using the sheep and goat dropping which is directly deposited on fields either while grazing or during night penning (Fig. 204). [SOURCE: Page_318]

Gross energy and indirect fossil energy flows of manure in the archetype village in 2022 All values expressed in GJ With the Green Revolution, the pump revolution and the White revolution, fossil energy has become a key cog of the agrarian system. All types of energy are represented and represented per ha. energies are overall much more important than the fossil energy. The labour energy largely is barely visible on the figure as it is largely outweighed by fossil energy and calorific energy (Fig. 205). [SOURCE: Page_319]

Figure 205. All types of energy consumed, produced and re-invested and produced and exported at farm-level in 2022 All the production systems, even the poorest and with no fixed capital, consume fossil energy: either directly from the diesel consumption of rented tractors for instance, or indirectly from the use of synthetic fertilisers and other plant protection products such has insecticides (Fig. 206). The pastoralists have the lowest fossil energy consumption per ha. Their fossil energy consumption is mainly due to the indirect fossil energy of groundnut hay bought to feed the sheep in summer. The fossil energy consumption from chemicals of non-irrigating production systems is high mostly because of the use of synthetic fertilisers and pesticides against thrips on groundnut. Production systems with irrigation have a higher fossil energy consumption from electricity because of the electricity consumed for irrigation. 25% of the fossil energy of large-scale fruit growers comes from the import of manure. This is because the quantity of manure applied per ha is huge, i.e. approximately 25 kg FW. One third of the fossil energy emissions of manure are covered by its transport 200 km away from the area. The large- scale fruit growers indirectly consume fossil energy with the import of manure for their fruit trees, which represents approximately 25% of their fossil energy consumption. The fossil energy from the electricity consumed for pumping water is comparatively fairly low. This is explained by the shallow depth of the groundwater table, measured at around 10 metres deep [SOURCE: Page_319]

319 [SOURCE: Page_319]

(own measurements) which induces a low consumption of electricity. If the groundwater table level was to decrease then the fossil energy consumption from electricity for irrigation would also increase. [SOURCE: Page_320]

Figure 206. Fossil energy consumption per ha at farm-level in 2022 On the scale of the village, the most important flow of fossil energy corresponds to the indirect fossil energy to produce synthetic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides. The direct fossil energy spent for irrigation (direct fossil energy from electricity) is fairly low compared to other types of fossil energy, but could be increased if the groundwater table was to go down, the consumption of electricity from pumps is directly proportional to the level of the groundwater table (Appendix 24). The flows of fossil energy have decreased the EROI not taking into account internal flows (EROIext-import), the energy self-sufficiency indicator (Eselfsuff) and the circularity index (Cindex) (Figure 207). Despite this, the EROIext-import is still above 1, which means that there is still more energy produced and exported than what is imported. This is explained by the productivity gains obtained from the different agricultural revolutions, and also because the main crop in the village is groundnut: groundnut is mostly exported (approximately 65 % of the groundnut production in GJ -pods and hay- is exported) and has a higher energy content than other crops (such as fruits and vegetables for instance). The circularity index has declined from 82 % to 29% (Fig. 207): the main flow that keeps circularity up are the flows of animal feed which represent 71% of gross energy flows circulating within the village. Those internal flows of animal feed are mostly driven by 1) the flows of grazed grass (which, as a reminder was counted as an internal flow of production systems) and 2) the flows of groundnut hay partly redirected towards the pastoralists who buy groundnut hay for their sheep in summer. Nonetheless, the production of groundnut hay consumes fossil energy, mostly from synthetic fertilisers, pesticides and diesel to prepare land and thresh the pods. The [SOURCE: Page_320]

320 [SOURCE: Page_320]

circularity of the village is therefore of different nature than the one in the 1950’s, as it is fuelled by pulses of fossil energy. [SOURCE: Page_321]

The representativity of the category is not proportional to the inflow of fossil energy in the village (Fig. 208). The non-irrigating categories with no livestock are responsible of 38% of the import of fossil energy in the village but they are also the most represented social category, i.e. 40% of the agricultural population. The large-scale fruit growers and the small-scale fruit growers on the hand are responsible of respectively 5% and 23 % of the fossil energy import but they represent 1% and 14% of the population (Fig. 208). [SOURCE: Page_321]

3.4. The shadow men and animals: labour energy hidden by fossil and gross energies, despite being vital Figure 207 on the scale of the village shows the very small flows of human labour and animal labour, compared to the flows of fossil energy and animal labour. [SOURCE: Page_322]

Today there are only 5 pairs of bulls left, whereas there were 130 pairs in the 1950’s. The population of draft animals has considerably declined, due to the replacement of animal power by fossil energy (electric pumps for irrigation, diesel for running engines for cultivation, harvesting and post-harvesting operations). In the 1950’s, animal power was very rarely sold out to other farms and the animal labour energy flows were contained within the farm. Today this configuration has changed. The farmers growing rainfed groundnut and rearing bulls sell the animal power of their bulls mainly for weeding operations on rainfed groundnut. In rainfed conditions, using bulls for weeding is more economically interesting than employing human labour. The bull population has strongly declined but it has not totally disappeared as they remain necessary for weeding. Figure 209 shows the central position of this production system and how it is connected to all the other production systems growing rainfed groundnut by thin flows of less than 1 GJ per farm. [SOURCE: Page_322]

322 [SOURCE: Page_322]

Figure 209. Human and animal labour flows in the archetype village in 2022 All values expressed in GJ In the 1950’s, the flows of human labour were represented by a thick arrow of 159 GJ flowing from the landless categories to the landowning ones and by a total of 379 GJ of family labour (see chapter 3). Today the flows of human labour energy are represented by much thinner flows circulating from the livestock less categories growing rainfed groundnut towards all the others. Even the farms within this latter category exchange labour (27 GJ) for weeding of groundnut. Nonetheless, the total internal flows of human labour in the village are of 596 GJ today, a value slightly higher than in the 1950’s. Despite the partial moto-mechanisation, the cropped surfaces have approximately doubled and many cultivating operations are still manual, such as groundnut weeding or the harvest of crops. [SOURCE: Page_323]

In the 1950’s all the landless categories were enough to fill the labour demand of the farmers with land (no labour from outside the village). Today the village labour is still enough to fulfil the demand but there is a small flow of human labour energy entering the village (Fig. 209). This corresponds to the labour for pruning and harvesting fruit trees. This labour is hired in batches from other villages in Anantapur district and are paid higher than the hired labour of village. They are called in batches by middlemen and employed by the large-scale fruit growers [SOURCE: Page_323]

323 [SOURCE: Page_323]

and the small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming. The human labour demand is fairly well spread out over the year because the perennial irrigated cropping systems create a labour demand all-year round (Fig. 210). The labour for rearing livestock is also constant, but compared in the 1950’s is mostly made of the labour of pastoralists which are more numerous than in the 1950’s (30 households instead of the previous 10 in the 1950’s). November is a peak period for the harvest of rainfed groundnut which is the main crop of the village (Fig. 210). The demand in hired labour in November is of approximately 7 000 man-days (6 000 MD for rainfed groundnut and 1 000 MD for irrigated crops), which is very close to the labour that the non-irrigating farmers with only rainfed crops and landless categories can provide. They constitute 244 workers in the village which can be hired. In the peak periods of September and November, the categories selling workforce are just enough to fulfil the labour demand. In the other months of the year, such as in August, or winter, the labour demand is much lower and not all the workers selling their workforce can be hired. [SOURCE: Page_324]

Figure 210. Family and hired labour monthly calendar at territorial level in 2022 [SOURCE: Page_324]

324 [SOURCE: Page_324]

Conclusion of chapter 7: The farms in Rapthadu rely on hired labour on a structural and permanent basis, making them patronal farms. Hiring labour enables to increase the family earnings. The socio-economic differentiation of farms is the result of various trajectories. The access to borewell irrigation, when it was possible, was a major socio-economic elevator. The ones who have not managed to drill successful borewells are heavily indebted and have to rely on rainfed crops. Livestock is not a game changer except for pastoralists who manage to earn an income similar to the ones of small-scale fruit growers with sweet lime but at the price of working day (grazing) and night (surveillance of the flock). The wash depressions are no longer the crux of the agrarian system: only rice and Napier grass is possible in those areas. Rice has a low value added and Napier Grass is only of use to farmers with dairy cattle. The rice growers of the wash depressions have a similar agricultural income than the non- irrigating groundnut growers with no livestock of the wash pediment. The rice growers of the wash depressions however do not live entirely from agriculture as most of their family members work in other activity sectors in cities. Rearing bulls and dairy cows enable farmers to increase their agricultural income. The labour productivity of livestock farming systems of rainfed categories is however low, and is only an advantage when the possibilities of selling workforce and working on other farms are limited. The agrarian system has been transformed by the use of fossil energy for pumping water from wells, run the machines to prepare land and harvest crops, but also to produce all the synthetic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides. With borewell irrigation, animal labour has considerably declined since the 1950’s. Today the surfaces cultivated by the non- irrigating farmers and the surfaces grazed by grazing livestock recharge the groundwater table, which in return enables the few irrigating farms to be able to extract water in a sustainable way. Those irrigating farms also need the labour of the non-irrigating categories to remove weeds between rows of vegetables and fruit trees, prune fruit trees and harvest fruits and vegetables. Human labour has not declined. On the contrary it has even slightly increased in the village since the 1950’s, despite moto-mechanisation. This is due to the increase in irrigated surfaces and the emergence of perennial irrigated cropping systems. The flows of human labour are however partly concealed by flows of gross energy of groundnut hay which add a new shade of interdependence between categories producing groundnut and pastoralists who buy groundnut hay in summer to feed their sheep. [SOURCE: Page_325]

325 [SOURCE: Page_325]

326 [SOURCE: Page_326]

CHAPTER 8: Merging the labour, energy and water questions into one: the agrarian question [SOURCE: Page_327]

Throughout this thesis, we have explored the changing social relations of production in the semi-arid agrarian system of Rapthadu. In this chapter we discuss the environmental implications of those changes. We do so firstly by discussing the changing role and nature of livestock. We then consider the implications of those changes on the relations of energy and water interdependencies which may display relations of domination and inequality. We conclude by outlining several key avenues of enquiry to compare Rapthadu with other agrarian systems, reflecting on the compatibility of social and environmental sustainability and on the future of agriculture with or without farmers. [SOURCE: Page_327]

1. Livestock: necessity or option of the agrarian system? 1.1. Livestock no longer of any use “as a whole” but still indispensable for “parts” of it In the 1950’s, livestock was a sine qua none condition to agricultural production, especially draft animals. Draft animals were an asset of the landowning social categories, which formed the wealthier part of the agrarian society i.e. the large holder farmers and the smallholder farmers. The multifunctionality of livestock was embraced in many forms. Muscular energy of draft animals was used for cultivation and transport, including lifting water from wells for irrigation. Dairy animals i.e. buffaloes and local dairy cows, provided food in the form of milk and other transformed products such as curd and ghee. The hides and skins of dead animals were used to make leather buckets for irrigation and other leather objects such as harnesses for draft animals. Livestock converted the biomass of grasslands and crop-by products into manure, thus either transferring nutrients from the saltus to the ager or recycling biomass of the ager. The excreta of livestock not only provided nutrients but was mostly a source of carbon and nitrogen to build up the organic soil matter. All the livestock farming systems were at least partially grass-based. The grazing areas -the ley fallows of the ager and the saltus- contributed to the groundwater recharge. Draft animals embraced all those functions at the same time while dairy animals and sheep supplied all functions except draft power. The combination of all these functions made livestock an absolute necessity “as a whole” and it was the keystone of the agrarian system. Without livestock, cultivation was impossible. [SOURCE: Page_327]

327 [SOURCE: Page_327]

Today, livestock is no longer the keystone of the system. However, it remains indispensable for some parts of it. The population of draft animals has been divided by 20, from 104 to 5 pairs in the archetype village. Although very few in number, those draft animals remain nonetheless indispensable for one very specific operation: the weeding of rainfed groundnut using implements pulled by bulls. Weeding of groundnut is indeed an operation which is not moto- mechanised and the use of bulls enables saving on human labour. Milk is still an important food item and is bought daily from the village shops by all social categories who do not have dairy animals. Manure remains vital for its carbon content and its function in soil water retention. The cost of manure is however very high, and is only bought by the wealthier categories, which are the large-scale fruit growers. The production of manure simulated in the village archetype in 2022 was not enough to fulfil the demand of farmers. For this reason, manure of large ruminants is usually not sold between farms. The large-scale fruit growers - who have totally abandoned livestock, buy large quantities of manure 200-km away from their own area to spread on their fruit orchards. The small-scale fruit growers still have a few cross- bred dairy cows and buy manure from outside in much smaller quantities, only to complement their own manure production. The only type of manure which is sold between farms is the sheep manure collected and sold by sheep fatteners. The sheep still play an important role – as they already did in the 1950’s- as fertility transfer agents, to fertilise land of farmers who no longer have livestock. Those farmers cannot afford to buy cattle manure and pay pastoralists to pen their sheep at night on their fields. The function of livestock for increasing groundwater recharge through grazing areas has remained but is mostly carried out by the pastoral sheep farming system. Farms have on the whole become more specialised thus severely fragilising or even breaking -for the ones who have abandoned livestock- the crop-livestock integration at farm-level. This has induced a higher dependency on inputs (Garrett et al., 2020; Schut et al., 2021). as illustrated by the large-scale fruit growers who have abandoned livestock but now import large quantities of manure to spread in their fruit orchards. [SOURCE: Page_328]

1.2. Agrarian transformations which allowed to dispense of livestock The multifunctionality of livestock has dwindled since the 1950’s, impeded by the successive agrarian revolutions. The necessity of owning draft power was first fragilised by the change of variety of groundnut in the 1980’s, where owning three pairs of bulls to harvest groundnut became unnecessary. Then the pump revolution gave a final blow to draft animals as bulls were no longer needed to lift water from wells. In addition, the role of leather was weakened as leather buckets were disposed of, but this change was not very perceptible in the [SOURCE: Page_328]

328 [SOURCE: Page_328]

energy flow analysis because leather was represented by very thin energy flows, despite being important assets of the agrarian system functioning in the 1950’s. This underlies a limit of energy flow analysis in the representation of low-weight or low-energy content products which play an important role in the economy (Bahers et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_329]

Nitrogen inputs from manure were partially replaced by subsidised synthetic fertilisers. The transport of sediments from tanks, which also supposedly brought nitrogen^54, also ceased in the 1990’s with the generalisation of the use of synthetic fertilisers, the development of borewell irrigation and the shrinking role of draft animals which were previously used to transport tank soil. With synthetic fertilisers, nutrients could be provided more easily, with much less work than what was previously needed, e.g. feeding and herding livestock throughout the year, collecting manure, digging tank silt and spreading the material on the fields. Most farmers gradually abandoned cattle and buffaloes to devote themselves fully to crop cultivation. The excavation of tank soil resurfaced again in the 2000’s with the emergence of fruit plantations, but this time not based on draft animal transportation: today it is the large- scale fruit growers who use tank soil as they have the financial capacity to rent backhoe loaders to excavate this matter. [SOURCE: Page_329]

In Rapthadu mandal, when access to irrigation was possible, livestock was gradually abandoned. The perfect example of this transition is the one of the former sheep pastoralists of the 1950’s who managed to drill borewells successfully. By decapitalising part of their herd and having won the borewell drilling gamble, they eventually managed to invest in small fruit plantations. They totally abandoned sheep and are now small-scale fruit growers, making them the “nouveaux riches” faction of the society. [SOURCE: Page_329]

A similar process involved the farms who were formerly purely rainfed and who managed to gain access to irrigation. Many specialised in milk production with the adoption of cross-bred cows. The agrarian history of the area indicates that dairy farming is however a temporary status in the capitalisation trajectory of farms and it tends to be abandoned when access to more remunerative crops such as fruits trees is possible. This is a dynamic which has been seen elsewhere in India (Aubron et al., 2023). It also resembles the one seen in a semi- arid Kenyan area, where access to irrigation of pastoralists was found to considerably reduce (to less than 30% ) the contribution of livestock in the household income. (Hemingway et al., [SOURCE: Page_329]

Although we didn’t analyse the nitrogen content of tank soil, we know from other studies that adding tank soil 54 [SOURCE: Page_329]

was a way of increasing mineral fertilisation providing nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus elements (Joshi and Deoras, 1955; Mohammed et al., 2009) and increasing organic matter (Adhinarayanan, 2017). [SOURCE: Page_329]

329 [SOURCE: Page_329]

2022). In Rapthadu, two form of livestock farming system have developed. The first form of livestock farming system is the development of crossbred Holstein Friesian dairy cows which were non-existent in the 1950’s. The second form is the intensification of the pastoral sheep farming systems (with a 6-fold increase of the sheep population), accompanied by the development of a lamb fattening system. The specialisation in meat production was speared by an increasing demand in meat which maintained prices high, making sheep rearing a lucrative alternative to rainfed cultivation. Nonetheless, sheep rearing is highly labour intensive and the labour productivity of a pastoral sheep system is low, which explains why, despite being a lucrative activity, it is still carried out by only 10% of households of the archetype village. [SOURCE: Page_330]

Today, livestock is no longer an essential cog in the agrarian system. The wealthier factions of society no longer need livestock to generate an income. Neither do most of the poorer households, as most of them live off growing rainfed groundnut and working on other farms. Livestock rearing is neither an asset of the rich nor of the poor. Some forms however generate a decent and stable income, the pastoral sheep farming system, at the expense of a high amount of family labour. Livestock being no longer a condition for agricultural production, the polarisation of the production systems has become the cause of a feed-food competition. In the 1950’s, livestock could use both the saltus and the ager by grazing ley fallows or feeding on crop-by products, thus lessening to some extent the competition between animal feed and human food (Tello et al., 2016). Today, dairy animals rely much less on grazing areas than before, as feed concentrates and Napier grass have been introduced in the feed ration. In the 1950’s, all the cropped areas provided crop by-products i.e. straw and hay. Today part of the cropped land, i.e. fruit orchards and most of the vegetables (except okra), no longer produce feed. Grazing sheep is also excluded from enclosed fruit plantations, which could have provided grazing resources in between the rows of fruit trees. The enclosure structure precludes access to grazing resources, as it does in other dryland areas of India such as Rajasthan (Agrawal, 1999, pp. 57–58). The difficulties for pastoralists in finding grazing resources during summer is buffered by 1) the purchase of groundnut hay and 2) their social capital as they have privileged access to the either uncultivated or harvested fields of their relatives, either from the same family or same caste. In winter, sheep graze on the horse gram which has been sown earlier during the monsoon. In the 1950’s, finding grazing resources during the monsoon was not a problem, but today, even during the monsoon, there is now much less grass availability for sheep. In Rajasthan (North-Western State of India, semi-arid area), the same problem occurs, with enclosures depriving pastoralists of grazing resources during the bottleneck [SOURCE: Page_330]

330 [SOURCE: Page_330]

monsoon months, and forces them to migrate more frequently and for longer periods than before (Agrawal, 1999, pp. 57–58). Nonetheless, some of the descendants of large holder farmers of the 1950’s have migrated to cities from the 1990’s onwards, thus abandoning their land on the wash pediment and the wash depressions. Although the land on the wash depressions is not usually grazed by the sheep^55 and are encroached with the invasive shrub Prosopis Juliflora, the abandoned areas on the wash pediment have become valuable reservoirs of fodder for the sheep population. This migration of large holder farmers descendants may continue in the future, thus releasing additional grazing areas for sheep and compensating the loss of grasslands by the expansion of fruit enclosures. [SOURCE: Page_331]

2. Inequalities over the use of groundwater: a fragile pumping-recharging equilibrium 2.1. A semi-arid context: a fertile ground for the development of inequalities The previous chapters have shown how the net groundwater recharge of the archetype village has slightly decreased between the 1950’s and today but is still positive, meaning that there is still more water recharging the groundwater table than what is extracted. [SOURCE: Page_331]

The Budyko framework (Budyko, 1974) allows us to go further in the analysis. This framework represents the evaporative index of a territory (meaning actual evapotranspiration - AET- of the soil and a given vegetation, divided by the mean rainfall), as a function of its aridity index (potential evapotranspiration divided by rainfall) (Fig. 211), which is a characteristic of the climate of the area. The framework is particularly useful to compare territories with different climates, but it can also help to visualise the impact of different land uses in a given climate, in relation to the limits allowed by the quantity of rainfall (water limit) and the evaporative demand (energy limit). Russian climatologist M. I. Budyko (1974) proposed this framework to predict the partitioning of water between evaporation and runoff for natural ecosystems. In humid and/or cold conditions (PET/P<1), rainfall exceeds the potential evapotranspiration: water is plenty and evapotranspiration is limited by the evaporative demand (called here “energy limit” as it is mainly driven by solar energy, or sometimes “demand limit”). In hot and/or dry conditions (PET/P>1), evapotranspiration is limited by rain (water limit). Budyko proposed a generic equation to represent the partition of rain water in different climates (Fig. 211): the area below the curve corresponds to the proportion of rain water evaporated and transpirated by the natural soil and vegetation, while the area between the curve and the water [SOURCE: Page_331]

55 The Parthenium weeds (Congress weed), also found in the wash depressions is toxic for animals. [SOURCE: Page_331]

331 [SOURCE: Page_331]

limit represent the proportion of rain water available for groundwater recharge and/or runoff. In arid areas, the curve is tangent to the horizontal asymptote y=1, i.e. evapotranspiration from vegetation and soil converges towards rainfall. At a later stage, Zhang et al. (2004) proposed a different equation, with a model parameter (w) allowing to adjust the curve to account for variations across ecosystems, linked with geomorphology, soil type, vegetation and climate (especially seasonality). In figure 211, we adjusted the w parameter to represent a territory with the land use of Anantapur in the 1950’s. Anantapur has an aridity index of 3.2 which is a characteristic of semi-arid areas: the village archetype is thus located on the x=3.2 vertical line on the right of the Budyko framework (Fig. 211). Using Zhang et al. (2004) equation, we draw the curve corresponding to the evapotranspiration of the vegetation of a territory with the same land use as Anantapur in the 1950’s. The areas with this land use but with a lower aridity index than in Anantapur will therefore have a lower evapotranspiration than in Anantapur, i.e the distance to the water limit is greater than it is in Anantapur. The areas with this land use but with a higher aridity index than in Anantapur will have a higher evapotranspiration than in Anantapur, i.e. the distance to the water limit will be shorter than in Anantapur. In other words, the drier the area, the shorter the distance to the water limit and the faster the evaporative index will move in response to changes of land use; the drier the area, the more polarised will be the agrarian society, between irrigating farmers (consuming groundwater) and those who live from rainfed cultivation or pastoralism (producing groundwater). [SOURCE: Page_332]

332 [SOURCE: Page_332]

Figure 211. Evolution of the evaporative index of a territory with a given land use in different climates, using the Budyko framework and the equation of Zhang et al. (2004) [SOURCE: Page_333]

2.2. The role of rainfed, irrigated cropped areas and grazed areas in the groundwater recharge: a sliding puzzle [SOURCE: Page_334]

In the 1950’s, the irrigated areas in the territory were less than 5%, the rainfed cropped areas approximately 20% and the grazed areas made up approximately 65% of the territory. The net groundwater recharge of the territory was positive and most of the water recharging the groundwater table came from surfaces grazed by draft animals, local dairy cows, buffaloes and sheep. Those grazed grasslands^56 were grazed once a year during the monsoon season. They had a low evapotranspiration and high net recharge (Fig. 212) [SOURCE: Page_334]

Figure 212. Actual evapotranspiration and net recharge according to different types of land use [SOURCE: Page_334]

56 As a reminder, grasslands in the 1950’s include the long ley fallows and the saltus which is mostly composed of mixed shrubland rocky hills. In 2022, grasslands are not as extensive. They include only the saltus which is now composed of abandoned land on the wash pediment and the same mixed shrubland rocky hills but which have been reduced. [SOURCE: Page_334]

334 [SOURCE: Page_334]

Since then, the population of large ruminants has declined (Table 26) and the most of large ruminants in the village today are non-grazing cross-bred dairy cows. Therefore, they no longer impact groundwater recharge. Between the 1950’s and today, the sheep population has been multiplied by 6 (table 26). [SOURCE: Page_335]

1950                                2022 Draft animals                             208                                  10 Buffaloes                               80                                  12 Local dairy cows                             64                                   7 Holstein Friesian                             0                                 124 crossbred cows Sheep (of pastoralists)                       240                                1 260 Fattened male lambs                             0                                 150 Total TLU (Tropical                           485                                 644 Livestock Unit)57 Table 26. Evolution of the livestock population in the archetype village (1950’s-2022) The available grazing areas have declined from 66 to 41% of the territory (Fig. 213) and the areas which were formerly neither grazed nor cropped have disappeared. This decline is the result of successive reconfigurations of the territory. First, the long ley fallows of the large holder farmers in the 1950’s disappeared during the Land Reform because most of the land which was distributed to landless categories came from those areas (Fig. 213). Then, three transformations happened almost concomitantly (Fig. 213) : 1) moto-mechanisation, and in particular backhoe loaders helped to partially remove the rocky boulders of the former saltus of the 1950’s and release new cultivable areas, 2) some of the large holder farmers who had land on the wash pediment and on the wash depressions migrated to cities before the development of fruit cultivation, thus leaving their land uncultivated – this made a few pockets of grazing areas available for sheep, 3) where borewells were drilled successfully, vegetables and fruit plantations were planted thus diminishing the grazing areas. [SOURCE: Page_335]
