All in all, the irrigated surfaces have increased from 4 to 15 % of the territory of the archetype village and rainfed cropped surfaces have increased from 19 to 42%, at the expense of a decline of grazing areas from 66 to 41% (Fig. 213). The grazing areas are also grazed more intensely, thereby lowering the evapotranspiration and increasing the net recharge (Fig. 212). [SOURCE: Page_337]

The respective land use of the village in the 1950’s and 2022 was plotted in Fig. 214. It shows that the evaporative index of the territory has increased since the 1950’s but is still far from the water limit (Fig. 214). This is explained by the fact that irrigated areas have increased only slightly and that their increase has been largely compensated in terms of evapotranspiration and net recharge by 1) the increase of rainfed cropped areas and 2) smaller but more intensely-grazed areas. Both the intensely grazed areas and the rainfed cropped areas have a lower evapotranspiration than natural vegetation (Fig. 212). The role of grazing areas and rainfed cropped areas in the groundwater recharge has also been seen elsewhere. Harris (2007) who studied the evolution of groundwater recharge in an Australian dryland catchment area with shrubland natural vegetation also mentioned this: “Catchment hydrology changes when clearing occurs. Both runoff and groundwater recharge increase, so that groundwater recharge under agricultural crops or grazed pasture is much larger than that under forest. For example, rates of groundwater recharge and downstream transport of materials have increased dramatically since Western agriculture was introduced in Australia. This appears to be due to a reduction in the leaf area of the vegetation and therefore a decrease in evapotranspiration. Compared with that observed under native bush, groundwater recharge in Australia has increased by at least an order of magnitude.” (Harris, 2007). Similarly, in the dryland Sahelian area, scientists noticed that in the past decades, the surface runoff increased over time, while rainfall decreased. This was explained by the decrease in natural uncropped and ungrazed areas. The clearing of vegetation decreases evapotranspiration and favoured runoff and indirect recharge from ponds or rivers. This observation, called “the Sahelian paradox” (Descroix et al., 2013) or “the Niamey paradox” (Favreau et al., 2006), is similar to the processes at play in Anantapur. Given the topography of the area, the rainfall which is not evapotranspired by vegetation can either infiltrate into the soil and recharge the groundwater (direct recharge) or run off at the surface and reach the river network, and finally fill the tanks, where it induces indirect recharge^58. [SOURCE: Page_337]

58 “Direct recharge refers to diffuse recharge, such as from precipitation, whereas indirect recharge results from the percolation of a part of runoff water through the stream beds, and localized recharge refers to concentrated recharge by preferential flow through cracks, joints and fissures” (Lerner et al., 1990; in Maréchal et al., 2009). [SOURCE: Page_337]

337 [SOURCE: Page_337]

Figure 214. Evolution of the evaporative index of the village archetype between 1950’s and 2022 [SOURCE: Page_338]

This means that except for the evaporation from the water bodies, or overflowing during heavy rainfall periods, most of the water “saved” by reducing evapotranspiration contributes to recharging the aquifer. By grazing, the sheep keep back the development of bushy vegetation, and especially the invasive Prosopis Juliflora shrub. This invasive shrub has a higher crop coefficient (Shiferaw et al., 2021) than the one we chose for the natural vegetation of this study, therefore a higher evapotranspiration than the one of natural vegetation in the study area. In the long run, grazing therefore maintains evapotranspiration lower than what it could be if those areas were totally abandoned, namely neither grazed nor cropped, and encroached by Prosopis Juliflora. [SOURCE: Page_338]

2.3. A territorial evaporative index with a high sensitivity to the changes of land use, a characteristic of semi-arid areas The evaporative index of the archetype village increased between the 1950’s and today, moving upwards but only very slightly, despite the significant increase in the proportion of irrigated crops (from 4% to 15%, see Fig. 213), some of which being now perennial, i.e. with even higher evapotranspiration rates Fig. 212). Why this only slight increase in the evaporative index, from 0.63 to 0.68? This is because the increase in irrigated crop area is compensated by [SOURCE: Page_338]

338 [SOURCE: Page_338]

the increase of rainfed crops and grazed area, both having much lower evapotranspiration rates than the irrigated cropping systems (see Fig. 212). In addition, between the 1950’s and today, the evaporative index of grazed areas has decreased because of a higher grazing intensity, and that of the rainfed crops has also decreased because groundnut has become the mainstream rainfed crop and has a lower evapotranspiration than most of the millets and pulses which were cultivated in the 1950’s. [SOURCE: Page_339]

The Budyko framework therefore tells us, and allows us to visualise, that the evaporative index of the archetype village hinges on very small variations. In the 1950’s, the territory evaporative index was relatively high because the low evapotranspiration rates of grazing areas and rainfed crops was compensated by the high evapotranspiration rate of irrigated finger millet and rice. In the 1950’s this equilibrium was not so much fragmented between social categories but happened within the social categories themselves, with some categories being net rechargers of the groundwater table and others net extractors. By this we mean that large holder farmers and smallholder farmers both cultivated irrigated crops with high evapotranspiration rates and rainfed crops with a lower one, and had grazing livestock. In 2022, despite the emergence of perennial irrigated cropping systems, which have much higher evapotranspiration, the evaporative index remains still fairly far from the water limit, because of the expansion of rainfed cropped surfaces, and also, to a lesser extent, due to the intensification of grazing areas. However, in contrast with the 1950s, this equilibrium is not achieved within farms, but between social categories. The social categories cultivating solely rainfed groundnut and the ones rearing sheep play a major role in maintaining the territory far from its water limit, to the benefit of irrigating farmers. [SOURCE: Page_339]

2.4. Groundwater: who controls who and what does it take to tip the balance? About the evolution of the net water recharge: If today the net groundwater recharge is still positive it is because a minority of farmers with access to irrigation coexist with a majority of farmers with no irrigation facilities (65%). The non-irrigating farmers are the main contributors to the groundwater recharge either by their grazing areas or rainfed cultivation activities. The minority of irrigating farmers exist not only from what others are missing – groundwater- but because of a non-conscious-form of exploitation where the labour^59 of [SOURCE: Page_339]

59 Pastoralists and rainfed farming actively contribute to the groundwater recharge by cultivating rainfed crops and by having grazing livestock: if they were not there, then the water recharge would be less. [SOURCE: Page_339]

339 [SOURCE: Page_339]

pastoralists and non-irrigating farmers enables the groundwater table to be recharged, therefore maintaining a sustainable use of the groundwater table. But then, who controls who? [SOURCE: Page_340]

About the evolution of the evaporative index: as we have seen in the previous section, Anantapur has a very high aridity index and because of the existing large gap between the climatic demand and the actual evapotranspiration (see previous section), the evaporative index is very sensitive to land use changes. In 2022, there is still a large gap between the evaporative index of the archetype village and the water limit. The expansion of irrigated surfaces through groundwater irrigation will increase the evaporative index, bringing it closer to the water limit (where the evaporative index equals to 1) and eventually to unsustainable levels. Considering the current rapid increase in the area under fruit plantation, which is promoted by the government, it is relevant to estimate how many has of fruit plantations it would take to reach (or cross) the water limit, under different scenarios. [SOURCE: Page_340]

Using the current situation as a departing point, we considered two scenarios of land use change impacting the two categories of current maximum recharge i.e. the non-irrigating farmers with groundnut, and the pastoralists. In both scenarios we looked at the impact of the expansion of fruit plantations, which are irrigated perennial cropping systems. We chose the case of sweet lime as it is a prime example of the fruit plantations of the region. We estimated the tipping point in each of those scenarios, above which the evaporative index exceeds the water limit. This tipping point also corresponds to the point above which the net water recharge would become negative: this would mean more water being extracted than being recharged, and therefore a structural decline in groundwater resource. [SOURCE: Page_340]

The first scenario supposes that the uncropped land of the village is partially planted with sweet lime trees. In 2022, grazing areas account for one third of the village. One of the current dynamics in the area is the installation of investors who rent or buy uncropped land to implement fruit plantations. Those investors can be urban investors who live most of the time in big cities such as Bangalore or Anantapur. They have either no connection with the area or are descendants of former villagers of the area. In both cases, fruit plantations are likely to impinge on the current grazed surfaces, and this is already under way (as shown on Fig. 129 in chapter 5). The major limits to the expansion of those fruit enclosures are the amount of capital it requires and also the labour availability. As investors usually are related either directly or indirectly to professional sectors other than agriculture (e.g. banking sector, trade), they are mostly wealthy and also well-connected to institutions with power. They can therefore benefit [SOURCE: Page_340]

340 [SOURCE: Page_340]

from bank loans with lower interest rates than those that villagers can get from other village inhabitants. The first limit can therefore easily be dismissed. Fruit plantation is also highly encouraged by the Central and State government as shows the implementation of the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) in 2014-2015. This scheme aims at developing the production of fruits and vegetables in India by setting up fruit tree nurseries, subsidising fruit plants, drip irrigation systems and also trellies to build pergola structures for running vines. The subsidies are shared between the Central Government and the State government at 60 and 40% respectively (Gov. India, 2022b). Andhra Pradesh is a focal point of this scheme as the aim is to make Andhra Pradesh the “fruit bowl” of South India. As for the second limit, the large-scale fruit growers mostly depend on hired labour for pruning and harvesting. This labour comprises of landless categories or non-irrigating categories of the district. They are hired in batches to work in the study area. As long as the proportion of non- irrigating farmers in the district of Anantapur remains high we can assume that there will be labour available to work on fruit plantations. If those non-irrigating or landless categories either manage to drill a borewell or migrate and work in other sectors than agriculture, then labour availability could be compromised. [SOURCE: Page_341]

The second scenario targets the poorest farmers, the ones who cultivate rainfed groundnut and have no livestock, which is the most represented production system today. It assumes a policy where farmers with only rainfed land and no livestock would benefit from subsidies for drilling borewells and implementing sweet lime plantations on their land. This scenario is however less likely to be realised than the first one as it implies a change of policy by the State government, and not just the consequence of an individual decision, which is the case for the investors in the first scenario. [SOURCE: Page_341]

Our model shows that the pumping-recharging water “tipping point” is reached when an extra 133 ha of sweet lime plantations are planted in the current grazing areas (first scenario) or when 135 ha of the currently cropped area with rainfed groundnut are replaced by sweet lime plantations (second scenario). This corresponds to either 22 investors with 6 ha of fruit plantations (the large-scale fruit grower production system) or 67 households belonging to the production systems of purely rainfed groundnut and no livestock (2 ha). This corresponds to 60% of the actual households of the category and 23% of the village households. The first scenario would also seriously impede the pastoral sheep systems, as the grazing land would also be reduced. As the fruit plantations are usually enclosed, sheep rarely have access to the grass resources in between rows of fruit plantations, casting them off as grazing areas. The [SOURCE: Page_341]

341 [SOURCE: Page_341]

second scenario would benefit the non-irrigating farmers who would have received the subsidies to drill borewells and plant fruit plantations. [SOURCE: Page_342]

Those examples exemplify how the irrigating and the non-irrigating categories, i.e. pastoralists and farmers cultivating solely rainfed groundnut, are interdependent. In other terms, the irrigating and wealthier factions need the labour and the water of the poorer ones, and the non-irrigating categories need the wage given by the wealthier. In the case where the tipping points would be reached or crossed, the groundwater table would start declining (like in other regions in India), the borewell yields would decrease (Baccar et al., 2023) up to a point where it would become impossible to pump water from some borewells, the shallower ones. The wealthier irrigating farmers would invest to drill borewells deeper and deeper in a desperate race with their neighbour to capture the remaining groundwater (Blakeslee et al., 2020). The water limit would however be crossed only for a short time, and after a few years, the feedback of the aquifer would constrain the system to reach another equilibrium – but with a huge economic and social cost. The categories who would not be in capacity to drill deeper borewells, would indeed have to stop cultivating irrigated crops and revert to rainfed groundnut. This cropping system has the lowest value added of all the cropping systems of the area. The wealth created per ha of rainfed groundnut is in a normal year 42 290 Rs and the wages are 14 800 Rs per ha, making a gross margin of 35 332 Rs per ha of rainfed groundnut (chapter 6). In chapter 6 we also provide the annual amount of interest to be paid back when a loan is contracted to drill a borewell. Most of the farmers who are already irrigating today have had to contract a loan to drill their borewell. In the case of a loan contracted to other villagers, i.e. the large-scale fruit growers, they have to pay back an annual interest of 28 000 to 76 800 Rs a year according to the depth of the borewell (chapter 6). If those indebted farmers had to revert to rainfed groundnut because of the decline of the groundwater table, they would not be able to pay back the interest for deep borewells with the income from rainfed groundnut. They would also be in a relation of financial dependence towards other wealthier groups. This situation of distress, has been well-documented in India, and has already led to the suicide of farmers (Galab et al., 2012; Reddy et al., 2010; Taylor, 2013). In other semi-arid areas in India, this risk is even greater as the value added of rainfed agriculture is lower than the annual interest to be paid for borewells (Fischer et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_342]

342 [SOURCE: Page_342]

3. Is environmental sustainability compatible with the social one? 3.1. 1950’s: an environmentally sustainable agrarian system based on strong social inequalities between landless and landowning categories In the 1950’s, inequalities were mostly driven by the relations of production between the land owning and the landless categories. The large holder and the smallholder farmers were neither linked by flows of labour energy (both hired labour from the landless categories and both had draft animals), nor flows of gross energy (both produced their own food and animal feed), nor flows of water (both contributed positively to the groundwater recharge). Although this has not been quantified, large holder farmers were most certainly wealthier than smallholder farmers because they produced more food and feed per family worker and also because they grew cash crops, i.e. groundnut. Debt relations convey towards this idea as large holder farmers were the money lenders of the smallholder farmers when needed. [SOURCE: Page_343]

The conditions of the agrarian system were such that it enabled the large holder farmers to accumulate surplus and become richer. On the other hand, the smallholder farmers could renew their family unit but were limited in the accumulation of surplus and capital. This was because they grew crops with a lower potential productivity than the large holder farmers. As rainfed crops, smallholder farmers could only grow millets and pulses as rainfed crops which had a much lower dry matter feed production than groundnut. It was therefore a vicious circle where their feed production conditioned the size of the herd which had to be partially fed on grasslands. As a consequence, only part of the manure was retrieved, and the input of organic matter from manure was therefore limited. Smallholder farmers didn’t have long ley fallows as they didn’t have enough land to do so. The only way of building up their soil organic matter content was to excavate tank soil and apply it to their land. Smallholder farmers had access to tank soil but were limited by the amount of labour to dig tank soil out and transport it. The conditions were therefore similar to other agrarian systems where the growth of the peasantry was limited by a vicious circle fuelled by unequal access to land (Gizicki-Neundlinger and Güldner, 2017). In Rapthadu mandal, access to grazing areas was provided as ley fallows were accessible to all and the saltus was a communal area. Access to land for cultivation was restricted by the land ownership and the means to cultivate this land, i.e. animal and manpower. Tanks were also a communal reservoir of fertility. Although in theory, everyone could have the right to benefit from tank soil, not everyone was able to benefit from it (Ribot and Peluso, 2003) as access to draft animals was necessary to transport tank soil to the fields. The ley fallow played an important role in the management of fertility as in other areas of the world (Badia- [SOURCE: Page_343]

343 [SOURCE: Page_343]

Miró and Tello, 2014; Tello et al., 2016). The disappearance of the ley fallow since the land reform, and much rarer use of tank soil today impedes the fertility of the agrarian system. The fertility is now dependent on chemical fertilisers for nutrients, which are subsidised in India – especially nitrogen fertilisers. The large-scale fruit growers also rent backhoe loaders for excavating tank soil to put at the base of their fruit trees. Buying manure and renting backhoe loaders to excavate tank silt is only possible for the wealthier categories: manure is bought 200- KM away from the area and the cost of renting backhoe loaders is high. [SOURCE: Page_344]

3.2. Human labour energy flows: a constant over time and a hallmark of Indian agriculture Even though the agrarian system has undergone major transformations since the 1950’s, the social relations of labour have remained unchanged in many ways. The division of labour between men and women was strong both in the 1950’s and today, as in other agrarian societies (Bourdieu, 1990). In the 1950’s, women had the exclusive responsibility of cultivation tasks which required no tools or very small ones, such as transplanting rice and finger millet, weeding groundnut and deshelling groundnuts. They were never in charge of driving a bullock cart or leading a pair of bulls, which was the sole responsibility of men. Some tasks were carried out both by men and men such as the harvest of crops. Today, the division of labour has not changed: women are still in charge of transplanting rice, weeding groundnut and vegetables, and are never seen driving tractors. We saw only once a woman and her daughter driving a tractor and spraying chemicals in a fruit plantation – they were large-scale fruit growers. Pruning, harvesting of fruits, loading fruits at the wholesale market are done by both men and women. [SOURCE: Page_344]

The calculation of energy flows at territorial level show that the amount of human labour energy circulating between farms today has not declined since the 1950’s. On the contrary human labour energy circulating within the village, i.e. either family labour or hired labour from the village, has increased from 538 GJ to 596 GJ (Fig. 215). An extra 56 GJ of human labour energy is also imported today from hired labour living in other villages of Anantapur districts and hired to prune fruit trees or harvest fruits. [SOURCE: Page_344]

In the 1950s’, all the flows of human energy were captured by the social categories with land, i.e. the large holder farmers and the smallholders. In 2022, the flows of human labour energy still circulate mostly from the poorer social categories (mostly farmers with only rainfed groundnut and no livestock) towards wealthier ones. The permanent relations of labours [SOURCE: Page_344]

344 [SOURCE: Page_344]

between the hired labour working under a gitam contract and the large holder farmers have disappeared. Today hired labour is exclusively paid in money, while in the 1950’s wages were frequently paid in king (grains, or even manure as seen in the previous chapters). The social relations of labour are today exclusively monetised and contractual, with labour hired and paid on a daily basis. The social relations of labour are therefore of “shorter duration, more contractual and monetised” (Breman, 2010) than the ones formerly carried in the 1950’s, what Breman (2010) calls practices of neo-bondage labour. The social categories capturing those flows of human labour energy are however more numerous than in the past. They correspond to the ones with at least one borewell today. As there are more categories hiring labour in 2022 than in the 1950’s, the total flows of hired human labour energy circulating within the archetype village are thinner than in the representation of the 1950’s where all the hire labour energy flowed towards two categories. Those comparisons show that the total human energy labour spent for agricultural production in the village has been multiplied by 1,1. The number of agricultural workers has been multiplied by 1.2 (Fig. 215). [SOURCE: Page_345]

345 [SOURCE: Page_345]

Figure 215. Total energy flows in the archetype village in the 1950’s and 2022 All values expressed in GJ [SOURCE: Page_346]

346 [SOURCE: Page_346]

The quantity of human labour energy spent per agricultural worker. varies among social categories at the two time periods (Fig. 216). Today farmers living from rainfed groundnut cultivation and working on other farms expend less energy from agricultural work than that used by smallholder farmers in the 1950’s, but expend more energy than that used by landless agricultural labourers in the 1950’s. The large-scale fruit growers (2022) and the vegetable growers with no livestock (2022) are the categories that have the lowest human labour energy expenditure on farm work among all categories over the two time periods. [SOURCE: Page_347]

Figure 216. Human energy labour productivity (human labour energy expended per worker) for each social category in the 1950’s and 2022 and per type of labour – family or sold out to other farms- [SOURCE: Page_347]

The transformations of the agrarian system of Rapthadu are therefore very different from the broad trajectories found in Western agriculture. Both have shifted from a ‘solar’ agrarian society to a ’mineral’ one^60 but in different degrees and ways. [SOURCE: Page_347]

Western agriculture has broadly undergone a process of moto-mechanisation resulting in a higher cultivated land surface per worker by means of tractors and other machinery (Mazoyer and Roudart, 2006). The European farmer population has also tremendously [SOURCE: Page_347]

60 We rely here on the terms of Allaire and Daviron (2018): “mineral” refers to a society which uses coal and oil and other minerals, and “solar” to a society producing biomass directly or indirectly by solar radiation or by the power of wind and water bodies [SOURCE: Page_347]

347 [SOURCE: Page_347]

declined. In Rapthadu, the evolution is very different, and similar to other places in India. The major difference is that the village workforce has increased (multiplied by 1.2) and that the cropped area per agricultural worker has decreased slightly from 1.2 ha/worker (including the ley fallows) to 1 ha/worker. The agricultural net production of the territory has increased from 20 648 GJ (including milk, leather, meat, grass and forage ingested by animals while grazing, distributed fodder, fruits, vegetables, grains, either consumed in the village or exported) to 67 039 GJ, meaning an increase by 3.24. The ager has remained roughly constant but the ley fallows have disappeared. The net productivity of cropped land (ager, including fallow land) has also increased from 36 GJ of agricultural product per ha to 118 GJ per ha. [SOURCE: Page_348]

Despite the irrigated area remaining still low (15% of the village surface), especially compared to other areas in India which have known an irrigation boom (Baccar et al., 2023; Fischer et al., 2022; Lucas, 2014), the irrigated crops still govern the flows of human labour as show figure 217. This figure shows the total quantity of human labour in man-days spent on the total surface of perennial irrigated cropping systems, one-cycle irrigated cropping systems and rainfed cropping systems. [SOURCE: Page_348]

Figure 217. Total human labour in man-days (top) and surface (bottom) of different types of cropping systems in the archetype village in 2022 Irrigated surfaces generate employment because of the multiplication of crop cycles and also additional or intensification of operations such as weeding or harvesting. The moto- mechanisation in Rapthadu mostly concerns irrigation, but also ploughing, harvesting of rice [SOURCE: Page_348]

348 [SOURCE: Page_348]

and post-harvesting operations of rice and groundnut. Weeding operations, harvesting of vegetables, fruits and groundnut, and pruning of fruit trees are all mostly manual. Agriculture in Rapthadu evolved in a different trajectory than in Western agriculture, where moto- mechanisation was concomitant with the decrease of agricultural workers and cropped surfaces increased per worker, allowing an increase in productivity of labour but also an increase of cropped surfaces per worker (Fig. 218). In Rapthadu, the net value added per day of work also increased but at the same time, the labour demand on irrigated crops and the irrigated surfaces also increased, therefore in fine decreasing the cropped surface per agricultural worker. Or the other way round: as the land surface per worker didn’t increase it was necessary to increase the labour productivity per worker via irrigation, otherwise farmers could not have continued living from agriculture. [SOURCE: Page_349]

Figure 218. Impact of moto-mechanisation on labour productivity and cropped surface per worker in Western agriculture and in India [SOURCE: Page_349]

The comparison of the total human labour and the surface under types of crops are an example of this labour intensification: irrigated surfaces still generate the most employment, despite representing a very small percentage of the territory (Fig. 217). [SOURCE: Page_349]

In Rapthadu, the village workforce has increased, unlike in Europe. The physical productivity of labour has increased from 43 GJ per worker to 120 GJ per worker. The physical labour productivity has therefore increased by 2.7, which is a lower rate than the 3.24-fold increase of the net agricultural production. This is an illustration of the “Lewis trap” or “poverty [SOURCE: Page_349]

349 [SOURCE: Page_349]

trap” (Dorin et al., 2013), which is an evolution pathway characteristic of Asian countries, and very different from developed countries. This is the opposite of industrialised countries of the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development), which follow the “Lewis Path” where the rise in labour productivity means that wages are increased and poverty reduced and leading to a world without farmers (Dorin et al., 2013). The Lewis Path carried out in Western Europe was possible because of the development of a labour-intensive industry and an emigration of labour to cities (Dorin et al., 2013). In India in 2010, 53% of the employed population worked in agriculture while 11% worked in industry and 11% in construction (Singh and Kalita, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_350]

3.3. Adding layers of inequalities on the human labour energy interdependencies Inequalities in the 1950’s were chiefly driven by flows of human labour energy: landowning categories captured the manpower of the landless categories. In 2022, the relations between social categories, and the inherent inequalities, have changed. The flows of human labour energy between social categories have been outweighed by flows of gross calorific energy of animal feed, especially flows of groundnut hay. They circulate between the farmers who have not much option apart from cultivating groundnut in rainfed conditions and farmers who have livestock and do not produce groundnut, i.e. pastoralists. [SOURCE: Page_350]

Today 4 388 GJ of animal feed circulate between farms in the village (groundnut straw and rice straw) while there was none in the 1950’s: all the feed was either produced on farm or grazed– we considered the grass grazed as an internal flow at farm-level. The 4 388 GJ of animal feed circulating in the archetype village exceed by large (7 times) the total human labour energy circulating within the village (596 GJ). However, concluding that flows of calorific energy of animal feed have reshaped the interdependency relations of farms in the village is partially incorrect. The first reason is that flows of human labour energy circulating between farms in the village have not reduced, quite on the contrary, they have increased. As there are more social categories in 2022 than in the 1950’s the flow diagram of labour energy of 2022 gives the impression that flows of manpower have thinned out (see previous section). The second reason nuances the importance of the energy from gross calorific energy of animal feed circulating in the village- mostly groundnut hay- compared to the flows of human labour. The comparison is problematic because both type of energies are not of the same nature and thus not comparable as such. This way of counting together types of energies or comparing them comes back to a “nonsensical aggregation of energy forms defined within non-equivalent narratives about energy transformations (e.g. summing joules of mechanical work to joules of [SOURCE: Page_350]

350 [SOURCE: Page_350]

orange juice).” (Giampietro et al., 2013, p. 2), an approach anchored in “the most obsolete among the various approaches used so far in energy analysis” and which imply a huge loss of valuable information (Giampietro, 2006). In reality the interdependencies materialised by flows of calorific energy of animal feed have not outweighed those of human labour, but they have added to the former interdependencies. To enable a better comparison of the types of energy considered in this study (i.e. labour energy, gross calorific energy, fossil energy) we could have made comparisons using a common unit, such as what is done in the “emergy” approaches where all types of energy flows are compared on the basis of solar energy (Amaral et al., 2016; Odum, 1983; Vigne et al., 2013a). In line with this idea, Hittner-Sánchez (2022) proposed to quantify flows of energy of manure as the “avoided” cost of fossil energy consumed when producing synthetic fertilisers. The consideration of biomass under flows of gross energy flows also can be problematic as some flows of organic matter are not directly metabolisable by human and animal living beings. Manure for instance was quantified in this study as the energy released when oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, i.e. calorific energy measured using a bomb calorimeter (National Research Council, 1981). Yet, the purpose of manure was to provide nitrogen and carbon to the soil and its quantification under a flow of gross calorific energy therefore seems, on second thought, ill-suited. Other type of materials, such as tank silt or sand, which were valuable types of matter used to make the agrarian system in the 1950’s function, could also not be taken into account in this energy quantification. [SOURCE: Page_351]

3.4. An increase in the energy efficiency of the agrarian system? 351 [SOURCE: Page_351]

and indirect fossil energy. However, despite the partial moto-mechanisation of agriculture in Rapthadu, the EROIext-import is still above 1, meaning that there is still more energy being produced and exported out of the village than is being imported. This goes against the general rule that industrialisation goes hand in hand with a declining EROI -this is verified in this study- and leads to an EROI lower than 1: “A first characteristic of agroecosystems is that, thanks to the photosynthesis, from a societal standpoint they produce energy as well as consume it. True, current industrialized agricultures use to have EROIs lower than 1— that is, they are net energy consumers instead of functioning as energy providers. But organic agriculture, through most of the past 10,000 years, could not function that way. By definition, farm communities needed to generate more energy carriers for human society than what they invested. Failure to do so literally meant starvation. Thus many agricultural systems typically have had, throughout history, EROIs higher than 1—of course, after having set aside in our calculations solar radiation taken as a gift of nature” (Giampietro et al., 2013; in Tello et al., 2015). In other territories which have entered in a moto-mechanisation process, EROIext-invest has also declined (Galán et al., 2016) but not always up to a point where it is below 1, i.e. more energy imported than exported. The interpretations of the maintenance of an EROI above 1 has to be analysed case-by-case. In Rapthadu, there are two major reasons. One of them is the fact that the territory is today mostly cropped with rainfed groundnut, whose both its hay and its pods have a high energy content, thus maintaining the numerator of the EROI at a high level. The second reason is in line with the idea developed in the first section of this chapter: agriculture in Rapthadu is two-headed where moto-mechanisation was not as complete as in Western Europe. Human labour still plays an important role in crop cultivation (mostly for cultivation of irrigated crops). This maintains the level of fossil energy lower than what it could have been if the degree of moto-mechanisation had been higher. The flows of direct fossil energy from electricity of pumps are fairly low because only 15% of the territory is under irrigated crops. Moreover, as the level of the groundwater table was measured at less than 10 metres below the ground, the consumption of electricity to raise water remains low. If irrigated surfaces were to expand and/or the net groundwater recharge go below the tipping points of the scenarios mentioned in section 2.1, then the groundwater table would start going down thus increasing the consumption of electricity per irrigated ha (Appendix 24). [SOURCE: Page_352]

From the perspective of solely the draft power and fossil energy to run engines that have replaced draft animals, we see that approximately 4 500 GJ came from the animal feed and labour power of draft animals in the 1950’s. Since then the draft animals have been replaced [SOURCE: Page_352]

352 [SOURCE: Page_352]

by pumps and motors. In 2022, approximately 2 500 GJ of fossil energy are spent to run tractors (diesel) and operate pumps from borewells (electricity). The energy of animal labour and the maintenance of draft animals was therefore greater than the fossil energy spent today and which has replaced draft power. This is linked to the fact that humans and animals, unlike machines, have to be fed all year round and maintained whereas a tractor or a pump is only used for the time of the work and the engine is then cut off. This is illustrated in the figure below (Fig. 219). In 2022, a man and his tractor can plough and till (using successively a subsoiler and a cultivator) 2 ha of land in one day (one day being 7 hours of work). In the 1950’s, 2 ha of land could be ploughed in one day but with 5 pairs of bulls and 5 men leading (one for each pair). Considering the energy of the feed and the food of animal and men, and the fuel expenditure of a tractor, we see that there is 30 times more energy consumed in the 1950’s than today to plough one field. The gap is even wider if we consider the irrigation operation, as today irrigation requires only turning the pump on. The representation of figure 219 is particularly telling in so far as mechanical energy is concerned. From this unique perspective, energy efficiency has increased. However, the replacement of draft animals by moto-mechanisation has other environmental downsides such as the dependency on fossil fuels (Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019) and higher greenhouse gas emissions (Aguilera et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_353]

Figure 219. Comparing energy of maintenance of animal and manpower in the 1950’s versus a tractor and his driver in 2022 If we calculate the second EROI of Table 27, taking into account the internal flows of the archetype village, EROIcircu, we find that it has increased between the 1950’s and 2022 from 1.1 to 1.3. This is a lower increase than what Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros (2019) observed in [SOURCE: Page_353]

353 [SOURCE: Page_353]

France, where the same indicator was found to increase from approximately 2 to 4 between 1882 and 2013. In Rapthadu the net agricultural production increased by approximately 3 since the 1950’s but energy invested (imported and circulating in the territory) to make the agrarian system function was multiplied by 2. In France, the net agricultural production was multiplied by 3 but the energy invested remain roughly constant (Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019) (Fig. 220). [SOURCE: Page_354]

Figure 220. Evolution of the energy invested and the net production in agriculture in France between 1882 and 2013 (Harchaoui and Chatzimpiros, 2019) [SOURCE: Page_354]

This can be explained by several factors. This is mostly due to the fact that the net productivity of the agriculture of Rapthadu has increased since the 1950’s, the increase has not been as spectacular as in France where the productivity gains per agricultural worker -grains- have been multiplied by 1 000 (Mazoyer and Roudart, 2006, p. 452) (Appendix 32). This is way more than the increase of physical productivity of labour observed in Rapthadu, from 43 GJ per worker to 120 GJ per worker. As mentioned earlier (section 3.2), the number of agricultural workers has increased in the village, unlike in France. Another factor, but less important than the previous one, is that although draft animals have declined in Rapthadu, the sheep population has increased and Holstein Friesian dairy cows have replaced most of the dairy animals which existed in 1950’s. The population of dairy animals has remained fairly constant (Table 26). 90% of the dairy animals today in the archetype village are Holstein crossbred dairy cows, which are non-grazing animals fed only on Napier Grass, rice straw, groundnut hay and feed concentrate. Those type of feed are high in energy content. The dairy animals in the 1950’s on the other hand were fed on straw, hay and also grasslands. The wild grasses have a much lower energy content than the feed of crossbred dairy cows. This also [SOURCE: Page_354]

354 [SOURCE: Page_354]

applies to the sheep population which was entirely fed on grasslands in the 1950’s and today mostly with horse gram forage in winter and groundnut hay in summer. Horse gram forage and groundnut hay have a higher energy content than the natural grass from grasslands. [SOURCE: Page_355]

The two EROIs are insightful to discuss the agricultural transitions. However, the improvement of EROIs and circularity indexes are often set as goals to embrace energy transitions. In the next paragraph we show that associating improved circularity and EROIs with sustainability is a moot point. [SOURCE: Page_355]

3.5. The search for circularity and efficiency, ill-formulated questions? The energy circularity of the archetype village has declined from 84% to 29% over the last 70 years, so has the EROIext-import (Fig. 215). The EROIcircu has increased but not as much as in other territories (see previous paragraph). This decline in circularity and EROIext-import was triggered by a partial decoupling of livestock and cropping integration, with fossil energy and gross energy now being imported in the village. In this paragraph we argue that seeking circularity and energy efficiency is not always a synonym of sustainability. Seeking a better EROI or a better energy circularity does not mean not relying any longer on fossil energy. Energy efficiency can be improved by increased yields from genetic amelioration of plants and breeds, but those improved breeds and plant species often require more fertilisers and water, such as the BPT rice variety introduced with the Green revolution, or the Holstein Friesian cows introduced with the White Revolution. We illustrate this based on the comparison of the energy inputs and energy outputs of a local dairy cow in the 1950’s and a Holstein Friesian crossbred dairy cow in 2022 (Fig. 221). The White Revolution enabled an increase in the production of milk: the milk yield of dairy cows has more than doubled since the 1950’s. However, this is at the expense of consumption of fossil energy which was previously non- existent. Further genetic improvement could increase the production of milk but probably at the expense of higher consumption of fossil energy. Even though the ratio of energy output per energy input may increase, this does not eliminate the question of fossil energy dependency especially with fossil fuels becoming rare. Seeking energy efficiency is therefore not always a synonym of sustainability. [SOURCE: Page_355]

355 [SOURCE: Page_355]

Figure 221. Evolution of energy outputs and inputs of dairy animals between 1950’s and today [SOURCE: Page_356]

The energy circularity of the archetype village has declined since the 1950’s but its nature has changed for two reasons. The first reason is that in the 1950’s circularity was composed only of feed and food gross energy flows, as well as animal and human labour energy flows. Today even though the system is not linear, i.e. the circularity is not nil, the circularity is fuelled by pulses of fossil energy imported in the village. The small-scale fruit growers with dairy farming illustrate this well (chapter 7, Fig. 189): the circularity index is the highest of all the production systems in 2022, i.e. 38% but fuelled by 1) the imports of fossil energy spent to run the pumps for irrigation of Napier grass to feed dairy cows, and 2) the gross calorific energy and indirect fossil energy of feed concentrates to feed those cows. The second reason deals with the origin of the internal flows of energy in the village. In the 1950’s, most of the internal flows of energy circulating in the village came from feed, food and manure which were in the case of feed and manure, exclusively internal flows of production systems: all the feed of the animals were produced on farm or grazed and manure was never sold nor bought. Today most of the internal flows of energy come from animal feed circulating in the village. 22% of the gross energy of feed circulating in the village circulates in between farms: this is mostly the groundnut hay circulating from the farms producing groundnut, towards the pastoralists who buy groundnut hay to feed their sheep in summer. Circularity today is therefore partly the result [SOURCE: Page_356]

356 [SOURCE: Page_356]

of a disintegration of crop-livestock integration at farm-level and a re-integration of crop and livestock between farms which have abandoned livestock or others which have kept it. [SOURCE: Page_357]

Production and exports of agricultural products have also increased. However, the level of circularity is still maintained at a fairly high level. This circularity is high because the crop- livestock integration which was found at farm-level in the 1950’s is now reconfigured at territorial level, i.e. between farms. It is high also because livestock, which makes matter circulate, has not totally disappeared. The level of internal flows of gross calorific energy of groundnut hay circulating in the village remains high. It is fuelled by relations of production of a majority of non-irrigating farmers growing groundnut with non-irrigating farmers not growing groundnut, but using their land and manpower to rear sheep, i.e. pastoralists. However, the nature of territorial energy circularity has changed over time: the circulation of gross caloric energy of groundnut hay between farms of the village is maintained by pulses of fossil energy which are either direct fossil energy for fuel for machinery used to prepare groundnut fields, or indirect fossil energy for the manufacture of chemicals. This is the same at farm-level: circularity at farm-level has considerably declined -or even disappeared- with the abandonment of livestock by most of the farms. The pastoralists have a much higher income than the non- irrigating farmers growing groundnut. Today the circularity of energy is partly due to the flows of gross energy of groundnut hay flowing from the non-irrigating farmers growing groundnut to the pastoralists. Circularity is therefore partly defined by the new social relations of production and on those economic inequalities. Environmental sustainability, seen here through the energy circularity, is therefore based on socio-economic inequalities. This example shows that environmental and social sustainability do not always evolve in the same direction. [SOURCE: Page_357]

357 [SOURCE: Page_357]

Conclusion of chapter 8: In this chapter, we showed how the agrarian transformations of the territory were closely tied with the changes of the role of livestock, mostly driven by a decline of draft power and the specialisation of other livestock farming systems towards meat or milk production. We also showed that the semi-arid conditions of the area contribute to strong relations of interdependence between social categories, which have developed since the 1950’s. New layers of interdependence have emerged. The first ones take the form of flows of water between farms pumping water and others recharging the groundwater table. The second are flows of gross energy between farms producing rainfed groundnut and others requiring groundnut hay to feed their sheep. The third are flows of fossil energy which are part of the functioning of all production systems, but involved under different forms: for example, direct fossil energy from electricity to pump water for the irrigating categories, or direct fossil energy from fuel to prepare land for groundnut cultivation and for threshing groundnut for non-irrigating categories. We discuss the compatibility of social and environmental sustainability by putting forward 1) the new form of energy circularity today which is fuelled by fossil energy and based on social inequalities, 2) the search for higher energy efficiency which does not necessarily imply the elimination of fossil energy dependence and 3) the sustainable us of the groundwater resource based on a socio-hydrological divide of categories where the wealthier categories need the labour of the poorest and the water which is recharged through their rainfed cropped areas. We show that this pumping-recharging equilibrium enables -for now- a sustainable use of the groundwater water of the system but that this equilibrium is fragile and could change rapidly. [SOURCE: Page_358]

358 [SOURCE: Page_358]

CHAPTER 9: Comparative agriculture, a new approach to social metabolism? [SOURCE: Page_359]

1. Social metabolism: origin and definition of the concept This work uses the flows of water and energy to illustrate the agrarian transformations of the archetype village. The quantification of flows of matter and energy is one of the characteristics of territorial analysis called territorial metabolism or social metabolism. In this chapter we discuss the potential bridges between the comparative agriculture conceptual framework and the social metabolism approach. Up to now, we have used the concept of “metabolism” in its purest and strictest form, i.e. flows of matter and energy. To draw potential bridges between the two frameworks we first have to clarify the key principles and the theoretical references of social metabolism. [SOURCE: Page_359]

1.1. The backbone of metabolism studies Studies which define themselves as metabolism studies are numerous but are part of a changing and evolving framework. There are many interpretations of metabolism. There is, however, a common denominator for all those approaches, which can be summed up into three main points: [SOURCE: Page_359]

-      Metabolism deals with links between entities of a given system and those links are brought by functional relations. Those entities however vary from one metabolism approach to another. -      the links between those entities are part of an autopoietic system (Haberl et al., 2016, p. 20) which is a “system making itself” (Giampietro et al., 2014; Maturana and Varela, 1980). This autopoietic nature enables the inter-linked entities to live, be sustained, grow and reproduce (Foster, 1999). There is thus an idea of dynamic, movement, in the functioning of the system which can be studied at different time periods. The word metabolism actually comes from the Greek, metabolê meaning “changed” or “altered”. There is thus an idea of self-maintenance, although this self-maintenance may be quite relative. -      the metabolism approaches are in all cases linked to matter: the way of analysing may be characterised by a materialist approach, or the object of the study may be a raw material which is consumed and or/produced, or it may be a primary energy carrier. [SOURCE: Page_359]

359 [SOURCE: Page_359]

1.2. From the metabolism of cells to the metabolism of societies The word “metabolism” was first used during the first half of the 19th century by German physiologists to describe the chemical transformations on the level of cells and organisms, in particular by the chemist Justus von Liebig who used the word Stoffwechsel in German meaning “material exchange” (Liebig, 2017). Karl Marx, who died only ten years after Liebig, then used the word on a wider scale, that of society, and added the adjective “social” to show this change of scale -social metabolism- (Marx, 1894, p. 195)). The concept therefore shifted: from a biological or physiological metabolism to a social one, defined as a set of “relations of personal dependence” and “all-round needs” (Marx, 1993; in Delbello, 2018). However, a temporary problem of translation caused the disappearance of the word metabolism in the works of Marx, until it reappeared again in the new editions in the 1970’s (Angus, 2018) (Box 12). [SOURCE: Page_360]

The Capital (Volume 1) Translation of 1888                                        Translation of 1976 “Capitalist production … disturbs the circulation of       “Capitalist production … disturbs the metabolic matter between man and the soil … while upsetting          interaction between man and the earth … by the naturally grown conditions for the maintenance of      destroying   the    circumstances    surrounding   that that circulation of matter, it imperiously calls for its   metabolism, which originated in a merely natural and restoration as a regulating law of social production,      spontaneous fashion, it compels its systematic and under a form appropriate to the full development       restoration as a regulative law of social production, of the human race.”                                        and in a form adequate to the full development of the human race.” The Capital (Volume 3) Translation of 1909                                        Translation of 1981 “In this way it creates conditions, which cause an         “Large landed property … produces conditions that incurable break in the interconnections of the social      provoke an irreparable rift in the interdependent circulation of matter prescribed by the natural laws       process of social metabolism, a metabolism of life”                                                   prescribed by the natural laws of life itself” Box 12. The changes of translations in the use of metabolism in the Capital of Karl Marx, identified by Angus (2018) At the time of Karl Marx, the industrial revolution was well under way in Western Europe, particularly in England. He uses the concept of metabolic rift to describe the material dislocation of nature and society incited by a new type of interaction between society and nature called capitalism (Foster, 1999). [SOURCE: Page_360]
